speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government intends for Budget 2024 to be a step towards Forward Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Forward Singapore exercise has three major goals for the decade and the next.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singapore must: first, have a strong and growing economy; second, develop a fairer society; and third, deepen our sense of unity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In doing so, the shared future that was distilled from various engagement sessions with the public was a Singapore that will be vibrant, fair, resilient, inclusive, thriving and united.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The real challenge to the People's Action Party (PAP), however, is for it to be open, and the extent to which it is prepared to accommodate the diverse views of Singaporeans on how to journey towards the destination envisaged by Forward Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: No doubt, PAP has asked for diverse views by demanding that the Opposition come up with alternative proposals, although one suspects they do so rhetorically.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: WP has responded sincerely and we have not been short of proposals that have ultimately been accepted by the Government in some shape or form, albeit after initial and sometimes significant resistance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the details may differ, the philosophy of supporting our involuntarily unemployed is one which WP championed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The same can be said for the WP proposals for anti-discrimination legislation to better protect our workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Unlike PAP, WP clearly stated these proposals in our election manifesto, and our Members of Parliament (MPs) have systematically and repeatedly raised these points along with others in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, the Government needs to be more forthcoming with information so that Singaporeans can participate more actively in policy discussion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, there is a growing mismatch in Singapore between aspirations and reality, which must be addressed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fourth, employers need to show more support for employees.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And fifth, we must work towards further strengthening unity among Singaporeans in this uncertain world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My first point is that the Government needs to be more transparent and forthcoming with information so that there can be meaningful participation by Singaporeans in the most critical matters affecting us.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is a recurring theme in my speeches, but I am by no means the only Singaporean to hold this view.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Straits Times carried an article dated 19 February 2024 titled, "Economists applaud 2024 Budget but some worry about sustainability." The economists quoted were concerned about the combination of large cash handouts with the lack of information about the sources of Singapore's fiscal strength.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the report, one former Nominated Member of Parliament (NMP) called on the Government to provide more information on how it funds its expenditures.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Another economist noted that Singapore is unique and does not follow standards set by global bodies, such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF), with regard to the difference between revenues and expenditures in the management of the fiscal balance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Yet another economist was quoted as saying, "As a society, we now have some very important choices to make and, unless we are well-informed, we will not be able to make those choices well." Sir, the latter point was about the Reserves, a subject which we debated earlier this month and where WP set out its five points of principle.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On 20 February, an opinion piece in The Straits Times was titled, "It's getting harder to project future Government revenue".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: His view was that gone are the days when Budget marksmanship of 2% was normal.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Two Budgets ago, I asked what the total estimated amount collected by the carbon tax would be.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government did not tell us, even though the preliminary numbers would not have been difficult to estimate and probably had already been tabulated by the Ministry of Finance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: No proactive update on how monies were spent on these programmes was provided until Parliamentary questions were put to the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have spoken about the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) Base Erosion and Profit Sharing regime, or BEPS, for some years now.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Finance Minister has laid out two possibilities that could affect us: one, of more corporate income tax being collected; and another of some multinational enterprises (MNEs) leaving Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Both could happen at the same time, if recent media reports are anything to go by: one, predicting the move of more MNE headquarters to Singapore from Hong Kong; and another reporting on the move of Electrolux's regional headquarters from Singapore to Bangkok.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of the implementation of Pillar 2, what are the estimated collections in either an optimistic scenario or a conservative scenario?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the first Budget debate of this term, WP called for the setting up of a Parliamentary Budget office, which was rejected by PAP as an idea that would only benefit the Opposition.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the spirit of Forward Singapore and in view of a greater need to track the effectiveness of Government policies and their expenditure outcomes, such institutions should be a feature of our democracy and the Singapore that the Forward Singapore report demands.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One economist quoted in the 19 February The Straits Times article said that Singaporeans outside this House desire to analyse and understand to a deeper degree what the Government is doing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These examples I shared put into relief the types of differences we can expect between the political Opposition in this House and non-politician Singaporeans outside of it on the one hand, and the PAP Government on the other.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such calls for information cannot be set aside as red herrings.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the Government was doing well on this score, we would not have private sector economists making the arguments and the points they do.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These calls represent a desire to shape a political environment that is fit for Singapore's purposes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans need to know how much there is to spend and where the money comes from.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These are basic requirements for having rational discussions on fiscal matters and for realistic alternative visions to emerge.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In any democratic society, the Government must facilitate such discussions and it should do so proactively by declassifying more information if necessary.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Sengkang Group Representation Constituency (GRC) Member Ms He Ting Ru will speak on the themes of deliberative democracy, transparency and accountability in her speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Will the Government spell out these initiatives in view of the commitment made in the Budget Statement, since some thought appears to have been applied to how much it will take to fund Forward Singapore plans?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just as PAP calls on WP to lay out its alternatives, surely PAP must lay out its proposals, too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A reference in the Forward Singapore report to the 5Cs of decades past was scrutinised by some in the media.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The 5Cs captured the aspiration to have cash, car, credit card, condominium and country club membership.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Forward Singapore report calls on Singaporeans to move beyond the 5Cs towards wider definitions of success.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Surely, that is an admission, perhaps unintended, that a fair number of the 5Cs are unattainable for most Singaporeans today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The reality is that things are very difficult for not a small number of Singaporeans, regardless of what definition of success one deploys.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A Business Times article from late 2023 reported the findings of an OCBC financial wellness survey.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Fewer Singaporeans can comfortably spend on things beyond the basics.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And more do not have sufficient emergency funds or savings to meet their families' needs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This was a rise from 71% in 2022.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the sentiments captured in this survey are anything to go by, there is a likelihood that the social compact may be precarious and uneven, particularly if the middle of society feels insecure about their financial future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To address this possibility, the structural moves to invest more in the future, particularly through SkillsFuture, are important and critical, even as the temporary cost of living support with the Budget are acknowledged and welcomed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP foresees a need for even greater investments in our human capital in future, especially in view of how rapidly the workplace landscape is changing and with more well-paying jobs requiring high-order skillsets, a point that will be further expanded by Sengkang GRC Member Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP sees the deployment of SkillsFuture credits towards economically productive courses with employment outcomes as an important policy initiative of this Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But we believe that many of the courses are likely to cost more than $4,000.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To further facilitate skills training and help Singaporean workers, the Government should introduce an interest-free SkillsFuture education loan.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP put this proposal front and centre in our General Election 2020 manifesto.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To start with, these loans can be calibrated towards courses, in either high-growth industries that lack Singaporean manpower or in other economically important areas.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The changes to the Central Provident Fund (CPF) Special Account (SA), announced by Deputy Prime Minister, will be addressed by Sengkang Group Representation Constituency (GRC) Member of Parliament Mr Louis Chua.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, I speak of retirement adequacy more broadly and as an ongoing concern for the decades to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It did not escape many Singaporeans, that all three core components of the Majulah Package: the annual earn and save bonus, the one-time retirement savings bonus and the one-time MediSave bonus, for Singaporeans born between 1960 and 1973, involved CPF top-ups.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Merdeka and Pioneer Generations will also get them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: From the vantage point of the WP, Sir, these moves make it clear that sufficiency of CPF balances for retirement is a serious and ongoing concern.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The moves to raise employer's CPF contributions through to the year 2030, must also be seen by employers in this light – of ensuring that all the workers are not left behind when retirement beckons.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Employers will have to redesign jobs, so that seniors can continue to work for far longer if they wish to.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The real risk of more redundancies in the years to come, arising from job displacement, adds impetus to the need for job redesign.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Recently, in a social media post, the Minister for National Development celebrated the 60th anniversary of the Housing and Development Board's (HDB's) Home Ownership Scheme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: History shows that the reception to the HDB Home Ownership Scheme, per se, was initially lukewarm.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would not be hyperbole to say: that the CPF changed from a statutory board in charge of Singaporeans' retirement to a subsidiary of the HDB, with the aim of helping Singaporeans purchase property.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Of course, many aspects of CPF policy have evolved since then.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But what is clear, is that Singapore is in a far different place compared to where it was in the early years of Independence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Specifically, younger Singaporeans cannot expect the same home equity appreciation that Singapore experienced from the 1990s.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Today, HDB affordability continues to remain an ongoing concern in the minds of many Singaporeans, in spite of the new Build-To-Order (BTO) classification system – which adds new restriction and increases subsidies for new flats.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In substance, the Government appears to acknowledge the point that affordability is an ongoing concern.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More money set aside for HDB flat purchase means less funds available for retirement, notwithstanding options to downgrade.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If property prices and general inflationary trends rise faster than wages, plans for retirement will have to start later for many – since they would have less to set aside for their nest egg, with mortgages to serve today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is time to closely examine how much CPF money should be set aside for housing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But if HDB prices continue to escalate, any move to reduce the CPF funds that can be set aside for housing, in favour of retirement adequacy, may backfire.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government may then have to commit itself to making HDB flats even more affordable by increasing subsidies further.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Make no mistake, direct subsidies for HDB flat purchases do not make HDB flats cheaper.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They merely transfer the cost to current taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP will continue to closely monitor PAP's moves on this point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We will be sure to hold it to account, if it allows HDB flats to continue to rise in price beyond wage growth and if it allows the retirement adequacy of Singaporeans to be compromised.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My colleague, Aljunied GRC Member of Parliament Mr Faisal Manap, will make some related points covering housing and low-income households in his speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, if Singapore really wishes to embrace the philosophy of Forward Singapore, then we need to show stronger support for our financially vulnerable workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is such an important ingredient of the future social compact.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Increases of the de facto minimum wage, should be seen as a step towards an inclusive and fair Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If we have a shared future, where there is a lack of support for paying our lowest-paid workers in step with economic fundamentals, that would reflect very poorly on Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When the economy grows or when support measures are extended to companies, workers must also benefit.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But consumers too, must be prepared to pay more for goods and services and it cannot solely be left to businesses to absorb the additional cost of wages.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The strongest social compact promised by Forward Singapore, also offers an opportunity to think about protections for our workers beyond wages.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Much has been said about the lack of recognition in Singapore for all blue-collar workers who use their hands to perform skilled work.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will speak more about this in the Committee of Supply (COS) debate for the Ministry of Manpower.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But there are areas where some employers have done well and displayed solidarity with the Singaporean worker.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, by implementing Flexible Work Arrangements (FWAs) in concert with the demands of a more modern Singaporean workforce.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We must also improve workplace culture and change attitudes towards skills upgrading and training, if Forward Singapore is to become a reality.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In a recent Ipsos survey titled "What Singapore thinks, feels and does", it was revealed that three in five Singapore employees – or 60% of Singapore employees – said that they were proud to work for their employer.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But this was some 14 to 19 points below the global average; 29% said that they plan to leave their current employer in under two years – nine points more than the global norm.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With the advent of artificial intelligence (AI) and the need to improve productivity, this is as good a time as any to significantly review HR policies: to align them with national imperatives and the lived experience of Singapore workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Member for Aljunied GRC Mr Gerald Giam, will speak more about productivity improvements in his speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit aims to encourage employers to invest and enterprise, and workplace transformation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It covers an array of programmes, including support for job redesign under the Productivity Solutions Grant.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These initiatives can be superimposed on the key HR workplace pain points identified by employees – particularly older workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As in previous years, the WP calls on the Government to report on the success, or otherwise, of these enterprise schemes that cause huge amounts of money.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Reporting on outcomes is a fundamental requirement for accountability.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Please give us information on what outcomes, if any, have been achieved on an industry-wide level.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Please let us know so that this House and industry experts outside this House can give inputs on how these schemes can be improved, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In this uncertain world, Singaporeans need to be committed to being united even as we must remain multiracial and multicultural.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Budget speech By Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, sought to put into focus an important message that many of us overlook as we remain peaceful and far removed from the prospect of conflict.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It will be more violent, it will be more fragmented, it will be messier and more unpredictable.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the same time as the world is seeing rising political polarisation and disenfranchisement, due to economic displacement, the world continues to struggle with common global problems, such as climate change, a subject Hougang Single Member Constituency Member of Parliament Mr Dennis Tan will touch on.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If Forward Singapore seeks to refresh the social compact to keep our society strong and united and to prepare for a difficult road ahead, all of us in Singaporeans – regardless of our political persuasion – will have to be our siblings' keeper.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Immigration and integration are good examples of where potential challenges lie.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Earlier generations of immigrants had little choice, or less choice, but to integrate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They could not live hermetically sealed off from their host population.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Only 30 years ago, it was prohibitively costly to make an international phone call.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Current immigrants can easily stay connected to their networks and countries of birth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One can be a new Singaporean or PR physically present in Singapore, but removed from Singapore society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Better integration between the races and communities must be an important feature of the new social compact.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We ignore this social objective at our peril, given how immigration is a permanent feature of Singapore's society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The prospect of constant information operations undertaken by state and non-state actors, is an acute threat facing all multicultural societies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As a multiracial and multi-religious society that relies on immigration to top-up the population, our bonds as one united people may be severely tested in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The reality of online misinformation of foreign interference, particularly if framed in nationalistic terms, or in the form of identity politics, can be insidious and highly damaging to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even as we seek more space to passionately advocate our views, including those on race and religion, we should be mindful lest we denigrate another group.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More communication is certainly needed, but we should never forget our common humanity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: None of us chose to be born into our race or religion, so kindness and empathy must be a dominant feature of the multiracial Singapore spirit.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As an opposition party with elected Members of Parliament (MPs) in Parliament, the Workers' Party will not self-censure but commit ourselves to bring up matters responsibly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Once mistrust between communities take root, we will not know what hit us.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP agrees with the posture taken by the Government, that polarisation must not happen in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And as a society facing an unpredictable world, we should not dismiss this potential reality.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We must gird ourselves against this prospect by deepening our commitment to fellow Singaporeans and representing them and their views faithfully.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A potentially more volatile outlook also reinforces the importance of the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) and Home Team and the importance of National Service.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Otherwise, Forward Singapore could easily fall victim to political cynicism.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such calls will not grow softer and they are not inconsistent with the findings and the desired outcomes of the Forward Singapore exercise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some of the differences between the PAP and the WP are of methods and approaches, and we must agree to disagree.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But there may be a few issues where there is consensus on the final outcomes, and yet, others where there is none.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We can see the imprints of Forward Singapore in many aspects of this year's Budget, including the various fresh approaches and moves to provide assurance to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are major initiatives to develop our people, to invest in medium- and longer-term capabilities and security, to support families and seniors, and to build a fairer and more equitable society.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We are moving forward amidst a more uncertain, more contested and more volatile world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: To adapt and thrive under this environment, we need to keep on reassessing our propositions and norms, but also, critically, to stay cohesive and united.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And in keeping with one of Forward Singapore key thrust that we are in this together and that we have got each other's back, this Budget continues to enhance the packages to help Singaporeans cope with the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Even though there are other measures and tools to help mitigate rising costs; nothing beats having more direct payouts and assistance from the Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And fortunately, we continued to have the fiscal capacity to dish out such upsized packages.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It will go some way to provide relief to the small enterprises and helping to mitigate some of the incremental costs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In addition to the AP, there are also other helpful features in this year's Budget that help Singaporean households and businesses cope with rising costs, such as the Workfare Income Supplement, the Silver Support, the preschool fee caps, the Progressive Wage Credits Scheme and so on.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I thank the Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister for his continuing assurances to help Singaporeans to manage the cost pressures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Besides the annual Budget measures, in September last year, the Deputy Prime Minister also came up with an additional off-budget $1.1 billion Cost-of-Living Support Package.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In that package, there was also an additional one-off public transport subsidies of $300 million to moderate the fare increase in 2023.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And this is over and above the $2 billion annual subsidy that the Government provides to keep public transport affordable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I hope that that the Government would continue to monitor the costs situation, including keeping an eye on the public transport fare; and to consider another one-off assistance to moderate the fare increase if the Budget position permits.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our people must be at the centre of any policy formulation and intent; whether it is to grow the economy, to build capabilities, to strengthen our securities and even why we manage our finances prudently.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We want our people to live a full and happy life.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: A major part of our life's pursuit is livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We work to earn income to provide for our families and ourselves; to live good lives and to have the financial means for contingencies and retirement.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As a Government, nothing can be more of a priority and worthy than to help provide good and fulfilling livelihoods to our people.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: That must be the foremost key performance indicator (KPI) for the Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, with the rapid technological advancements and a more competitive and disruptive economic environment, long-term job security will be an increasing and ongoing challenge.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The skills set that we acquire in schools and in the workplace now has a shortened shelf life.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Some old jobs will become obsolete, while new jobs that require new skills will be created.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And coupled with that, on the labour supply side, with an increasing healthy life span, we can now have a longer career runway.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We are living longer and we have more healthier years in our life; thanks to the quality of life that we enjoy today.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singaporeans understand this imperative and know that there may a time in their career where they need to do a pivot, in response to the changing landscape.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The introduction of SkillsFuture 10 years ago opened up our mindset about continuous learning throughout life.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Budget 2024 provides a major boost and a significant funding upsize to the SkillsFuture movement; with the aim to nudge Singaporeans in their forties, fifties and even sixties to embrace career resilience and to stay up to speed on their employability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme, with various subsidies, can greatly help to reduce the economic costs for training, a perennial pain point for the working mid-careers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is now more targeted in scope; and would only apply to programmes that can achieve the desired employability outcomes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister called it "another bite" of the education subsidies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I hope this new subsidised back-to-school full-time diploma programmes can also help produce more professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs); and hence, reduce the future need for more S Passes and Employment Passes (EPs).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Committing the funding is just first step and, of course, a critical enabler.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The real heavy lifting is in operationalising the entire value chain, where workers seek training that the employers sought; the educators being deeply plugged into the needs of industries and businesses and curate the skills proramme that matters; and the work unions and Government closely monitoring, facilitating and anticipating the next few bounds ahead.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is in keeping with the current reality, where we will see more disruptions that will impact businesses and jobs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am glad that we are now ready to move on this.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is very much part of what we meant a functioning, social compact and that we have got each other's back.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: (In Mandarin):   There is a saying that people have no fixed position and water has no constant form.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The rapid development of technology today has led us into an era of constant change in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The transformation of economic operations has directly impacted the workplace, changing the employment model and shortening the value and lifespan of skills and knowledge.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In response to this situation, this year's Budget has also strengthened a response strategy, enhancing and introducing new policy measures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In addition to the enhanced SkillsFuture subsidies of up to $4,000, the Government has also adjusted education subsidies, allowing middle-aged Singaporeans to re-enter educational institutions to pursue professional diplomas and enhance their employment potential.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: From these measures, we can understand the Government's intention to enable Singaporeans to maintain employability, expand employment opportunities and have a better future.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Learning and upskilling is a challenging endeavour, with economic cost and personal time commitment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is why the Government is investing significant financial resources and strengthening policy measures to alleviate this burden on the individual.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Ultimately, whether we can achieve results depends on whether workers have that willingness and passion to seek skills and knowledge, and whether employers have a flexible, rewarding and long-term mindset to support this.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In this process, we also need to curate more courses that can be applied to enhance employment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will be a very difficult road, but we have no choice.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I can see the Government's determination, and in the future, it will require everyone and the entire system to work together to implement these enhanced upskilling policies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: (In English): Sir, on the economy, I fully agree with the Deputy Prime Minister that we need to continue growing the economy, so that we can improve the collective well-being of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And given the inherent constraints stacked against us, such land, labour and carbon, our next phase of growth has to be productivity and innovation driven.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is not going to be easy, as bigger countries that are better resourced and with the scale of domestic economy are also doing the same.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The strategy that we have adopted to overcome our limitations and which has placed us among the top economic value-add country per capita in the world, is by continuously attracting high quality and high value investments to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Attracting such investments help us leapfrog the riskier and the capital-intensive build-up phase; and enable our economy to always stay at the frontiers of cutting-edge technology.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, anchoring high value and innovative MNEs to base and hub here continues to be a compelling strategy for an economy like ours with minimal scale.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And thanks to our best-in-class investment attracting agencies like the Economic Development Board (EDB), the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and Enterprise Singapore (ESG), we have been able to attract these high-quality investments, despite the intense competition.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I often read the annual reports of EDB, to get a sense of how much investments we are attracting each year.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Besides reporting the fixed asset investment (FAI) commitments and the total business expenditure per annum (TBE), EDB would also report the jobs expected to be created and the value added to the economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am heartened that our economic investment agencies never lose sight on the ultimate motivation on why we bring in investments, which is to create good jobs and to contribute to our gross domestic product (GDP).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How could our local enterprises benefit from the presence of MNEs?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The key is in finding ways for our local firms to be the suppliers and servicers of the MNEs; and playing a part in their value chain.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The enhanced Partnership for Capability Transformation aims to increase the range of modalities for MNEs and small and medium enterprises (SMEs), to collaborate and to help the SMEs up the game.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This could be the pathway for our local enterprises to break out of the size trap, level up to be the emerging regionals or niche champions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On AI, I am glad that Singapore has a head-ups in developing AI capabilities with our National AI strategy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Last December, I happened to be in Taiwan for the holidays, with my family.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: At that time, the Taiwanese Presidential and the Legislative election campaign were in full swing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And out of curiosity, I popped into a couple of election rallies in Taipei and watched the local news there, to hear what are the issues that the candidates were talking about.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is not uncommon in Taiwanese elections, to hear opposition politicians there using Singapore as an example to criticise their government for not doing as well as Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, in this election there, it was again not surprising that Singapore got a few mentions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: One of them was where the opposition politicians ridiculed their government on why tiny Singapore can be listed as the top 10 countries in the world, leading in AI research and technology; and Taiwan is not there.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They lamented that Taiwan is losing out in this AI race and will severely impact its overall competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many jurisdictions including Switzerland and Hong Kong has announced their plans to implement it in 2024 and 2025.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: BEPS 2.0 will reset the level playing field for global competition for investment and that is why it is critical that we keep improving our overall offerings such as introducing the Refundable Investment Credit to strengthen our competitive position.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: One issue of considerable interest is the revenue impact from introduction of Domestic Top-Up Tax.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the near term, it is expected to provide additional revenues to the Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In an OECD report released in January 2024, OECD provided estimates that imply a revenue gain of around 15% to 40% in corporate income tax for investment hubs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In February 2024, Hong Kong which will introduce Pillar 2 in 2025 has estimated its own revenue impact to be around HKD 10 billion, or S$1.7 billion.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There was another estimate by Switzerland in August 2023 which estimate the impact for Switerland as CHF 1.6 billion, or S$2.4 billion.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Both the Hong Kong and Swiss estimates seem to be point to a lower revenue impact than what the OECD estimates would imply, which is up to about S$10 billion for Hong Kong, up to about S$15 billion for Switzerland.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Of course, OECD has cautioned that there is a wide range of uncertainty in their estimates.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Furthermore, the OECD report does not factor in the impact of Pillar 1, which will have a negative revenue impact for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: When both Pillar 1 and Pillar 2 are taken together, it would be difficult to pin down on the net revenue impact.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This discipline about a balanced Budget is of critical importance especially where the trajectory of our spending is heading higher.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Often, commentators would like to use characterisations such whether the Budget is left-leaning or right-leaning or centre-left or centre-right to describe a Budget.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But it may not be that straightforward for this year’s Budget.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Rather than to characterise the budget as being more left or right-leaning, I would say this is a budget that is forward moving and upward progressing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have every determination to move Singapore forward; and in this forward journey ahead to ensure that there will be upward social mobility and cohesion and importantly upward progress for everyone.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We even see policy innovation where the Government provides Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme Vouchers for families to rent an HDB flat in the open market for one year, to supplement the strong demand for temporary housing whilst families wait for their BTO completion.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Those with less will receive more, but there is something for everyone.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, we must be very careful to calibrate handouts to ensure that these are sustainable, as people may grow to rely on them over time.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It may become a challenge to wean them off expectations of such broad-based support in the future.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Also, the generous direct transfers to cushion residents from elevated inflation may, ironically, add to further demand and reverse early signs of moderation on inflation.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Last year, I had raised similar concerns about Government handouts increasing demand and creating a vicious escalation in prices.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Helping people cope with rising costs is a worthy policy but it must be balanced against the risk of prolonging inflationary pressures.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: After all, it would be unsustainable to dole out assistance to fight inflation if such help ends up keeping inflation higher for longer.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I call on the Government to keep a close eye on this.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The economy grew by only 1.1% last year, down from 3.8% growth the previous year.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Real income declined 2.2% for the first time in over 10 years.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore’s continued growth in the new era of global development is not guaranteed.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We face challenges in an international tax environment where global minimum tax regulations are upon us, and where countries around the world are fighting for high-quality investments.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In order to succeed in our next phase of growth, we need to pivot towards high-value, innovative economic development.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This shift necessitates a profound change in our skills and capabilities, far beyond what has brought us success in the past.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In an era dominated by rapid technological advancements, our focus must pivot towards nurturing skills in innovation, research and development (R&D), digitalisation and AI.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These fields have transformative potential to boost our economy, but require a new breed of industries and professionals who are adept in these cutting-edge domains.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The magnitude of this transition cannot be understated.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced the launch of a refreshed incentive toolbox with new fiscal schemes, such the new Refundable Investment Credit scheme and top-up of existing funds to further advance capabilities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is 10 times the amount set aside to help companies cope with near-term challenges.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, Sir, many of the initiatives will only be effective to the extent they are taken up.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Significant effort must be directed to boost usage in order to achieve the intended outcomes of the respective schemes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The number of companies tapping into R&D grants is insufficient, and SMEs still struggle to decipher the multitude of schemes and the complexity and onerous application process.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The support schemes available to us is a springboard, but the impetus to leap forward lies within us.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Embarking on a journey of transformation is akin to preparing to scale new and uncharted mountains.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This journey compels us to traverse unfamiliar terrain and to overcome obstacles that are inherent in scaling any worthy peak.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We are comforted by the knowledge that, in this journey, we are not alone.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The support schemes available are akin to tools, maps and safety gear, provided to ensure that our climb, our ascent is not only successful but also safe and secure.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These resources are designed to assist us in navigating the complexities of change, offering guidance, training and support at every step.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But, ultimately, it is only we who scale the mountain; the gear alone cannot do it for us.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But, unfortunately, the announcement to close the CPF SA for those aged 55 and older attracted the most attention.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst I support the rationale behind the Government's move, the sudden closure of SA accounts affects many middle-income seniors.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Based on established CPF rules, they have systematically saved and trusted this scheme to build up their retirement nest-eggs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many rely on CPF savings as a key source to fund their retirement.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This sudden unexpected change disrupts their retirement planning.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As a policy move, it may be fairer if the Government could grandfather the SA scheme for existing 55 and older CPF members.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Over the years, I have advocated for a higher ERS, enabling CPF LIFE to better cater to the retirement needs of middle-income Singaporeans, especially for those considering CPF as their primary source for retirement planning.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is really important that the CPF serves middle-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The rule of thumb for the income level required to maintain a similar lifestyle in retirement typically involves replacing a certain percentage of your pre-retirement income.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is commonly suggested that retirees will need approximately 70% to 80% of their pre-retirement income to sustain their lifestyle.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This estimate of 70% to 80% as what they need in retirement, assumes the decrease in certain expenses, such as commuting, work-related expenses or mortgage payments, while anticipating an increase in others like healthcare or leisure activities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: While CPF LIFE should not be tailored to meet the needs of the affluent, it must and it must serve as a primary source of retirement income for our low- and middle-income seniors, ensuring they have financial security and peace of mind in their golden age.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The final financial outcome for FY2022 diverged notably from the initial projections, going from an anticipated deficit of $2 billion into a surplus of $1.7 billion.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This represents a significant widening from the earlier projection of $0.4 billion deficit.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In the light of these developments, I would like to ask how the Government projects revenue and expenditure to ensure a level of predictability that informs crucial decisions, such as the need to raise taxes to balance the budget.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: While I appreciate the fiscal discipline demonstrated by setting aside funds that are committed for future programmes that we promise the people without burdening future budgets and generations, I want to seek clarification on several aspects.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Additionally, I am interested in understanding how undrawn amounts are treated and how drawdowns are optimised across funds to smoothen out expenditures.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will come as a great relief to many Singaporeans who are still struggling to cope with the high costs of living and an uncertain job environment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will first address the support measures and how we can take bolder steps to support Singaporeans in coping with the rising cost of living.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will then discuss Progress Singapore Party's (PSP's) views on the proposals in the Budget to support lifelong learning and develop the full potential of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Singaporeans are feeling that their wages are unable to keep up with rising prices, leading to feelings of anxiety and insecurity.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This feeling is borne out in the wage statistics.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, the Consumer Price Index, or CPI, which measures inflation, does not take into account loan repayments.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that the higher interest rates which resulted in higher mortgage payments and other loan payments are not taken into account in the calculation of inflation and real wage growth.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's response has been to provide subsidies and rebates that help households in the short term, for instance, the Assurance Package.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While these short-term support measures are welcome, PSP has always maintained that these are not long-term solutions that address the root causes of the rising cost of living.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While it is true that rising prices are subject to global forces like oil prices, food prices, disruption to supply chains due to pandemics, wars or climate change, there are also domestic factors driving prices.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These domestic factors include our property prices, Certificate of Entitlement (COE) prices, population policy and Government taxes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, I will only talk about property prices and Government taxes and leave the discussion on COE and population policy to another day.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Suffice to say that COE increases our transportation costs and population policy affects the overall demand for all goods and services, thus putting pressure on all prices.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One root cause of the rising cost of living is rising rents.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that when you walk into a shop to buy a product, 30% of the cost of that product is due to the shop's rental and this has not yet taken into account the suppliers' rental costs which had been built into the cost of goods sold.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Similarly, in the food and beverage (F&B) sector, rent forms about 27% of business cost.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Rent therefore has a big impact on the cost of living of most Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP once again calls on the Government to take action to moderate excessive commercial rent increases in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For a start, guidelines on reasonable annual rent increases can be issued, similar to how the National Wage Council (NWC) issues guidelines on wage increases.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the rate of rent increases can be moderated, it will not only be beneficial for Singaporeans but it will benefit businesses as well.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition, Government is the largest landowner in Singapore and yields significant influence over the property market.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If it has the political will, it can push outcome in the direction it wants.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another root cause of rising cost of living is home prices.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For most of us, buying a house is the single largest expenditure of our lifetime.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will greatly ease the burden of housing costs on young people and allow them to more easily build up their retirement savings.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It might even provide some with the leeway to take risks with their careers and pursue any entrepreneurial dreams without being shackled by large mortgage payments.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Government taxes form part of the cost of living, with the most obvious being the Goods and Services Tax (GST).

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Budget 2022, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said that healthcare expenditure is increasing due to the ageing population and is expected to hit $27 billion in 2030.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: GST therefore needed to be raised to fund the expected increase in healthcare expenditure.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the Government share whether there are any further plans to raise taxes to fund the increase in healthcare expenditure?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, the Government helps Singaporeans cope with GST increases and cost of living increases by giving cash grants, rebates and vouchers, resulting in a situation whereby the bulk of the population are now in regular receipt of Government handouts.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In any society, there will always be people with different income levels and it is normal for Government to give grants to the lower-income families.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But if the bulk of the population need Government handouts to cope with cost of living, then that cannot be a healthy situation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should also be circumspect about the fact that the bulk of the population is getting used to the idea that it is a norm to receive Government handouts.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It may be the easier route to provide handouts to cope with the cost of living, but we must focus on taking steps to keep costs in check.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For a start, we ask the Government to reconsider exempting a list of basic necessities from GST.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can list specific products rather than broad categories to minimise classification issues and limit price levels to those generally consumed by lower- and middle-income families.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The need for this measure will become more pressing as GST rate increases.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The way that the Government currently treats land sales proceeds and prices HDB flats is also adding to taxpayers' burden.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: HDB must pay Singapore Land Authority (SLA) for the land used to build HDB flats.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These land sales proceeds are then locked away in past reserves and are paid for by large Government grants.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These Government grants must be paid by taxpayers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, in effect, taxes are being collected to be locked away in the reserves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Further grants are given to HDB flat buyers in order to make flats more affordable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These grants must also be paid by taxpayers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have previously proposed that land sales proceeds be treated as revenue divided over the duration of the lease.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is heartening to hear the Prime Minister acknowledge that this is not an unthinkable proposition during the Public Finances debate earlier this month.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As this measure can relieve the tax burden on Singaporeans, I hope the Government will consider it seriously.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Apart from containing costs, another way to cope with rising cost of living is through raising wages and ensuring that they keep pace with the rising cost.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One major way of doing so is through education and training.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Before I talk about education, I wish to declare that I own a private education company.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe that full-time training will be more effective in enhancing the employability of our workers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Temporary financial support would be greatly beneficial to retrenched workers seeking a new job.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Any delay in the implementation of this scheme has real consequences on the retrenched employees.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We hope the Government can finalise the scheme as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition, if a retrenched worker decides to enter full-time training a few months after they were retrenched, we hope that the size of their training allowance will not be impacted by their period of unemployment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We seek the Government's confirmation that their training allowance would be based on their last drawn pay when they were employed.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We whole-heartedly support the intention of helping our ITE graduates, but feel that the ITE Progression Award does not quite fully meet that objective.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since most of those who qualified already chose to progress into diploma courses, the Award has limited scope to encourage more to do so.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The $5,000 top-up to the education accounts does help to ease the financial burden of ITE graduates enrolling for diploma courses; but the $10,000 CPF top-up less so and, furthermore, is actually going to a group who are no longer just ITE graduates, but a specific group of diploma holders.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An issue of parity amongst diploma holders arises here.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Giving $10,000 to some diploma holders, but not others, based solely on the route they took to enter polytechnics can get controversial.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are of the view that a better way to help ITE graduates would be: one, help more ITE graduates qualify for polytechnics.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Entry requirements can be reviewed to recognise the value of relevant work experience rather than just grade point average (GPA).

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Those who decide to take the "O" levels in order to qualify for polytechnics should also be supported.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This can be done through promoting or expanding the ITE General Education course; or providing education grants to those doing so as private candidates.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, help those who enrolled in diploma courses successfully complete their programme by conducting bridging courses to cover the gaps between ITE programmes and "O" level programmes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A TODAY article in July last year, cited students who expressed the need for such courses in areas, like mathematics and essay writing.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The above support measures should also be extended to those who had dropped out of school even before completing ITE, but now wishes to return to the education system to upskill or upgrade themselves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP hopes that the Government will consider our suggestions so that together, we can find a more permanent solution to the challenges faced by Singaporeans in coping with the rising cost of living.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With global tensions and conflicts exacerbating shortages of supplies and disrupting logistic chains, prices of goods and services have risen substantially and are expected to increase further.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unfortunately, it is challenging for our workers' wages to keep up with the pace of price increases and inflation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the face of an uncertain global operating environment, competing priorities and the need to balance our budget, I welcome the Ministry's decision to provide greater assistance for the lower-income group and bigger households with elderly and children.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On this note, I would like the Government to consider pegging this or future batches of vouchers to the number of persons per household.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If three or four generations or an extended family live at one address, it could be due to financial limitations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, all the more reason for a headcount-based CDC Voucher system.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the other hand, if the reason to stay together is to facilitate mutual care and support, the household should similarly not be penalised for this.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, I would like to take the opportunity to appeal for more middle- and long-term support for the sandwich generation – whom I would refer to as the group that has to provide for the care and expenses of children and elderly parents, while having to prepare for their own retirement needs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have to factor in longer lifespans, which mean that they have to support their parents over a longer period even as they themselves become senior citizens.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As family is the most important unit of society, we need to continue providing the relevant support needed by this group in order to safeguard our families and our society.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope a similar scheme can be introduced for elderly with similarly low incomes during their working years but who are living with their family members, albeit in the lower- and middle-income brackets.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such a support programme will also help to alleviate the burden on the sandwich generation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also like to speak about our families with genuine needs to ferry young children and elderly parents at this stage in their lives – who need cars but find car ownership difficult to afford.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Government also consider recalibrating our vehicle COE system to take into account the changing car usage patterns, including the rise in car-sharing services and yet continue to keep car ownership affordable for families who need it?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In recent years, their property taxes have been increasing, which affects this group of senior citizens living off their savings.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While the annual value bands will be raised and they will be allowed to pay via a 24-month instalment plan without interest, some of them may still face financial issues.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, I would like to propose for an arrangement where IRAS will review, discuss with and advise affected landowners the various payment options and alternative solutions appropriate to their specific cases.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   I would like to surface feedback regarding retirees living in landed properties.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In recent years, their property taxes have been increasing, which affects this group of senior citizens living off their savings.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While the annual value bands will be raised and they will be allowed to pay via a 24-month instalment plan without interest, some of them may still face financial issues.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, I would like to propose for an arrangement where IRAS may review, discuss with and advise affected landowners the various payment options and alternative solutions appropriate to their specific cases. : This is a forward-looking Budget that is focused on steering the whole nation ahead while not leaving anyone behind.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, I will speak about the culture of work in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, I will speak about uplifting the wages of workers in the professions of the hands.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This will help to ensure that our workers are able to keep themselves relevant and future-ready.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But these schemes will not bear fruit if our workers do not have the correct mindset and our culture of work is not conducive.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The culture of work in many countries, including in Singapore, is changing.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I welcome some of these trends, like flexible working hours and working from home, as they can help to create work environments that are conducive to an ageing population and supportive of couples having more children.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I am more cautious of other trends and suggestions – like a very short workweek and a right to disconnect from work.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Many of these trends originate and emanate from developed economies.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is, of course, also a developed economy, but we are very different from many of these other countries – some of which have natural resources or hinterlands that they can tap on.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's sole resource is our human resource, upon which all our success has been built.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew said, and I quote, "You know the Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: He is a hardworking, industrious, rugged individual; or we would not have made the grade." The quote, of course, continues to say that he is also a champion grumbler.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But that it is fine if he has worked hard, then he has earned the right to grumble.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore it falls to reason that if our workforce weakens, our competitiveness and attractiveness as an economy weakens and this threatens our continued ability to sustain our way of life.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As such, we should be very careful when we look adopting some of these trends and we should determine their sustainability for Singapore and the consequences of implementing them in legislation and in policy.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Let us look at the practical effect of this legislation.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, there will always be some workers who decide to forego their rights and to remain connected.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These are people who simply do not want to disconnect for various reasons.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And among these people, we may be likely to find the future leaders of organisations, future entrepreneurs, inventors, young lawyers who aspire to become senior counsel, workers who want to go the extra mile to delight their customers, administrative service officers who want to get their promotions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There is simply no alternative to hard work, putting in the hours, putting in the steps.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And being in a global city in a super-connected world, a contactable and responsive worker is invariably a more valuable worker.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, while the worker that refuses to be contacted would not be penalised, the worker that remains contactable may get a boost in his performance evaluation.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: He may be more likely to get the increment and the promotion because an organisation must reward those that are more valuable to it and that are more willing to do more than they have to.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Third, there may be tensions that arise because the worker who exercises his rights strictly may have expected that he would have had spots as the worker who forewent his rights, who would in turn expects that he does better precisely because he had put in more work than is expected.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Such legislation creates more questions, more tension that could be disproportionate to any good that could conceivably come out of it.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that such legislation does not come before this House.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We should be careful as to what trends and fads we decide to champion in this House.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They may have severe consequences on the productivity and competitiveness of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not forget how the Great Resignation came and went as fair as doomed.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There is a trend promoting an aversion towards material success, as if it was some form of scarlet letter, in favour of a more relaxed attitude to work.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Being overly materialistic is, of course, not a good thing.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But I hope that this does not trickle down to become an aversion to hard work, ambition or the pursuit of success because we have to face it that many successful people are motivated by material success, and that that pursuit of it may lead to the creation of successful companies and jobs and opportunities for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, let us encourage those who want to work hard and who want to work more, in pursuit of whatever their dreams are and let us avoid a culture against work from forming in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: On a related note, at the last Sitting, we had a lengthy and very important debate on mental health.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad that Deputy Prime Minister Wong has stated that mental health is a national priority and that there will be an expansion of mental health services.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I am, however, troubled with some narratives that suggest that mental health and hard work are on polar opposites and that they are mutually exclusive.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I have heard people say things like: "I'm not going to put too much effort into this job because I am prioritising my mental health".

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Yes, excessive work stress can lead to mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But I am sure that there are also many people who work very hard, who take on a lot on themselves professionally, who have difficult working hours – and who also have good mental health.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I imagine that there are many Members in this House who would fall into this category.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We should therefore avoid giving paid to such narratives even as we tackle very real mental health concerns amongst our workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I am concerned that the Singapore worker may be becoming complacent in believing that our way of life is a given.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, as Deputy Prime Minister pointed out in his Budget speech, we cannot afford to become complacent.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We are vulnerable – if we have slow growth similar to what we saw in the previous year, Deputy Prime Minister said, we would be in trouble, and we would not be able to improve our collective well-being, and our standard of living would be affected.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, we must constantly work at it and we must guard against trends and ideas that can negatively affect our competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But at the same time, there is no point working hard to maintain the lead and then not enjoying it ourselves.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And it is not about working well either.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is about working hard and living well.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is the work culture we should seek to promote amongst Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, perhaps we can aim for our workers to have it all – and to put that forward as the ideal for our Singapore workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My vision of a Singapore worker is someone who works hard and tries to do his best at his job.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: He is proud of his professional achievements and confident that he has the skills to take on future roles and to compete with foreign talent.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: He is compensated adequately to have a good Singapore standard of living, including spending quality time with his family and pursuing his personal interests.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is a vision of a holistic Singapore worker – one who does his best to work hard and is able to live well.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, I would like to encourage our workers to use this as a mantra and a hashtag online: #workhardlivewell.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: You do not have to fell "pai seh" posting about your leisurely pursuits or holidays with your family, or just having gotten or bought something nice for yourself.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Because you worked hard, you achieved it, and you deserve it. #workhardlivewell.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They are in what may be called the professions of the hands, that is, jobs that are manual in nature and that do not have a high academic criterion for entry.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Many of these are in Progressive Wage Model (PWM) sectors like cleaning, retail, F&B, security and waste management.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I declare at this juncture, Sir, my interest as the President of Security Association Singapore, a trade association in a PWM sector.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In the first instance, Sir, I think that we need to recognise that these jobs require that workers have certain skills.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We must recognise and accept that these are skilled jobs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
