text: Last week, there was some online chatter about a SkillsFuture course on washing toilets, which is part of the mandatory training for workers in the cleaning industry.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: A post that was widely circulated commented that these skills could be learnt during National Service or at home.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Just because one can grow a cactus on their office table does not make them an arborist or horticulturalist.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This course teaches workers on how to clean toilets on a commercial basis.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And there are many things that go into it, from safety elements like putting up a sign outside the toilet while it is being washed and when to remove it, to the use of various types of cleaning equipment, and chemicals, some of which may be dangerous if not used properly.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It goes into basic custodial checking and time management because these workers have to manage the cleanliness of several washrooms in a day.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, let us not ridicule the work that people do or the training that they undergo.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The second thing that we should recognise is that these are jobs that are physically demanding.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I would challenge naysayers to wait tables at a restaurant.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: You are on your feet throughout your shift, walking from tables to kitchen or to the bar, carrying food and drink that can be heavy.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There is a public relations element to the job because you should be pleasant with patrons and there may be some amount of entertaining that you may have to do as well.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is not as simple as some may make it out to be.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Third, there are significant shortages in the manpower supply for these jobs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The shortages become worse when there is a surge of demand for security officers during major events, like the Formula One (F1) Race.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We therefore need to be able to attract more Singaporeans to enter these professions and to pay them well.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Fourth, these jobs are important jobs that have integral contribution to what Singapore is and what Singapore aspires to be.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If we look at the trademark physical attributes that Singapore is famous for – clean, green and safe.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: All of these are managed by PWM sectors.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister said that we should embrace a broader definition of a good job and recognise skills and competencies, instead of overly focusing on paper qualifications.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister said it is not just about re-shaping the labour market, but also about shifting perceptions about work.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I was further encouraged to see the Forward Singapore report include "respecting and rewarding every job" as one the objectives we would seek to achieve.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is important that we not only reward workers in these jobs, but that we also build respect for their professions, so that we can equalise how all jobs are viewed.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The report also called for a further reduction of wage gaps across professions including through the PWMs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is quite clearly a Government priority, which I applaud, to achieve a mindset change so that all jobs in Singapore are viewed as good jobs, and that the gap in the compensation for workers of different professions is made smaller.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The current PWMs look at closing the gap between lower-wage workers and the median income.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I ask that they consider setting as a long-term objective that the average wage of workers in each PWM sector rise to be on par with the average wage of fresh university graduates.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I make this suggestion because although the Forward Singapore report addresses the matter of increasing rewards, it does not touch much on how to improve respectability, aside from encouraging it through some form of moral-suasion.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Pegging average wages of professions of the hands with that of academically-inclined fresh graduates could provide a more tangible indication that both these categories of jobs are equally worthy of respect and hopefully, trigger a cultural shift in how our society views these jobs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to ask the Government and the tripartite partners to also accelerate the PWM wage increases so that our lower-wage workers can also live well and enjoy the fullness of the standard of living that Singapore should provide for its citizens.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: For, say, a 40-year old officer, after deductions for CPF, he would take home about $2,120 – a sum that would go into supporting his family and himself.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I am not going to go into the various calculations, that have been aired in this House before, of what is a minimum living wage in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But let us just be honest with ourselves and ask ourselves if $2,120 a month is this sufficient.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Will such a wage entitle that security officer to live the life of a Singapore worker that I envisioned earlier?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Will he enjoy the good Singapore standard of living?

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If we are honest with ourselves, I think we know that it would not be sufficient.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But the silver lining is that security officers will in fact see fairly rapid wage increases over the next four years.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that the tripartite partners negotiating the security PWM beyond 2028 will consider my suggestion to peg the average wage of security officers across all the ranks with the average wage of fresh university graduates.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: While my proposal may be seen as bold in the Singapore context, it is in fact a norm in many advanced economies.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, the average wages of waste management personnel and security officers, in particular, tended to be higher than that of fresh university graduates.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, it does appear that Singapore is somewhat of an anomaly amongst comparable advanced economies in the wages we pay our workers in these sectors.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Wong said at the IPS Conference, consumers must be willing to pay more for certain goods and services to uplift the wages of those who provide them.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I am on all fours with Deputy Prime Minister's observation that, and I quote, "We cannot demand for services delivered by our fellow citizens to be priced cheaply and in the same breath lament that their wages are too low.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is completely inconsistent." But another observation is that the initial few PWM sectors were all in the facilities management sector and were servicing mainly private condominiums and commercial buildings.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The buyers of these services actually can afford the increases in prices, but unfortunately, many of these buyers still retain the mentality that these services are manual services and therefore ought to be cheap.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: They have therefore been reluctant to increase prices in recognition of value and have largely continued to adopt a cheap-sourcing approach.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I hope the Government will do more, in partnership with the respective trade associations and trade unions, to change buyers' mindsets.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that our workers will continue to have a mindset that is cognizant of our innate vulnerability.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We have to put in effort in order to maintain our way of life.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The corollary is that those who are working hard, including in professions of the hands, are able to get their just rewards.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that we will collectively be able to enjoy the Singapore standard of living, regardless of our professions and educational background.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What is noteworthy is that this is not solely on the back of volatile revenues such as stamp duties or vehicle quota premiums, but on the back of record levels of corporate income tax, personal income tax and of course, GST revenues, all of which continued to break new record highs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This was not surprising, given news of record profits from some of the larger Singapore corporates, from DBS Bank to Sembcorp Industries.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Positive revisions to FY2022 data also meant that instead of a revised deficit of $4.2 billion, FY2022 saw a surplus of $1.7 billion instead.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is important to put into context the record operating revenues and improved fiscal position of the Government against the challenging economic environment that we faced in 2023.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: GDP growth slowed to a mere 1.1%, while inflation was a source of consternation for many Singaporeans, which was what led the WP to raise the cost-of-living Motion in Parliament late last year, to share ideas and possibilities of reducing cost of living pressures by way of policy change, many of which are structural.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In line with the theme of providing constructive feedback and ideas, I have two revenue measures for the Government to look into, after studying the revenue and expenditure trends over the past years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would be in addition to revenue raising moves that my colleagues and I have shared in past Budget debates, such as the issue of wealth taxes which I have raised previously, where even though we may have raised the highest personal income tax bracket and property taxes, the likes of wealthy individuals earning dividends and capital gains income from their vast wealth while renting luxury apartments in Singapore will still not be taxed directly.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In line with the spirit of wealth taxes, there is room to study the potential to have liquors being taxed on an ad valorem basis, in light of our suggestion of raising so-called “sin taxes”.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This need not result in any increase in duties on everyday alcoholic beverages, but it would be much more equitable if the so-called “atas” wines of the world, which easily cost thousands of dollars a bottle, incur a higher excise duty compared to the $20 a bottle wine found in the supermarket.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Second, I note that casino taxes were raised in 2022.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In spite of this, betting taxes as a percentage of GDP have been flat in past years at around 0.5%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moving on to the main body of my speech today, I will touch on the importance of structural changes compared to one-off handouts, where I will highlight the need for structural improvements to personal income taxes and corporate income taxes to better support individuals and businesses while keeping our tax system progressive and up to date, and also touch on the urgent and important topic of retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Conceptually, I believe that: one, it is important to put in place structural levers in our system as opposed to relying on one-off schemes, which may either be new or have to be refreshed year after year, incurring a lot of administrative costs and resources to operate on the part of the Civil Service, and creating much uncertainty on the part of Singaporeans; two, it is also important to direct our resources to those who need them the most, rather than broad-based handouts to everyone, which could lead to allegations of Budget measures being part of an "Election Budget." Take the CDC Voucher scheme, for example.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While I am sure all Singaporeans appreciate cash handouts amid the cost-of-living crisis, the CDC Voucher scheme evolved from one aimed at helping Singaporean lower-income households defray their cost of living in 2020 to one where all Singaporean households are eligible.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The amounts given have also varied quite significantly over the years, and it remains a question whether the scheme will be a permanent one, or if so, whether all households will continue to qualify and just how much are the vouchers going to be worth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, as opposed to the existing GST Voucher scheme, there appears to be many operational challenges faced by Singaporeans when trying to claim the CDC Vouchers, such as those who are renting their flats and sharing the same address with other households, those living in shelters and also those who no doubt may belong to the same household but are facing difficult familial relationships.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On personal income taxes, I note a tax rebate worth 50% of tax payable, or up to $200 was introduced in YA2024, similar to YA2019.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, instead of a one-off rebate, we are better off raising the bottom-end of marginal resident personal income tax rates and increasing the tax-free threshold for the first $20,000 of chargeable income to reflect inflation over time.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This was what I raised in a Parliamentary Question back in 2022.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In my speech on the Income Tax (Amendment) Bill in 2021, I suggested raising the level of progressivity in our corporate income tax regime to better support our local SMEs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even as other support for companies to build capabilities is being strengthened, I hope the Government would consider providing greater tax relief to our SMEs, such as by raising the tax exemption limits or by introducing schemes similar to the two-tiered profits tax rate regime in Hong Kong, which they introduced in 2018 to relieve the tax burden for SMEs in particular.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is important given that in Budget 2018, the Government announced tighter restrictions around our tax exemption schemes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Having such corporate income tax reforms built into the tax regime would also provide for greater certainty, as opposed to the current CIT rebates which significantly vary year after year from 20% to 50% in terms of the rebate, to a cap of $10,000 to $40,000 in the last decade from YA2013 to YA2024.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is critical to ensure that we continually re-invest in our local SMEs, the backbone of our economy representing 99% of all enterprises here and responsible for the jobs of 71% of employees, to enable Singapore to stay competitive in a post-BEPS world.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Otherwise, we could well see a reduction in our tax base and employment levels, should our local SMEs shift more of their activities to other jurisdictions in response to the new business environment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Touching on the topic of BEPS2.0, which I have also spoken about in past Budget debates, the time for introducing adjustments to our tax system is finally before us.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong has also announced the introduction of two components of Pillar 2, the Income Inclusion Rule and the Domestic Top-up Tax.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I have asked last year, while precise numbers may not be feasible, does MOF not have a range of blue sky and grey sky projections as to the impact of the implementation of a domestic top-up tax?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Especially when we are looking at the Income Inclusion Rule and the Domestic Top-up Tax taking effect in less than a year’s time, for businesses’ financial years starting on or after 1 January 2025?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If this is factually incorrect, given that the MOF will have a better basis to make its own estimates, then I hope the Deputy Prime Minister can correct this in his round-up speech.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Instead, the Deputy Prime Minister shared in his Budget speech that he does not expect the new moves to generate “net revenue gains,” due to the “significant spending required to stay competitive.” To say so is just akin to saying any forms of tax rate increases, from personal income tax, stamp duties to the GST, is not going to generate net revenue gains due to higher spending needs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I understand that this could be due to the introduction of Refundable Investment Credits and the net effect of BEPS 2.0 and the Refundable Investment Credit is to an extent also dependent on just how generous the EDB and ESG are in awarding these Refundable Investment Credits to companies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I agree that only time can tell when it comes to the actual revenue gains, as we await the roll-out of Pillar 2 globally, but it would be a sad day if countries go against the spirit of the reforms in the first place.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The BEPS 2.0 reforms were introduced to stop the race to the bottom when it comes to sovereign tax policies, and to facilitate international collaboration to end tax avoidance.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope the additional tax revenues from BEPS 2.0 will not simply be in substance returned to MNEs through other forms.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is also a pressing issue which requires urgent and decisive action, given our rapidly ageing society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While there are several good moves to improve retirement adequacy, like raising the ERS and enhancing the Silver Support Scheme and MRSS, I am concerned about the closing of the CPF SA after the age of 55, and the lack of longer-term measures to help Singaporeans grow our retirement nest egg sustainably.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In itself, I do not have qualms about the closing of the SA.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, this is a step backwards when it comes to ensuring the retirement adequacy of Singaporeans, and much needs to be done to truly strengthen retirement adequacy for the seniors today and tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: When the compulsory annuity scheme CPF LIFE was introduced, the SA continued to provide flexibility to CPF holders to access or “touch” their retirement savings, while providing a decent interest rate floor of 4%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong said in his Budget speech, “The remaining SA savings will be transferred to the Ordinary Account (OA).

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Of course, members can voluntarily transfer their OA savings to the Retirement Account (RA) at any time, up to the revised ERS, to earn higher interest and to receive higher retirement payouts.” Is this the full picture, though?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Singaporeans will know that funds in the RA will be used to pay the premiums for their CPF LIFE plan, meaning to say we can no longer withdraw the funds as we wish.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I understand that this is the concept behind annuity schemes to enable members to get lifetime payouts.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But it also means that even though the stated interest rate of the SA and the RA is identical, the actual yield that is earned by the two accounts could not be more different.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And that based on the latest average life expectancy of Singaporeans, it is unlikely that the effective yield for RA savings will exceed that of funds that would have been in the CPF SA.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, whenever I raise the issue of CPF interest rates in Parliament, the response by various political officeholders has been to stress the attractiveness of prevailing risk-free interest rate floors of 2.5% for the OA and 4% for the Special, Medisave and Retirement Accounts (SMRA) over the past two decades of protracted low interest rate environment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The closure of the SA from age 55 takes the shine out of such counter-arguments, in my view.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Wong reminded us, we are facing a change in environment from very low interest rates to a more normalised period where interest rates will be higher for longer and the era of easy money is over.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is in the context of this sea change that we should look at CPF interest rates going forward.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How then should we allow the laws of mathematics and compounding to work for our seniors’ retirement funds?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I continue to stick by what I spoke about in the Reserves Motion earlier this month, and that is to enable all Singaporeans, not just our reserves, to directly participate in the long-term returns from the Government's fund manager, GIC, with adequate safeguards in place.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is especially pertinent when we consider the source of funds for the GIC in the first place, a part of which is indirectly derived from CPF savings via the Singapore Savings Bonds (SSGS bonds).

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The effects on our ability to save for our own retirement is tremendous.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I listened to Minister Indranee Rajah's explanation that in 2014, then Deputy Prime Minister Tharman explained in Parliament at great length how we set our CPF interest rates and manage CPF proceeds.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I went to do a bit of research on this into the Hansard and realised I was far from being the first to bring this up.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Then Deputy Prime Minister Tharman's explanation was in response to PAP Member of Parliament Mr Inderjit Singh, who also questioned whether our 2.5% interest rate paid out to the CPF OA is fair compensation for Singaporeans who have left their savings locked up for so long.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In fact, if I go back further in time, many MPs from the PAP, WP, NMPs, have all suggested allowing regular Singaporeans access to better investment returns from the Government's investment entities like the GIC.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: PAP MP, Dr Lily Neo, called on the CPF Board to work with GIC, and perhaps peg the interest rates at two percentage points below GIC's returns.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: NMP Mr Siew Kum Hong quoted an academic paper which stated that: "To the extent that the GIC's return on investments has been higher than the return actually credited to CPF members, a recurrent, highly regressive, largely implicit tax on the CPF wealth has been borne by CPF members." PAP MPs Mr Ong Kian Min and Mr Sim Boon Ann called on the Government to share with CPF members surpluses it makes on CPF monies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And Mr Ong even said, "I cannot understand how the Government can say it will not be responsible for providing for my retirement, but I must lend the Government my retirement savings for investments and any gains earned on my money is not my money." Finally, Ms Sylvia Lim from the WP also called on the Government to do more to boost CPF returns while managing the risks, especially after the 2002 Economic Review Committee's recommendations to do so via private pension plans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These are all words of wisdom by those who came before me, and two decades on, continue to resonate so deeply with me.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How many more Singaporeans today could have met their retirement sums, compared to the four in 10, five in 10 today, had we implemented these suggestions back then?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Let us remember that eight years ago, in 2016, then Minister for Manpower Mr Lim Swee Say, had then on behalf of the Government, accepted the recommendations within part two of the CPF Advisory Panel's report, which included the introduction of the LIRS as an additional investment scheme.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And finally, we are all aligned with the urgent need to strengthen Singaporeans' retirement adequacy, so let us not shut Singaporeans out of attractive, sustainable and practical solutions to boost our retirement funds.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore continues to remain vulnerable to macro forces that are beyond our control and influence.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we continue to keep an eye on global developments with trepidation, I am glad that this year’s Budget has reflected the Government’s commitment to the Forward Singapore movement by introducing specific and targeted support to areas of concerns highlighted by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am particularly glad that the Government is providing additional support to seniors on ageing, healthcare and retirement during such times of uncertainty and rising cost.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is an assurance to seniors, including young seniors like myself, that the Government will provide older Singaporeans a social safety net during their silver years, particularly when senior Singaporeans are facing the twin challenges of ailing health and reduced incomes.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I had asked a Parliamentary Question on this topic in July 2023 and I am grateful to the Government for responding with this policy change.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would give senior single Singaporeans more flexibility to unlock the value of their initial larger properties, or more valuable properties during the later years of their lives, without having to bear the financial burden of ABSD, which under the previous policy would have reduced their retirement nest egg by a significant amount.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that this this is an important policy change, assuming that single Singaporeans are unlikely to have the same level of economic support that married senior Singaporeans with children would have.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Allowing a refund on their ABSD would help them to better meet their retirement needs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe this policy will give younger single Singaporeans more flexibility in their housing options if they wish to unlock the value of their private properties, especially to meet unexpected financial needs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The refund policy for younger single Singaporean could be scoped more tightly than that for senior single Singaporeans to prevent abuse and profiteering.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, the younger single Singaporeans must hold their first property for a specific number of years before they are entitled to the ABSD refund on their second smaller property and, perhaps, such refunds can only be claimed once or a maximum of twice in their lifetime.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My next topic will focus on SkillsFuture and continuous education training (CET).

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Apart from supporting senior Singaporeans with their ageing, healthcare and retirement needs, I am heartened to learn that the Government is also putting increased emphasis on our middle-aged Singaporeans with the SkillsFuture Level-up Programme.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Having once spent many years working in Temasek Polytechnic, I am confident that our polytechnics and IHLs are equipped to design and develop CET courses that can help upskill our mid-career Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That said, with industry needs evolving at such a rapid pace, our educators at the polytechnics and IHLs might not be fully equipped with the latest industry knowhows and insights to design and conduct courses that meet industry demand entirely.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At present, there are very few courses offered at polytechnics and IHLs that are co-developed, co-taught and co-certified with industry partners.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Co-taught and co-certified CETs are especially important for mid-career Singaporeans in equipping them with the latest knowledge that can positively impact their career.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: After all, having attended a co-certified programme with a leading industry player sends a strong signal to employers that their employees have learned from the best in the industry, not just from the staff at the polytechnics.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the same note, I strongly urge our polytechnics to co-create new diploma courses with industry partners to take advantage of the Mid-Career Enhanced Subsidy.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Rather than have mid-career Singaporeans join an existing diploma programme with PET students, specific industry-oriented programmes with different teaching methods, pedagogies and learning outcomes should be created for them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is important for us to recognise that adult learners have very different learning needs and learning styles from teenagers or younger adults.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Putting adult learners on the same diploma programmes is unlikely to help them to acquire the skills needed for a career switch or career step-up, since both groups of learners have very different levels of industry experience and cognition.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe this would encourage more mid-career Singaporeans to take up such courses since they can still be employed full-time while undergoing upskilling and retraining.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Almost four years ago, in June 2020, I made a speech that urged MOE to consider extending the provision of PLDs to all students in Singapore, particularly those in primary school.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think it is timely for MOE to consider providing PLDs to our students in the primary schools given how the education technology landscape has changed significantly in the past four years.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To reiterate some of the arguments that I have previously made: the ownership of PLDs for all levels of learners in Singapore is a bold and ambitious step in realising Singapore’s ambition to embrace smart learning.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such a device will enable students from across all levels of education to learn everywhere and anywhere and is the textbook of the future where all forms of education and submissions can be made on a single unified platform.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Introducing the ownership of PLDs at an early age would help induct our students, our younger students, to the notion of self-directed e-learning, encouraging them to take ownership of their own learning pace and performance at a younger age.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This undoubtedly, will have a knock-on effect when they are older, especially when e-learning and continuous learning on-the-go become second nature to them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While a significant portion of the Budget is focused on providing near term support to cope with the cost of living in the form of CDC Vouchers, Service and Conservancy Charges (S&CC), U-Save and income tax rebates, the Budget is also forward looking in providing support for seniors and mid-career Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened to know that the Government is taking active steps to address this concern early through the Forward Singapore movement and the following policies that it is rolling out.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Government can accelerate the pace in which support programmes for seniors are being rolled out and to consider how to better cater to the needs of this group of Singaporeans who have contributed tremendously in early years to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, Sir, I end my speech in firm support of the Budget.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Today, I would like to speak about two things: how to help our people thrive in their jobs; and how to support our seniors to age with purpose and dignity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I will also speak briefly about the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We spoke about unemployment support in this House for years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Based on my conversations with my residents in Kebun Baru, it is not yet a top-of-mind concern for them.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To give some context, four in 10 of my residents live in private estate homes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Because the residents trust that the Government will support them if things get tough, as during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I also want to point out that major insurance companies do sell unemployment insurance, but the take-up is not high.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But conceptually, I believe Singaporeans, including myself, are open it to if it is properly designed, as the world and the job market are changing at breathtaking speed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Two weeks ago, OpenAI stunned the world with their text-to-video capability, Sora.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Sora was able to generate life-like one-minute videos from text prompting, where everything in the video obeyed the law of physics!

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Being able to ensure that every interaction in the animation abides by physics.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This has some veteran Hollywood producers suggesting that in three to five years, generative AI can do the bulk of small screen television series production.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But what happens to creative professionals globally, including in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The same story can be replicated across many industries, many countries.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We want our people to lead in this new wave of change.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Most people do agree with the central idea, but yet, there are also many questions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: If the Government pays for it, how much tax do we all have to pay?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To address this concern, we should be clear on what we want and what we do not want.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Of course, we want our people to be confident in the face of change.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We must focus on the central issue, which is an unanticipated cash flow challenge that most people face when they lose their jobs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We want this kind of support to be different from those who fall below the poverty thresholds.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Right now, we support Singaporeans only when they have exhausted their wealth and their familial support.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But moving forward, when Singaporeans lose their jobs, we want them to focus on reskilling and upskilling by providing them with some financial peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Unemployment support should not only come when their savings have been wiped out.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We do not want abuses or the shirking of personal responsibility.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We do not want our people to make uninformed career reskilling decisions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Some of my residents also want the freedom to opt out.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Of course, we have to think through this carefully.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It will be easier to persuade people to join in in this insurance if the premium is affordable.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Two, we must preserve a strong sense of personal responsibility.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As the cost of living differs widely, we should give our people a choice in how to manage their lifestyle in the event of a major cash flow disruption.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The Government can also work with financial advisory associations to provide affected people with free financial advisory.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The third point is to provide sufficient Government support which is largely funded by tax.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I hope the Government can offset some of the cost of the insurance and get things started.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In short, in implementing unemployment support, Singapore, we, must find our own way forward.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We must do so by ensuring personal responsibility, risk pooling among our people, and Government support complement and not undermine one another.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: To ensure support, I also hope we can actively consult the silent majority before rolling this out and move carefully, start with a modest programme and review that over time, because if we are to fund this programme through a further tax increase, there might be some fatigue amongst our taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: There is broad support amongst people for the enhancement of Skillsfuture.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Singaporeans are deeply appreciative of the monthly support for adult Singaporeans to go back to school full-time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is something that Members of this House, including myself, have advocated over the years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It fills a critical gap in our efforts to upskill and reskill our people.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Of course, our Government must also do our level best to ensure that the skills training in most industries is relevant and useful.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Now, let me move to my second topic, caring for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Now, we must quickly implement these services as we are facing a silver tsunami.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In addition, I hope the Government can consider the following.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I hope the Government can support not just foreign manpower quota but also set aside spaces in HDB estates, so that the professional caregivers can be sited there comfortably, respond to our seniors quickly, without incurring too much transportation cost.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Second, even as we level up our Active Ageing Centres (AACs), I hope the Government can consider funding senior-related services in trusted nodes where our seniors gather, such as places of worship: mosques, churches and temples.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Third, to ensure that our nation's ecosystem of senior-related services always has a focus on serving our private estate residents as well.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our private estate seniors have caregiving and emotional support needs, even though they are better off financially.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But through them, we can also get a preview of the needs of future Singaporean seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Before I end my speech, I would like to speak briefly about cost of living.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I also hope that the Government can actively identify supply-side solutions and fixes, which can bring down the cost of doing business and, therefore, the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Can we increase the number of purpose-built dormitories and, in the meantime, allow for more onsite dormitories to ensure that our foreign manpower housing cost is manageable?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Also, once we implement the special economic zone with Johor, can we improve the connectivity of our more manpower-intensive operations and industries with our immigration facilities, so we can tap on more manpower from Johor to come over to work and go back to Johor daily?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Can we further re-energise our pro-enterprise panel to identify areas of red tape that cost the private sector time and money, so that we can reduce the cost of transacting with the Government?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Lastly, I hope the Government and my fellow Members in the Chambers can think through the cost-of-living implications when we pass new laws, regulations or ask for more enforcements.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For many of us in business, we instinctively know that a higher quality or service level usually means higher cost.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Yes, the law is more precise but it is also more complicated.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Moving forward, most landlords will need lawyers to do contracting rather than let agents and landlords handle the drafting of lease as it is now.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Moving forward, every time there is a change in the areas being surveyed, the landlords will need to hire a surveyor.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These will cost landlords at least a few thousand dollars.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Yes, it is harder for errant landlords to disadvantage the tenants, but all consumers will have to pay for the higher cost-of-living associated with higher rents.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I hope we can all be more measured when we call for more rules, additional studies and Parliamentary Questions, if it is only because we want to be seen conveying moral outrage after a tragedy or to signal virtue to a more particularly vocal part of our electorate.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I am fully aware that we speak up in Parliament to voice the views of our people.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But let us remember that there is a real cost to society, through higher cost of living that the silent majority must bear when we pile on excessive regulations and enforcement.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: In fact, I hope that when we speak about laws in Parliament in the future, we can speak clearly of the regulatory and enforcement cost imposed on society, businesses and our people.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With that, I stand in strong support of the Budget.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because of this, Budget 2024 will give some benefits to almost every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the monies in the endowment and trust funds will fund social spending over many years into the future and only a small amount will be spent this year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP has explained the workings of the endowment and trust funds during the Public Finance Motion three weeks ago and why capital transfers to these funds should not be considered as current-year spending.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, Budget 2024 falls short on immediate spending in the current year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While we welcome the $1.9 billion Assurance Package and the effective reduction of the owner-occupier residential property tax increase announced in 2022 by the revision of the annual value bands of the properties, these supports are hardly enough for cash-strapped Singaporeans to cope with the current cost of living crisis.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will impact the retirement plans of many Singaporeans who can no longer enjoy a higher CPF interest rate and withdrawal flexibility of their CPF funds at the same time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Government tell us how much interest it is paying these SAs currently and how much will it save in interest payments?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, we are pleased to note that Budget 2024 has addressed some of the issues that have been regularly raised by PSP in this House.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will be a great help to young Singaporeans looking to form their own families and PSP strongly supports it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since Budget 2021, we have pointed out that the long waiting times to get a BTO flat is among one of the major factors pulling down our total fertility rate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As it is not possible to ramp up the BTO supply fast enough, PSP has always urged the Government to increase the number of rental flats and improve the quality of rental flats to enable young Singaporean couples to get a place to stay while waiting for their BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While we support the PPHS (Open Market) Voucher, we are concerned that this scheme may negatively impact other groups of Singaporean tenants who are not eligible for PPHS.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We urge the Government to go further to establish rental flats as a viable housing option going forward.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the COS debates, I will explain why the PSP’s Millennial Apartments Scheme is a superior and more all-rounded policy compared to providing vouchers under PPHS.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We recognise this increase in LQS as a step closer to the Minimum Living Wage concept that PSP has proposed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP has long advocated for a Minimum Living Wage of $2,200 per month for all Singaporean workers, which translates into a take-home pay of $1,800 per month.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While we support the increase in the LQS, we are mindful of its negative impact on SMEs which need Singaporean headcount in order to employ foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We hope the Government will introduce complementary measures to minimise the impact of the LQS increase on the business viability of our SMEs, which are operating in a rising high-cost environment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, a new SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme will be introduced to support mid-career workers with a $4,000 credit.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague, Ms Hazel Poa has already affirmed our support for it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is good that the Government has now tied SkillsFuture training programmes to better employability outcomes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP has long argued that the SkillsFuture programme, which costs about a billion dollars of taxpayers’ money a year, has contributed little to the employability of Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Much more still needs to be done to ensure Singaporeans have a larger share of good well-paying jobs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To that end, we would also suggest a level-up for the Skills Development Fund so as to co-opt employers into the process, thereby ensuring that the training undertaken by workers are relevant to raising productivity in their current jobs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The handout approach is characterised by the existence of around 60 support schemes and services, each offering short-term handouts for a targeted segment of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is not uncommon, however, that multiple schemes are applied to solve one particular socio-economic problem for one recipient, which often, and very understandably so, makes it very confusing to the recipient.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, during Budget 2022, the Minister for Manpower presented an example of a low-income 65-year-old landscape worker who enjoyed a total income of $27,570 a year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While this figure works out to be about the same as the Minimum Living Wage that PSP has proposed, the total income was not paid from one source, but consisted of a base income of $17,400, presumably paid by the employer, and $10,170 paid by the government through seven different schemes, namely the Special Employment Credit, the Annual Progressive Wage Model Bonus, the Workfare Income Supplement, the Workfare Special Payment, Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) subsidies, the Care and Support Package and the U-Save and GST Vouchers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, seven schemes were applied to achieve the one socio-economic objective of ensuring that the worker had more to cope with the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, such a system may contribute to lower self-esteem among lower-income workers because their basic pay is still very low and there are little incentives in the schemes to motivate them to improve themselves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The handout approach also comes with a high administrative cost because needy Singaporeans usually need external help to navigate through the maze of eligibility rules to qualify for a particular support.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, to deliver welfare benefits to a Singaporean, very often the Social Service Office (SSO), the People’s Association, the Silver Generation Office and many other private charity groups are involved at the same time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Slightly more than half of the 60 schemes also require applications.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They may not have the time or energy to pay attention to what schemes they qualify for, even if these schemes can help them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They also lack the English language proficiency to understand these rules.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, despite the good intentions of the Government, the complexity of the handout approach means that many needy Singaporeans may not enjoy the benefits of the many schemes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of them may also not get the help they need fast enough, and this can be especially troubling when urgent help is required.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP is a strong advocate for more support for Singaporeans, but the taxpayer’s money spent must motivate Singaporeans to strive for higher goals and not breed dependency in handouts.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PAP under the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew always sought to avoid breeding dependency.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In contrast, the PAP Government of today is relying on a patchwork scheme of vouchers, rebates and top-ups that lower-income Singaporeans are increasingly dependent on, instead of pursuing systemic economic reforms such as reducing rent-seeking in the property market, strengthening labour protections, or introducing a Minimum Living Wage.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is this system dragging Singaporeans into a social trap rather than providing a social trampoline that allows Singaporeans to bounce back?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This may be the reason why although the PAP Government has increased social spending very significantly since about 2011, it did not seem to have improved the financial well-being of Singaporeans proportionately.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The main weakness of the handout system developed by the PAP Government, is that it does not empower the individual.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The objective of empowerment is to give the individual the means to take initiative to better his or her own life.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP believes this begins with providing the individual with a minimum level of support and then incentivising him or her with attainable goals.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Once the individual has reached these goals, he or she will be motivated to strive for more.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This whole process requires a "permanent scheme" approach and not a handout approach.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have been advocating this permanent scheme approach since my first Budget debate in 2021, but my proposals were completely ignored by this Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I shall repeat three of those that I have recommended repeatedly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In our opinion, the AHS will be the beginning to many potentially positive socio-economic outcomes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For a start, it will immediately reduce the cost-of-living pressures on Singaporeans and allow them to have enough CPF savings without downgrading their HDB flats when they reach retirement.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most importantly, this peace of mind for housing and retirement will also apply to all future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the AHS, we will not need to enhance the retirement adequacy of Singaporeans through schemes like the Matched Retirement Saving Scheme and the occasional top-up of CPF accounts.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The resources in all these schemes can be consolidated into one permanent scheme namely the AHS.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As PSP have said in our manifesto 2020, anyone who puts in an honest day’s work should have enough to live with dignity.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minimum Living Wage is a social standard that we should establish that is not completely linked to the productivity of the worker.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, we have proposed the Minimum Living Wage to be co-funded by the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The co-funding can come from many handout schemes as mentioned before.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To minimise moral hazards, Singaporeans will have to co-pay healthcare expenses from their Medisave accounts.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government can supplement the Medisave accounts with a Healthier SG bonus every year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For Singaporeans who practise healthy living, this bonus will become excess MediSave balances which can be transferred to their Retirement Account to boost their retirement income.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP envisages that with the majority of Singaporeans covered under a few permanent schemes, the Minister for Finance will not need to distribute handouts to millions of Singaporeans during every annual Budget.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We must be aware that we have the ability and responsibility to do more for ourselves, for Singapore and also for the world.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Just for your information, I gave you an extra 30 seconds.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Kindly keep to the time that is allocated to everyone.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This ambition is easy to state but it is tricky to strike the right balance.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are mutual trade-offs in pursuing equality and growth together.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is also important to ensure that no one slips through the cracks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While I have heard and read some opposing viewpoints, the general feedback from my residents is that the Budget payouts are generous and they can see that the Government is trying to transfer more from the well-to-do in our society to give to the lower- and middle-income segments in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To paraphrase Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong from two Budgets ago, "those who have less, get more".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, I am also aware of our budget constraints and, most importantly, we need to be aware of our sustainability issues going forward – especially in terms of our revenues and how we intend to spend going forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I will speak on three selected areas on our move to enhance equality in our economy and social space, which reinforces each other.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, enhancing transport welfare and supporting the middle and upper-middle group.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, on our two-pronged approach to sustain our economic growth – attracting investments and talent to Singapore; and boosting our local enterprises.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Just like the previous years, those who are successful will contribute a little more for the less well-off and less able.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Support for preschool expenses and a one-year Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme Voucher for eligible families who rent a HDB flat in the open market are also significant and welcomed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, one important aspect of daily expenses that has not received the targeted attention is transportation and health costs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I will focus on the cost of transportation in my speech.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The cost of owning and maintaining private vehicles in Singapore is recognised as one of the highest in the world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, our transportation cost is still quite low compared to other major cities, with the Government providing support to reduce the impact of fare increases on commuters and ensuring that our infrastructure and transport network remain up to date.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can we further extend PTV as part of our budget transfers, such as CDC vouchers, in the future to help more Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Public transport assistance is more likely to benefit the lower and middle income groups, compared to the higher-income groups who generally use less of our buses and trains.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, if such assistance will encourage higher-income individuals to use public transport rather than private transport, that will still help us in our sustainable transport objectives.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have a resident at Toa Payoh who needs help in terms of public transport vouchers to go for job interviews and also to work in a location that is far away.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are some middle-income earners who were retrenched and are now looking for work but need temporary assistance in terms of transportation cost.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I hope that the Government will introduce transport cost assistance in the form of a temporary financial support scheme for those who are retrenched and are now looking for jobs, for example. : We must also support the upper-middle income group, not just the low income.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are also experiencing the same rising costs but may not be getting as much in benefits compared to the lower- and middle-income groups.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One of the things in Budget 2024 that is also made available to the upper-middle income group, is the SkillsFuture enhancements.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That must be correct, if we want continuous skills upgrading to be a key pillar in our social compact.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, how likely will the upper-middle income group utilise the specific enhancements, in which are targeted at pursuing a diploma, degree or certification after age 40?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Do we have data on the utilisation of SkillsFuture credits by income deciles?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What do those trends tell us and will we be refining our approach to ensure that upskilling becomes a whole-of-society movement?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must also ensure that schemes like SkillsFuture is not abused.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Among other reasons, we do not want to allow those who are not in need to exploit and profit off these programmes, diverting away the help that should have gone to those who need it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is scary to think that a criminal syndicate fraudulently made away with almost $40 million in grants between April and October 2017.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While the more involved participants have each been sentenced to 13 to 17 years' imprisonment, are we still doing anything today to recover the $21 million that is still lost?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I also welcome the revision of the Annual Value (AV) bands of the owner-occupied residential property tax rates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When this property tax was raised in early 2022, it was not foreseeable that market rents would soar to the extent it did.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a result, more of our upper-middle income homeowners saw the AV of their properties and their property tax bill increase.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For owner-occupied residential properties, these homeowners would not have directly benefited from the bullish market rents since they are not renting their properties out.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They were thus left poorer as a result as they had to pay property tax up to a higher bracket.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would there be more frequent and periodic reviews of our property tax structure, considering the volatility of market rents in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More fundamentally, is it time to stop pegging property tax for owner-occupied residential properties to AVs which are, in turn, pegged to market rent levels?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, our quest for socioeconomic equality must obviously include the protection of vulnerable segments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I will just focus on two such groups of vulnerable individuals.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Among other things, the Government-supported increase in our seniors' CPF contribution rates, the raising of the ERS and the enhancement of support schemes, like Silver Support and Matched Retirement Savings Scheme (MRSS), which will boost the nest eggs of our seniors to retire and age with dignity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Government be willing to reconsider relooking at the OA interest rate mechanism?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One suggestion would be to include some of the qualifying full banks, in addition to the three major local banks that are now being referenced.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That may potentially shift the needle and is more reflective of funding conditions in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another suggestion is to take into consideration the promotional interest rates that are offered by the banks instead of just the board rates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While it is true that a consumer might have to meet certain conditions to qualify for the promotional interest rates, that may not be a good reason to deny CPF members higher return on their OAs – especially given the cumulative size and certainty of the funds that the CPF Board is given to invest.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government can, of course, subsequently apply some negative credit spread or a slight discount to the interest rate – to reflect the lower risk of putting money in the CPF, as compared to bank risk.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But my general point is that given the significant change or potential rapid changes in the global interest rate conditions recently and going forward, the longstanding calculation mechanism may be quite stale and no longer fit for current conditions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, we will need more details to scrutinise if the scheme can be implemented without eroding our work ethic and design ways to mitigate the moral hazard of financing unproductivity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When does the Government expect these details to be announced and when do we expect the scheme to be implemented?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can Deputy Prime Minister and MOF share a bit more on how this scheme will be funded over time?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I await more information on this eagerly, as it is truly a big shift in principle by our PAP Government to help our Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am heartened that this Government will not shy away from slaughtering "sacred cows", if it considers it to be in the interest of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is no shame in walking back if the circumstances so require.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While on the note of income volatility from unexpected unemployment, I would like to resuscitate my proposal again and again to give Singaporeans the option of assessing personal income tax on a current-year, pay-as-you-earn basis.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As opposed to a preceding-year basis, this system can help taxpayers better manage their cash flow by matching tax payments with contemporaneous income.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our push for greater equality cannot come at the expense of our growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To help Singaporeans cope with rising costs in a sustainable manner, we must focus on growing their opportunities and wages instead of relying on one-off distributions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, part two of my speech – therefore – turns to our two-pronged approach to sustain our economic growth: attracting investments and talent to Singapore; and boosting our local enterprises.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a resource-scarce nation, our economic miracle has been built on attracting businesses to build up a base or some part of its operations here, even if it may service foreign markets or conduct substantial operations abroad.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These inbound businesses and investments create employment opportunities and also downstream or partnership opportunities for Singaporeans and Singapore companies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I am glad to hear the moves to enhance our competitive advantage in the semiconductor and finance industries, but why is there no mention of our entrepot trade and transshipment hub and specific initiatives to defend or stretch our lead?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On the other hand, our seaport reached an all-time high in arriving ship traffic, recording over three billion annual gross tons in vessel arrivals in 2023.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I will be filing related cuts during the COS debates and I look forward to hearing the Transport Minister's plans to preserve and enhance our status as an international aviation and shipping hub.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The implementation of Pillar 2 of BEPS 2.0 will also cause some loss of attractiveness as an effective corporate income tax floor is put in place across different jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, which of the financial incentives offered by the EDB and other agencies to draw foreign companies can we continue to offer under the global base erosion rules?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This would help with the relatively higher land, manpower and transport costs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the specific support rates for a project will be commensurate with the economic or decarbonisation outcomes that the project is expected to bring, what will happen if it eventually transpires that the project outcomes were never close to what was expected?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will there be a lookback period where support can be clawed back from those who can pitch and market a project much better than they can implement them?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More fundamentally, have we landed on a system of measuring and verifying decarbonisation outcomes?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More than two years after we debated the "Low Carbon Society" Motion in this House, I do not think that any carbon measurement standard has achieved ubiquitous or common usage in this part of the world yet.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is there any preliminary indication of support from other countries for the playbook that is currently being developed by the National Climate Change Secretariat (NCCS), Gold Standard and Verra?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To attract businesses and investments, we must also maintain our attractiveness as a liveable city for foreign talent.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It would be too parochial to assume that we know everything and have nothing to learn from others.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That is why other countries have been taking some big steps to woo foreign talent to their shores.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In May 2022, it launched a High Potential Individual (HPI) visa which allows a young person who graduated from a global top 50 university to go to the UK with their family for two years to just "explore, work, study and invent".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How has our Overseas Networks and Expertise (ONE) Pass fared in attracting top global talent to live and work in Singapore since it was launched in August 2022?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How does it compare, given the heated global competition, to woo talent through a mix of easier visa routes, relocation grants and other benefits?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is well-known that we are also one of the most expensive cities in the world for expatriates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides the issue of soaring rents, foreign expatriates also do not enjoy the substantial healthcare subsidies and utilities support from the Singapore Government.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, there is a limit to how much we can tax these higher-income expatriates before they flee to a different country and we lose their tax base, their assets and their expertise.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How does our taxation of expatriates compare to other talent hubs, such as London, Frankfurt, New York or Dubai?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What are the concrete next steps following the publication of our National AI Strategy 2.0 in December 2023?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We cannot forget that AI goes hand in hand with data.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would we extend our AI-catalysing initiatives to activities that are data-centric, even though they might not be AI-centric?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, research into large volume data processing or sustainable data collection and processing would be key enablers of our AI objectives.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, what are we doing and what are we planning to do for our data sector?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The circumstances that we see today combine high inflation, high interest rates and possibly for longer, in an increasingly uncertain world featuring frequent shocks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is not even considering COVID-19, which, today, seems more like a bad dream than a lived two-to-three-year experience.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But through the Forward Singapore exercise, we know where Singaporeans want to head.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Help involuntarily unemployed jobseekers bounce back stronger, supporting families and seniors, empowering and uplifting those in need, this Budget hews closely to Singaporeans' aspirations to build a more equal society while not compromising on the economic growth that underpins our security.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In Singapore, in the 1960s, those born then had a life expectancy of 64 years.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In the 1980s and 1990s, it improved to 70 to 75 years.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Today, we have a life expectancy of 84 years.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Over the last 60 years, our life expectancy in Singapore has increased by 20 years, a 31% increase.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How do we value a year of good health?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These consistent investments in building up capabilities of our healthcare workers, of our infrastructure, it is a complex and long-term commitment.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These capabilities require a confluence of investments in infrastructure, equipment, training and education.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
