text: There must be sound and sustainable healthcare policies, coupled with a culture of excellence and a spirit of innovation, pushing the edge and frontier of medical research and technology.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: What does it mean for all of us?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Five of Singapore's hospitals are in the top 150 in the world, with Singapore General Hospital being the top 10.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: So, imagine, whenever our grandparents or parents are in need of medical care, a surgery or emergency medical treatment, have comfort that there is a team of highly competent and motivated healthcare workers who are one of the best in the world doing their best to deliver world-class care.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For ophthalmology, Singapore National Eye Centre is ranked third in the world, and Singapore Eye Research Institute is ranked fifth in the world.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Today, Singaporeans continue to age well and are healthier than before.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: More can be done and the results are clear.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Today, most of our five-year-olds can expect to live up to the age of 100.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And by 2050, living up to 100 will become a norm for our newborns.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The question then again is: how do we value life?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: What would you do to have an additional year of good health, an additional 20 years of good health to do the important things in life?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: If you have an extra dollar, where will you place it?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Every marginal and incremental dollar, how would you spend, manage and invest it?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How do we get the incremental dollar to live longer, better, healthier and more meaningful lives?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Singapore comprised two-thirds of that, at $141 billion.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I repeat: two-thirds of all the FDIs in ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Singapore ranks eighth globally for inward FDIs and first in the Asia-Pacific.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It refers to investments made by a company or individual from one country, investing and having business interests in another.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And how much advantage and wealth does that generate for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: That is particularly important for Singapore, as it displays the forward-looking economic trajectory.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: FDI creates quality employment, facilitates and encourages technology transfer.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It spurs infrastructure development and increases our export capacities.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Singapore's economic achievement today is built over decades, with leadership, bonus and collective teamwork.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This requires a confluence of economic and social factors, balance for sustainable future for all.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is not by sheer luck that we could earn that one incremental dollar.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It matters because we must understand the difficulty and the amount of collective effort, as a nation, to be in a position of strength.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The investment climate, how connected and coherent is our infrastructure?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Our legal frameworks, technology and innovation, our international agreements?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There are also social factors that are equally important: our social and political stability, our healthcare systems, education and quality of life.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: All these factors are what attract companies and individuals to invest time and resources here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It remains attractive because of what we have been doing for decades.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It must be so for the next 50 years and it must be so for the next hundred years.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How do we value our future and our future generations?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The lifespan of a country is 158 years, whilst an empire is about 250 years.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This is historic data, and we are at our 59th year mark and approaching our 60th.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: On this land that we stand and live upon for the last 700 years, it has been tumultuous.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: From the 13th century, starting with history from Palembang, the Srivijaya empire to Majapahit, to Melaya then to the British, then to the Japanese, back to the British, Malaysia and then Singapore – all these in the last 700 years.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And we must remember our vulnerabilities as a nation-state.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: History is replete with lessons to be learnt and relearnt.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The ancient Republic of Venice, the Republic of Genoa, Carthage, Sparta, the Byzantines – where political fragmentation and external pressures eroded state powers and the Hanseatic league.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How determined are we, that after a hundred or 200 years, that we are still a sovereign and independent state, against all odds and statistics, to surpass beyond the average lifespan of empires and countries?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Some estimate that our Reserves are just below $2 trillion.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To put things in perspective, assuming that our estimation is accurate, our Reserves are worth less than Apple.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is worth less than Google and, more recently, Nvidia decided to be more valuable than us.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: So, when you make your next purchase of an Apple product, Microsoft or Google, or the next graphics card with Nvidia, remember that their market capitalisation is higher than our entire national Reserves.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Our Reserves are worth less than the companies that I have mentioned.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is worth reflecting on how we plan to save, invest and allocate our resources for the future.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We are fortunate to have the Reserves that can power a Budget that we have today.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is made possible because of the prudence and the value of our founding and past generations.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is this consistent act over numerous decades that enabled us to take care of all Singaporeans, for all to lead a longer and better life.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How do we value the lives of our children?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Save the Children ranked Singapore the best place to grow up.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We give our very best to our children and our future generations.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We have the basis to debate about education every now and then because we have gotten the basics right.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Remember that we are of that generation 20 to 30 years ago where we had much less resources and knowledge.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is not perfect, but we progress and make relevant.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We embark on lifelong learning, instil adaptability and self-learning to ride the tides of changing technological advancements and build resilience to our relevance of skills and competencies.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In the past, work was more linear and the pace of change was gradual.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We saw how we restructured again and again, securing one generation after the other and building on one another's success.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Today Singapore's workforce stands amongst the most proficient in terms of management, vocation and technical skills.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This year ITE celebrates its 32nd anniversary and it continues to build strength to strength.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We do not say that we are doing well, that we have accumulated enough capabilities and that we can invest less in our education system.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We do not say that we are too high in our rankings and that we can afford to drop a little, because this is insidious.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Is there space for a city state to be a bit lower in our commitment to the future – to our future generations?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We cannot because as Singaporeans deep within our core, we know what it takes to be relevant and we know what it takes to take care of our future generations.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: More importantly, how do we cherish it, respect it and be good stewards of the life given to us?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Gaza has one of the youngest populations in the world.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The median age is just 18 in 2020.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Those age 65 years and above are less than 3% of the population.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For women, it has declined from 76 to 70 years.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And it is not just about war and conflict alone.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Countries with high levels of violence experience lower levels of life expectancy more than peaceful ones, estimating a gap of around 14 years – between the least and the most violent countries.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is not just conflict related, but also many other factors – homicide, violence, quality of life, education and all.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We are building version 1 and version 2, just like how internet browsers and applications evolved, with progressive and improving versions.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must do so and build better versions ourselves and for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We cannot expect to be perfect in all we do.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And we try harder, in delivering better capabilities for better life every day.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is called building – building for the future.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And as we build for today and for future generations – a life that is longer, healthier, more meaningful, more fulfilling and inclusive for all.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Just like our shining examples – Singapore Airlines and Singapore Changi Airport.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It was not a rare occasion marked by a cosmic alignment of constellations.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It requires effort – collective effort from all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: So, let us all build together for a better tomorrow.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Just the other day, I met a young Clementi family – daddy and mummy with their little girl, just a few months' old.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We talked about how the world has become more dangerous; more uncertain; full of challenges – a dangerous world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A world where big countries bully small countries and sometimes invade them – invasion and occupation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A world where small nations and small communities can come under siege, have their water supply cut off; electricity supply cut off; food and access to medicine blocked.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A world where climate change is accelerating, where sea levels are rising and that means a world where some islands in 50 to 100 years' time, will be underwater; a world where some island-nations may not exist by the end of this century.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And as we were talking – this Clementi family and I – we realised that their little girl and her children and her grandchildren will know whether our generation today made the right choices.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And the choices before us will require much imagination and resolve.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Eleven years ago, in the TODAY newspaper, I wrote about how we need to imagine the unthinkable before it happens – not just bigger versions of yesterday's challenges, but new challenges which did not exist before.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today I will speak about three of these challenges.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Challenges which in our time, will require fresh thinking – a fresh approach: artificial intelligence (AI); Singapore's energy security; and keeping Singapore's society together as a people.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Less than two weeks ago, just before the Budget Statement 2024 by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong – our Finance Minister, there was another announcement, halfway across the world from Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Just one year ago, during the Debate on the President's Address in April 2023, I had spoken in Parliament about the age of AI and how fast things were changing – how software, like ChatGPT, GPT-4 and Midjourney V5, had appeared in the market within less than a year or so.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: AI which can hold a conversation with you and can write an essay for you – that is ChatGPT.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: AI which can take high-school exams, advanced placement exams in the United States curriculum and outperform many humans – that is GPT-4.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: AI which can create photo-realistic pictures of events that never happened – that is Midjourney V5.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Just one year ago, I had spoken about how with increases in computing power, once you go from generating one make-believe image to 30 images a second, you go from AI-generated photos to AI-generated video.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: At the time April 2023, I had expected the technology to take another two to three years.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As it happened, it took place faster than I had imagined.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, that is the world today – technology disruption happening very quickly.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, we cannot hide from these changes.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: No country, no economy can hide from these changes in the world with AI.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Even if an entire country tries to prevent AI from entering its borders, other economies will do so – your competitors will do so.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because it recognises that in a world that is changing so quickly, what you learn in school – in education – at age 20, may have changed, transformed and have been replaced by a new world by the time you are age 40.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It recognises that change and supports middle-aged and older workers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And having mid-career workers learning new skills alongside younger workers – a middle-aged mid-career worker alongside someone who is 18, 19, 20-plus years' old, learning together, that will also transform the education experience in our IHLs because older workers bring life experience, life skills and living wisdom into the classroom.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Even as they bring that into the classroom, they also learn new skills, together with the younger students.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: These students, by working with each other, they lift up one another.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They will transform the classroom even as it allows the older and younger worker to form new friendships, new networks and new opportunities together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our electricity supply today does not just keep the lights on at home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It does not just keep our workplaces and hospitals going.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our energy supply is needed, so that our NEWater plants can expend energy to purify water and make it fresh and consumable again.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our energy supply is needed, for desalination plants to work against the salt gradient and produce fresh water without the salt that comes with the seawater.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our energy supply, our energy security underpins our water security.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And all of us know what it means for Singapore if our water supply is ever called into question.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And that means, we have to consider our energy security the same way too.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Two years ago, in the 2022 Budget debate, I had spoken about this: why we need to diversify our energy sources; why 95% energy generation from natural gas is not good enough for the future era; why 95% can be a concentration risk?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I also spoke about how we need to go beyond looking at importing low-carbon electricity through a cable from overseas – because in a challenging world with all kinds of dangers, a cable may break down; a cable may have a technical incident; many things can happen to a cable anywhere in the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And looking beyond to the future means that we have to consider new low-carbon technologies, such as hydrogen or even the newer next-generation of nuclear technology as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I called upon the Government to look at moving ahead of the market – especially for hydrogen – and for Singapore's potential as a hydrogen hub.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, data centres are energy-intensive yet so essential for AI.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: You can keep a data centre offshore for cloud computing in the commercial sector.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On social togetherness, Mr Speaker, no amount of fiscal firepower, no amount of policy prescriptions, is going to be sustainable or implementable, if we, as a people in Singapore somehow become divided, fragmented or splintered.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If we are splintered, we are going to be less than a dot in the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And there are deep forces around the world, driving people apart, forces that change societies because with digitalisation, more digital world, it means people are less likely to meet, face-to-face naturally.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The social media algorithms that almost everyone has on their handphones, the social media apps; many of these algorithms feed you more of what you have seen before.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They bring you to listen more of what you have heard before, leading to echo chambers and, as a result, sometimes, leading to polarisation in society as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Also, there will be troublemakers outside Singapore, trying to undermine our unity, cohesion and togetherness.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In the world today – and we have seen many case studies far away from Singapore, some a little bit nearer – the first shock in a conflict may not be kinetic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It may be an op to undermine the social unity and trust in a society. see how in other countries, certain players are trying to polarise and divide societies.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It will be even more challenging in the age of AI.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What happens when deepfakes are able to create videos of events which never happened?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What happens when you have deepfake videos of public figures on any side of the House, saying things they never said, doing things they never did?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What happens if there is a deepfake video of people from different communities arguing or even fighting, a deepfake video of something that never happened but which has the potential to be spread widely and undermine our social harmony and social togetherness?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What happens when deepfakes become so similar to reality that people no longer trust what they see or hear even when it comes from a reliable source?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What happens when people can no longer tell the difference between what is true and untrue, what is fact, what is falsehood, its big implications for societies, big implications for democracies around the world?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There are no easy solutions in a world where anyone has access to the computing power to create a deepfake.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But Singapore is small enough that we have a fighting chance.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Singapore is small enough that we can bring our people more closely together, build more face-to-face interactions, deepen human relationships.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We can do this in a way that larger geographically spread countries are not quite able to do.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have the state capacity, governmental capacity for agencies to work together in teamwork, in cohesion, something that many other countries cannot quite do.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We saw that during the pandemic and it will be essential for this next challenging future that we face.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we must keep building that sense of togetherness so that amidst different views, different backgrounds, different dispositions, everyone in our community sees ourselves as fellow citizens, fellow brothers and sisters, in that Singapore dream, in the idea that is Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That means, across Government, urban design and social policy must actively lean in, to encourage people to meet face-to-face in day-to-day life.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: All this can help maintain social trust, cohesion, togetherness, even amidst a wave of AI and the deepfakes that will come.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we must ask ourselves, when a new HDB development is built without the traditional void decks and in a shape that makes it harder for neighbours and their children to naturally meet one another, naturally play with one another, on the way to work, to school and coming back, we need to ask, are we inevitably weakening our social reserves, compared to the older HDB void deck designs?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Are there revenue-neutral ways of designing an HDB block differently, so that people are more likely to meet, connect, get along, in a very organic and natural way?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When a neighbourhood centre is being built in a new estate, do our planners lean in favour of having more hawker centres, more coffee shops and getting these amenities to start up and activate sooner rather than later?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When we design our education policies and education system, do we encourage our younger generation, in addition to their Mother Tongue, to learn the language of another Singaporean community, not as an examination subject, not just because of the economic opportunities near us in Southeast Asia, but also because it builds understanding and helps deepen our identity as Singaporeans?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because just like fiscal reserves, our social reserves can take generations to build up, much effort to maintain and yet, are so important when a crisis hits.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And the world ahead will have more than its fair share of troubles.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And at the same time having to face a major crisis – a terrorist attack at home, a pandemic, or a regional conflict where two old friends ask us to choose between them." Sir, we do not get to choose when the next crisis will hit or for that matter, what the next crisis will be.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we can choose how we deepen our togetherness, how to prepare today.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We can choose how we strengthen and deepen our social togetherness, strengthen Singapore's social reserves so that in a world of troubles, no matter what comes, nothing and no one will ever knock Singapore down.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Insights from works like Ronald Wright's "A Short History of Progress" and Arnold Toynbee's "A Study of History" underscore the vital lessons history teaches us about the risks of unchecked progress that had collapsed civilisations.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Understanding why civilisations collapse is a complex matter, with no singular cause universally recognised.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, several critical factors have been identified that contribute to such declines.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The first factor is climate change and environmental degradation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These elements played crucial roles in the decline of various ancient societies, including the Anasazi, Maya and the Roman Empire.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This factor contributes to social unrest, erode social cohesion and weakens a society's ability to effectively tackle societal, ecological and economic issues.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As societies become more complex in their attempts to solve emerging problems, they may reach a point where the costs of complexity outweigh its benefits, ultimately precipitating collapse.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In the context of Budget 2024, these lessons from history underscore the importance of a balanced approach to progress.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is not enough to pursue growth for its sake.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We must ensure that our growth is sustainable, inclusive and even resilient to the tests of time.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is why the Budget's focus on advancing business and worker capabilities, building for the future and caring for society is so crucial.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Commitment to green innovation, renewable energy investments and the development of resilient infrastructure that can withstand the challenges of climate change ensures that our progress today does not come at the expense of future generations.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The SkillsFuture top-up for mid-career workers, the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme, and extension of the SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit are positive moves towards building up the long-term skills stock of our Singaporean workforce.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I particularly like the enhanced Partnerships for Capability Transformation (PACT).

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: PACT will provide support for companies to partner each other on capability training, internationalisation and corporate venturing.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Such partnerships with large companies will help our SMEs grow and become industry leaders in their own right, providing more good jobs for the future.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The enhanced Assurance Package will provide much needed relief for lower- and middle-income households.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Improving the affordability of preschools and special education schools, enhancements to retirement support schemes, introduction of a new unemployment support scheme and the new ITE Progression Award will enable us to advance social mobility and create a Singapore that everyone can contribute and belong to.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Collapse, however, is not absolute and history has shown that societal resilience may be able to delay or prevent collapse.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Evidence from around the world indicates that "economic diversity", the range and complexity of a country's exports, is linked to the skill level of its population, suggesting that a more skilled populace is better equipped to tackle crises as they emerge.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore business sector acknowledges the importance of collective efforts to advance the Forward Singapore vision and strengthening societal resilience.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As a Council Member at the SBF, I have seen first-hand how in 2019 SBF launched a business-led initiative, proposing six recommendations to support the employment of the elderly, the less well-off and those at risk of job disruptions in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This Sustainable Employment initiative engaged over 50 business leaders, representatives from trade associations, Government, IHLs, non-government organisations (NGOs) and foundations, showcasing a nationwide effort to uplift disadvantaged and vulnerable workers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In 2022, SBF established the Alliance for Action (AfA) on Business Leadership Development, aiming to prepare Singaporean talents for global leadership roles.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Engaging with over 200 business leaders, human resource (HR) experts and young professionals, the AfA produced a report with recommendations for individuals, businesses and Government to foster the next generation of leaders.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Just this month, the Human Capital Action Committee within SBF has been tasked to implement these recommendations, ensuring that the report's insights are effectively put into practice.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, TACs have now offer over 100 Career Conversion Programmes, supported by Workforce Singapore, targeting various sectors, such as construction, marine and offshore engineering, electronics and manufacturing, alongside specialisations in internationalisation and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: To achieve our annual growth rate of 2% to 3% over the next decade, our economy and businesses will have to keep focusing on productivity, innovation and labour growth while keeping business costs competitive.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Government is boosting productivity by significantly investing in SkillsFuture, aiming to cultivate a skilled workforce.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, in addressing our Manufacturing 2030 vision, there is a pressing need for more local talent in manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Our first recommendation is that training should extend beyond introductory topics to include advanced technical domains, and sector-specific modules, ensuring it meets the real needs of workers, businesses, and the economy.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: To further enhance employability and cultivate a skilled workforce, more emphasis on workplace training is needed.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Workplaces should be qualified as extensions of our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs), so that learning can be more practice-based and application-oriented.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For SkillsFuture to be successful, not only employers should be responsible, workers must also have the right attitude and upskill voluntarily.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This approach will enable workers to gain deepened industry skills beyond basic and general skills, boosting employability for the long term.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Our next recommendation is centred on driving innovation in new areas of AI and sustainability within our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: To further support SMEs in adopting these technologies, the Government should consider implementing a tiered grant model.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This model will enable businesses eager to innovate beyond basic level ‘plug and play’ solutions to do so, without being constrained by cash flow issues.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, it is essential that we provide SMEs with support beyond technology access, particularly in developing governance frameworks and ethical guidelines for the responsible use of AI.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: To support SMEs in sustainability efforts, more assistance and education are essential.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We urge the Government to collaborate with sectoral TACs to create and improve sustainability programs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Grants for consultancy, implementation, and training can help SMEs effectively manage and report emissions in compliance with sector standards.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Given our aging population and persistently low birth rates, while businesses continue to reskill and upskill our local workforce, we can work closely with government to identify and unlock untapped manpower pockets.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: By harnessing smaller labour pockets, like gig workers looking to transit back to traditional economic jobs, women and older workers who are keen to re-enter the workforce, and students who might be incentivised to take on relevant part-time jobs or acquire real work experience that can count as academic credits offsets, we can collectively expand our labour force to support our economic growth targets.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, pursuing our growth objectives necessitates a harmonised alignment of both local and foreign labour forces.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The business community continues to advocate for strategic augmentation of our workforce with controlled foreign labour growth, tailored to specific sectors and job roles, where either local talent or local workforce participation is scarce.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Such targeted augmentation is crucial for driving industry transformation and ensuring the long-term economic prosperity of Singapore. : Mr Speaker, Sir, at the beginning of my speech, I have highlighted that societies can falter under the weight of their own complexity.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: My final and fourth recommendation is for the Government to engage with the business community closely, working together with various Government agencies and unions with the aim to reduce bureaucratic complexity and expediting efficiency towards co-curating a conducive environment that fosters business competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to conclude by drawing to two additional factors contributing to the collapse of civilisations, which I have not previously mentioned.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Often symbolised by the metaphorical "four horsemen" – war, natural disasters, famine and plagues.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's advantageous position today, bolstered by our substantial reserves, grants us a unique capacity to mitigate the impacts of these external shocks and the uncertainties of randomness.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Observing Budget 2024, I am reassured by its prudent and balanced nature, which thoughtfully avoids excessive depletion of our reserves, but rather strengthens our ability to secure a resilient and prosperous future for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Societal resilience can prevent collapse and Budget 2024 is a step in that direction in building this.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Let us continue to take inspiration from the past, a country born from mud flats and swamp and now a shining metropolis.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Let us muster the will together to ensure Singapore will not simply fade out of existence and not be a nation that began with a bang and end with a whimper.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Together, let us be confident to create a Singapore that stands as a beacon of sustainable progress and inclusive prosperity for generations to come.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.45 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 3.25 pm until 3.45 pm.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, I will shift away from talking about mental health and focus on discussing how the Budget lays the foundation of a resilient and inclusive society, focusing on education and lifelong learning as a vehicle for social mobility.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These are not just policy areas, these are the lifelines that will propel our nation forward, ensuring that every Singaporean – regardless of their starting point in life – can thrive in the face of adversities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is about equipping our youth with the ability, the agility to navigate the complexities of a future that we can only imagine.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Lifelong learning is our commitment to every worker, ensuring that their skills remain relevant, that they are capable and robust in an economy that is perpetually evolving.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In our pursuit of social mobility, we reaffirm our promise to every citizen that their dreams, aspirations and hard work – not their circumstances at birth – will define their future.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In this era of relentless change and disruptions, safeguarding employability through strategic investments in skill development and productivity, enhancement is a paramount concern.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The substantial increase in SkillsFuture credits highlights the imperative of ongoing training and upskilling in navigating the complexities of a contemporary job market.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A person who stands to gain from this opportunity is Mr Thomas Tan.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: He is currently working in a beverage company and has recently completed a certificate in business analytics.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: On hearing about the top-up, he is now eager to get back to study and complete a few more modules so that he can obtain a diploma.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But what excites him most is not just getting that diploma, but the chance to learn new skills that he can apply in his work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I recall my own endeavours, when I decided to take a two years leave to pursue my studies full-time.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I was already married and I was about to have my first child – to be born that year – and I had to use my savings and spend money prudently.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I also believe the allowance and two years of full-time studies could positively impact one's mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is especially so for those who may feel burnt out and want to move to a new sector or industry.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Those who come back are often refreshed and ready to share new ideas that they would like to apply in their new job.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Despite these enhancements, concerns persist among individuals and businesses.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Individuals need guidance on what is the right programme for them: what could help them in the future, what could propel them further?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: On the other hand, businesses seek assurances that whatever training the individuals go to, they would benefit the company and, in turn, fostering productivity and innovation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To address these concerns, a multi-faceted approach is necessary.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We should and must continue to engage industry leaders and businesses from various sectors through advisory panels and feedback mechanisms to further enhance the SkillsFuture courses with emerging demands.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We could also enhance career advisory services to help individuals select courses best suited for their careers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We also probably need to shift towards what I call an outcome-based training model, where the success of training programmes is measured by tangible outcomes, such as employment rates, career progression and salary increments.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This ensures the courses deliver real value to participants.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Addressing these concerns can significantly shift lifelong learning participation and employer recognition.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, I would like to talk about the ITE Progression Awards, Sir.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Now, this move is not merely about financial incentives.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a profound statement against the stigma traditionally associated with skills-based education, reaffirming its value and indispensability in our economy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The wage gap, as in many parts of the world, reflects not just economic disparities, but also the value placed on different types of education and skills.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The median gross starting pay for ITE graduates has increased – signalling a positive momentum – yet the gap remains significantly different compared to their university peers or from other Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs).

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Far too long, pursuing degree qualifications has been seen as the only path to success – sidelining the immense contributions of those with technical talent.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The ITE Progression Award challenges this outdated notion by creating more robust career pathways for ITE graduates, ensuring they are not unfairly capped in their career progression.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As Singapore's economy diversifies and specialises, the need for technically skilled professionals in advanced manufacturing, IT and healthcare, for example, is growing.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: With the hands-on training and industry relevant skills, ITE graduates are well-poised, well-positioned to meet these needs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Recognising these values is essential for us to narrow the wage gap and ensure our economy has the skilled workforce it needs to thrive.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, I welcome the ITE Progression Award as it is the step in the right direction.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I told them I will ask in Parliament.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But it just shows how much interest and positivity this move has generated.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: One such person that would benefit from this award is Mr Adil.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: He is a part-time ITE student, who is also currently working as a manager at a pizza outlet.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Upon hearing of this, he quickly checked what courses are available for him.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: He believes that this is an opportune time for him to pick up a new skill in automation and he is raring to go.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By ensuring the ITE graduates have equitable opportunities for career advancement and adequately compensated, we signal a broader shift in societal values towards a more inclusive appreciation of skills diversity.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This paradigm shift requires not just policy adjustments but a collective change in mindset from employers, educators and society at large.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To that end, ITE should no longer be stigmatised as "It's The End".

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In fact, we should now rename it, "It's The Evolution".

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It reflects the evolutionary process of personal and professional development the students undergo and a change in mindset in the community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I believe that we all have our strengths and there are pathways to success for each and every one of us and this, in turn, helps us in our mental health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my maiden speech, I highlighted the pivotal role of early childhood education as the cornerstone of lifelong learning and a vehicle for social mobility that cannot be overstated.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But despite these positive steps, some concerns still remain.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, questions are asked about the quality assurance.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: How are we able to maintain high standards of education?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: At the same time, questions also arise about teacher retention and the training to ensure that we have quality teachers and we have enough teachers out there.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But for me, I have always questioned about the enrolment rate of preschool education and the attendance that comes with it.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, to address these concerns and fully realise the benefits of increased support for preschool education, I would like to suggest the following.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That means we need to establish a more robust quality assurance mechanism in our preschools, against standardised benchmarks.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We also need to enhance support for teachers – through comprehensive programmes and professional development opportunities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But finally, and this is something I have always mentioned – the need for compulsory preschool education.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And this can only come if you make it serious enough for them to take it seriously.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By embracing lifelong learning and mastering new skills continuously, especially in the growing sectors such as technology, green energy, and bio-medicine, individuals can respond to the challenges of a rapidly changing job market and seize new opportunities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I admit that it is quite difficult for us to encourage individuals to continue their education because they are concerned about their advanced age or are busy taking care of their families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, the support provided by this year's Budget towards lifelong learning initiatives is a proactive step to encourage all levels of society, and this includes our community, to continue to grow and adapt to the needs of the present and future workforce.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Through the enhancement and expansion of the SkillsFuture programme, this year’s Budget offers various pathways for individuals to acquire and renew their skills and expertise that are relevant to current industry trends.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This provides specific impetus for individuals in this age group, to learn new skills or further develop existing skills.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, a worker in the service sector can choose to learn about information technology to further enhance his digital capabilities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, an employee in the manufacturing sector can attend courses in the management of green economy projects, and thus enable him to take advantage of job opportunities in this rapidly growing industry.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This initiative provides opportunities for those who wish to pursue further education but have financial constraints.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, an assistant preschool teacher may take advantage of this subsidy to obtain a Diploma in Early Childhood Education, strengthen her professional qualifications and see more career opportunities open up for her.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To harness lifelong learning, as a society, we need to promote a culture that values and promotes lifelong learning.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This requires us to support those who are be bold enough to make the leap to study again, and they need to be steadfast and patient when embarking in a new field.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: My hope is that our community will take advantage of these budget initiatives to actively engage themselves in lifelong learning.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is not just about improving oneself but also about contributing back to society, family and country.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There are several components to this, and one component is that there will be an expanded network of Active Ageing Centres (AACs) providing a wider range of programmes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: First, I would like to ask the Ministry of Health (MOH) what is the current situation with the staffing as well as the recruitment efforts for our AACs?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How will MOH assist our AACs to recruit and maintain additional staff to tackle the manpower needs for a bigger scale AAC landscape?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Does the Government have a guideline in mind for the manpower staffing per centre under AAC 2.0, of course, taking into consideration that requirements for clusters may vary according to the size of the cluster?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: AACs have a mix of staff and volunteers while staff strength of AACs may vary from centre to centre and volunteers are also an integral part of AACs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Volunteers may not always be able to take over the roles, expertise and, indeed, professionalism of the professionals in our AACs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, for the group of seniors who do not wish to be involved in their AAC activities or do not desire to keep in contact with their AACs, I would like to know what are the plans that Age Well SG may have for them as far as outreach and keeping in contact are concerned?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This will be in line with tackling loneliness and addressing the need for seniors to be socially connected, as mentioned by Deputy Prime Minister Wong.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am especially concerned with those who live alone, keep to themselves and who are not close to their families or neighbours.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Beyond having more or more varied activities, we need to study what approach can be taken to better enable AACs to keep in regular contact with this group, at least to provide support when it is needed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Studies should also be done to see how AACs can attract better male participation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong also mentioned in his speech of silver upgrades to our residential estates to enable seniors to live more independently and safely in the community by way of amenities, such as therapeutic gardens and barrier-free ramps and senior-friendly home fittings, such as wider toilet entrances and shower seats.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I look forward to more details from the Government, including how these amenities will be made available to residents in their homes and in our common spaces.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong also mentioned that there will be improvements to infrastructure for seniors' mobility and safety, such as more sheltered linkways, bus stops with senior-friendly features as well as safer and more pedestrian-friendly roads.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As recently as August 2022, in an answer to a Parliamentary Question, the then-Minister for Transport said that there were no plans to expand the criteria of Land Transport Authority's (LTA's) existing covered linkway programme covering a 400-metre radius of major transport nodes, such as MRT, LRT stations and bus interchanges.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope that there is now a rethink about this approach for covered linkways, especially on lands administered by LTA or other state lands.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: LTA should consider linking at least the heavily utilised bus stops to nearby housing estates.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, working with Town Councils to link up such heavily utilised bus stops with the nearest covered walkways within the HDB estates.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can the Government look at increasing the cap for the MediSave withdrawal limit for seniors with multiple chronic conditions so that such seniors, especially seniors who are retired and not working or are unable to work, will be less out of pocket when paying their bills?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I know that the MediSave withdrawal limit was revised in January 2021.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Would it now be timely for the limit to be raised, at the very least, to keep up with elevated inflation?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance Lawrence Wong emphasised in the Budget that the Government would strengthen its support for the elderly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope the relevant Ministers can share more details on this.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong mentioned that the refurbishment and enhancement of senior-friendly facilities in neighbourhood to enable the elderly to live more independently and safely in the community.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This includes expanding sheltered walkways and bus stops with elderly-friendly features.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In August 2022, the then Transport Minister stated that the Land Transport Authority (LTA) did not have plans to expand existing sheltered walkways.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Currently, LTA’s sheltered walkway coverage is limited to within 400 metres of MRT stations and bus interchanges.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope the Government can reconsider this strategy, especially in LTA managed or state-owned areas.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, LTA could consider collaborating with the Town Councils to connect HDB neighbourhoods with sheltered walkways to busy bus stops.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Furthermore, the Budget also includes a one-time MediSave Bonus for eligible Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For elderly individuals with multiple chronic illness would need frequent outpatient care, especially those who are retired or unable to work, if the annual withdrawal limit remains at $700, this top-up may not provide much help to them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The withdrawal limit was last revised in 2021.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In times of rising prices, will the Government consider raising the withdrawal limit for MediSave to reduce the cash outlay for retirees?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will the Government also consider increasing the withdrawal limit for MediSave by the same 20%? : I will next touch on the issue of support for adults with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I welcome Deputy Prime Minister Wong's announcement that he will provide more support for adults with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He said he will expand spaces in sheltered workshops and day activity centres where they can undergo skills training and launch more enabling services hubs to provide community support to persons with disabilities and their caregivers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I believe that, as a society, there is a lot more we can and should do for adults with disabilities among us, in particular, adults with serious special needs as well as their caregivers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Earlier this month, I filed a Parliamentary Question asking whether the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) will consider increasing the number of day activity centres and residential homes for adult persons with autism.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I believe that we really should increase our resources to provide continuous training for adults with disabilities, including but not limited to special needs adults, such as those with moderate to severe autism beyond their time in the SPED schools.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In my view, there are multiple possible benefits.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We should continue to think of ways to improve long-term post-SPED school education or training, providing further education and skills training, if possible.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: More studies should be done to increase the possible range of work training these adults can undergo and the range of work they can undertake in society.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This will enhance their lives and promote better integration with society.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At the same time, spending time at day activity centres rather than at home, with structured programmes, activities and interaction with others will enhance the mental well-being of such adults.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: My heart also goes out to senior caregivers and their special needs adult children, wondering what is going to happen to the care of their children when their health gives way one day.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Even when these parents may have other children who are non-special needs, is it appropriate to expect them to take over care of their siblings when their parents pass on?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Should we not provide adequate residential homes for these adults with more structured care and development?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And can we also consider for these homes to allow some of the special needs adults to be able to go home to their families on weekends, providing some balance between residential care and home care, allowing family members suitable respite in the process?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Minister Masagos also said that MSF has been working with the sector to develop plans to better support adults with autism and their families, given the increase in awareness of autism and in the clarity of its diagnostic criteria and that MSF will share more details in the coming months.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Indeed, I hope that MSF is able to share such details during COS, including details of any studies undertaken recently.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In November last year, I filed a Parliamentary Question asking the Minister, among other things, whether the Ministry keeps a record of the current number of elderly caregivers who are caring for adult persons with intellectual disabilities and whether the Ministry will consider developing and implementing early identification and support programmes for such caregivers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How mentioned in his reply that MSF does not directly track the number of elderly caregivers who are caring for adults with intellectual disabilities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In December 2023, news broke that one of my Hougang residents, an adult with special needs, stayed in his flat with the body of his elderly father after his passing for five days while continuing to attend day sessions at the day care centre.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While I am extremely thankful that the authorities and stakeholders were commendably quick to assist and arrange for care for the son thereafter, this case reinforces the need for us to consider developing and implementing an early identification and support programme for elderly caregivers who are caring for adults with special needs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such a programme could adopt a multi-agency approach that involves our AACs, day care centres for adults with disabilities, healthcare providers and even service providers like lawyers who may have interactions with family members in the course of their related work, for example, doing Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA), as well stakeholder agencies like Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) and MSF, such that each party can trigger another party to provide necessary checks or support for the family concerned.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Studies should be done to see how contact and support can be appropriately maintained by one or more stakeholders for both elderly caregivers as well as the special needs adults.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Last year, I said in my Budget debate speech that we should work towards AACs, which cater to the different needs of seniors, whether social or medical, or for more specialised areas like mental health or disabled persons who are seniors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The centres should still be referring centres even if other organisations or sub-units are involved.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Indeed, an expanded AAC can also perform the coordinator or contact role for elderly caregivers of adults with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Last year, I said in my Budget debate speech that we need a detailed roadmap for retraining workers in these sectors as Singapore decarbonises.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I asked whether we have sufficient sustainability-related courses that businesses and workers can afford to attend, both in terms of time and money.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In my speech today, I will go on to talk about the quality of the education to be provided.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the context of climate change and sustainable development, upskilling is now necessary to ensure a just transition and that no worker is left behind.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: IHLs form the backbone of this shift and there exists a multitude of courses available to build capacity and upskill the existing work force in areas such as environmental, social and governance (ESG) and carbon services and trading.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The MSc programme in data science for sustainability was also launched in NUS to train data scientists who can integrate their knowledge and skills with an understanding of sustainability issues.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Nanyang Technological University (NTU) has the Asian School of the Environment and offers majors in environmental and earth systems science, public policy and even a second major in sustainability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These are examples of positive development in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But to ensure that graduates are well equipped to meet the demands of the times, all such courses must go through sufficient policy and industry validation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For instance, IHLs should, if they have not done so, internalise the SkillsFuture reports to assess SkillsFuture needs in these areas and assess what skill sets they have to teach undergraduates and graduate students.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We should also encourage our course providers to ensure that all courses provide adequate time, emphasis and coverage on Singapore, so that students can really understand how to green Singapore and the challenges that Singapore face.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Do knowledge providers have the right people to teach and impart such knowledge and skills?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some form of impact assessment is necessary to track lifelong learners' progress, comprehension and application.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Second, knowledge and content providers across the IHLs also need to be given adequate support to do this important work of providing the knowledge and skills for the workforce.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Hiring practices at university need to reflect contribution to society beyond traditional publication and impact factors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If Singapore is to succeed in our green transition, more emphasis needs to be placed on hiring experts that have real-world experience in solving complex sustainability challenges.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Demand is also growing for Singapore to help build regional and international capacity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Overall, there is growing demand for Singapore's experts to be ready and available to impart valuable knowledge.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To do so, we need more Singaporeans to step forward with the right knowledge, skills and attitude to help grow our local, regional and international sustainability talent.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Indeed, we need to actively grow our pool of educators.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Climate change demands urgent action from everyone, across all sectors of society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Whilst it is not flawless, it does stand as evidence of our Government’s commitment to listening and understanding ground realities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am very grateful to my residents, grassroots activists, fellow volunteers and my Central District CDC councillors and partners for sharing their insights on Budget 2024 with me.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many of them have expressed admiration for its comprehensive suite of benefits to individuals, households, seniors, businesses and families with children in preschools and special education schools.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Budget’s positive features are widely recognised and appreciated.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In my speech, I wish to focus on three areas of concern: firstly, the need to scrutinise if the intended outcomes of Budget 2024’s initiatives will be met; secondly, the sustainability of escalating social development costs; and thirdly, the need to foster a more robust ecosystem of partnership to make the Budget theme of “Building our shared future together” a tangible reality.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, the devil, as they say, is in the details.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For instance, while attractive financial incentives are provided for ITE graduates below age 30, to pursue further diploma studies, several questions remain unanswered.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is unclear to me how many are eligible for these targeted diploma courses and whether the potential opportunity costs of not working will deter them, and if they will receive adequate career guidance to ensure alignment with their strengths and job market needs?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The same questions also apply to the mid-career reskilling plan for Singaporeans aged 40 and above.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is also a profile who similarly needs to be urged to undertake the reskilling initiative for better future employability.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I therefore would urge a careful study of the response of the target pool of ITE graduates and mid-career Singaporeans to further improve the chances of success of this potentially game-changing investment by the Government.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Government can consider an even more aggressive move of specifically approaching the lower-skilled gig economy workers, for instance, and others whose industries or jobs are at risk of being obsoleted by technology, including AI.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The investment in our younger ITE graduates and mid-career Singaporeans is not the only ones that need careful eyeballing and tweaking if need be.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some initiatives such as the corporate income tax and personal income tax for everybody, the reduction of fees in preschools and SPED schools are blunt measures that signal Government's care and empathy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Yet, they may or may not be needed or appreciated by some Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: An option for those not in need to redirect their benefits for a common pool for those more in need should be considered.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Much like how unused CDC Vouchers are channeled to charities with an Institution of Public Character (IPC) status.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I therefore urge Government to undertake a proactive mitigation strategy to guarantee the effective execution and success of Budget 2024's well-intentioned initiatives.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, I would like to touch on the worrying trend of rising national expenditures, especially in what is categorised as "social development costs".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This investment in social development reflects Government's priorities and commitment to improving the quality of life for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Yet as we increase spending in these vital areas, we must also consider innovative ways to sustain this investment.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Our Singapore society is not accustomed to higher personal and corporate income taxes for various reasons.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How sustainable this funding model is remains to be seen.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There must constantly be found ways to pay for the ever-increasing expenditure.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Some people I have spoken to call for an even more resources, for example, to be channeled to GIC and Temasek Holdings for them to invest, so that the NIRC base can be enlarged.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The two investors have, over the years, delivered decent medium- and longer-term returns.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And others call for more public-private-people partnerships for more innovative and flexible funding.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Whatever it is, the concern over the sustainability of the current funding model for our ever-rising national expenditures should not be underrated and underestimated – and that is my second point.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong’s clarion call through Forward Singapore and through Budget 2024 to “build a shared future together” is an important call to action for every sector of society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Already, Singapore is working with partners in areas such as community hospitals, hospices included, special education and other social services.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I refer to hon MP Dennis Tan's lament about the adults with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And I just want to share that all of us have a role as well.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In my Kampong Glam division, for example, we have tested and piloted in the last two years with the People’s Association (PA) grassroots and CaringSG, a special programme that is called "Purple Hearts".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a special needs families' network, where more than 20 volunteers from the ground, led by some of our grassroot leaders and me.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We regularly visited, befriended, tried to find out the needs and then referred and directed the needs of these 200 families to the different agencies, some of them in Government and some are non-government.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am very happy to share with Mr Dennis Tan and also other MPs, if they are interested, to at least make this happen in their area.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Already, Singapore is working with a lot of partners in this space.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But let me just propose some ways by which our Government can take a better lead in ensuring the building of a shared future together, especially in the non-profit charity sector, where I actively volunteer.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is a sector that is full of heart but is fairly fragmented.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, the Government can play a crucial and more helpful role in facilitating this ecosystem to ensure more informed decision-making and impactful outcomes.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In recent years, substantial resources have been allocated to governance of the partners, which is vital of course – audits, governance and so forth.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, there needs to be a deeper understanding among both donors and recipients about the landscape – identifying the key essential services, causes, beneficiary groups, key gaps and expectations, as well as clarifying the Government's participation in these gaps and how others can contribute effectively.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, major donors in Singapore, such as Ngee Ann Kongsi and various foundations, could be better supported to invest in the essential areas sustainably.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The back-end of any effective social service ecosystem lies in its operational capabilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Currently, many social service agencies and charities face challenges due to fragmented support structures in governance, procurement, risk management and internal controls.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Not their fault; it is just that they are operating with very limited resources.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They cannot afford to pay for what one Member called “bureaucratic complexity”.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, operating with limited resources, these charities and partners often find it very difficult to establish systems that meet Government operating and audit standards.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Improving support in these areas therefore is crucial.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For instance, having good senior public servants from the Public Service for Good movement started by Minister Chan Chun Sing to sit down with key sector leaders and help set reasonable standards and install cost-effective back-end functions – this is one way of moving forward for a shared future.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, on supporting manpower needs in this non-profit charity sector, the Government can play a pivotal role by being sensitive to and supportive of the workforce dedicated to its non-profit partners.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The manpower challenges faced by organisations, for example, like Dover Hospice, which I just visited, where healthcare staff, despite their experience, face tenure limitations; and partner homes, nursing homes, residential homes, which see staff leaving for other sectors, for example, the public sector, due to more attractive connect plans or compensation packages.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: All these underscore the need for a more supportive and sensitive framework by the Government, together, working as partners.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Essential and emerging needs should be carefully identified and receive more support.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
