text: These include healthcare, lifelong education, care facilities for adults which Member Dennis Tan has mentioned also, and I raised many times in the House here and outside, for persons with disabilities and their families, especially the adult ones, and also support social enterprises that lead to job creations for the vulnerable, such as our neuro-diversed, disabled and lower-educated Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Instead of relying only on donations and grants, charities as the Government's partners should be encouraged to fish rather than being fed in the long term.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Social enterprises play a critical role in addressing societal challenges through business solutions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But social enterprises are some of the most difficult businesses to run, having to achieve both financial and social output bottom lines.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The money goes into the charity and not into any individual's pockets.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, this approach will not only foster social innovation but also contribute to the economy in a meaningful way.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Public procurement policies that favour social enterprises can create a more inclusive economy and drive social value creation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And I look forward to the Government double-clicking on what I have shared on these five items, so that we can build a shared future together.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And I also look forward, of course, to its considered responses in this Budget season.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Only with a vibrant ecosystem can each one play their role to the best and bring to reality the spirit of ForwardSG and Budget 2024.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Now picture Encik Ali, struggling to choose between essential groceries and his medication due to inflation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They represent the daily struggles of a sizeable number of Singaporeans, both young and old, feeling the squeeze from rising costs of living across the board.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I meet some of these residents at my Yio Chu Kang Meet-the-People Sessions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While Budget 2024 deserves recognition for its priorities, the affordability crisis casts a long shadow, threatening not just the financial security of our seniors but the very fabric of our diverse society.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us act before affordability becomes a barrier to opportunity and well-being for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We can do more to make Singapore an affordable place to live in, particularly in transport, housing, CPF and social support schemes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we need to ensure affordable and accessible transport for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While our public transport network continues to expand, car ownership remains a critical aspect of life for many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Families with young children, seniors, individuals with limited mobility and those with special needs often rely on private vehicles for their daily commutes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Despite its world-class efficiency, our public transport system experiences sizeable crowds at most hours.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: During peak periods, the situation intensifies, with limited seating availability for vulnerable passengers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While private hire vehicles (PHVs) offer an alternative, their costs and waiting times are rising, not to mention that there are peak-hour surcharges.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Recent experiences during festive periods like Chinese New Year, with reported waiting times of 30 minutes, raise concerns about their reliability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Of course, this is understandable as PHV drivers have families, too, and will join in the celebrations during this festive season.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But this also means that there is a certain market failure in the PHV network which may require some intervention.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Skyrocketing Certificates of Entitlement (COEs) threaten to push car ownership out of reach for the average Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is not a luxury car problem; it is a family car problem.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The recent Parliamentary debates on this issue demonstrated the urgency of addressing the affordability issue.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have raised this issue in Parliament on several occasions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This issue centres around the fairness and impact of placing PHVs and individual buyers in the same COE pool.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: PHV companies often have access to greater financial resources and can be more aggressive bidders, ultimately, passing on the cost to passengers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Companies are likely to prioritise higher bids, compared to individual buyers purchasing for personal use, knowing that they can recoup the money in the future.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Hence, creating a separate category addresses this imbalance between corporations and individual buyers, ensuring a fairer and more equitable system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Speaker, Sir, we need to protect our seniors from seemingly unfair property tax increases.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While the recent adjustments to AV brackets and property rebates are a positive step, their delayed implementation presents a pressing concern for our retired seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They have acquired their private properties decades ago and lived in them for a long time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A sharp property tax increase can devastate these retirees who lack the income to absorb the cost.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need a fairer system that protects our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They lack the readily available cash flow to absorb any significant rise in property tax associated with increasing AVs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps the Government should provide more assistance to retirees with no income who possess a single owner-occupied home.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By all means tax more for those with a second property, a third property and so on.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What the Government is doing now is essentially asking retirees staying in their own home who cannot pay their property tax to sell away their home and uproot from the environment that they are familiar with.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will put stress on our seniors and affect their mental health.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It might even cause dementia to set in earlier.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We also need to implement a fairer property tax system considering residents' unique circumstances, especially for owner-occupied homes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can we encourage our banks and financial institutions to have reverse mortgages?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Monetise some of the lease of the houses, but with the option of paying back when the house is eventually inherited.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This may create a market and allow price discovery and competition, too.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We also need greater clarity on the relevant physical attributes that are being considered when calculating the AV of the home.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will IRAS assess the condition of houses, both private and HDB, that are located in districts with higher property value but have not been renovated in many years?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we need clearer communication and targeted support for CPF changes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While the closure of the Special Account (SA) and the transfer of funds to the RA simplify the system and offer potentially higher interest rates, I seek clarification on the 1% of members who cannot transfer their SA savings to RA.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on who falls under this exception?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will moving funds from the OA to the RA be voluntary?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will members be informed of this option, its benefits and drawbacks, and receive assistance on this if needed?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Numerous residents have expressed concerns that they have to replan their retirement due to this change.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Years of financial planning based on the SA's higher interest rates are disrupted, leaving them with limited time to adjust.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The limited withdrawal options from RA raise concerns about accessing emergency funds, unlike the SA, which has more flexibility.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Conversely, leaving funds in OA means lower interest earning and retirement savings, impacting our seniors' long-term financial security.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Minister to address these residents' concerns and explore ways to minimise the impact of the SA closure on members aged 55 and above, particularly regarding withdrawal flexibility.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on specific measures to help them grow their retirement savings?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we need to refine means-testing processes for essential schemes to ensure inclusivity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Seniors in larger flats may face other financial limitations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They may share the roof with many family members and do not have the option to downsize or monetise the house.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Hence, it may not be right to equate housing type with wealth.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The current means-testing based on housing and family income might not accurately reflect the true financial situation of all seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the increasing trend of later marriages and singlehood, many young Singaporeans live with their parents while striving for financial independence or waiting for their BTOs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Denying subsidies based on these further disadvantages young Singaporeans and impacts their decisions regarding marriage and family planning.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us view Singapore as a grand, age-old tree, deeply rooted in our values and traditions, providing shelter and sustenance to all who seek refuge beneath its branches.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Just as we cherish and nurture our seniors, so, too, must we ensure that they are sheltered from the storms of uncertainty and hardship.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They grew the tree, and now it is their time to enjoy the shelter it should provide.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is evident that action is needed to address the affordability challenges facing Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have made several suggestions in my speech.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to explore separate COE categories for PHVs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Tailored policies and capped increases can alleviate the burden on seniors and home owners.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Thirdly, in CPF, greater awareness of policy changes and targeted support are critical to help seniors grow their retirement savings, especially for lower-income earners who struggle to reach the Basic Retirement Sum.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, in social support, refining means-testing processes for essential schemes like Silver Support and medical subsidies is necessary to ensure a holistic view of individual and family income.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Government to prioritise these measures to ensure affordability for all, especially for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us not wait until rising costs become insurmountable barriers for Singaporeans of all ages.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By working together, we can build a more inclusive and equitable society where everyone thrives, regardless of their circumstances.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Together, let us make Singapore a truly affordable place to live in, and a nation where everyone can chase their dreams without being crippled by financial hardship.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We are lucky that in Singapore – against massive odds – we have continued to do well.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Budget 2024, which is a part of the Forward Singapore movement, aims to keep the upward trajectory going.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But even as we grow our economy, the immutable fact is that resources will always be finite but wants unlimited.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Our needs rise with each generation and their aspirations for a brighter and progressive future imply we have to keep adapting and evolving.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We need to take deliberate actions to stretch every dollar we spend to ensure we continue to meet the growing aspirations of our citizens and expand our economy in a holistic manner.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Thus, strengthening key areas and preventing unnecessary resource wastage, while ensuring that our wealth and social equality keep pace across different segments in society, is necessary.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In this Budget 2024 Statement, there are four areas stood out for me.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: First, I agree with the need for our economy to continue growing at a healthy pace, but not at all costs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I applaud the Government in planning for the future of economy and setting a direction of what industries and jobs will anchor this little red dot beyond a decade or two.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, we have to be careful not to be blindsided by the potential unseen structural and social costs that such development could bring.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We have to plan for such economic activities in a holistic and calibrated manner and, most importantly, as part of a whole-of-Government effort to ensure we consider all dimensions of each plan.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For example, as we pursue new high value activities, such as R&D, we should not neglect strengthening our foundational engineering capabilities or to continue encouraging our high value-add manufacturing base.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The pandemic has shown that over reliance for core parts of a supply chain globally has its downside.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Offshoring some of these jobs not only impact our blue-collar workforce, but it could also risk Singapore losing our ability to effectively translate innovation into market-ready products.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: On the long run, this limits Singapore's capabilities of being a "one-stop" shop for such innovation deployment.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, we must continue to support capability development in tradecrafts and some blue-collar domains, to ensure we have a holistic workforce to drive our economic plans forward.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I hope similar schemes would continue to support and enhance our workforce to develop mastery in key skills which are needed to drive some fundamentals in Singapore's growth forward.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: To be clear, I am in full support of our future economic thrust, such as preparing for the digital and green transition, continuously moving up the value chain and finding niche areas where we can be globally competitive and differentiated.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But while we push the frontiers of innovation – and it is critical – it is the ability to imagine the future of Singapore's economy that presents hope and possibilities to all segments of workers that will keep our economy going.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: These spendings are important to ensure that Singapore remains a good participant of global climate action and potentially be a beacon to other countries in transiting towards cleaner energy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: These infrastructural developments are, however, costly; and could entail higher risk of being stranded, given the uncertain energy landscape.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: A prudent allocation of these funds must go beyond just evaluating the capital.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It requires Government leaders to make good judgement calls on the risk of such investments and to consider the potential high recurring cost and approach to maintain such infrastructures for usability over a defined lifetime; so as to prevent wastage both now and in the future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In the same vein, we should follow this philosophy when developing any infrastructure projects to ensure we can stretch every dollar spent.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Take, for example, many sheltered linkways have been constructed to provide increased convenience to our citizens and give them the comfort during the hot and wet weather.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, some of the sheltered linkways are not built at areas with heavy footfall and they are under-utilised.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The lightings that are required to keep them bright for usage at night is also drawing more energy from the grid when it is already lighted by parallel streetlights.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: To ensure the safety of these structures, especially the ones spanning across the roads, are both expensive to construct and maintain.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Have we considered how to minimise high recurring expenses to maintain these assets for decades?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Were there options to modify the usage of these sheltered paths to serve a wider community, or other innovative and cheaper ways to provide such shelter?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Such decisions do require some level of judgement.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Given our limited resources and the possibility that some day, we will have little foreign workers to serve our daily needs, will the public works regulatory evolve to allow citizens to volunteer their expertise or knowledge on potential technology and designs that can be used?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: For a young nation with relatively high median income, it is hard for some to apprehend that we have amongst us the low-income workers, a sandwiched middle-income group and seniors or retirees who may not have sufficient financials to support their retirement.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With impending global headwinds that may adversely affect our economy and our ageing population, I am concerned for the future for this group of citizens, especially given the uncertainty it may bring.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While the country prospers, a key topic we have to face squarely is whether our wealth and social equality is keeping pace across the different segments in society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While such schemes have instant effect to address current inflation challenge, the long-term deployment of such schemes, likewise places a fiscal burden on the Government.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: There is a need to continually track the impact of such packages and to regularly benchmark it with the intent of the package or the policy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With Singapore's continued investments into new high value economic growth areas and as we continue to support upgrading our workforce to undertake higher value jobs, I am hopeful that the real wages for Singaporeans will continue to grow.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I am not against the provision of financial support for targeted groups of individuals who have needs and are unable to support or manage without additional support or truly needs a helping hand in that manner.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Everybody likes "free money", but it is important that we always prioritise our fellow Singaporeans who might need a bit more help and continue to support them as a national family.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: And this brings me to the last aspect of helping those who need more support and in a targeted manner.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I am very encouraged by the announcement of the increased support to be provided to families of persons with special needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I believe that inclusivity is an important pillar in our social fabric, and we should continue to aspire and rally more Singaporeans to support and integrate people with special needs into our community to the largest possible extent.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: To be a caregiver for someone with special needs is not only a matter of financial cost, but it also takes a toll on the entire family as their lifestyle completely changes beyond one about affordability, to one that focuses on how best to enable the special needs person to live a life.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: One resident who approached me for help recently had an issue with her daughter's application for a transport concession card.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The issue of not getting the approval was one around definition of disability and the assessment criteria.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The fact of the matter is her daughter has been diagnosed with varying degrees of disability since young.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Now at 20, her condition has not improved, and she faces other societal challenges and the lack of opportunity to participate in the workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: What her parents are concerned about is not merely about a transport concession card, which is lesser in value than GST Voucher or even the CDC Voucher support that were generously given.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The concern they have is that the availability of options their daughter has for rest of her life is determined by what others are willing to provide and the decisions to support rely on rulebooks that are seldom exercised with a sense of understanding.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I do ask if there are more we can do as a community to support such individuals.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I am heartened to see that there are more commercial facilities setting aside space and adjusting their operational procedures to make spaces that are more welcoming to those with special needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Other similar efforts are also taken by corporates, such as Frasers Property and its tenants, who chose to be the inaugural "Inclusive Champions".

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Proliferation of such community, as well as commercial-led efforts are essential to ultimately mainstream the inclusivity of special needs individuals into Singaporeans' daily way of life.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I hope the Government will expand its support for such ground-up efforts, both in the commercial and the community space to help those with special needs.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Deputy Speaker, to conclude, I am optimistic about Singapore's growth ahead despite the global headwinds.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Budget 2024 provides a view of how we can shape our economy to embrace a new demand, which also ensures our workforce can be better placed for future job propositions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While the Government plans for the nation, I also seek fellow Singaporeans to take an active role in our path forward.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This country can only benefit from our collective wisdom, efforts and willingness to see it succeed.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Success is not simply a definition of being the best, but one where we feel proud and comforted that our success includes those who are needy and vulnerable in society as well.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: And with that, Sir, I rise in support of the Budget.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It takes care of the immediate cost-of-living challenges, provides support for families and our seniors, supports individuals and businesses to be future ready for growth and jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The introduction of measures to anchor quality investments, invest in new economic sectors and major moves to decarbonise the economy, are welcomed but require large funding.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The question is, will we be able to continue to afford such large funding.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I hope that we continue to be able to share as we progress on our specific initiatives.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: My speech will focus on four areas: better growth; jobs and opportunities; healthcare and senior care and the property tax adjustments.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the continuing geopolitical situation, slower economic growth and decline in real income, Singaporeans and businesses have been challenged in coping with inflation, higher cost of living and of doing business.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But we do need to give focus to growth and quality growth.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is vital if we want better lives for Singaporeans and for businesses to be able to thrive.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This point was aptly articulated by one of our residents in Changi Simei last year during our Budget dialogue.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As we were discussing budget measures to support cost-of-living pressures, he reminded us that while support measures are needed, we must also "grow the pie".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If we do not grow, we will be worse-off in the long run as we will be relying on a shrinking pie and there will be less to count on.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is the stark reality and a timely reminder.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Global uncertainties, disruptions and structural shifts, driven by technology and climate change, require us to make fundamental shifts and innovate to achieve good and sustainable growth.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singapore needs to continue to remain an attractive hub for businesses to invest their high quality projects, as this brings cutting-edge capability, knowledge and technology, and more importantly, it creates good jobs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We have always had a very competitive culture in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This has served us well in many ways, from the excellent performance of our students in schools to our efforts the top global rankings and everything from corruption perceptions to business friendliness.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans are not looking to the Government to shield them from global competition.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, we detest unfair competition where people who do not play by the rules or follow local norms, still get ahead.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, when Singaporean workers see colleagues getting hired and promoted not on the basis of their ability or hard work nut because their manager prefers working with people who share his cultural background, this creates a profound dissonance in them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Because Singaporeans have been brought up to believe that meritocracy is a guiding principle in our society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We want a Singapore which rewards workers and professionals based on their competence and hard work, not connections or tribal loyalties.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, while we strive to shape the Singapore that we desire, we are but a small drop in a vast ocean.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We have to teach our children and students to deal with the world as it is, not how we wanted to be.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They must be taught at home and in schools to speak up when they have something to contribute, not stay silent in the background.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They must be encouraged to ask for what is due to them and not simply accept what others decide for them without question.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And they must be willing to network with a wide spectrum of people from different cultures and nationalities and understand what motivates them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore is often viewed as a nation of excellence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In local parlance, we do things "swee swee".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Give Singaporean a task and when they say they have done it, we can trust that it has been done well.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must never let this culture of excellence slip.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is our advantage in an increasingly competitive world.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: AI and robotics both have both burst into mainstream consciousness in recent years, with the launch of generative AI and self-driving cars.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These technologies could provide a path to boosting Singapore's productivity by enhancing the speed, accuracy and efficiency of various tasks and processes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There are many studies of AI's measurable impact on productivity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These are amazing opportunities for Singapore to take advantage of.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government can spur a broader uptake of AI and robotics, not only for our scientists and businesses, but also for general purpose use by ordinary citizens.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In February 2024, I proposed the creation of a national AI Healthcare Foundation Model which can be used to predict and intervene in a broad spectrum of diseases.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These are not just national initiatives but possible precursors to greater regional scientific cooperation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore needs the right institutions and opportunities in order to attract and retain the best minds, including talented Singaporean students, scientists and entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need interventions to steel our citizens against AI-driven job redundancy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is better for us to be the architects of our own disruption than to allow technology to change us for the worse.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is tempting to pull out the old playbook or pouring money into training programmes and encouraging workers to attend courses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, this approach may not succeed in upskilling an entire workforce in disrupted new technologies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must also embrace tacit learning, through the hands-on use of AI and robotics.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Using AI tools or robots needs to be made as easy and as commonplace as goggling for answers on a web browser or operating a television remote control.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Robots should be deployed more widely in our environment so that the public get used to seeing and using them every day.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Giving every Singaporean hands-on practice with AI and robotics will better ensure that the gains of these technologies go to everyone, manual workers and knowledge workers, civil servants and entrepreneurs, MNCs and SMEs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: AI tools make workers more productive and we should give our people more opportunities to use them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must strive for the whole breadth of Singapore society to have contact with the best AI models and robots.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Only by trying them out as a first mover and being willing to accept and learn from failure can we gain and retain the thousand points of knowledge that no instructor can teach.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In his Budget Statement, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong rightly pointed out that we are now in an era of armed conflict, confrontation and terrorism, with major powers prioritising national security over international cooperation and that there is a diminished willingness to tackle global issues.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must work within the realities of this new world order as the old order is probably not coming back anytime soon.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong said that we will pursue better jobs and better growth.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: He made a commitment to improve wages across professions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In particular, he said that the wages and career prospects of ITE graduates should not be too far behind polytechnic and university graduates.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I hope the wages of skilled tradespersons will come much closer to par with knowledge workers, because of the value they bring to our economy and our society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I will elaborate further on this during the Committee of Supply debate on MOM's budget.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong said it is to be used for selected training programmes with better employability outcomes, including part-time and full-time diplomas and undergraduate programmes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can I ask the Minister, how did the Government arrive at the conclusion that these diploma and degree programmes have better employability outcomes?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Is there empirical evidence to support this and if there is, are the better outcomes due to the greater skills that these graduates have acquired or because local employers continue to emphasise paper qualifications over skills and experience?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In fact, it has been recognised that one of the most effective ways to pick up employable skills is through on-the-job training (OJT) and apprenticeships.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As such, I would suggest that the Government subsidise OJT and apprenticeship programmes to the same tune as diploma and degree programmes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In his Budget Statement Deputy Prime Minister Wong mentioned briefly about how the Government will do more to support those whose jobs are made redundant, through a temporary financial support scheme for the unemployed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: He said the Government will be working out the details later this year.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How much longer will it take to flesh out?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: More importantly, how fiscally sustainable will the scheme be?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, Singapore should move towards equalising the fees for SPED schools and mainstream schools.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While I am aware that the cost of providing education at both types of schools is different, the school fees should be the same.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Then SPED school fees should also be $13 a month not $120, which is the current average.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even lowering it to $90, while commendable, is still not equitable.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is especially so considering the higher costs that parents of special needs children incur in many other areas besides education.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The additional costs of SPED schools, should be socialised in the interests of creating a more inclusive and equitable society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: School bus fares remain another significant concern for the disability community.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: But we know that SPED school students face a higher increase in their school bus fares, due to the smaller pool of bus operators who are able to meet their more complex needs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am aware and appreciate that there are various school bus subsidy assistance schemes, like the MOE Financial Assistance Scheme (FAS) and the Enabling Transport Subsidy (ETS).

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While I understand the need to keep the school bus operators sustainable, the adverse impact of the cost of living crisis has made the cost of school bus transport an added burden for many parents of students with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many rely heavily on school bus transport to commute to and from home, school and social service agencies to attend programmes, such as the Early Intervention Programme for Infants and Children (EIPIC), daycare centres, sheltered workshops and special student care centres.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, the students also need to be ferried from their school to the programme, creating a double whammy in transport costs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I would, therefore, like to call on the Government to increase the monthly household income limit for both the FAS and the ETS, especially for households with special needs members.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In addition, more subsidies can be provided to match the inflation of school bus fares.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This would ensure that more families can access and benefit from these subsidies to cover the ever-increasing cost of living.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By nurturing an ecosystem that champions fair competition, leverages the transformative power of AI and robotics and places the welfare and progress of every Singaporean at its heart – we can secure a robust and flourishing future.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Let us remain committed to building a society with access to opportunities, a culture of excellence and the value of each individual's contributions shape the Singaporean journey for generations to come.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Implicit, as I see it, are the key words – Building, Shared Future and Together.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In listening to Deputy Prime Minister Wong deliver the Budget on 16 February and subsequently reading his speech again, more than one time and reflecting, I feel very grateful that despite the uncertainties we will encounter, we are well-placed to face these together as one people.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2024 addresses immediate issues whilst continuing to structure our future social compact.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2024 continues to encourage and support necessary economic growth, albeit at a slower pace.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Our Budgets typically attract the interest of the financial and business community.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I do hope, though, that more Singaporeans will find time to read Budget 2024 in totality.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that even as the financial and business communities evaluate and debate the Budget from fiscal perspectives, that they will play a part in communicating the essence to a much broader constituency.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Possibly, one reason for the limited engagement in the Budget details by our broader population is a historical implicit trust in our Government.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: However in this age of misinformation, it becomes essential that every Singaporean increasingly appreciates facts and realities.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It needs to be seen beyond simple statements, such as Government handouts, if we are to be a part of contributing toward our shared future together.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Much has been spoken in our recent debate on our reserves and the prudent fiscal stewardship exercised by our Government over the past decades.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: But we need to understand that we started building our reserves with what we can assume was a smaller initial sum and, over the decades, have grown this significantly.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In terms of our own economy, we started our economy from a challenging base and today we have been able to attract significant international investments and also develop a strong local business sector.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2024 has acknowledged current challenges and has therefore provided support in a number of areas for both individuals as well as for businesses.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Growth in our local business sector will come organically and will also come from new initiatives.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We need to ensure our SMEs continue to thrive.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We need to encourage entrepreneurship to stay vibrant and relevant.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Innovative entrepreneurship can come from intentional support of budding social entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2024 provides for the welfare of those in our community who are more needy and vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Owing to structural shifts in our domestic economy and also in the global economy, some of our workers will find themselves involuntarily unemployed.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Support may be helpful in conveying – they are not facing this alone and that both Government and the community are ready to help.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I also hope and request that the approach we introduce will be wholistic.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I would also encourage individuals who are unfortunately affected to try to stay positive in planning their future.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Some may become involuntarily unemployed owing to physical or mental incapacitation.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: There are some existing avenues to help this group.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is likely some will fall in the gaps.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Our social sector must continue to retain talent and attract new talent to be ready to support both current and future needs.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: As we define success under our new social compact, I am hopeful that we will find many who will see this sector as a fulfilling vocation.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Our youths and seniors will need a variety of targeted support and interventions.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This Budget has outlined support for our seniors to improve their retirement adequacy amongst other areas of support.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In this area, employers need to step up and provide opportunities for seniors seeking to remain in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Many of our larger local companies are doing well.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It is troubling that drug use is increasing amongst our youth.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: While enforcement may seem to be natural response, have we been able to identify what are the systemic issues that we may need to address?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In a recent opportunity to hear from MHA, I am heartened that there is increased efforts to help early drug abusers rehabilitate and hope we can keep supporting this.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: There is also the issue of decline in mental wellness and the recent increase in suicide rates amongst youth.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Again, what are the possible systemic issues that we may need to address?

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, Mr Speaker, Sir, we have been beneficiaries of economic and material success.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We are also a nation that is one of the safest and, largely, most secure in this rather troubled world.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Many of us will describe this as being a nation that has been truly blessed.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The proposed plan to help those who desire to help others is a tangible step to building a cohesive and generous society.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It enables those in our community to play a part in contributing together toward our shared future.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Engaging the Community Foundation of Singapore, MSF and Community Chest is an excellent starting position.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: So is the objective, which is to uplift the lower income members within our community with collaborative programmes and initiatives.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I would note that, as a country, we have responded generously to appeals over the years without the tax deduction.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The Government is stepping forward to support acts of humanitarian assistance, which should see increase in our levels of response should such unfortunate events occur.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Last week, I had the opportunity to attend the City of Good Summit organised by the National Volunteer and Philanthropy Centre (NVPC).

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: One of the keynote speakers spoke on the issue of water and the continuing challenge of clean water in many less-developed parts of the world.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Many communities could live their entire life with little or no access to clean water.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Our Embassy in Myanmar has helped communities access clean water.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Clean water solutions have been initiated by Lien Aid in Cambodia, which I have had the opportunity to visit and to learn.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: I also had the opportunity to meet the Wateroam team in the Singapore International Foundation Young Social Entrepreneurs event, when they were in the early stages of startup.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Wateroam was founded in 2014 by three Singaporean undergraduates while at NUS.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: When Hyflux was still an operating business, I was able to promote their portable filtration system for use in rural communities.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: When we talk about water solution, we also need to acknowledge the early efforts of Dr Jack Sim – founder of his very own WTO.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: For the benefit of Members here, WTO in this case is World Toilet Organisation.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Dr Jack Sim has done a great deal in promoting clean water and proper sanitation.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Lien Aid is serving in four Asian countries.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: As access to clean water will require varied approaches across countries, much more will need to be done globally to resolve this problem and to help develop lasting solutions.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Solving the global water challenges will transform communities, address health issues, generate improved economic standards and improve access to education.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore can play a key part – bringing together existing and new providers and delivering a coordinated plan to solve this global challenge as a partnership of public, private and people sectors.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: There will be future challenges – some we may foresee while others may confront us suddenly, as with the recent COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: However, as Deputy Prime Minister Wong has mentioned, we have pulled through challenges over the past decades and often emerged stronger.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We are embarking on a new social compact that will shape future generations.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2024 continues to support our shared journey together.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: It is imperative that we stay united and build collective resilience.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is welcome news, in fact, based on the feedback of my residents.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With such supporting resources to tackle immediate challenges, our families should be in better positions to take advantage of the longer-term programmes to upgrade and upskill – so that they can continue to fulfil good jobs and earn higher incomes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There were some calls to dip into our reserves in the past so that more handouts and subsidies can be distributed.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The House had debated on this issue recently.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Our parents and even ourselves, will give the best food to our children.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even though it is food that we ourselves enjoy, we will tell our children that we are not hungry, or that we do not like this food, but this is not true.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All parents would want to give the best and save the best for their children and grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our young and future generations are our children and grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, we have the responsibility to give the best to them to take care of them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With regard to the full disclosure of our reserves, it is in our national interest that the Government needs to guard against the ill-intended that may try to scheme away from us.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Hokkien, there is a saying, "capable or not, you will know once you try." In fact, in the past, there were more than one attempt by those with malicious intentions to attack our currencies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These attempts have all failed in the end.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That was because we have strong reserves to deter attacks by the others. : Sir, as Prime Minister had said, our reserves is a precious resource which must be protected.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have to strike a delicate balance between meeting present needs and future emergencies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For now, let us work with this balance and find ways to increase productivity and augment our economic pie, so that we can finance the needs of our own generation and have some extra to contribute to the next generation, as our predecessors had done for us.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The war in Ukraine, Gaza and the resulting security threats in the Red Sea, disrupt supply chains.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The invisible cybersecurity networks have further extended the dimensions of threats from land and sea, and to the air.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The lessons from the Ukraine war have given a new perspective and definition of warfare.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It becomes clear that we are vulnerable to the use of the technology that we have used to our advantage.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, we need to continue to invest in R&D and support innovation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The family offices in Singapore should be encouraged to allocate resources to support the R&D and innovation initiatives in Singapore, including attracting top talents and scientists to Singapore to work with our researchers and scientists.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They may include projects to strengthen our food and energy security.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am supportive of looking into the latest and safer nuclear technology, such as small modular reactors for deployment offshore as the additional green energy solution for our energy needs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, just before I came in, I saw that one country has even successfully launched satellite from a platform in international waters.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will enable our working seniors to build up more CPF savings for their retirement.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is a perception that persons age above 50 face greater challenges finding employment.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For non-PMETs – at 2.7% – it is the lowest of all age bands.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, I would like to urge for more job search support and matching for older persons who wish to continue working, especially those who have been retrenched.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Of the employees retrenched in the last two years, does the Government have the details of their age groups, the duration of their job searches and how many remain unemployed presently?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the success rates of retrenched workers age 50 to 55, 55 to 60 and those age above 60 respectively, in finding employment within six months?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Government consider tie-ups with employers, including the Public Service, to place those who have completed the relevant training to meet the job requirements?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How about providing incentives to employers to offer jobs to seniors?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Government provide more details about how it is helping workers who are actively looking for jobs and what are the measures to detect and minimise age discrimination in hiring practices?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Subsidised rental housing under the PPHS and the one-year PPHS (Open Market) Voucher to support eligible families who rent a HDB flat in the open market are both excellent schemes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As moving house is one of the most stressful life events, it is no wonder that some couples choose to delay having children until they have moved into their own flats.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When I speak with many business leaders, the key concern always revolves around manpower.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Given our low birth rate, it is difficult to hire enough Singaporeans to support the growing economy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Additionally, many of the business leaders say that many manual jobs and roles outside air-conditioned environments are not favoured by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Companies tell us that they sometimes have no choice but to hire foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, the strict foreign worker quota and the continually rising minimum salary requirement for S Pass renewals are pain points for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is commendable that the Government is encouraging SMEs to invest in technology, particularly in the fields of AI and green initiatives.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Before I proceed, I would like to declare my interest as the CEO of Strides Premier, a company that leases out vehicles and provides services to vehicles, including the maintenance of specialised vehicles such as fire engines, ambulances and oil tankers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We would like Singaporeans to have more time to date, get married, to have children, to spend time with the families or care for their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: So, it is very essential for this retail sector to supplement its manpower with foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Similarly, in environments without air conditioning, Singaporeans are also reluctant to work.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In fact, many SMEs would like to appeal to MOM to increase the foreign worker quota for jobs that are not favoured by most Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In addition, many entrepreneurs among my constituents in Nanyang lament that they have to substantially increase the pay of skilled foreign workers when they renew their S Passes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Most Singaporeans would unlikely experience a 15%-pay rise in a year, even with a promotion.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Such a significant increment for foreign workers' pay not only increases the costs of SMEs but also creates discord among their Singaporean co-workers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thus, I hope MOM can consider a more moderate minimum salary adjustment for S Pass holders.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The Home Team Science and Technology Agency (HTX) is one good example, where the procurement needs of the Police, Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF), Prisons and Central Narcotics Bureau are centralised for better synergies and transparency.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Many civil servants are diligent in protecting the Government's interests when writing the tender specifications.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For example, some Government tender contracts specify that payments will only be made upon the full delivery of expensive items, tools, specialised vehicles or only big payment on completion of projects, and they do not give any down payment or make progress payments.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: While this practice protects Government from receiving substandard products or reduces the risk of incomplete projects, it makes things very difficult for the SMEs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is difficult for SMEs because with no down payment or progressive payment, it adds to the financing costs of SMEs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Given the current high-interest-rate environment, it will be challenging for SMEs to bid for such Government projects.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Project tenders that do not offer deposits or progressive payments typically favour the large companies with deep pockets, especially MNCs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: So, therefore, I urge the Government to review such practices to level the playing field for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thirdly, on land use: thanks to the Ministry of Transport, we now have more Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) lines.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Residents in the West, including those in Nanyang, are excited about the upcoming Jurong Region Line.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The Jurong Region Line is not an underground line; it will run on MRT viaducts similar to most of the lines in the North-South and East-West MRT lines.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The space below the MRT viaducts along the current MRT lines is not well utilised, unlike in other countries like Japan.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Currently, we do see some of the spaces below the viaducts used for cycling paths.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But these viaducts are near MRT stations and they are valuable land so we hope the Government can allow the space below the viaducts to be used by the private sector, especially for SMEs that provide important services such as childcare and eldercare services for the convenience of the residents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I have spoken on this topic several times before in this House.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Many residents, including those in Nanyang, are pleased with the 2024 Budget announcement of the additional $600 in CDC Vouchers for each Singaporean household.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I have previously mentioned that CDC Vouchers are a better way to help Singaporeans mitigate the impact of inflation on two aspects.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The heartland shops benefit from these CDC Vouchers a lot.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Unlike cash given under the GST Vouchers, CDC Vouchers cannot be spent abroad, especially across causeway.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In addition, CDC Vouchers also have multiplier effects, as reported in the press quite widely.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For households that do not need the CDC Vouchers, they can choose to donate the vouchers to those who need them more or simply refrain from spending, allowing the Government to redirect the resources to other more urgent needs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The CPI component could function similarly to the price index used by the Energy Market Authority to determine electricity tariffs and how the Public Transport Council uses the price index in the fare adjustment formula to determine the adjustment of public transport fares.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This price index is crucial, as inflation has been high over the last three years and is likely to remain elevated in the next couple of years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is a double whammy for low-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When nominal income increases, many Singaporeans no longer qualify for financial assistance, as the Government only adjusts the income criteria very infrequently.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the same time, these low-income Singaporean families require more financial assistance as their real income has decreased in a high inflation environment.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I understand that MOH and the MSF have promised to review the income criteria for blue CHAS card and financial assistance periodically.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: From experience in the past few years, "periodically" means once every few years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This is acceptable when the inflation rate was low in the pre-pandemic situations.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Last year, I rose to speak on three areas in my Budget Debate speech to urge strong efforts by the Government to: one, support working adults; two, care for our seniors; and three, support our young couples and families.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For this year’s Budget, I would like to continue focusing my speech on considerations and support for these three groups who made up most of the residents in my Jalan Kayu Constituency.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the Jalan Kayu constituency, the largest segment is aged between 20 and 60 years old.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are mostly working adults who may be embarking on their first job to sustaining employment as far as possible in their senior years, all with the hope of retiring with comfort and confidence.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I am concerned about the low take-up rate of individuals attempting to upskill or consider mid-career switches through the SkillsFuture Scheme so far.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand from some of my residents that despite the generous SkillsFuture Credit, time for attending approved courses is a major factor in them using up the credits.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, I would like to ask the Government how it can further support employers to enable their employees who are motivated to upgrade, to be given more training leaves and time-off to pursue upskilling courses and more so, to embark on another diploma programme as the new top-up to the scheme will enable.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Another consideration is the age of the Singaporean interested to utilise the top-up credit to stay employable.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Lee came to my Meet-the-People Session and shared that he held a diploma in mechanical engineering from Singapore Polytechnic and an advanced diploma in manufacturing technology many years ago.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: He had also taught modules and given lectures to ITE students previously.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Lee is healthy and hopes to continue working but he struggled in his job search due to his age.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I worked with Workforce Singapore (WSG) to make referrals and tried to assist him in the journey.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: His case highlights the need for a more inclusive, flexible approach to career continuation for our older workers besides upskilling.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For a case like Mr Lee, how likely would SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme help in his job search if he does invest time to take up another diploma?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is something in the mind of some of my residents in their 60s who are keen to continue to pursue life-long learning and to work well into their 60s and 70s, if they are in good health.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, let me move to another group of important Singaporeans, our young seniors in their 50s.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During my house visits and grassroots events, many of these young seniors have shared with me that they welcome the move by the Government to introduce the Majulah Package to better assure their retirement needs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A group of them are, however, full-time caregivers to their elderly parents who are in their 80s and 90s and who are frail.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They shared with me that the Majulah Package would have been helpful for them too, but family caregiving is not recognised as a formal employment.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Government be open to adjusting some of the criteria for the Majulah Package's Earn and Safe bonus, such as by establishing the family members' genuine needs for full-time caregiving, and the duration of caregiving provided, to include this group of young senior caregivers, who are also concerned about their own financial needs, so that they can also benefit from the package?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also welcome the move by the Government to raise the Enhanced Retirement Sum from three times the Basic Retirement Sum, to four times, to allow more members, aged 55 and above, who wish to put more of their accumulated CPF savings to receive higher CPF payouts on retirement.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nevertheless, I would like to raise a concern for some single seniors, aged 55 years old and above whom I have met at my Meet-the-People Sessions, who have yet to settle their housing needs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The latest Population Trend 2023 showed that the proportion of singles rose across all male and female groups aged 25 to 49 years, between 2012 and 2022.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This would inevitably mean that we would have more individuals who are approaching the age of 55 years old, who are still single.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During my Meet-the-People Sessions, I have come across cases where the single seniors, who are 55 years old and above, who have finally succeeded in balloting for their own HDB 2-room Flexi flat, and were looking forward to having a home of their own as they reach retirement, but they are unaware that the sums from their Ordinary and Special Accounts, that have been transferred into their Retirement Account when they reached 55 years old, could not be used when their house came, for payment beyond the loan they can get from HDB at that old age.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of them were disappointed that the extra sums transferred into their Retirement Account could not be reversed when they needed the amount to pay for these BTO flats.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even though they have tried to appeal to the CPF Board for the withdrawal of their Retirement Account for their flat purchases, the recourse for them is limited, as the CPF Board also needs to ensure that the Retirement Account amounts are maintained to support their retirement needs.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have encountered many residents coming to seek help at my Meet-the-People Sessions to secure HDB flats to start a family.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are usually young couples who have not been successful yet in their balloting for new flats – be it BTO or Sales of Balance flats – but hope to have a home to start a family soon or have a baby coming on the way.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, the request for assistance in balloting for new flats usually forms the majority of my Meet-the-People Session appeals to HDB for my young residents, especially during the BTO launch seasons.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As Budget 2024 looks towards supporting families at each stage of our lives, I hope that the Government can consider placing more importance on implementing comprehensive strategies, such as creating a social support ecosystem for mentoring young couples in financial planning, financial management, so as to reduce their financial anxieties associated with raising children in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: From working adults striving for career advancement, seniors navigating their golden years, to young families dreaming of a brighter future, our policies must continue to be inclusive, flexible and forward-looking as we prepare for the next decade.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us continue to work together to uphold the values of inclusivity, resilience and unity, ensuring that every citizen, regardless of age or life stage, can look forward to a thriving future, prepare for the challenges of today and the opportunities of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Both of them agreed that there is no place for populism in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is also recognition of the fact that in countries where populism has taken root, societies have become divided, people have become polarised and the trust between the people and the Government weakened.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The agreement, however, presumes that we know what populism is.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Most academics and commentators agree that the core feature of populism revolves around the division between the "people" on one hand and "the elite" on the other.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Cas Mudde stated, "It is a thin-centred ideology that considers society to be ultimately separated into two homogenous and antagonistic camps, "the pure people" versus "the corrupt elite"; populist politicians advocate that they represent the "whole people" whereas the elite represents "special interest", regardless of the truth of the matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The framing of issues is usually confrontational, antagonistic and emotive.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This sort of populism – once we see it for the grandstanding and posturing – is really not very hard to reject.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is mere opportunism played out in the political arena.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But there are two further elements to populism.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, it is not always easy to see through grandstanding rhetoric and recognise opportunism in its true face.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, populism is not always mere words – it also reaches into real policy action with a specific approach, which I call a "fool's gold" promise.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Populism in action lulls people with the promise of easy money, soft compromises, zero trade-offs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These two elements – words and deeds – make up what I call "strong populism".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And notwithstanding the forging of the agreement in Parliament, there remains no guarantee that this sort of populism will not take root in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is because, as in all modern democracies, we have a representative government, where a minority – that is the elected – represents our people, the majority, and has the mandate to govern.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The suspicion that this representation is imperfect will always be there.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have seen several examples where people's fears, especially during crises, are capitalised by populist politicians espousing radical change.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I will give two examples: one from the right and the other from the left.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is poised to feature in a coalition government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Should that happen, it would not be difficult to imagine the impact on the cohesion of the country across race and religion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As President, he launched programmes that offered free or highly subsidised goods.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the end, the country's economy shrunk and hyperinflation set in, despite it being an oil producer.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Again, let me identify the specific populist lever – which is to use price-distorting policies to give short-term, apparent benefits to people, at the cost of the country's long-term economic health.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Both these acts are forms of strong populism to me.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: From my research, I noted a number of writers, particularly Prof Simon Tormey, who have observed that in recent times, the world is facing a populist insurgency.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The fact that such political opportunists have taken in so many voters across so many countries, shows us that it is no easy matter to see populism for what it really is.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We, as a country, therefore, need to develop the capability to recognise and emphatically reject this insidious and seductive form of divisive politics.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If we do not do this, the consequences for us as a small nation will be serious.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
