text: Just last week, I learnt about a speech that our first Foreign Affairs Minister, the late Mr S Rajaratnam, made in the UN General Assembly in October 1971.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said to the effect that small nations need to keep their own houses in order, to be able to secure their places in the world.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In other words, small nations need to ensure that they retain social cohesion and political, as well as economic stability for the long term.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Unlike bigger countries, small nations like Singapore, when they fall victim to divisive politics that populism brings, they will be easy for the picking.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They would no longer be taken seriously by their bigger neighbours.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Once that happens, small nations would not have the ability to protect and promote their national interests in the international arena anymore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In other words, we will have a "double whammy", domestically and internationally.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Therefore, our commitment to reject populism in its strong form, must therefore carry a commitment to educate all Singaporeans to recognise it when we see it and call it out.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The rejection of strong populism commits us to a specific duty.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is a duty to make hard choices, to be accountable to the people of Singapore, by way of political and practical solutions to the social imperatives of our nation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The critical difference between this "hard choice" approach and a populist approach to policies is two-fold.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, this should be done without the histrionics that populism often attracts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I must say here that I am for even more scrutiny of policy proposals and performance from political leaders, from both sides of the aisle.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What I am against here the chest-beating, sabre-rattling politicisation of issues that get in the way of true analytical discourse.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Without the "noise", there will likely to be better engagement on the substance of the matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the end, there will be clarity on what parties are agreed and what they are not.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I feel that this distillation process is essential.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Otherwise, there is a danger of performative politics entrenching itself in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have reached a point in our country's development where solutions to most things are complex, and sometimes, finely balanced.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is characteristic for populist politicians to be short on details when advocating for a policy change.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We politicians, from both sides of the House, need to do the homework, understand the background facts, and also understand how the status quo was forged, highlight the trade-offs inherent in the policy proposals, separate facts from fiction and then, go on to make arguments as to why the balance should be struck one way or another.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Political leaders in office should eschew the tendency to just label policies as "populist", even though they may in fact receive broad support of citizens when what they really want to do is to make the policies sound unreasonable and irrational.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a point that Francis Fukuyama made – and I agree with him.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is incumbent on leaders to go beyond labelling, highlight the precise aspects of the proposed policies that they are concerned about.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is this process of responsible contestation and distillation of ideas and proposals which, in my respectful view, will serve as a bulwark against the emergence of populism in its strongest form in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Through this process, there will be better accountability to our people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our people, noting the areas where politicians are agreed and where they disagree, will be better placed to choose which future they wish to ascribe to through the ballot box.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In opening the debate, the hon NCMP Mr Leong Mun Wai highlighted what he referred to as "social ills" that must be addressed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These included cost of living, social inequality, mental health and declining total fertility rate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To this list, the hon Leader of the Opposition, in his speech during the debate on the Motion added healthcare costs and intergenerational equity.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I, for one, do not see these human conditions as diseases or "ills" but as imperatives for the Government of the day, as moral directions for us to apply our best minds and our utmost resources.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These social imperatives cannot be denied, but they cannot be solved by mere handwringing, or by profligate spending.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our duty is to be accountable in the way that I have outlined above, by a serious political commitment and spending our time, energy and resources in formulating and explaining our policies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Importantly, we need to be aware of the parameters of the hard choices at play and to reject the "fool's gold approach".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These points were articulated so well in my hon friend, Mr Shawn Huang's speech which I heard earlier today.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Putting aside the use of monies from the reserves for the moment, I think there are two points arising from what both the hon Members have said that will find agreement on both sides of the House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, that the social imperatives identified by both of them are legitimate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These imperatives require the attention of this House and the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, I would say, as a backbencher, much of what I do in my constituency for my constituents revolve around dealing, amongst others, with such issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, as responsible MPs, both sides of the House will reject spending for merely the sake of spending.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, to make the case to spend more money will involve taking at least the following steps.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, an examination of the existing programmes that the Government has for the imperative in question.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, a calculation of how much the Government is committing or spending on these programmes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Third, a performance assessment or review of the programmes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And finally, the articulation of the case for more spending on the imperative which will have to include dealing with the Government's points on "passive income" that the reserves currently provide and having sufficient ballast for the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At this point, I would like to deal with the hon Leader of Opposition's point raised in his speech earlier that the Government should be even more forthcoming with information to make better decisions on the Budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, at the last Sitting, the hon Prime Minister gave us a Master Class.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We also know that the variance of the operating revenue and the expenditures within a band of about plus or minus 4%.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Of course, there would be situations where the predictability may be affected by, say, market situations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, for property tax, it went up because the AV went up and that is a function of the market.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For that kind of situations, all we can do is we make best predictions and then make adjustments as we go along.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But these will be the inputs for which we would have available for the purposes of making sure that whatever we are articulating as policy proposals for more expenditure can be supported and fiscally prudent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Leader of the Opposition made reference to an article which appeared on 19 February in The Straits Times and he pointed out that some economists had also made the point about lack of information being forthcoming from the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One point to note, as he had stated, is that most economists lauded the Budget.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One economist had asked about the use of pre-funding Government programmes, for example, the Pioneer Generation package and he suggested that there should be more transparency in relation to this plan.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But the reality is, every year, the statement of accounts is presented to Parliament.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That statement of accounts is actually audited by the independent auditors.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All MPs can ask questions and it is also subject to scrutiny of the Estimates Committee.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And, of course, drawdowns are also subject to scrutiny of the Auditor-General.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Another economist felt that the amount of past reserves should be disclosed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For these reasons, I would say that there is no real obstacle for anyone of us in this House to articulate holistically why more money or more resources should be spent for a particular policy imperative.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I will now provide an illustration on the working of the framework that I suggested by dealing with the Cost-of-Living imperative.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In October 2022, the Government unveiled a support package to give Singapore households additional help to deal with rising prices.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is entirely open to hon Members who wish the Government to spend more to tackle cost of living issues to make the case that the 50% mark is insufficient for middle-income households and argue that it should be higher, say, 60%, 70% or even 100%.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They should articulate how such a move would be in the better interest of Singaporeans and Singapore as a whole.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What then this leads to is the crystallisation of a sum that is needed to fund the advocated policy proposal from the reserves or elsewhere with the accompanying reasons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The political office holder responding to hon the Member's proposal, if he disagrees with the proposal, will be well advised not to simply shrug it off by labelling it as populist.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Rather, he must tackle the proposal head-on and explain why the current spending levels are sufficient and should be maintained, having regard not just to the specific issue but the big picture as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Through this, we will gain a clear understanding of the points of agreement and disagreement as well as the reasons in support of the respective contentions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singaporeans will be better able to follow the debate and the implications of the policy proposals should they be implemented or rejected.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is, of course, open to hon Members across the aisle to make their plans part of their election campaigns even if they may be rejected by the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But they must have such plans in the first place.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If they do not, it is merely promising Singaporeans as a share of a piece of gold that disappears after election day.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I view this as healthy politics as both sides will then present their cases to our people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the end, it will be fellow Singaporeans who will judge and decide through the ballot box.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is how we prevent populism from rearing its head in our politics.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is how a high level of accountability to our people will be maintained.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: If that is the case, I will just end off by saying that the social imperatives are upon us.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We all know this and it is no great epiphany to point these out.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: If we are to really say that we have a serious Government and a serious Opposition, as exhorted by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, the focus must fall on the generation of solutions to such imperatives and a reasoned articulation of why these solutions create better outcomes for our people whilst being fiscally prudent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And by democratic acclaim, let us stand behind the ones which we believe, as elected Members, most benefit the people of Singapore for now and the future and by so doing, reject populism in its strongest form.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I have been trying to follow very carefully what he has been suggesting.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the broad strokes, typical of Mr Murali Pillai, you would not really disagree with them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But in terms of populism, I thought it would be important for me to just come down to some specifics.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: He mentioned some references in my speech to the 19 February Straits Times article.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the point that I made in my speech was that article showed how people outside of this House, Singaporeans, in the context of the Forward Singapore exercise, were also looking at fiscal sustainability, fiscal balance, how the Government raises revenue and its expenditure policies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And in that regard, the point I made was we had put forth a proposal to smoothen that conversation, to better that conversation for the benefit of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I understand he moved on later to talk about certain proposals that we have made for which the PAP has a conscientious objection.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think that is where I would like some clarification from him.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If there is a conscientious objection, then what happens to the populism argument?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Is it wrong for the Opposition to bring up those points?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second clarification I have is, again, bringing it down to an example.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In this debate so far, we have the PAP Members speak up about building BTO flats in advance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: What sort of numbers would the Member expect from anyone across the aisle or even in his own party, raising in Parliament, to substantiate that argument?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: For the moment, I will leave it at these two clarifications.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, that is the reference to our conscientious objection.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And it was in the context of referring to one of the economists featured in the article which the hon Leader of Opposition referred to.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: There, the economist said that we should know the full amount; then, we would know whether the spending is high or low.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As far as the issue of the purpose of referring to the article itself, I take the hon Leader of Opposition's point.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I understand that it is really with the view to provide further feedback on the Forward Singapore exercise and I welcome them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: What I think would happen through this articulation, using this framework, would be a laudable outcome, which is that the people of Singapore outside this House would know that it is something that is being proposed, there is seriousness in the proposal because the facts and figures are there and then you could juxtapose what is the Government's position on the matter against the hon Member's position.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just a quick response to Mr Murali Pillai on his clarifications.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In the case of the BTO example that was raised as part of this debate by a PAP Member, that example then would actually fail the test that Mr Murali Pillai has brought up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am assuming that in Mr Murali's schema, that analysis would also have to follow.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is an exhortation not specifically to the hon Leader of the Opposition, or rather, hon Members from across the aisle, but it is actually from both sides of the aisle.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And for anybody who wishes to make a proposal that involves extra spend, then you need to go through the analytical framework and I think then there will be clarity as to whether or not, ultimately, it is in the better interest of Singapore and Singaporeans to proceed with the extra spend.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, just to push the Member a little bit more.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I think I will just basically deal with it on a point of principle, and while he can take suggestions from my colleagues from the PAP, I can also refer to suggestions made by hon Members from his party.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I still remember an example of setting up the Parliamentary Budget Office and that was a proposal made in this House and there was really no understanding as to how much money that would entail in not just setting up the office but in terms of its operations as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, I would rather that the points I made not be obscured.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Let us stick on the principle and the focus is really to make sure that the ugly head of populism does not rear in our politics.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And, thankfully, that is a bipartisan point and I do hope that, on both sides, there will be an opportunity to reflect on the contributions I made in this House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: First, I would respectfully disagree first that, with his claim that just because all the necessary information was provided by Prime Minister Lee with regard to this back-of-the-envelope calculations, it would be therefore reasonable for us to take his calculations as self-evident.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But I believe that he introduced a number of assumptions about expected returns to reserves and GDP growth and, indeed, about the amount that would be returned to the reserves based on the way that the Government calculates the primary surplus vs the IMF recommendations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, my question is: if the Member accepts that these assumptions are not necessarily self-evident, is it reasonable, in a debate, for us to question these assumptions?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My second point builds on this and I ask if the Member would think that the Government would be comfortable with making the kind of public policies that they have proposed just based on the publicly available information that is currently available to the Opposition or whether the Government would actually require more information that is not made publicly available.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, from the perspective of anybody proposing to spend more, these facts would be important.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I do accept that my hon friend across the aisle may have a different view about the extent of the information that is needed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: But the point I am making, and I guess we can agree to disagree, and I said this advisedly, that this actually is a red herring.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, for these reasons, I think we are not disadvantaged.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As far as the second point is concerned, and I stand corrected, I think my hon friend mentioned about whether the Government would be comfortable—I am sorry that I kind of stopped there, if the hon Member could just clarify the purport of his question, I will try my best to answer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, my question is whether the Member thinks that the Government would be willing to be comparably hamstrung in terms of only making public policy on the basis of all the publicly available information or they feel that the Government can only make policy when there is additional proprietary information.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I think there is a false premise in the question.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is about the Government being hamstrung in relation to public information.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, I see this as based on a false premise and, therefore, I will not answer the question.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, the Member Murali has mentioned repeatedly that there is a red herring, that we have all the information that is required based on the fact that the share of NIRC is stable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Does he think that this stable share has nothing to do with the assumptions about expected returns or GDP growth?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, there is no — I mean, subject to the assumptions inbuilt in the framework, it is not just plucking a figure out of the air.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, it seeks to address immediate cost-of-living pressures.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2024 is also about building our shared future together.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: If these phrases sound familiar, it is not just because we have heard them many times today already, but because they are the same phrases used to describe Forward Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, Budget 2024 is the first step in bringing Forward Singapore, the vision of our nation's future, to life.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Forward Singapore mentions "inclusiveness" as a shared value that must be upheld.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The word "inclusive" or "inclusion" has likewise been used many times in this House.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: When a word has been used so often, it runs the risk of losing its meaning.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: When was the last time we paused to think what "inclusion" really means?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In this context, I would like to dedicate my speech today to talk about inclusion or social participation of persons with disabilities in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: At its core, social participation refers to the active engagement of individuals in all aspects of society.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Today, I will look to cover five areas, from education, transport, sports, housing, to employment.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: To prepare for this speech, I thought it would be best to hear directly from the voices of young persons with disabilities (PwDs).

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I wanted to know how they saw Singapore, through their unique lenses and lived experiences.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Underpinning this is a firm belief that understanding this well will guide us towards more inclusive and effective policies.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: To those who earnestly contributed, thank you for indulging in my unpolished attempt at gathering feedback and for your valuable insights.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I will be sharing some of your ideas and hopes today.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For PwDs, social participation is not only essential for their personal well-being but also for fostering a sense of belonging and inclusion within society.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Social participation encompasses the ability to interact meaningfully with others, access shared public spaces and services, and participate in enriching and fulfilling activities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: True integration enriches the social fabric for everyone, cultivating a culture of empathy, diversity and mutual respect.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It should not be surprising then that education should serve as the foundation for social inclusion.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Education, especially at a young age, equips PwDs with the knowledge, skills and opportunities they need to succeed in life.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Programmes, such as the TRANsition Support for InTegration (TRANSIT), is a great way to positively integrate students with behavioural difficulties into mainstream settings.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: To ensure a smooth transition from school and foster a truly inclusive society, it is also crucial to address the social challenges faced by PwDs with special education or SPED school backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Thirty-one percent of the autistics I surveyed said they rarely interacted with students without disabilities during school activities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Outside school, 35% said they rarely interacted with their non-disabled peers and 15% had no such interactions.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The two most common reasons given were previous experience of name-calling or bullying and concerns about acceptance.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In the face of this, we have to ask ourselves what can we do to minimise such seemingly common negative experiences.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: One possibility may lie in bridging the awareness gap.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: School settings are a great way for mainstream students to benefit from meaningful interactions with their peers with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It breaks down social barriers and will reduce awkwardness later in life.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: One suggestion that was shared with me, was to incorporate awareness lessons specifically about disabilities into the school curriculum.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We could also go one step further and impart such lessons organically during Physical Education (PE).

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: When I was in school, I was often – by default – entrusted with the role of safeguarding my classmates' mobile devices when they did their PE lessons.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It was always my honour to be given such great responsibility at a young age.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This role, though, kept me on the sidelines.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I vividly remember one exception, when I was first invited to play a game of poison ball in Primary school, by our favourite PE and form teacher.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It was a rare opportunity for me to bond with my classmates in lighter settings.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: To foster awareness and acceptance of others, play time is the best time.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: How can we do more of this, rather than relying on the spontaneity of a few good teachers?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Could MOE study ways in which we could institutionalise more inclusive PE programmes in mainstream schools?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Sports is often regarded as a powerful social leveller; this is a great opportunity to harness the same to weave inclusivity into the fabric of early education.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In the face of Singapore's restrictive car ownership policies, this is doubly important.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: PwDs do appreciate the accessibility features in our public transport network.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Some that were shared with me include: wheelchair zones in buses and trains, generally well-designed MRT stations and the MyTransport.SG app, which shows bus arrival timings.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: As a regular MRT user myself, I share these positive observations.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Compared to many other cities in the world, we are blessed to have an MRT system that is generally quite accessible for wheelchair users.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: However, there is more that can be done in this area.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Difficulties encountered when using public transport include: platform gaps in the MRT system, slippery floors on buses that cause wheelchair sliding even when the wheels are locked and unexpected closure of the only accessible route.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Other PwDs also face different types of problems while taking public transport.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: One PwD shared that no one offers a seat on the MRT even when a yellow card with details about their medical condition is prominently displayed.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Another also shared the same concern about the lack of acceptance of invisible disabilities – this individual has neuropathic pain due to surgery and sometimes needs to sit down to minimise pain.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that the Ministry of Transport (MOT) through LTA has been working on this area, introducing programmes, such as the priority cabin pilot and the invisible medical condition card. "Hardware" solutions like gap fillers, while not able to fully solve for the height difference between the platform and train floor, helps to narrow the train gaps and enhance safety.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Given awareness and acceptance of less obvious conditions still fall short, could MOT study ways to further elevate the visibility and understanding of the invisible medical condition card?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Earlier, I made a brief mention of sports in the educational setting.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In the broader context, sports and recreation plays a vital role in promoting physical and mental well-being among PwDs and promote social inclusion.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Competitions like the Special Olympics and the Paralympic Games, provide opportunities for PwDs to showcase their talents and abilities on a global stage.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: These events not only empower PwDs to pursue their passions and flourish, but also challenge stereotypes and limiting perceptions about disability.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Our national athletes fly the Singapore flag high at regional and world level competitions and are elite performers in their respective fields.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: But what about those who do sports recreationally?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Access to sports and recreational activities remains a challenge for many PwDs due to a lack of inclusive programming or facilities, their medical condition or a combination of these factors.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) has been making progress in ensuring that more sports facilities are accessible and inclusive.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: On top of this, SportSG is developing an inclusive ActiveSG gym orientation programme, to encourage gym usage by PwDs, which is a good initiative.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Interestingly, based on my findings, 67% of those with physical disabilities have not used any of their free ActiveSG credits.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This is 59% for autistics and 58% for those with sensory disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: During the weekend, I did my regular swim at an ActiveSG Sports Centre – a routine I have kept up for many years now.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: As always, I observed no other wheelchair user in sight.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This is despite facilities being outfitted with accessible ramps and toilets.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Apart from improving infrastructure, we must therefore make the effort to help more PwDs feel empowered and safe to exercise and play sports in shared spaces.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Boosting PwD sports participation is something that we should strive for and I will speak more about this during MCCY's Committee of Supply.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Moving on, housing is the cornerstone of the Singaporean dream.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, 48% of those with physical disabilities rated the likelihood of purchasing a house between one and three out of 10, with 10 being the likeliest.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Thirty-four percent of autistics I surveyed rated the same.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Much like everyone in Singapore, cost of housing is a common concern for these groups too.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We must do more to facilitate home ownership among PwDs.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: There are significant financial barriers to PwD home ownership, because of additional expenses they incur in their lifetimes and/or lack of stable employment.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: One suggestion raised to me is subsidised rental programmes for PwDs.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: As independent living may be a daunting prospect for some, why not lower the barriers to entry – let PwDs and their families have a tangible experience of what is possible in a financially accessible way, while they work towards home ownership?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Access to good housing fosters a sense of community and a sense of having a stake in our country.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We must explore innovative solutions that empower PwDs in this regard, tailored to their varying levels of independence.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I will also raise the topic of inclusive housing policies during Ministry of National Development's (MND's) COS debate.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Meaningful employment is vital to economic independence for any adult and adds to the feeling of having achieved.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: However, for PwDs, the path to meaningful employment is often clouded by challenges and barriers that hinder their potential and opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: One PwD shared that during job interviews, interviewers did not think that they would be able to work.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This was despite years of different job experiences.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Another shared about their very low income level.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Many PwDs also work part-time, often not by choice.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Some of the key barriers often encounter by PwDs in relation to employment is discrimination, lack of accommodations and limited access to training and career development opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It becomes crucial to understand the Government's strategy for ensuring that PwDs receive the reasonable accommodations they need to participate in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We must address how to prevent these accommodations from being left to the discretion of individual employers, which could lead to subjective biases.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: At the workplace, the welfare of PwDs is also not something to be overlooked.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Thirty-nine percent of those I surveyed said they were often or always experiencing feelings of loneliness at their workplace.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Some PwDs hoped for more support from their teammates at work.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For others, it is as simple as being invited for lunch.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We spend so much of our time at work.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: A little more attention and effort from each of us could go a long way to make a positive difference to those around us.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In Budget 2024, SkillsFuture has been presented as a key pillar of Singapore's social compact.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, it serves as a social leveller in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: To ensure it truly serves its purpose, we must ensure it is accessible to all groups of Singaporeans – including PwDs.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: According to feedback gathered from PwDs by the Disabled People's Association (DPA) Singapore, PwDs still face significant barriers in accessing the SkillsFuture system.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This ranges from course materials not in accessible formats or training providers unwilling to provide reasonable accommodations.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The Enabling Academy also curates courses specially for PwDs as an alternative.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Although well intentioned, these courses are significantly limited in scope compared to the extensive offerings available within the broader SkillsFuture system.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This not only restricts opportunities available to PwDs, inadvertently causing them to fall further behind, but also risks further segregating them from wider society.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In light of this, I strongly urge the Government to deepen its commitment to inclusivity in Budget 2024 and ensure that we make SkillsFuture accessible to all users.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Harnessed correctly, SkillsFuture has big potential to not only enhance career opportunities and professional enhancement for PwDs but also to cultivate greater societal integration and strengthen our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In preparing for this speech, I recalled the words of American writer, Max Ehrmann, "You are a child of the Universe, no less than the trees and the stars; you have a right to be here." Mr Speaker, inclusion is not just a matter of accessibility or accommodation; it is not merely about enabling one to hold on to a job, make a living.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It is about ensuring that every person, regardless of their abilities or disabilities, has the opportunity to fully engage in community, to enjoy life and pursue their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Society must give every Singaporean the courage to dream.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: By breaking down barriers, challenging stereotypes and fostering inclusive environments across various domains, we can create a society where all individuals – including PwDs – can be a part of a greater whole and contribute meaningfully.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Let us work together to build a more inclusive Singapore, where everyone has the opportunity to reach their full potential.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Let us make Forward Singapore a reality for all.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I appreciate the efforts by the Government for the financial policy of the Government to look after everyone.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: There are provisions to help individuals, help families, workers and businesses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many people view the Budget Statement as simply an announcement of the goodies which the Government dishes out for its citizens.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I really hope that we can change that mindset.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The financial policy of the Government must be not just to help our citizens tide over their current issues but also to provide a roadmap for Singapore's future.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If the Government does not plan for the future, then we are merely putting out fire every time a crisis happens.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It should not be seen as an "ang pow" or as gift to citizens, but it is meant to alleviate the increased expenses that every household is facing today.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: However, my concern is that such cash, CDC Vouchers and other rebates cannot be a long-term solution.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: After a while, citizens may keep asking for more and more cash handouts and rebates.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Eventually, we may possibly develop a crutch mentality for such handouts.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Hence, I wish to urge the Government to review the reasons for the increasing costs and to find ways to mitigate such increases.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Many businessmen that I speak to complain that the two main reasons for costs inflation is firstly, escalating land costs; and secondly, labour costs.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The businessmen lament that if the Chief Valuer continues to assess properties at a high price, then the rental of shops, offices and other industrial buildings may never come down.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: A case in point is when the Government rejected a bid for the Marina Gardens Crescent site because the bid was too low.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This means that if the Government maintains that the right price for land is a higher price based on the valuation set by the Government, then land costs will always remain high, and this will in turn cascade down to the ultimate user of the properties, who are the tenants.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For labour costs, I believe that many businessmen gripe about being unable to find workers for some of the less-desired work that Singaporeans shun.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This will help businesses survive and help keep the costs of labour more manageable.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Next, I will talk about preparing for the future.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I applaud the efforts of the Government to strengthen SkillsFuture.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The programme was launched in 2015 and each Singaporean received a credit of $500 into their account.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: A further top-up to the SkillsFuture Credit was made in 2020.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The SkillsFuture programme is an important principle that learning is for life; every Singaporean must do their part to continually upgrade themselves.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It has been many years since I attended formal lessons in classes.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: As expressed by the hon Member Dr Wan Rizal, I was very nervous about having to attend classes and eventually I was told that I had to pass a test before I could make a claim for the SkillsFuture Credit.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But these lessons has allowed me to build up confidence that with some effort and perseverance, we will be able to adapt to learn new skills.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, my intent is to try to pick up conversational Bahasa Melayu sometime this year or next.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And sometime later, I would like to take up a basic course in plumbing at ITE so that I can learn some life skills or take some courses to learn how to maximise the use of AI to improve my life.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They can also tap on various other Skills Development Fund grants to help pay for their courses.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Next, Sir, I would like to talk about supporting the retrenched workers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In March 2017, I had asked the Government to consider mandatory retrenchment benefits for workers who had lost their jobs due to retrenchment.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In my speech made seven years ago, I had said that for the worker who is retrenched without any compensation, it is a frustrating time for him as he struggles to provide for his family.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Thus, I am truly glad that the Government had in principle agreed that we can do more to support workers who are involuntarily unemployed because displaced workers are already straining to make ends meet.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I look forward to hearing more details of the scheme so that citizens who lose their jobs involuntarily can have some temporary relief while they re-skill themselves and find another job.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They have worked hard their entire life to contribute towards building up Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: And some of them have the fortune to invest their savings into buying a private property for their golden years where they hope to live the best part of their life.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Lim, you are a good role model of life-long learning – lawyer, future plumber and for those who do not know, he is also a black-belter in Taekwondo.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I look forward to adding more senior-friendly facilities and amenities in our housing estates.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, I hope that beyond adding hardware, we can also use the funds for heart-ware programmes There are two areas I would like to address.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: One, inter-generational preparation and safeguards towards degenerative ageing conditions like dementia, and two, programmes that will increase social sustainability amongst the elderly.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In my October 2022 Adjournment Motion, I shared three ideas on impending dementia emergency for inclusion in the Healthier SG framework.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Today, I would like to highlight how dementia and community mental health efforts can be part of a broader social-health integration.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In recent years, as more caregivers come forward to share their struggles caring for loved ones living with dementia, Singaporeans are increasingly aware of this condition.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Presently, almost every child is using digital devices.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This is largely due to the prevalent use of computers, mobile screens and digital computing.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Dementia as a societal reality will affect our population as a whole.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: MOH should consider commissioning similar studies to look into how we can prepare for the fight against dementia.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: At Sembawang West, we have initiated some programmes and these are some examples.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Back in October 2022 and at around the same time of my previous Adjournment speech on dementia, the Sembawang West team brought together a panel of community leaders, local caregivers and people living with dementia.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The purpose was to discuss the difficulties that the caregivers face and for the community leaders to understand the user experiences these individuals would prefer.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Since then, regular discussions facilitated by AWWA CREST and Dementia Singapore have been organised.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Together with AWWA CREST, Republic Polytechnic and People's Association and grassroots volunteers, the working group also convened a four-day hackathon for hyperlocal dementia ideas for the Woodlands region.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In addition, a Community Living Resource initiative for the Woodlands Region will be launched soon.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This will be organised by agencies such as Care Corner, Club Heal and Sembawang Town Council.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We are glad to see how the awareness and public campaigns of dementia-friendliness have spread across Singapore since the first dementia-friendly community was launched in 2012 at Yishun.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These DementiaFriendlySG efforts could only be possible with our "many hands on Deck" collective efforts across the various community partners in Singapore over this past decade.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We appreciate what you have done for us.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: On another note, I would like to highlight what many of us are very concerned about these days – mental wellness of caregivers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Many of my fellow MPs have been speaking about mental wellness.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: But in the context of dementia, many caregivers living with people with dementia are likely to be psychologically impacted.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We have to ensure that all caregivers and community volunteers are regularly monitored and that they are constantly supported by social workers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: My next point is about the integration of health and social services.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: More synergies can be unleashed if service boundaries across health and social services are integrated.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: MOH campaigns such as Healthier SG, National Mental Health and Wellbeing and Action Plan for Successful Aging are efforts towards achieving a healthier nation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our medical, health and social services are structured to serve different boundaries across Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Restructured hospitals are clustered intuitively to serve the East, North, Central, and West and South regions of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As a result, professionals from agencies such as the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) and MSF have to understand their service boundary in detail while also being well-informed of the service boundaries of other services.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Some services such as MSF's co-funded programmes like the Family Service Centres have bespoke boundaries based on the geography of where the majority of social needs to be focused.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Other services such as AIC-co-funded programmes like CREST and COMIT mimic grassroots and constituency boundaries so that they can have greater synergy with the grassroot leaders.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: MSF's Social Service Office (SSO) and AIC's Silver Generation Office (SGO) are located all over Singapore with the intention to develop the networks of ComLink and promoting active aging respectively.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These regional offices, despite being similar in nature, have different considerations in determining their service boundaries, like MSF's SSO using the Urban Redevelopment Authority's (URA's) planning area regions and the AIC's SGO using constituency boundaries.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This synergy would exponentially improve the community social-health integration and strengthen our overall national heart-ware resilience.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And even after all the announcements are made on the full extent of the Budget, when asked for their views, there are some who continue to focus on the immediate needs, such as how much more Community Development Council (CDC) Vouchers they will be receiving.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, more and more residents come up to me and share that they are getting increasingly worried about our future, if Singapore can continue to grow and prosper and if this trajectory and Budget is sustainable.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The phrase used by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong in his Budget speech was, "cautiously optimistic".

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong shared that there is considerable uncertainty in the outlook and the risks are tilted to the downside.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What struck me was the challenges that he shared ahead.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He mentioned how the international environment has darkened dramatically, something that was also picked up by the Leader of the Opposition yesterday.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And the Deputy Prime Minister also mentioned that the world will be more violent, as we see a growing zone of impunity involving armed conflict and terrorism that cannot be easily resolved by the global community.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When we look around us, the world seems to continue to be more fragmented as major powers are prioritising national security over economic interdependence.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong also mentioned that it would be messier and more unpredictable.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If we take a step back and observe the world around us, we can see many examples of conflicts or of communities wedged apart by differences, or of fragmented post-election struggles to form government and of parliaments in deadlock that they cannot pass important bills to help the country.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Very often, the fractures and the wounds driven by wedging differences often lie so deep that it will take generations to resolve and mend.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If we look at the world around us, Singapore sticks out like a sore thumb, for what we have is an anomaly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And this did not happen by chance and should not be taken for granted.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the past few years, how Singapore came together – not without our own fair share of challenges – has enabled us to sail through this storm.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the uncertainties and challenges ahead, how we continue to stay together with our refreshed social compact and our focus on keeping our society strong and united will be integral to define how well we can navigate the uncertainties ahead, turn challenges into opportunities and progress for Singapore and ensure that even with all the challenges, we continue to look out for one another and care for one another, in a vibrant, resilient and inclusive community.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And it is through that lens that I will respond to Budget 2024.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And lastly, how do we ensure that the progress is sustainable for our future generations?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must have a strong, vibrant and innovative economy which will then bring good jobs and hence, better lives for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That is the formula for economic progress in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A conversation that I had with a Senior Executive of a large MNE at the Singapore Airshow best sums it up.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond the buzz of the dynamic display, he mentioned, while overlooking the hall, "There is no place in the world where we have such a clear view of the ecosystem of support for any investment, such as that shown in Singapore." True enough, at the front of the hall, we have the Economic Development Board (EDB) hard at work attracting the investments.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We then have JTC Corporation championing sustainable industrial development.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We then come to the next question of how to develop the workforce capability?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We had Workforce Singapore (WSG) in the exhibition hall promoting the sector, encouraging the Career Conversion Programme to bring more mid-career professionals into the industry and skills upgrade, through SkillsFuture, to better prepare the workforce for the growth of the industry.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the side of the hall, we had AeroCampus, where schools were sharing courses on aerospace engineering to prepare our talent pipeline, and the students toured the AeroCampus, learning more about the industry from seasoned professionals.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There is no single ingredient of how we continue to attract quality investments into Singapore, but rather how our schemes, policies and agencies continue to collaboratively synergise.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Working together to create a vibrant and innovative economy is our competitive advantage to the world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While I support the intent, given the size and scale of the NPF, how do we ensure that the funds are effectively used by businesses to drive real productivity, add value to the industry and transform the industries?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given that the proposed top-ups to NPF is half of the budget of the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY), how do we measure success so that we can quantify the returns on this investment?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I will elaborate more on it in the Committee of Supply (COS) debates.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Something that I have also always talked about in this Chamber is the rising cost of doing business and the uncertain impact of the implementation of Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) 2.0.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is something that I have raised in the Goods and Services Tax (GST) amendment Bill in November 2022, Budget 2023, National Productivity Fund Bill in August 2023 and in this Budget debate again.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the GST amendment Bill, I have also challenged the perception from some of the Members that BEPS 2.0 alone will be sufficient to make up the "hole" left behind by not raising GST.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am glad that in yesterday's speech, I may have heard Mr Louis Chua agreeing with Deputy Prime Minister Wong's position, that there will be spending to offset impact of implementing BEPS 2.0 and there is still a lot of uncertainty on how businesses and countries will react.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Member goes on to say that he hopes that the introduction of Refundable Investment Credit does not go up against the spirit of the global BEPS 2.0 implementation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He also mentioned that he hopes that it is not returned back to MNEs in other forms.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I find that as an extremely worrying position.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chua mentioned that we should not go against the spirit of BEPS 2.0.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But I am worried if, philosophically, he is comfortable with limiting the capability of the tools that we have to attract investments?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To attract investments – our lifeblood for Singapore – here is where theory diverges from reality, where we are fighting tooth and nail for more investments into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Is this what Mr Louis Chua is advocating for?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I can assure those in the Chamber that attracting investments into Singapore will continuously be more challenging and we want to equip ourselves with the full disposal of tools to attract good investments into Singapore to create good jobs for our people.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am pleased to hear the continued commitment to upskill and reskill our workers through our SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme, provide enhancement support to our low-waged workers through the enhancements of the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS), SkillsFuture Mid-Career Training Allowance and the introduction of the Institute of Technical Education (ITE) Progression Award.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Enhancing the effectiveness of SkillsFuture to focus on capability building and real productivity improvement is something that I have often spoken about in Parliament too.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lastly, how do we ensure the Budget is sustainable for future generations?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are many challenges ahead of us and there will be pressures to spend more.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Budget addresses the key challenges and builds our capability as we look ahead and it does so with a balanced fiscal position, where we do not spend beyond our means.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am heartened to hear the reassurance from Deputy Prime Minister Wong on upholding the ethos of fiscal discipline and responsibility to ensure our fiscal position always remain balanced, sound and sustainable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These days, when younger commuters give their seats up to me on the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT), I no longer feel insulted but accept with grace.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, with better life expectancy and health, 60 is the new 40.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We still have much to contribute as citizens.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, I wish to focus my speech on older workers and how we should be tapped on as a resource for the good of the nation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Last week, veteran Hollywood director Martin Scorsese won the prestigious honorary Golden Bear at the 74th Berlinale for lifetime achievement.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For close to 60 years, Scorsese was at the helm of countless groundbreaking films, the latest being "Killers of the Flower Moon" released last year, starring Leonardo DiCaprio and Robert De Niro.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He announced that his next project would be a film on the life of Christ.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The late Ms Teresa Hsu Chih, who died at the ripe old age of 113, was dubbed Singapore's Mother Teresa.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The retired nurse founded charities caring for the aged, the sick and destitute, and was still actively involved in charity work after turning 110.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Over the years, I have met many older residents whose job search suggests age discrimination.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There was a male resident who had decades of experience in healthcare management.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He was well-groomed, communicated well and seemed fit.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Yet, he found it near impossible to land an interview, let alone secure a job – in the same industry, healthcare – in positions either equivalent or less demanding than he had previously held.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Younger seniors aged 40 and above are also not sparred.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Just last month, the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) released a radio documentary on ageism in the workplace and interviewed mid-career Singaporeans; they shared their difficulties on just getting employers to give them a chance to show what they were capable of.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Yet, the fact is that there are jobs waiting to be filled.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The ratio of job vacancies to job seekers was at 1.58, which was higher than pre-pandemic periods.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The sectors that saw significant vacancies included Health and Social Services, Information and Communications, Professional Services, and Financial and Insurance Services.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While there may still be some physically demanding sectors that may not be suitable for older workers, this space has decreased over time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is clear that jobs have evolved in the advent of technology and artificial intelligence (AI).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On this issue, Dr Helen Ko, Senior Lecturer at the Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS), wrote a commentary for CNA entitled: "Seniors do well at their jobs yet ageist myths and negative stereotypes persist." She opined that it was not the age of a worker that was the most important, but whether the demands of work exceeded the worker's capabilities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: She noted that in this modern era, health and technology improvements meant that there were few jobs that the average 70-year-old could not do.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The World Health Organization (WHO) has put out many studies on ageism in recent years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The WHO literature refutes many misconceptions about ageing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It has been noted that there is no typical older person, and that some 80-year-olds have levels of physical and mental capacity that compare favourably with 20-year-olds.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thus, age should not be used as a proxy for capability.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Also, as life spans increase, many older people experience longer health spans.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, each cohort of the older population is effectively younger and should not be discriminated against because of age.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Having older citizens engaged in the workforce has immense benefits for society as a whole.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If a significant proportion of older and middle-aged people are unemployed, especially those in the lowest income groups, they will become more dependent on informal family assistance, Central Provident Fund (CPF) savings and Government transfers or charity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This will increase social stratification and social division in our country.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These include various grants and the Senior Employment Credit (SEC), which offers wage offsets.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While these incentives are appropriate and necessary, I believe we can attain even higher labour force participation of older workers if we change any ageist mindsets.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I am looking forward to the anti-discrimination legislation to be unveiled later this year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The various stakeholders involved have rightly identified age discrimination as something to be tackled.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To make the legislation more effective, it should permeate the entire human resource process.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the UK, for instance, I understand that the Equality Act 2010 protects people of all ages regarding employment, recruitment, promotion, reward and recognition, redundancy and vocational training.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thus, for example, the UK legislation has made it illegal for recruiters interviewing potential hires to ask their age or date of birth.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If our upcoming legislation has this effect as well, it would potentially be a game changer.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, I would like to turn briefly to the related topic of how to ensure our older workers can retrain.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While there is a minimum age of 40 to access these measures, there is no maximum age.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even if so, I would say that there is utility in this, as it keeps the minds of seniors agile and keeps them healthy longer.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It could also allow them to become effective volunteers in our non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and charities, even if they are not earning a salary.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Many of them do not come from privileged backgrounds and they value the second chance, as it were.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For adult learners to succeed, having course fee subsidies and employer support is critical.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: CET is a worthy cause, as it is an important aspect of social mobility.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have focused on how older workers are a national resource that should be leveraged on, for the benefit of society.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We still have work to do to tackle age discrimination if we are to maximise our country's potential and well-being.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: All of us should be lifelong learners, or risk becoming obsolete.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As I said at the start of my speech, 60 is the new 40.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Let us embrace this reality with renewed confidence.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Lim, like you, I am also a "young senior".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And like you, I, too, enjoyed the movie "Killers of the Flower Moon".

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My suggestions and clarifications stem from business owners, newspaper reports and forum letters, which I have encountered since 16 February 2024.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I applaud the Government for being nimble and progressive in reassessing Singapore's existing suite of tax incentives, noting that other jurisdictions are also undergoing tax incentive reforms, ahead of the landmark move.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a tax credit with a refundable cash feature, it is an attractive and flexible scheme supporting a range of high-value economic activities, including manufacturing, green transition activities as well as research and development (R&D).

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The proposed Refundable Investment Credit seems to be based on qualifying expenditure.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government make the scheme available to businesses which are not as expenditure-heavy, such as the ones that are tech solutions related, but also can bring economically beneficial activities to Singapore?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Government consider awarding tax credits on output and volume-based features as well?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, may I appeal for the scope of qualifying activities under the Approved Foreign Loan incentive to be expanded beyond capital-intensive productive equipment investment?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Under the scheme, the withholding tax is exempted or is applied at the reduced rate on interest payments on loans taken.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also recommend that the withholding tax concession be extended to support companies in undertaking other economically productive activities in Singapore, including commodity trading, intellectual property (IP) rights acquisitions, mergers and acquisitions (M&A) activities as well as R&D.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government consider expanding the scope of qualifying IP rights under the Intellectual Property Development Incentive to include other intangible assets, such as plant variety rights, designs and utility models?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, would the Government further liberalise GST treatment for input tax claims on carbon credit trading-related expenses?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Enhanced tax deductions would be helpful for the businesses that purchase voluntary carbon credits to manage their emissions targets.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can all yields deriving from certain qualifying green investments made by Singaporean investors overseas be exempted from corporate tax here, similar to the foreign-sourced dividends?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To develop Singapore's workforce further, I also propose to increase the cap for tax relief on course fees for personal development.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Course Fees Relief has been capped at $5,500 since 2011, for individuals taking courses to upskill or gain academic, professional or vocational qualifications.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As costs increase, it may be time to increase the cap, to further encourage individuals to invest in their future by upskilling.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To better support the families amidst rising costs, I propose that the Government reviews the quantum for the Qualifying Child Relief when computing personal income taxes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: More targeted funding support can be provided to SMEs to invest in carbon-pricing and modelling solutions, as well as projects such as value-chain emissions management and decarbonisation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These measures can include a further deduction on the expenditure incurred or co-funding on such projects, subject to a cap.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Enhancing partnerships to include capability training, internationalisation and corporate venturing is highly beneficial for our SMEs in a world where advances in technology are progressing at an unprecedented rate in a turbulent global environment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Sustainability is an area where the SMEs can work with the MNCs who are usually the "queen bee" buyers, on opportunities to become more competitive.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Presently, environmental, social and governance reporting only applies to listed firms, but SMEs should take stock of their carbon emissions as legislation in some other countries require firms all along the supply chain to comply with sustainability standards.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Recently, many SMEs are constrained in what they can bid for, such as projects like the JTC proposed Coastal Development Tender, which award points to bidders that have the experience of completing projects overseas.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am cognisant that this criterion is not compulsory.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, few Singaporean companies have the experience of securing projects overseas, thus Singaporean companies feel disadvantaged to earn these additional points.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In order to earn these additional points, local companies are encouraged to form a joint venture (JV) with larger Korean or Chinese companies, so that the JV has a higher chance to win large infrastructural projects in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I was informed that there is limited transfer of knowledge as these large JV partners are only interested in the manpower resource, which include the foreign workers quota that their Singaporean JV partners possess.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, the transfer of knowledge is very limited.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many business owners had informed me that there is a shortage of heavy vehicle parking lots near their drivers’ residences and many business owners even pay for their workers' extra transport expenditure.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government convert vacant premises like schools or JTC sites into carpark lots, regardless of how short term it may be?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government could also review the current foreign worker quota to allow them to be pegged to job roles, instead of the current classification. : Would the Government consider providing more incentives to companies which practise inclusivity hiring of seniors, the disabled and those with special needs?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
