text: Presently, the Government provides an Enabling Employment Credit paid to employers of persons with disabilities (PwDs) aged 13 and above and earning below $4,000 a month and the Open Door Programme Job Redesign Grant by supporting up to 90% of the job redesign costs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I propose going further by giving tax rebates, higher quotas for hiring foreign workers and more points awarded when bidding for Government projects.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Companies have noted a shortage of local talent in some areas but, sometimes, part of the problem is that they have inherent biases and refuse to consider certain groups of potential employees, even if they have the matching skillsets.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These include young seniors or the group defined as being between the ages of 50 and 60.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A challenge for them is finding meaningful work that allows them to use the skills they have developed over the years.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many young seniors are medium-skilled for the most part, with some high-skilled workers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They have higher expectations for the jobs that they are doing and are less likely to be willing to take lower-skilled jobs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Like many of the older Singaporeans, they face challenges like age discrimination at the workplaces, questions about whether they can continue in their current roles, seniority, salaries and so on, until they reach the retirement age.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Along with encouraging this group to work for as long as possible and as long as they want to, it is also important to incentivise businesses to configure jobs in a way that actually makes it more acceptable for them to work longer.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As wages become more stagnant, would the Government consider extending progressive wages to more sectors and up the income ladder?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While social support schemes, such as ComCare and the recently enhanced ComLink+, have been introduced to boost lower-income households, these schemes tend to target the lowest income group in our population.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, many Singaporeans who fall below the 20th percentile of population by household income need more help, too.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: WIS has been enhanced over the years to better support this larger group of lower-income workers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, an individual worker is often responsible not just for themselves but for their dependants, too.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As WIS is still disbursed at the individual level, it does not fully account for the heavier financial burdens that some of these workers may face when raising young children, supporting elderly or caring for family members with special needs, especially with the cost of living rising.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The annual review of WIS can be administered similarly to the Public Transport Council's annual fare review exercise.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: An increase in the proportion of WIS payouts allocated to cash can also help households to meet their immediate needs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With current inflation outpacing the CPF Ordinary Account interest rate of 2.5%, it would be more practical for WIS recipients to have more cash in their hands.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: WIS should also be recalibrated to take into account household incomes and size.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The current WIS is pegged to an individual, using the worker's age, employment status and income to determine the disbursement amount.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But this supplement is provided even to a lower-wage worker in a wealthier household.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Instead, a household-based WIS would provide a higher monthly payout to lower-income households with more dependants.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will be a more holistic approach to take into account the overall financial situation of a household.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore has many social support schemes for lower-income families with different eligibility criteria.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Essential workers need the help most but they have the least time and capacity to navigate their eligibilities and to apply for the various schemes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They also face challenges learning about and taking advantage of the latest upskilling measures, including those introduced in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They may lack the awareness and knowledge about where and how to apply for training programmes and what kind of courses suit them.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, in view of the number of job and training scams in the market these days, we also need to help them navigate and avoid this pitfall.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Government consider a more systematic framework to reach out to and coach these workers on the safe path to training?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With this, I would like to conclude with my support for the Budget.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: With the advent of emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), coupled with a proliferation of social media yet to be fully understood and its impact realised, the world is moving incredibly fast and at a blistering pace.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: The pace of change in the world today and, indeed, in Singapore, is no longer just a function of linear years, months, weeks or days, but the pace of change globally has profoundly accelerated since the turn of the century.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Stasis today no longer means we will be left behind by a mere few steps but inevitably left behind exponentially further and further with the passage of time if gaps are left unaddressed.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: When we talk about social mobility, a few things come to mind.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: First, whether some of us care to admit it or not, each and every one of us here have benefited from some form of privilege.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Whether we may have been born into some form of wealth and socioeconomic privilege, whether we had the privilege of good health, a decent upbringing, stability in the household and loving parents, or the privilege of teachers, confidantes, mentors or friends who looked out for us, gave a word of advice or nurtured us to who we have become and where we are today.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: My humble view is that no story of any success bore out of the efforts of a single individual alone, but it had to be that alongside that valiant individual's effort, the village around him or her made it possible for success to first take root.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Second, we know not everyone has this privilege.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: We hear of children born into dysfunctional families, suffering abuse and afflicted by trauma.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: We know of families where breadwinners or other members are suddenly saddled with debilitating illness and disability and how that can catastrophically change the outlook of a family within an instant.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: We hear tales of families so big relative to the size of their physical house that the only true privacy one has from the shared space is only when he or she is in the washroom.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: We also hear of neighbourhoods of rental flats where children grow up in less than savoury environments, confronted with an early introduction into a life of antisociality, drugs and crime, and where Police presence is not uncommon.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Third, that the true distance between the two, having such privilege or otherwise, can actually be quite the fine line.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: It is a fallacy to think that our station in life is set at birth and that things cannot upend themselves.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Sides can change, illness can hit and jobs can be lost.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: In our fast-paced world, despite our best efforts, sometimes change can be unforgiving, dramatic and merciless.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: In this paradigm, an understanding of the importance and acceptance of social mobility is critical for our society.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: At the level of the individual, as much as we do not wish it for anyone, we cannot ignore this vulnerability and pretend like it cannot happen to any of us.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: We must accept with some humility that the success that has befallen us is not necessarily the result of hard work alone but that of our favourable social milieu, the people around us and, some would argue, chance to a significant extent.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: The reverse also holds true; that for many individuals and households assessed as low in their socioeconomic status through a measure of their income or financial ability, many find themselves stuck, not by virtue of a lack of hard work, effort or intellect.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Some have not yet been blessed with the privilege of opportunity and mentorship, they may be encumbered by ill health and disability, or just born into circumstances that snared them early into a cycle of poverty, scarcity and hardship.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: When we take a deep look at success through the lens of inequalities and social mobility, we then are able to view our own successes with some modesty and romanticise less about the gallantry of our own efforts, and we view the lack of success in others with much concern and interest into their well-being and life circumstances.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Many Members have, before me, spoken about social mobility in this House in the past.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: It allows for individuals to move up or down the social escalator of life, regardless of their initial background, ethnicity or economic status.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Some would describe it as a social ladder, but I contend that things are moving at such a pace that makes an escalator a more apt descriptor.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: In our dynamic and fast-paced world, trying to achieve social mobility remains a constant moving target and it has not been easy to keep pace and ensure full equitability in opportunities for all.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: For without social mobility, there is little hope, opportunity, growth and success for the underprivileged and most vulnerable amongst us.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: There will be entrenchment of privilege and, in fact, distrust and discrimination will only fester and proliferate, gnawing and tearing at the social cohesion we have taken so long to build and strengthen.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Everyone, regardless of their life circumstances, deserves a fair and equitable chance at success.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Today, Mr Speaker, we are perhaps more coordinated than we were decades ago in wanting to gain traction for social mobility.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: We have the hon Minister in-charge of Social Services Integration as well as the Rehabilitation and Social Mobility Policy Department, as part of the Policy and Planning Directorates of the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF).

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: We recognise that in wanting to empower and uplift the most vulnerable, it requires a whole-of-Government approach.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: We cannot afford to take on the issue of social mobility and its layered challenges piecemeal.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Problems relating to early access to education and health, employment opportunities and steps towards housing ownership must be addressed collectively.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: We know that ComLink+ attempts this today and the intent is to take a holistic and wrap-around approach to support families.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: I can see how some of the proposed changes in the Budget will help address social mobility to some extent.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: For example, enhancing the Assurance Package lends confidence to each Singaporean household that there is something for everyone and no one is left behind, especially at a time when there continues to be inflationary pressures and rising costs of living.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: When coupled with the Enterprise Support Package, even as businesses seek to transform and strengthen their workforce, the true yield and benefit also go to the Singaporean workers, for it gives them opportunity to upskill, develop and grow alongside that of the business enterprises they work for.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: That the Government continues to pay close attention to local enterprise, especially smaller firms, is heartening and we hope that this seeds confidence for our local businesses to grow further and for them to flourish even beyond our shores.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: I echo the Deputy Prime Minister’s call that we need to deepen this culture of lifelong learning and skills mastery to develop every Singaporean to their fullest potential and for each and every one of us to have the opportunity for productive and meaningful careers.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: The SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme actually makes me feel young again.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: What this programme does is that it gives a second wind of opportunity to learn a new skill, especially in a world where things have moved so quickly and technology has outstripped skillsets learnt from what feels like a lifetime ago.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: I wonder if it were possible to consider introducing this at a younger age, say, 35, and whether degree programmes could be permitted as well.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: While some individuals may be keen to spread some breadth to their knowledge base by taking a diploma unrelated to their existing expertise, others may be keen to dig deeper into their field of interest and pursue a degree instead.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: From time to time, I hear of young talented ITE graduates who do well in their courses but stop short of wanting to continue.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Sometimes, the draw of the gig economy or full-time employment in the short term, coupled with the pressing need to contribute to the family’s household income looks like a reasonable option to enter the workforce, rather than be confronted with another three years of education at a pace of learning that is faster than before.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: When they enter the polytechnic after finishing ITE, it will also be apparent that they are older than their peers who may have come directly from secondary schools.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: The adult in the room will recognise that in the longer term, a diploma would be of natural benefit, but consider also a young person from a family of less privilege, pressed with imminent caregiving responsibilities of his siblings and wider family at an early age and no direct sight of the longer-term implications of such a decision.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: My view is that through the ITE Progression Award, while relatively modest and encapsulated within the CPF construct, there are practical benefits that could nudge more to consider strongly to move on to diplomas if they qualify.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: This would go a long way in helping them move forward into the next phase of their lives and in giving their best to their current studies.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: This is harder to quantify and we can never emphasise this enough, for it is a delicate process and we need to get it just right.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: For those of us who have ever tried a hand at making bread, it is the yeast that makes bread rise.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: We can knead the bread with all our might and effort, add the ingredients like flour, water, salt and sugar, and yet it still does not rise in the bread pan.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Yeast is one of those delicate ingredients in bread that can be hard to quantify, and its introduction into the recipe is almost an art and takes careful judgement.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: It is not a mere insertion of quantifiable ingredients and an anticipation that things will rise automatically.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: The Budget is helpful, the funds are important and so is the structure to enable it.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: But we must remember that the exercise of social mobility is also just about maintaining dignity and autonomy.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: It is about knowing that society has your back and are rooting for everyone to succeed.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Our social policies can only come to life when, at the last mile, we deliver them with a genuine and determined desire to uplift, with a care and concern deserving of a fellow brethren with a shared Singapore identity and a genuine belief that the vulnerable, having been played a card of less privileged circumstances in life, deserve to succeed, too.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Because of her background, she genuinely had no access nor sight to see beyond what her lived reality could offer, and her aspirations and ambitions were much constrained and reduced from what she could have easily attained.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: The truth was neither she nor her family had the social capital to envision a future beyond the horizon of what they could reasonably see.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: There are gems in the rough arising from many of these families.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: They are borne from a life of adversity, hardship and challenges, and what some of their children need is really a fair and equitable opportunity.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: These children often grow up faster than most, their negotiation skills drawn from the uncertain and harsh environment they have grown up in, and they possess an adaptability and resilience that can be hard to replicate and teach in the classroom.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Especially when we see deep potential and exceptional qualities in an individual child, if we were to fully affirm our ethos of social mobility, we must be able to give him or her access to the full swathe of options and the full mile to realise their potential.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: And when we shed light on these options, it must be coupled with a genuine desire that they deserve to be successful, too.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Across all Ministries, whether it be in addressing inequalities of access to health, education, housing and social support, I believe, Mr Speaker, we have the structures and unitary components in place.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: In theory, the bread pan is ready and we have got all the ingredients for the bread in the mix.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: The yeast sometimes can be a little tricky and fickle to get going, and it takes patience for the bread to rise.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Similarly, in delivering a Budget towards realising social mobility, the constitute ingredients like funding, structure and processes matter, but they do not matter as much as how we approach the issue in a spirit that genuinely cares and is concerned for the most vulnerable in society.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: We have done well in our 58 years since Independence.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: We must recognise that in as much as Singapore starts from a strong position today, that we are doing well through our fervent efforts to improve and strengthen Singapore society, and that we are on a reasonable cadence for continued success, we must also have the humility to accept that we arrived here in 2024 with a little luck against the odds stacked against us in history, recognise the privilege of standing on the shoulders and wisdom of leaders before us, and that the starting point for Singapore today in 2024 has arisen from inherited structures and efforts of generations of Singaporeans prior.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: There are others who may not be as fortunate to be where we are today and we remain a country many others seek to emulate.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: We must guard this privilege well and be custodians of Singapore’s continued prosperity, but at the same time, we cannot also turn a blind eye to other calamities in this world, such as places of war, conflict, crises and disasters.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: This is an extension of our lived ethos and values as a Singaporean society that everyone deserves a chance at success, that not all lived realities are made equal and that privilege exists in many shapes and forms.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: It is not wrong to live a life of privilege, to compete fiercely and strategically for our survival, and to want to do well for ourselves, our families and our next generation.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: However, with the blessings of privilege, we must recognise that our environment, the people around us and chance had a significant role to play.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: Tempting as it may be to only give ourselves a pat on the back, we cannot discount the role that others have had to play in our success story, be it our accomplishments as individuals and as a nation.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member):
text: The humility keeps us grounded, informs us of a worldview of care and concern for others and further fortifies us as a society of ethical values, compassion and kindness.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, we are at the cusp of a transformation that ranks among the most profound of them all, the AI transformation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many have spoken on this, so I rise to speak on two specific aspects.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, how this transformation affects our social compact, and second, how Singapore has and should continue to approach the governance of AI.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To truly understand the societal implications of AI, we need to, first, understand what we are dealing with.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While there are many kinds of AI systems out there, most contemporaneous AI systems are based on machine learning (ML).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: ML systems are trained on data to produce insights and predictions, and they have become more prevalent in the early to mid-2010s.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the late-2010s, deep learning, a subset of ML, grew in prominence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This utilises neuronetworks, which comprise layers of nodes similar to a human brain that process inputs and produce outputs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These systems are also able to adjust their weights, thus increasing the model's accuracy over time.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Most recently, the technology that has taken the world by storm is, of course, generative AI (genAI).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: GenAI utilises deep learning, but the difference is that through new techniques and mechanisms, they can be trained on large sets of unstructured data.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The result is foundational models, that is, models capable of producing output for a wide range of tasks without having to be specifically trained for it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yet, notwithstanding the capabilities of AI today, we must remember that we are talking about artificial narrow intelligence (ANI), which is able to only do specific tasks well, rather than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which connotes AI that is able to perform a wide range of tasks that a human can normally do.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have spent some time delving into the technicalities because I believe it is important to bear this in mind when we talk about AI affecting our social compact.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I do not wish to rehash what had already been said.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead, I believe we must be careful on how we tread this line in encouraging AI innovation and adoption while continuing to support our people and their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One concern is how the AI age will affect jobs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Alarmist headlines emphasised the loss of jobs to AI, but actually, the key to making AI-enabled jobs rather than replace jobs is to allow people to find their passion with new responsibilities that require uniquely human abilities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With every industrial revolution, the economy changes and so do jobs where what is required of humans also change.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, that, in fact, is a net gain in jobs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But what we must ensure as a Government is that no one slips through the cracks, to ensure that every Singaporean, as we become an AI-enabled society, will have that opportunity to learn and grow, and none of us need fear being replaced.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must also consider that not everyone can make such transition at the same time and at the same pace.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But, through the right assurances and infrastructure, we must help every Singaporean realise their core and unique human skills and show them how these skillsets remain relevant and even while their job scopes encompass more decision-making and creative responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: ANI systems have limits beyond which human intervention is required.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, the more unprecedented and complex the situation, the better humans are at managing it, because we have a sense of judgement, empathy and values that no AI system can foreseeably replace.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With the help of AI, we can feed datasets into deep learning models to look upstream and understand the root causes of various societal issues.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Not only should we aim to figure out how to support those who are vulnerable in our society, especially those vulnerable to the coming changes, we should also try to ensure that they do not reach that point of vulnerability in the first place.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the contrary, we have been moving very thoughtfully and proactively in the realm of AI governance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The model framework provided organisations with practical guidance on how to deploy AI in a trustworthy and responsible manner, and as the first of its kind globally, positioned Singapore well in the global discourse on AI governance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 2020, the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA), PDPC and the Lee Kuan Yew's Centre for Innovative Cities at the Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD) launched a guide to job redesign in the age of AI.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The guide adopts an industry-agnostic and human-centric approach to show how existing job roles can be redesigned to harness the potential of AI so that AI augments, rather than replaces, jobs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The guide also provides real-life examples of how companies have empowered their employees through job redesign and training.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Further, just this month, Singapore led the release of the ASEAN guide on AI governance and ethics.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These, which are just the tip of the iceberg, showcase the thought leadership that Singapore wields regionally and, I might say, globally in the space.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Over 60 nations around the world have some form of regulation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore's approach has never been to take another country's approach and apply it wholesale.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead, we watch global developments closely and tailor them to our needs while introducing fit for Singapore measures.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But what we also need to watch out for is the risk of international fragmentation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is where countries adopt their own unique regulations of AI, resulting in a patchwork, often quite irrational, of global regulations and heavy compliance burdens for companies looking to provide AI products and services across borders.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is why international corporation to build regulatory into operability is important.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore points double down on these efforts while developing our governance approach in a risk-based and pragmatic way.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should also study how our international counterparts address the impact of AI on jobs, societies and the social compact, and act decisively so that we maximise the benefits of AI for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The GenAI technology behind ChatGPT showcased exactly the benefit and risk dichotomy AI technologies present to our societies and economies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With Singapore's pragmatic and forward-thinking approach, let us plant the seeds and shape the future of trustworthy AI today.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That was meant to have been the concluding remarks of my speech.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I would like to also make some comments on the hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim's speech, a couple of speeches before me.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As I understand, Ms Sylvia Lim's position is that we should not disenfranchise our senior workers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If one were to study the Budget speech delivered by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, there are a number of key initiatives.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, a whole raft of measures that are targeted to assist our seniors to not only age actively, but also to reskill, upskill and re-enter the workforce.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I enjoin the hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim to have a care and look at what we are doing, the $3.5 billion for Age Well SG.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Or a MediSave bonus of up to $300 for all adult Singaporeans born in 1974 to 2003.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We will increase quarterly payments from the Silver Support Scheme by 20% and raise qualifying household income thresholds to $2,300.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But specifically, if I have not misunderstood hon Member's speech, is the aspect of re-employment and jobs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I have learnt, over the years, in this Chamber, that statistics do not necessarily make the point as well as stories do.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, let me share with you that while we have all these measures in place and there is a lot of deliberation, a lot of the need to balance competing interests and pushing out new policies, funding them, ensuring the revenue is there for them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But at the end of the day, as MPs and Members of this House, at least, the elected ones, have a duty to ensure that these policies and measures meet their intended need on the ground.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a story of a resident, Mr Subramaniam, whom I have known for a number of years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some years ago, we met and he shared with me that he is looking to upskill himself and he wants to get a security guard licence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I said, "Mr Subramaniam, why would you like to get a security guard licence?" He said, "Because I will be able to upskill, earn more money for my family.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have a wife, and I have one son, Ramasamy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We live in our one-room one-hall flat in Ghim Moh", an area in the ward that I am responsible for.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I said, "Yes, we will do our best to get you a security licence." He did.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He went from Henry Park Primary School to Fairfield Methodist Primary School.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He did well enough to get into ITE.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He got a 4.0 out of 4.0 GPA in ITE.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He went on to Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) and he did one semester in Glasgow, and he is doing very, very well.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And along the way, when we meet, whether at market visits, home visits or when he comes in for Meet-the-People sessions and we have a chat, and the relationship is now a friendship.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I asked Mr Subramaniam, "What did you do with your upskilling and reskilling?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He said, "Mr de Souza, I got a job in Changi Airport." So, I said, "Changi Airport?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How long does it take for you to get to Changi Airport?" He said, "An hour, an hour and 20 minutes." And I said, "And an hour and 20 minutes back." So, he said, "Yes." I said, "Why?" He said, "Because at Changi Airport, the pay is better, and I want the best for of my son." So, when we talk about wanting to provide for our seniors, I agree that policies and statistics can be quite clinical and impersonal.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The bridge is us and it is for us to accomplish that vocation to the best of our ability.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I must say that I am really rather puzzled by Mr de Souza's response to my speech and perhaps, respectfully too, I may suggest that he has misheard me.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: First of all, you know, he says to have a care as elected Members of Parliament (MPs) for what the Government is going and, in my speech, actually, I strongly endorsed the continuing education and training (CET) initiatives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Having been a person that has been involved for more than a decade in managing and teaching CET courses, I see the value and I did say so in my speech.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I have also acknowledged the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme in detail.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I think he has misunderstood or has not heard what I have said and kind of accused me of not acknowledging Government's efforts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: While I am happy to hear that his resident has done so well, has he not come across any residents who are older who have faced age discrimination in the workplace?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I did not hear the hon Member talk about all the different measures that we have in place to support the seniors which I went through.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The Member may have alluded to the upskilling which I alluded to.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I think what is important is to not dichotomise, not say, "Look, this is water and oil and what we are going to do at the policy level doesn't actually trickle down to the low level." It does.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And the reason why I gave an example is to show that we are meant to be the bridges.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: If we see that there is ageism, as I have seen and as I have tried humbly, to the best of my ability, to bridge, then we should.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, I do not think I misread or misheard Ms Lim's speech.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I think it was largely based on ageism and my humble response to that is, if you look at all the fiscal measures, and the grind and the work of the MPs on the ground, I think we do have a chance of a winning formula for our seniors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I think the Hansard will speak for itself of what I have said, and I do not agree with what he has accused me of saying.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I think "accusation" is a very strong word.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I am summarising what I think her point is and her point is really that there is this stark, prickly, difficult and possibly unassailable issue of ageism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I agree that it is a difficult issue.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I agree that it is an issue on the ground.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I seek to re-orientate the House into how the Government is vested with this issue and has put in place all the initiatives to try to overcome it.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I assure Members that everything that is said here will be captured in Hansard.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We also face sharp shocks to the economy from time to time, most recently with the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Colleagues would remember the five Budgets that we had to approve in 2020.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Responsive monetary and fiscal policies can provide stabilisation through the cycles and shocks to ensure that we do not fall into a deep hole.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But in order to grow our economy for the long term and to grow sustainably, we need to embark on structural changes, structural policies which would transform our economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Only then can we create good opportunities for Singaporeans and generate the resources for uplifting our people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Such structural policies include what Ms Denise Phua said of the potentially game-changing investments to support and uplift workers, a theme which many of you have also spoken on.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, growth is important, but it is also getting harder to achieve because of both internal and external factors.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As a small and open economy, Singapore depends on our connections to the region and the world to grow and thrive.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: While globalisation over the past three decades has brought great benefits and progress, the mood has since shifted from collaboration to competition.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is, in part, driven by technological innovations, including automation and AI, which are reshaping jobs and competitiveness across industries and countries.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some major economies have turned more protectionist and insular and even adopted industrial policy to support strategic industries. "Friend shoring" and "de-risking" are quoted as strategies to strengthen resilience.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These have reconfigured economic linkages and global supply chains.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: From globalisation anchored in economic competitive advantage, we are now seeing fragmentations based on political alignment.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This, together with the recent upsurge in geopolitical unrest, has brought new uncertainties.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Internally, our domestic environment is also more challenging.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Singapore's economic structure is now closer to that of a mature economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The days of "catch up" growth are over and our resource constraints – labour, land and carbon – are becoming biting.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Economic growth is the sum of labour force growth and productivity growth.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But with our ageing demographics, the local labour force growth is shrinking quickly towards zero.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, we must therefore find ways to double down on productivity-driven growth.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many advanced economies have only managed to achieve average real value-added per worker growth of less than 1% per annum over the past decade.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And even as we invest in strengthening productivity, such as growing depth in certain industries, it is impossible to match the scale and size of larger economies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Put together, these sound pessimistic, but I am, in fact, upbeat about Singapore's prospects.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Overcoming challenges and finding new opportunities has been in our DNA since Independence.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Each time when the odds were against us, we rallied together to find new ways forward.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our sound monetary and fiscal policies have enabled us to stabilise our economy through various economic cycles.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They also provided the confidence for long-term planning by companies and households, and ensured sustainable economic growth.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: First, our economic transformation movement has achieved steady momentum.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To sustain this, there must be shared ownership and leadership in the coming years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Second, we are shaping and strengthening our innovation ecosystem to enable high value, cutting-edge work to be done in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Third, we must lean in to foster greater connection and collaboration and strengthen Singapore’s standing as a Global-Asia node for technology, innovation and enterprise.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: When the Future Economy Council was formed in 2017, a key piece of work it embarked on was the Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs).

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The ITMs were not merely about developing plans to be executed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The process of doing so was equally, if not more, important.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The process involved 23 industries each identifying trends, challenges and opportunities they faced, then developing strategies to enhance productivity; restructure jobs and reskill workers; strengthen innovation; and internationalise.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The ITMs represent a more mission-focused and industry-driven approach to tripartism, where our Government agencies collaborated with businesses and trade associations and chambers (TACs), while our unions worked with companies to support workers' reskilling and enterprise upgrading.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Through the ITM process, stakeholders across each industry built trust, identified synergies and shared resources and experiences.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In so doing, they supported one another towards the shared goal of ensuring that their industry, enterprises and workers remained relevant and competitive.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In 2021, the ITMs were refreshed to take into account post-COVID-19 realities, including the importance of resilience and sustainability.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This shared ownership of transformation is critical in today's world of accelerated changes and shifts, as it affords greater agility in our responses.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Government plans and programmes will remain important, but when enterprises and workers embrace transformation, they can be at the forefront of seizing opportunities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In some countries, transformation invokes anxiety and trepidation as it is associated with job loss or companies being forced out of business.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In contrast, our 2023 National Business Survey showed that almost all businesses polled recognise the importance of business transformation, up from 61% in 2017.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our workers are not only aware of the need to upskill and reskill, but have also taken action.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: While the efforts will take time to bear fruits, the indicators, so far, are positive.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Even amid structural shifts and sharp shocks from the COVID-19 pandemic, our economy has performed well and enabled us to grow the economic pie for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is stronger than that of advanced economies like South Korea, the US, the UK, Germany and Switzerland.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: With these productivity gains, businesses were also better able to cope with the inevitable cost increases.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Incomes rose as our economy and productivity grew.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will release a fuller report of the ITM efforts in a few months' time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have been able to sustain this transformation and achieve good outcomes because of our unique approach to tripartism.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This productive collaborative relationship between employers, workers and the Government enables us to shape transformation and growth to be fair and inclusive.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is a very precious asset to keep Singapore dynamic and harmonious.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In a world that is more fast-moving and complex, working in concert is even more important now so that we can harness one another's strengths to move forward faster and together.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Like any successful movement, it draws strength from the trust and confidence of each stakeholder to collaborate.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: One change which I observed, which we must build upon and expand, is how we have evolved our tripartism towards co-ownership and leadership.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For instance, we convened the Emerging Stronger Taskforce at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic to explore how Singapore could rebound stronger.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: A key idea of the task force is the Alliance for Action (AfA), which mobilised private and public sector leadership to tackle specific, high-impact issues.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For example, the Singapore Business Federation and leading business leaders proposed an AfA on business leadership development.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This AfA put together a concrete set of initiatives to grow our local timber and groom global-ready talent.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Another AfA, on supply chain digitalisation, led to the establishment of the Singapore Trade Data Exchange (SG TraDex), a common data infrastructure that enables the trusted sharing of data across the trade ecosystem.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This has grown more pertinent with the supply chain disruptions that we are now experiencing from geopolitical unrest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, I thank members of the Emerging Stronger Taskforce and Minister Desmond Lee and Mr Tan Chong Ming for co-leading the task force.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our TACs also helped their members navigate challenges and seize new opportunities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: During the COVID-19 period, our Chinese, Indian and Malay Chambers of Commerce and Industry encouraged and supported SMEs to digitalise, both to ride out the pandemic and to position themselves well once business resumed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) has been a significant leader in transformation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In line with its commitment that “Every Worker Matters”, NTUC has gone beyond the traditional notion of unions by partnering companies to transform and provide better prospects for their workers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Over the past five years, NTUC has worked with nearly 2,000 companies through the company training committees (CTC).

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Through ops-tech roadmapping or operations technology roadmaps and skills gaps analysis, these committees helped to uplift companies’ organisational capabilities and improve work prospects for their staff.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is highly commendable that NTUC is not fearing technology, not fearing how technology will displace the workers, but is actually taking concrete action to uplift workers with technology, and this will become even more important as technology advances and more of our workers grow older.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, I hope that this House will embrace this same spirit when Members are debating the importance of technology.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: One company which benefited from such a committee was Elitez Group, which provides human resource solutions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Partnering the Food, Drinks and Allied Workers Union, Elitez Group tapped on the CTC grant to implement two business transformation projects.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These enhanced productivity and freed up capacity for its staff to be trained in higher-value tasks.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As a result, 15 of their senior and professional workers were upskilled and received wage increments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: A small step, but a big lesson for everyone.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is also heartening to see larger companies serve as “SkillsFuture Queen Bees”, leaning forward to help other companies within their industries transform.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For example, our logistics industry comprises many SMEs and is highly fragmented.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: ST Logistics, as the appointed SkillsFuture Queen Bee, shared its expertise and provided guidance on workforce transformation to smaller companies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In doing this, we upgrade not just individual companies, but tap on the broader ecosystem to achieve synergies and grow together.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Most importantly, we should be proud that our workers are taking ownership of their lifelong learning journeys and career development.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This complements ongoing efforts to create pathways for continuous learning and upgrading through our Institutes of Higher Learning, often in the form of stackable micro-credentials, to build industry-relevant skills.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In fact, I would encourage colleagues to look at the websites of all our universities to see the range of programmes that they have.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And, as Mr Darryl David said yesterday, we must strengthen the linkages of our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs), businesses and unions further.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Taken together, Singapore’s approach to transformation is a proactive and collaborative one involving different stakeholders.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is unusual and enviable, as it enables us to build capacity and capabilities not just in certain pockets, but across the board.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is how we ensure that the opportunities and benefits arising from transformation can be shared by all, and Singapore grows in an inclusive manner.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I have spoken about how we are sustaining our transformation movement, through implementing the ITMs and strengthening collective ownership across different stakeholders.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I earlier mentioned how technology and innovation are reshaping competitiveness across industries and economies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is something that the ITMs take into account so that industries and companies can remain competitive and ahead of the curve.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza earlier had spoken at length on AI, in particular, generative AI, and so did Dr Tan Wu Meng earlier.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For Singapore, technologies, such as AI and automation, augment our human resources and if we learn how to use this well, AI can be our augmented intelligence, as the Member mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, we should think hard about how the future of jobs and skills will be transformed with automation and AI and, in turn, how we can restructure our work and reskill our workers proactively to take advantage of these changes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Singapore’s next bound of growth must be powered by an economy that is technology-intensive, innovation-driven and sustainability-focused and provide good jobs for our workers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: First, to capture new opportunities, we must be at the forefront of understanding, discovering and translating science and technology to advance existing key economic sectors while building capabilities for new economic drivers of the future; researchers in our universities and research institutes to generate the body of basic scientific insights; companies and startups to translate these insights or discoveries into innovations and solutions that can be applied to industry needs or market demands; and finally, the right training and support for workers to take on new jobs created by these opportunities, which I had spoken about earlier.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This value chain is what we call the research, innovation and enterprise (RIE) ecosystem.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The objective is to establish winning advantages in key economic sectors to strengthen Singapore’s position, uplift our local companies as well as create good jobs and opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To achieve this, the Government must work closely with our RIE stakeholders – researchers, IHLs, startups, local companies and multinational enterprises – to co-fund and grow the ecosystem.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Given our inherent small size, we need to develop our local researchers and nurture our enterprises and startups while also attracting leading global companies and top research and entrepreneurial talent to form a strong ecosystem.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many Members have earlier spoken about AI, and I would like to add that AI is one form of deep tech.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: There are many other forms of deep tech, and our biomedical sciences industry is a good illustration of this.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Biomed is a deep tech area where scientific expertise is critical but the impact may not be immediately apparent.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Over the past two decades, we had steadily built up the ecosystem of researchers, companies and a skilled workforce.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: When COVID-19 hit, these capabilities enabled us to contribute to the global fight, including the development of diagnostic tests.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This patient investment has also nurtured Singapore startups, like MiRXES and Lucence, whose groundbreaking solutions are making good progress in their next phase of development in large overseas markets like the US.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many MNEs have chosen to site their research and development (R&D) and innovation centres in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We also attract global startups, funders and founders to Singapore through a vibrant slate of events, from the Singapore Week of Innovation and Technology (SWITCH) to the Lee Kuan Yew Global Business Plan Competition.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our institutions and researchers have developed strong niches in areas like biomed, quantum and material sciences.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must now press on and continue to strengthen commercialisation and translational capabilities, to produce more “output” and capture value amid shortening innovation cycles and intensifying competition. mRNA technology, the basis of COVID-19 vaccines, is a very good example.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: While the scientific research had begun in the 1970s, it was only in the 2010s that drug companies saw the potential in nucleic acid therapies and invested in translating the science into therapeutics.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This was how they were able to develop effective vaccines within such a short time span.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: With such a long gestation period, it is important that we proactively shape and grow the ecosystem with other RIE stakeholders, including global companies, startups and funders.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Even as we continue to attract the right companies and stakeholders to grow our ecosystem, we can do more to deepen the innovation capacity of our students, researchers and enterprises.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We want to foster a generation of entrepreneurial youth and there are opportunities, such as the National University of Singapore (NUS) Overseas College and the Nanyang Technological University (NTU) Overseas Entrepreneurship Programme, to provide exposure to our students.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Patsnap, one of our homegrown unicorns, is a product of such efforts.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Co-founder Jeffrey Tiong first developed the idea of building a patent and technical intelligence search engine during his NUS Overseas College internship in Bio Valley in Philadelphia.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For our researchers, the opportunity to work with other global researchers is a valuable one.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Through our Campus for Research Excellence and Technological Enterprise (CREATE), we are convening groups of top researchers from partner universities and local institutions to address complex interdisciplinary challenges in fields like urban planning and climate change.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have more than 20 corporate laboratories, such as Applied Materials' partnership with the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR) and NUS, which is geared towards Advanced Packaging and Advanced Materials research for the semiconductor industry.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is especially heartening that Nanofilm, a nanotechnology unicorn spun off from NTU, recently set up a corporate lab there in NTU.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We hope to encourage more of such examples, to inspire our students to strengthen our ecosystem.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We also have the Industrial Postgraduate Programme where students do full-time postgraduate studies while undertaking an industrial R&D project at participating companies to help them gain industry-relevant R&D skills.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In the area of deep tech, where innovation output is potentially high impact, but the process is lengthy and high-risk, we are doing more to support venture building, complementing efforts by the private sector.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The objective is to support deep tech startups in overcoming technical, financial and market challenges while accelerating their growth.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: NUS' Graduate Research Innovation Programme and NTU's Innovation and Entrepreneurship initiatives are just two platforms to do this.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Both universities recently partnered Xora Innovation to pilot the launch of deep tech startups that are globally competitive and can address large global market opportunities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Amperesand plans to deliver their first systems worldwide by 2025.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are also supporting our enterprises, especially SMEs, to engage and participate in R&D, innovation and capability development activities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our SMEs need not worry about their lack of scale, as they can tap on the research expertise and resources of our polytechnics to support them in their innovation journeys.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: There are 12 Centres of Innovation, covering sectors like aquaculture, built environment and electronics.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Technology for Enterprise Capability Upgrading (T-UP) Programme supports pioneering SMEs in developing innovative products and processes by seconding public research scientists and engineers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Lion TCR, which develops new cancer immunotherapy products to treat life-threatening viral-related cancers in Asia, is one example.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: With the support of two scientists from the A*STAR Singapore Immunology Network, Dr Wai Lu-En and Dr Sarene Koh, Lion TCR's R&D efforts enabled its product offerings to be more cost-effective than current options and also improved its production efficiency.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This has fueled Lion TCR's business growth and contributed to the company's global expansion.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For innovative local enterprises, joining up with larger companies provides opportunities to capture a steady stream of business and upgrade their innovative capacities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We just had the Airshow and top global companies, like RTX and Rolls Royce, have chosen to anchor in Singapore to tap on our strong base of precision engineering companies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Avionics companies, like Thales, are also having a deep presence in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Under the enhanced Partnerships for Capability Transformation Scheme that was announced at Budget, SMEs can partner larger companies to scale up and go overseas.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And this is how we overcome our constraints of a small, domestic market.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is also a win for larger companies which can tap on the innovative capacities of the smaller companies to stay ahead of the competition.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The RIE ecosystem is wide-ranging with numerous players.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For it to work well and result in tangible outcomes for Singapore and Singaporeans, we must invest in the different domains while weaving them together intentionally to build strong and reinforcing connections.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our IHLs and research institutes must continue to invest in basic research and building up world-class capabilities, while also linking up with the industry to translate peaks of excellence into viable commercial products.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must continue to encourage our local enterprises to innovate and tap on larger local companies and MNEs to scale up and grow.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The goal is for them to be key regional or global players in their own right, providing solutions that the market seeks.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: By developing a stronger innovation ecosystem, we create a conducive environment for leading local and global companies to deepen their presence here and attract global funders and startups to be a part of our ecosystem.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And in so doing, we sustain a virtuous cycle of creating more opportunities for Singaporeans and for Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Given today's contested and uncertain world, Singapore must deepen our standing as a Global-Asia node for technology, innovation and enterprise to create new value for ourselves, the region and the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It plays out in the way we build transformative capacity across different sectors and stakeholders and shape a strong RIE ecosystem that brings together the strengths of domestic and external stakeholders.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These two elements reinforce our reputation as a trusted connector and node and our value add in a more volatile and uncertain world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our robust regulatory and legal frameworks are longstanding strengths that provide the confidence that Singapore is a trusted and reliable partner.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have also strengthened connections to innovation nodes around the world through our Global Innovation Alliance.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Thus, even as the rhetoric grows and cooperation slow, businesses and countries know that Singapore continues to be a constructive and neutral location for business, innovation and talent.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is how the Economic Development Board (EDB) has, over the past two years, managed to secure investment commitments, which are above its medium- to long-term goals.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Singapore continues to be among the largest sources of foreign investments into China and India, reflecting our value as a gateway for companies to explore opportunities there as well as in ASEAN.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must, therefore, lean in to foster greater connection and collaboration at all levels.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Domestically, it is about fostering co-ownership and leadership through the ITMs and our ongoing transformation efforts so that our industries, companies and workers are empowered and confident as they ride through new waves of change.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is about deepening linkages across our innovation ecosystem and connecting with other ecosystems and stakeholders, so that we can harness science and technology to find solutions to global challenges and unlock economic value.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And beyond that, it is about leveraging our trusted reputation and extensive networks to encourage like-minded partners to grow in Singapore, through Singapore and with Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: (In Mandarin):   Since the founding of our nation, Singapore's economy has developed rapidly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Besides the relentless efforts of our people, maintaining economic openness, promoting trade and attracting foreign investment have also been key to our success.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Contestation between major nations, wars and disruption to the global supply chain and other factors have cast a shadow over the economic outlook.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Will our economy continue to thrive, and will Singapore continue to prosper?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: My answer is: I am very certain that Singapore can achieve this.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To continue promoting economic growth, we must continuously increase productivity, facilitate economic transformation, strengthen the innovation ecosystem and enhance international connections and cooperation, leading Singapore forward through a multi-pronged approach.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In 2017, we established the Future Economic Council and formulated the ITMs, which has enabled our economy to maintain a steady momentum in the face of challenges in recent years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In a conducive environment for innovation and business, leading companies can expand their operations here, enabling us to attract more investors and startups to develop in our country, creating better jobs and opportunities for our people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Therefore, in the current trend of global instability and a slowdown in international cooperation, we should uphold our consistent approach and continue to strengthen international cooperation, allowing international partners to recognise that Singapore is a reliable partner and giving businesses the confidence to invest here.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Whenever we face difficulties, we will unite and seek new paths forward.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Therefore, even in the face of current challenges, I believe that Singapore's future is still bright.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Because I am confident that we can unite and move forward together to build a better Singapore for our people and our future generations. : Let me now conclude in English.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But I have laid out the strong basis for my optimism that a small and open economy like Singapore can continue to thrive and secure our next bound of growth.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And with tripartism fuelling our collective transformative capacity, Singapore and Singaporeans can remain well-placed to partner others and seize new opportunities with confidence.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is how we can continue to keep our economy innovative and vibrant, and build a better Singapore with opportunities for all.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could give results by helping them to boost their productivity at work, for example, summarising long documents or drafting professional emails and reports.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In the first place, there are already a range of courses and, as I have said, when we look at the industry transformation and the workers' needs, what is very important is to ensure that the training and the utilisation of the skills are done in tandem.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is very good that workers are taking ownership of this training to upgrade themselves, but the impact will be even greater if they work together with the companies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Which is why I mentioned in my example of how the NTUC is working with the company to do operations and technology (opstech) roadmapping, to do transformation and, in tandem, work on the redesign of jobs and the reskilling of workforce.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is in every domain of the technology that we want to make use of, that we want the society which is a lot more digitalised.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If you remember, even for our digital payment system, during the COVID-19 pandemic, we rolled out the CDC Voucher scheme, for which the Mayors came out with the idea.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Huge efforts were put in by our agencies to train our hawkers to install these devices and to learn how to use it.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Just last evening, I was talking to a group of my residents during the Meet-the-People session, about what they were doing and how they were learning to use this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, our approach, whether it is the use of AI, the use of mRNA technology the use of simple digitalisation tools, has been an inclusive one.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is, we look at what needs to be done and deploy the right tool for the right task, and not just AI.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
