text: So, understanding what the real needs are and what you can serve, what are the safeguards that we need to put in place to ensure its proper use and how to put this together in a way that advances not just R&D work, but also the reskilling of workers, has to be done in an integrated way, and not in bits and pieces.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I appreciate Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat's discussion of the importance of SkillsFuture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In principle, I do not disagree with the potential benefits of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: You can look at it as a glass half empty or glass half full.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Name me a country which has started such an extensive SkillsFuture framework.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I was the Education Minister for five years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our students have done so well and now, our older workers are working hard to learn new skills.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Name me a country where the NTUC is not only accepting change, but is embracing change and being a partner for change, in working on the Company Training Committee, in working with companies to do, not just training, but surprisingly, opstech roadmapping.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They were trained by researchers from A*STAR to look at how companies can adopt technology and, in the process of adopting technology, how jobs can be redesigned and reskilled, so that workers can take on better jobs, with this huge amount of SkillsFuture funding and the range of courses.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I think the Education Minister and the Minister for Manpower will speak more on this later.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, we will have to take a different approach for different groups of workers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For those who are able to take ownership and do the courses on their own, who want to change their jobs, there is a range of options available.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There are many companies that are taking action to redesign their workflow.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have been working very closely with the Singapore Business Federation (SBF) and that is why I mentioned earlier that the SBF has also set up an AfA on business leadership development.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have met the team who are doing this and, in fact, they are making very good progress.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, we have got to upskill everybody at all levels, including the CEOs of companies, to embrace change.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is very good, in my view, that we are able to achieve this progress over time.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And, in fact, instead of saying, "Oh, I am skeptical, I am pessimistic", if the Member has good suggestions on how we can do this better, play a constructive role, because with his professorship, he would know this well – play a constructive role, be a part of the team.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have so many members of the academia who are working with us and giving us excellent ideas.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, if the Member has great suggestions, I am open to considering.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: My point was that training has its limits and the adoption of the SkillsFuture credits is nowhere as much as what we would have hoped for.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: And so, the glass is not even half full, in that respect.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: To acquire skills, workers need hands-on practice, which is why we are calling for an expansion of the use of SkillsFuture credits to use it for, perhaps, subsidies for the use of AI tools, so that they can increase their productivity and get some hands-on experience.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Speaker, I remember Mr Gerald Giam's question is whether it can be expanded for other areas in a more appropriate way.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is certainly an area which the Ministry of Education (MOE) and MOM will be happy to consider if you have specific good suggestions about exactly how it can be used.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have tried to sketch out what different people are doing – from the company training committees of NTUC to what the IHLs are doing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I suggested to all Members earlier to take a look at the websites of our universities and polytechnics, and they can see the range of courses that people can undertake and, with the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme, there are even more courses that they can undertake.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For workers who need help, support and encouragement, we should all do our best to encourage them.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That is why WSG and SkillsFuture Singapore have been mounting lots of programmes to reach out to residents, not only in trying to get a job, but also, my residents are asking, what are the courses they can do?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I myself have participated in many of those outreach programmes and I must say that the response of many of our workers, including senior ones, is very encouraging.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: You are right that training is not everything.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: You need a collective effort, including by the managers and owners of businesses, to say, "I am going to take training seriously, but more importantly, not just training for its own sake, but how training can be translated into better job performance.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And therefore, we can have productivity growth and I can reward my workers better".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I absolutely agree that the SkillsFuture is a good programme in principle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And the challenge that I would put to the Government is how to ensure that it fulfils its original objectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: As for our participation in various suggestions for how we can improve it, I have made suggestions within the context of this House, but if we receive invitations from the various Ministries for us, or any of my Workers' Party (WP) colleagues to participate in these kinds of discussions, we would be more than happy to do so.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, you do not need an invitation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And by the way, let me make it clear that I have heard MPs on both aisles speaking about workers, and we have a very strong presence of our union MPs here and they will be speaking even more on this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, we all care about Singaporeans, and we want to do the best for them.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, you are welcome to give me your ideas, if you have very specific ones.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But let me say that I would have to consider it, together with all the other good ideas.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Denise Phua, did you raise your hand earlier?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We might actually be a victim of our own success.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Because of the big push for lifelong learning, I think, during that time and even now, there are many free courses that are implemented.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, I know that many IHLs – NUS, for example – have given a lot of free CET courses that do not require the use of SkillsFuture credits, in a sense.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: When the CDCs implemented the CDC Vouchers scheme, we had the whole pool of IMDA Digital Ambassadors who went all out to teach our merchants and our seniors, for example, how to use the digital vouchers.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It did not require the use of SkillsFuture credits.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At the same time, I think, because what NTUC does – the free trainings, the training plans and so on – those courses are sponsored and paid for by the companies.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But I just want to say that, let us not get too hung up on the adoption of the SkillsFuture Credit, because there are indeed, many courses that are free for now.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, peer learning is a very important aspect of that learning.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Because a lot of the infrastructure and a lot of the courses are already there.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is not a question of why do you not do more of this or more of that.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I think we can all focus on how we encourage everyone, young and old, to learn something and you can learn from anywhere.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It does not mean you must take a formal course.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These households have been most affected by the rising cost of living in Singapore and the issues they face are multi-faceted.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: When Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong delivered the Budget Statement earlier this month, I was heartened that there was significant attention given to this segment of our country's population.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In response, the Government has ramped up support packages for the lowest earners in this year's Budget, adding onto the measures that had been announced and implemented in 2023.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has also provided some details on the ComLink+ progress packages, where families with children from low-income households can receive financial top-ups when they work with family coaches assigned by the Ministry of Social Development and Family (MSF) on an action plan to meet certain goals.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These goals include having children enrolled in preschool education, gaining employment, improving their financial stability and saving for home ownership.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In my experience, most, if not all, parents want to send the children to preschool and share a common desire to see their children get a good education.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: What often prevents them from sending their children to school are other tangible factors, such as the lack of places in nearby centres, concerns over their ability to pay the fees even after subsidies and financial assistance, pick-up and drop-off timings because the parents are working shift, among others.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Top-ups to the Child Development Account (CDA) are useful throughout a child's education journey.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, they have far less of an impact on the immediate challenges a household may face in trying to keep their little ones in preschool.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I welcome the lowering of fees at childcare centres under the Partner Operator and Anchor Operator Schemes as well as the expansion of subsidies.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe this will go a longer way towards helping lower-income families send their children to preschool.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: On the matter of employment, low-income earners are among the most vulnerable segments of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Aside from their lower wages, job security is another concern for many low-income earners, particularly those in professions with no specialised skills.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Low-income earners worry about being replaced easily or retrenchment, which can have an upsized impact on their families' livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I look forward to receiving more details about the assistance that the Government is planning for the involuntary unemployed.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The WP has called for the introduction of redundancy insurance since 2006.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: By whatever name, a scheme that provides a net for Singaporean workers who find themselves suddenly out of job due to events out of their control is something that is needed in a time where job security is not assured.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe that despite this move, there will remain a sizable portion of our population that is wary, not because of the support level but because they are unsure of whether undergoing reskilling will improve their earnings and job security.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The other generations may also need more help in assessing their training funds under SkillsFuture as many of them are not IT-savvy.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: But for young Singaporeans from low-income households, the path to home ownership is more fraught with risks.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The two primary concerns are affordability and availability.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I note that support under the employment and saving packages are kept at $30,000.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: After including the grants, the price of a 3-room flat in the February 2024 launch of Build-To-Order (BTO) projects ranges between $127,000 and $172,000.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Assuming the household successfully applies for a housing loan, the downpayment involved could range between $25,400 and $34,400.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Families with children find it more difficult to save to buy their own house because there are more immediate needs to be met daily.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The wait for a BTO unit can range from around three years at the fastest, assuming there are no construction delays.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Even for Singaporeans from middle-income families, the long wait throws a spanner in the works when they are planning for marriage and children.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For lower-income families with children, the wait can have a bigger impact.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is a sad and unfortunate reality that the living environments in rental flats are often not conducive for young children.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: There are stresses and pressures that arise that have an impact on their longer-term development.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A more proactive approach may be required, for example, giving such households, which are ready to purchase their own home priority in the in the Sales of Balance Flats exercises or providing them assistance with purchasing a resale flat at subsidised prices.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: They are not eligible to apply for a flat under the Public Rental Scheme as that spouse is not a permanent resident (PR).

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: They also do not have enough income and/or savings to purchase their own flat.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The situation affects their relationship with their spouse.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe this is the sentiment all of us can get behind.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It includes enhanced Assurance Packages, rebates, SkillsFuture support and more CDC Vouchers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These measures show our commitment to Singaporeans that we have got their backs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Budget 2024 also recognises that these are short-term measures.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the medium to long term, we need to boost real incomes in the face of rising inflation, especially for the middle-class.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is the only way to improve our standard of living.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To do this, we must equip our workforce with the skills for new jobs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We also need to support our employers to find new markets and grow.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Workers should remain relevant and firms have to remain competitive.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Workers' real wage growth can only be sustained when employers grow.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have advocated in this House for measures that bolster businesses' competitiveness, enhance local enterprises' capabilities, such as carbon accounting to align with new procurement criteria, facilitate firms' growth through initiatives like Partnerships for Capability Transformation, and ensure retirement adequacy for seniors along with the creation of age-friendly facilities for them to lead active and purposeful lives.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am heartened by the additional support allocated in Budget 2024 for these crucial areas.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thirdly, I will explore alternatives to promote inclusivity and a sense of ownership among employees, enhancing their motivation and contribution to their companies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lastly, I will propose a focus on Enterprise Singapore accreditation programmes to incentivise companies to prioritise inclusivity and social equity, fostering a more inclusive and sustainable economic environment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Most of our workers are employed by our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, support for our SMEs is critical to uplift local workers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A key area of concern for our SMEs is cash flow.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Employers often tell me they struggle with hiring the needed talent to transform.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This challenge has also grown due to rising manpower costs and a tight labour market.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is a commendable initiative to support individuals in pursuing skills development and career advancement.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The eligible courses are selected courses that are oriented towards meeting industry and employment needs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is crucial to ensure that these programmes are aligned with the evolving needs of the job market and provide relevant skills for the future workforce.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Job Skills Integrator Programme, introduced in Budget 2023, identify the nexus between new skills workers need and corporate objectives.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Human resources (HR) play a vital role in guiding employees to maximise benefits for the company with clear objectives.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to examine how can HR act as an in-house career advisor.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With enhanced SkillsFuture funding, the challenge is to ensure that employees, while in their jobs, can identify and acquire new skillsets aligned with corporate objectives.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To do this, HR roles, particularly in our SMEs, will need to broaden.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: HR's spectrum ranges from administrative payroll tasks to the HR business partner (HRBP) role, which interfaces with the business to support its needs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, most SMEs may not have an HRBP role, leading to a lack of corporate alignment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For SMEs without an HRBP, chief human resource officer (CHRO)-as-a-service can be a solution to mimic the HRBP role and maximise SkillsFuture credits.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This service could provide significant value for the SME sector and help grow SMEs to be large local enterprises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another feature of the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme is the Financial Support for Full-Time, Long-Form Training.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is yet another major shift in our nation's support of life-long learning.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This addresses the basic cost of living needs of an adult learner.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, some employers have expressed concerns regarding the depletion of their workforce, as more employees take time off to pursue new diplomas.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Could full-time diploma programmes be adapted to allow workers to continue working part-time in a firm?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This arrangement benefits employers by mitigating manpower shortages while enabling workers to stay abreast of industry trends during their diploma pursuits.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, how does SkillsFuture Singapore's existing career transition place and train programme align with and support this new initiative?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This alignment between employees and employers maximises the translation benefits of the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thirdly, as we strive for innovation and technological advancements, we must promote greater inclusivity at the firm level.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given the increasing disruption in job scopes, there is a pressing need for improved job re-design capabilities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Alongside the support for acquiring new skills announced in Budget 2024, it is essential to develop measurement tools and benchmarks for employers and HR to equitably assess salary ranges for newly acquired skillsets.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This ensures that as employees upskill and both the individual and firm productivity improves, the gains are equitably shared between employers and employees.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, there is a growing body of evidence indicating that returns on labour are increasingly overshadowed by returns on assets, exacerbating the wealth gap in our society.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Concurrently, employers are contending with high staff turnover rates and seeking effective talent retention strategies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Often, there is frustration due to misalignment between employees and the firm.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, I suggest implementing measures that enable employers to share in asset appreciation upsides while strengthening the alignment between employees and the organisation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: ESOPs grant employees the option to purchase shares at a set price upon meeting performance goals, aiming to retain key staff long term.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Psychologically, ESOPs instill a sense of ownership, boosting motivation and performance.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This benefits both employees and employers, enhancing motivation, ownership and long-term success.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This change, effective from January 2023, helps employees manage the financial burden of taxation on stock options.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Bulgaria, amendments to the Commerce Act have led to the creation of the Bulgarian variable capital company, tailored to start-up technology companies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This new company type offers greater flexibility, for example, by reducing administrative requirements related to shareholding structures.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Ireland, some schemes allow for share allocation or options to employees, which include tax benefits after a certain period of shareholding.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, in the US, companies offering Phantom Stock Plans or Restricted Stock Units (RSUs) may benefit from tax deductions when the awards vest, providing they meet certain conditions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This encourages companies to implement such plans as part of their overall compensation strategy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This could involve introducing specific tax deductions or grants for companies adopting Phantom Stock Plans, RSUs or other innovative compensation models, thereby promoting a more flexible, diverse approach to employee ownership and participation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lastly, as we strive to create a more inclusive environment within the firms, it is also essential to consider how we can leverage investment and purchasing decisions to promote social equity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This brings us to the concept of impact investments and the importance of environmental, social and governance accreditation programmes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Encouraging investors to support employee-focused companies drives change.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The rise of impact investments creates opportunities to direct investments toward inclusive firms.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This presents an opportunity to connect capital with accredited enterprises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The landscape of capital flows has evolved to bolster impact-driven enterprises.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This evolution entails a blended approach that merges philanthropy with investments.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Blended capital encompasses grants, recoverable grants and equity, reflecting a convergence between philanthropy and impact investments.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With increased consumer awareness, especially among the younger demographics, individuals prefer supporting positive-impact enterprises for societal gains.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Environmental, social and governance-based accreditation can catalyse a shift towards virtuous purchasing and investing, fostering greater societal impact through these enterprises' endeavours.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To incentivise companies to prioritise inclusivity, I have called for the promotion of accreditation programmes, such as Company of Good by NVPC and B Corporation (BCorp).

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These accreditation programmes are important for investors and consumers to evaluate businesses that promote greater inclusivity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Acknowledging companies' commitment through such programmes deepens their impact.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A prominent local illustration of NVPC's Company of Good accredited entities is ABR Holdings, renowned for operating the popular Swensen's chain of restaurants.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: ABR Holdings collaborates with organisations, like Association for Persons with Special Needs (APSN), Asian Women's Welfare Association (AWWA) and Yellow Ribbon Singapore, to offer training and employment opportunities to individuals with special needs and ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: ABR Holdings not only serves delectable cuisine but also dishes out kindness to our community, exemplifying its commitment to social responsibility.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By amplifying the prominence of ESG accreditation schemes, fostering blended capital investments and promoting purchasing support for inclusive firms, we initiate a cycle of investment and social impact, ultimately advancing toward a more inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By addressing the needs of our lower-wage workers, enhancing workforce training, promoting inclusivity within firms and leveraging impact investing, we are charting a course towards an inclusive and sustainable future.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These initiatives underscores our dedication to ensuring that all Singaporeans share in our nation's success.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: A familiar face that a PwD and their caregivers can talk to, candidly on future-care planning, employment or, perhaps, even where they could pick up a recreational sport in the community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Along with that, 14 focal areas, such as "learning beyond schooling years", "inclusive employment" and "inclusive public spaces" were highlighted.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Consistent with the recommendations of the masterplan, I maintain that more can be done for this community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Since the launch of EMP2030, we have continued to push ahead with our agenda of disability-inclusion.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The ESH and EBH symbolise our ambition to do better as a society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: One where PwDs can partake freely in the community, just as any other abled-bodied person can and would without fear of stigma.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: It also paints our vision for a more inclusive workplace, one where more PwDs can sustain gainful employment, thrive and flourish.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: As we continue pushing in this direction, I hope that as a society, we can work together to empower our brothers and sisters of all abilities, enable them to realise their maximum potential and to lead meaningful lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: To do so, policies and programmes alone are not enough.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We also need persistence and participation – your participation, everyone's participation – to make disability-inclusion a hallmark of Singapore society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In many areas, such as inclusive employment and availing of independent living options, the Government can and will take the lead.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Yet, in other domains, such as the shifting of mindsets, everyday accommodations, community organisations, social service agencies, individuals like you and I, we all have a role to play.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Today, I dedicate my speech to the sharing of some everyday challenges that PwDs and their caregivers face, particularly those that exist at the intersections of service provision.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I recently spent good time talking with Dr Lim Hong Huay, a developmental and behavioural paediatrician.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Beyond her professional credentials, she is a mother and caregiver to two children with special needs and, to her, I owe a vote of thanks for the central ideas in my speech today.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: I will touch upon three key ideas, namely: one, the critical role of the caregiver; two, better information and awareness; and three, stronger professional collaboration.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: All of us, disability or otherwise, visit a doctor occasionally.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: How differently then does a PwD experience the healthcare system?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: A point Dr Lim made left a deep impression in me.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The difference, she said, "was in the medical professional's practice of "the art of medicine"".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: According to an article in the Canadian Medical Education Journal, the "art of medicine" is simply a clinician's way of being when interacting with patients and family members.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: How doctors, nurses and allied healthcare professionals diagnose, explore treatment options, communicate and promote healing, these are examples of "the art of medicine".

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This made a lot of sense to me.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: After all, we are first and foremost, human beings, not merely humans doing.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For patients with disabilities, particularly those who cannot effectively express their own thoughts and feelings, the practice of the "art of medicine" becomes even more cogent.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: How a patient with disabilities respond to prescribed medication, side effects they may experience and so on, is often told through the keen lens of the observer, and that is their caregivers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Therefore, how healthcare professionals interact with and co-opt caregivers in the process of promoting healing is instrumental.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Caregivers are also often best placed to advise healthcare professionals on potential triggers, for example, bright lights, colours or sudden loud sounds, that might spark adverse reactions in their charges.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Triggers differs from patient to patient and, therefore, including and intimately involving caregivers when working with patients with disabilities would, in many instances, aid the work of healthcare professionals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: To be sure, there are many well-meaning healthcare professionals who want to better serve patients with disabilities and their caregivers by planning out their service experience in advance.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: They can be supported to do so if they have more ready access to information, such as an individual’s disability status, and are more aware of their accommodation needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For instance, in healthcare, a longer stretch of consultation may be scheduled for patients who may face difficulty expressing themselves.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: All of these are plausible, and these tweaks can be quite easily made, so the service experiences that PwDs and their caregivers have with the healthcare system can overall be more positive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In their life course, PwDs and their caregivers interact with professionals and organisations from different sectors – doctors and nurses in the hospital or clinic, teachers and allied educators in the special education (SPED) schools and occupational or speech therapists in the social service agencies (SSAs).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Across different sectors, we need to grow a culture of tighter collaboration.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Cross-disciplinary sharing of professional practices would be a great start.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For example, risperidone is an anti-psychotic medication quite commonly prescribed to manage psychosis-induced agitation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We sometimes hear anecdotes of PwDs being taken off such medication prematurely, sometimes due to caregivers’ concerns or purely streetside hearsay about the potential side effects of such medication.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Having non-healthcare professionals who interface with the PwDs and their caregivers on a more frequent basis – for instance, their speech therapists – can help to allay unfounded concerns of family members and overall, this represents a net positive for the PwDs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In other instances, tools such as visual scheduling used by social service professionals to communicate a sense of routine and rhythm, particularly for autistic individuals, might unfortunately not be well understood and, hence, much less deployed as a communication strategy by healthcare practitioners when working with these individuals.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: My wish, therefore, is to see more sharing of professional practices across domains, so that there is not only better appreciation of each other’s work, but the opportunity to enlist one another in mutually reinforcing each other’s work is not lost.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: There are obvious benefits to be had if professionals in different sectors could understand and help reinforce key messages among PwDs and their caregivers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: When PwDs move across different service sectors in the course of their lives, there almost always exist, today, an inevitable resolution loss in terms of what each successive organisation knows about the PwDs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This goes back to the point I made last year about taking on a case management perspective for each PwDs and how we should support them and their caregivers more systematically throughout the course of their lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, the Enabling Masterplan 2030 has outlined our country's vision and plan to build a more inclusive society over the coming years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We hope that every individual in our nation will have the opportunity to reach their full potential.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In my speech today, I would like to propose three key points for consideration and discussion.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: First, in supporting the journey of PwDs, caregivers play a pivotal role.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Where feasible, we should allow caregivers to participate in professional processes, such as medical consultations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Third, professionals from different industries, when serving PwDs and their caregivers, can also collaborate more closely to provide a seamless service, focusing on the PwDs. : Mr Speaker, our journey in disability-inclusion has been built upon the hard work, sweat and tears of many professionals in the social service, healthcare, education and many other sectors, as well as the many PwDs and their caregivers who have worked tirelessly to get us to where we are today.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Standing on the shoulders of those who have come before us, it is now up to us to pick up the mantle, carry the torch and strive towards the day we work the word "inclusion" into obsolescence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I rise in support of the Budget Statement made by the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I resonate with that and share this belief.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome the approach to draw from fellow Singaporean’s collective experience, expertise and feedback during the Forward Singapore conversations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Budget takes those conversations forward and make them into concrete actions for our future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am particularly interested in the measures to help our households and providing more assurance for families and seniors.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My speech will be focused on housing options and enhancing liveability in the housing environment for families and seniors.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: During last year’s Budget debates, I raised several proposals to further refine the balloting process for BTOs for families and young couples.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am glad that the Government has not only adapted such recommendations but also ramped up the supply of BTO flats to meet the demand for housing.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: White waiting for their BTOs, I met many young couples in Keat Hong who are living with their parents.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They are newly married and waiting for their flats in exciting new BTO developments in Bukit Batok and Tengah.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Most importantly, while living with their parents, they get to save up and enjoy the support to take care of their children and access to many childcare centres and amenities in the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Keat Hong, where they grew up, is a place of warmth and familiarity.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This helps young couples who are waiting for their BTO flats to have temporary housing.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Previously, they need to join the waiting list for rental flats from HDB and the open market rental are out of reach for them financially.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: All of these policy changes show that the Government listens intently to the various feedback via numerous consultations or through the Meet-the-People sessions appeals that we MPs sent on behalf of residents, for me, every Monday in Keat Hong and, after careful studying, implements them into action.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Government lends a listening ear and extends a helping hand.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Malay, Sir. :   This Budget provides more support for families in terms of financial assistance and housing.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This comprehensive approach means that the Government not only helps specific groups but all levels of our society, from senior citizens to families to workers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One issue of concern is housing matters, especially for young couples with young children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Last year, I suggested a way to further fine-tune the application process for HDB BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I observed that the suggestion provided was not only considered but it was also employed to help young couples who have just got married.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To help them, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has also announced a new voucher scheme that helps young couples to rent a house from the open market during the period when they are still waiting for the completion of their BTO flats.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This voucher will help many from our community to get interim housing.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One of my Keat Hong residents, Mdm Nur, together with her husband and child, are living with her sister’s family while waiting for their BTO flat to be ready in four years’ time.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A total of eight persons are living in the 4-room flat.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Her elderly mother who has mobility issues is also living with them.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, she applied for a rental flat from HDB.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, the PPHS application opens once every two months and each application will take about four to six weeks to process.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the meantime, she is expecting another child and so, she would like to have some certainty and stability in her housing arrangement.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: During my Meet-the-People session, I appealed to HDB on her behalf, not just to get a rental flat, but also proposed alternatives like subsidies in the open market.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am glad that the proposal is now being considered by the HDB with the availability of rental flats vouchers in the open market.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will provide greater stability for themselves and their children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope more support can be provided to help our young couples and families alleviate their concerns for housing.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I look forward to the announcements from the Ministry of National Development in this regard.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The hon Mr Faisal Manap had earlier suggested that residents of public rental houses be given priority to buy houses.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But for me, this refers to just one aspect.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should not view the housing issue in silo.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is because there are many aspects of family life that should be considered and addressed.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, with the joint effort of partners such as M3@Towns and the Dian Project, which engages families living in rented homes, we can provide support in various aspects including health, children's education and family matters.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: All these help families to move from rental homes to their own flats and not only for them own their homes, but also to ensure that they have stable jobs, educated children, a healthy family and a happy marriage.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By having all of that, there will be stability in their lives, which is what we wish everyone to have.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is the way. : Mr Speaker, Sir, one other aspect of housing is having lift access.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chua Chu Kang Town is undergoing various exciting developments, like the Jurong Region Line and a new hawker centre to be constructed in the town central.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are many residents who have lived in Keat Hong for decades and so they wish to live out the rest of their lives here.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As I had stated earlier, there are also many young couples drawn by the exciting upcoming developments and have moved into the estate.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, there are several blocks that had been designed originally without direct lift access, though they come with added privacy and exclusivity for their home owners.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Nevertheless, as residents live in their blocks over the decades and age in place, direct lift access has become more important to them.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I had raised this issue numerous times in this House.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are segmented HDB blocks which have segments that do not have direct lift access, meaning that affected residents would have to take the lift to a floor, walk along a corridor or passageway, navigate and thereafter take the stairs up or down to their unit.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For residents who have been living in such units for decades, they now face difficulties and inconvenience as they age in place.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have spoken up previously on the LUP, the Lift Access Housing Grant and other solutions to support these families.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I wish for more support in this regard.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One resident, Mr Tan, is an elderly man with an adult son who had suffered from stroke.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He had been taking care of his son for decades.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They live in a segmented unit in Keat Hong with no direct lift access.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Previously, going to medical appointments would be a hassle, with him carrying the son down the flight of stairs to the next floor and navigating the corridors to the lift lobby.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Now, with the Town Council, we provide complimentary stair-climber services that Mr Tan can call on so that we can assist him and his son the flight of stairs using a stair-climber machine.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Food or package delivery personnel also find it difficult to deliver because of the block layouts and differing lift access navigation routes.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some furniture or bulk delivery services are not available as well to these segmented units without hefty charges.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In times of fire or medical emergency, our first responders also may find it difficult and there is a time lag to reach these segmented units in time.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: To help with the situation, we have introduced the Keat Hong WayFinder Maps at lift lobbies in segmented blocks.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This was held in our segmented block in Chua Chu Kang.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And during this detour, contestants had to find the right lift lobby, go up the correct flight of stairs to get to a segmented unit, where a contractor with a distinctive look in yellow boots will be waiting for them.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It was Phua Chu Kang in Chua Chu Kang!

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: After many frustrating attempts, contestants finally managed to find the unit.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My point is this: if the segmented blocks are so hard to navigate that they are deemed a worthy challenge in an international reality TV series, imagine the daily struggle for our residents, especially the elderly and those with young children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have to acknowledge the changing dynamics of our communities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With an ageing population and an increasing number of families residing in our flats, the need for adequate lift access is more critical than ever.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Lifts are not merely mechanical devices; they are the lifelines to connect us to our homes and communities.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With age, stairs can transform from a simple climb to an insurmountable obstacle.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Accessible lifts provide a sense of autonomy and dignity to our elderly community members.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The same scenario can be applied to our families with young children and strollers who will need to navigate up the multiple flights of stairs daily.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, may I propose the following?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Thirdly, where technical solutions are not possible, perhaps HDB can consider compulsory acquisition of such units and convert them to public rental housing, so that the occupants of such units will not be inconvenienced by the permanent absence of direct lift access because they are transient and will only be living for a short period of time.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, revisit the funding criteria model for LUP.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Instead of considering the directly affected units, HDB currently only takes into consideration the affected units which are directly affected by the lack of lift access.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should also consider the other benefiting units which will benefit from the additional lifts that can add as contingency or redundancy plans.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should not discount the generosity and empathy of fellow Singaporeans to shoulder the burden of such LUP costs together.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope we can study these proposals and help our family residents.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In making our common spaces more accessible, we create environments that promote social cohesion and well-being.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In helping our young couples to attain their dream homes, we not only fulfil their aspirations, but we also provide hope for their children.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In embracing the importance of the lived environment and housing, we foster a sense of unity and belonging among our fellow Singaporeans, making this country truly a home we love where we live.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong mentioned the need for Singapore to remain steadfast and united to weather the storms ahead. "Ships do not sink because of the water around them.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Ships sink because of the water that gets in them." We must be united in spite of the foreign disruptions, divisions or influences.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Budget is a stark reminder to all of us to remain so in facing future challenges together.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In the WP 2020 Manifesto "A Singapore For All", we outlined our vision for Singapore, which has a place for each and every one of us.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is a positive development that we have agreement across aisle for ideas, such as supporting involuntarily redundant workers financially through a difficult period as they look to find their feet again.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As a nation, we should be proud to see such good policies come to fruition because they work towards making sure that everyone benefits from our nation's progress.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To take the next step forward in Singapore's development, we should work on our expanded vision of progress and this vision can only truly and meaningfully be expanded if we have trust.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In other words, we need to trust others with different views from us that they, too, are acting in good faith, even though they may differ in perspective.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In particular, apart from asking people to trust our public institutions, we should ask ourselves if we trust our people.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How do we work to ensure that trust is a two-way street?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I will highlight some examples showing how trust is not yet a two-way street in Singapore, and try to explain why and how we should make it a two-way street.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The second half of my speech will speak of how we measured dividends we will reap if we achieve this mutual trust, and I will set out what this expanded vision of progress could look like.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, what does the public know and what should the public know?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While official secrets are a concern whenever we talk about the military, is there really no middle ground in offering detail on the expenditure?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How does one debate whether this spending is economic, efficient, effective or even enough?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, with the Enterprise Support Package and a myriad of other schemes announced in the Budget, would there be publicly available targets published as to how many firms are reached and how the money is being put to use?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How does the public know if schemes such as these, which is spent out of the public purse, are successful?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Do we measure policy success by how much is spent or is success a measure of its outcomes?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The WP called for the creation of an Independent Parliamentary Budget Office three years ago, but what is more fundamental is the willingness to publish details.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In 2012, then-Deputy Prime Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam said, "Trust and transparency are two different parts of a system of accountability".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While there are admittedly security concerns, which means full transparency is not always possible, the solutions that WP has brought up in the past, like the Independent Budget Office, disclosing more information to Standing Select Committee members with secrecy safeguards can help negotiate this often difficult balance.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Government needs the err on the side of transparency, publishing as much as possible, and it needs to agree to publish what is asked for, balanced against security interests.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Legal instruments, such as formal right-to-know legislation, will help define what can and cannot be published.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But the right to know is not accountability for accountability's sake.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It helps us to have debates in good faith.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If the Government sees that it has already been held accountable, then it debates with different views in good faith, which is the second point I would like to make.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With the Gini coefficient, for example, the Government has said that there is less inequality than other countries in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) before taxes and transfers, but does this feel like the case when we speak to our residents?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With over one in four Singaporeans marrying non-residents, some of these workers are also integral parts of our families here in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But perhaps, a more significant contributor to this feeling is that there is another way of looking at our wealth, namely, wealth inequality.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The OECD also states that we need to use a different measure to measure wealth inequality, and I believe that this can apply here, too.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, data on the distribution of household wealth is not easy to come by.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Government previously said in 2018 that its Gini coefficient calculation needs to reflect the full range of Government policy interventions that are unique to the Singapore context.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore does have unique policy interventions, given its small size and open economy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But this rationale, this focus on insisting that there is a right context, should not be justification to block the publication of data that people would like to see.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Trust is a two-way street and the lack of trust from the Government in not providing data to debate certain topics will breed the distrust in it in some quarters.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On tackling inequality, aside from what specialists with an economics background tell us, I can only express what my constituents say and feel.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If the public sees a gap in the information, then public agencies should, within reason, fill the gap with the correct information rather than say that there is no need to fill the gap.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My third point is that the Government should probably trust citizens to co-create.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But we can take reference from the concept of citizens' assemblies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Its findings on issues, like abortion, helped inform a referendum on the issue, with some praising the process for being depoliticised, bringing logic to a divisive issue and providing a space for listening, understanding and empathy to differing opinions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Further exercises, similar to Forward Singapore, can thus bring in more independent expert testimony to provide evidence to participants, and these experts can and should have conflicting views.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Exercises could then be designed to accurately reflect Singapore's demographics.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Just as importantly, the Government should take up the task of responding directly to the findings and explaining what recommendations it would sign into policy and which it would not.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There should be periodic independent public reviews of the extent to which goes out and such exercises have been met.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is only with building our trust in the public can we meaningfully move forward to build a shared future together, which means proper transparency and accountability.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To bolster this, we need to properly measure our progress and to measure things that matter to us.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For many years, both within this House and without, we have heard proposals of how important it is to measure how our country is doing beyond gross domestic product (GDP).

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, periodic reassurances during Budget, Election and national conversation times that we are looking at Singapore's other factors of development apart from GDP are not enough.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Measuring progress beyond GDP has to be part of our DNA.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is already not a new idea, and we can take a leaf out of New Zealand's living standards framework dashboard.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The New Zealand treasury publishes details about the measurement to use and for ministries on priorities for informing well-being, and it is fully disclosed to the public for transparency.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The indicators show trends over time, distribution across population subgroups and, importantly, give the Kiwis a direct chance to view how their government is doing in improving their country's well-being.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Earlier this month, during the Motion to debate mental health, I had spoken about our collective and individual well-being and what we can do to develop our strengths to protect against ill mental health and to promote flourishing.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I had also, in 2022, spoken about issues relating to our environmental footprint.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Thus, I will focus today on the areas of unpaid work and investing in our people.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, unpaid work, that is what which does not receive directly remuneration but which nevertheless has an impact on our economy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is usually broadly divided into informal care and domestic work, unpaid reproductive labour and voluntary work.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For informal care, in particular, the Forward Singapore reports states that the Government will give more assurance to Singaporeans that they will be taken care of.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is particularly important to probably understand the often unpaid and unsung work and needs of our carers who are already delivering on our nation's collective responsibility.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In 2020, I called for, among others, time-use surveys to be conducted to better understand the work being done by our informal carers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Since then, the National Council of Social Service (NCSS) has published a survey in 2022, which aimed to better understand issues surrounding quality of life for carers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This comes after the 2013 survey of informal caring in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While it is good that we are paying attention to the topic by having periodic in-depth surveys on specific issues relating to the provision of informal care, what these surveys do not contain is a regular and easily quantifiable measure of the contribution that is being made to our society and also indirectly to the economy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Various academic papers have pointed out that the lack of a measurement of the total value of informal care giving in Singapore makes it challenging to inform and guide public policy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What strikes me, though, is that many of these policies have an underlying assumption that informal carers want to and are able to stay in some form of paid work as much as possible.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Likewise, there is also little public information to measure the amount of unpaid domestic labour and voluntary work being undertaken in Singapore to formally acknowledge and incorporate the contributions that are being made to the nation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Measuring the value of involuntary work was a call made by a 21-year-old undergraduate in the forum pages recently, which I quote, "We should do so, in order to give a fuller picture of how our economy is performing." Having an annual figure of measuring unpaid work should also allow us to directly see if there are any effects that external shocks and events have.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, whether and how the amount of informal care is affected by an economic downturn, which segments of the population are more affected by it and to allow the public to measure on a regular basis – the impact that our policies are having to support unpaid work.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Moving to our people; our only natural resource.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is another way of measuring how we value and consequently invest in our citizens.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The New Zealand Living Standards Framework measures this as an integral part of the wealth of the nation in the form of human capability, defined as knowledge, physical and mental health and cultural capability.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It includes in educational indicators as well as measurements on not just life but healthy life expectancy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In line with an increasingly VUCA world – that is, more volatility, uncertainty, complexity and ambiguity – there is now rightfully more emphasis on lifelong learning and enhancements to the SkillsFuture movements are undoubtedly welcome for those who are considering pursuing midlife or mid-career training.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Increasingly, we are also hearing about how paper qualifications should and will become increasingly obsolete.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, I hope that policies to encourage ongoing training do not inadvertently perpetuate an emphasis on paper qualifications.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In short, we have to address structural barriers that may be preventing Singaporeans from making use of the schemes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, many workers have cited issues, such as the lack of time and the opportunity costs associated with attending classes, and have expressed reservations about forfeiting annual leave entitlements or the need to forego hourly wages to do so.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, there have been concerns raised about the inclusivity of SkillsFuture clauses raised by non-governmental organisations (NGOs), such as the Disabled People's Association, which ask that more can be done to get training providers to provide reasonable accommodations to enable PwDs to attend courses.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There are also reservations about having courses exclusively catered to PwDs, such as those through the Enabling Academy, which many in the community feel may be well meaning but ultimately, exclusionary.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This would include care skills and training programmes in the wake of the accelerating needs of our ageing population, and also training in the fields of mental health, such as psychology, psychotherapy and counselling, and towards building a sustainable and strong contingent of the newly announced family coaches, whom MSF will deploy to work with vulnerable households.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To conclude, I hope that more than half a century of nation building means that we have now arrived at a stage where a diversity of views has a place in our society and that respect for disagreement is a hallmark of trust that is a two-way street.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Greater transparency and more meaningful in-depth discussion may mean that we may take a more deliberative approach to public policy, which, in turn, should be seen as a means to improve.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is this approach to transparency and accountability, together with measuring our progress beyond GDP, that will ultimately help better inform our public policy debates and co-creation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One of the highlights of this Budget is the strong support for the upskilling and reskilling of our ITE graduates and middle-age and older Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Reinforcing a continuous learning mindset and identifying improvement opportunities among Singaporeans will enable the population and Singapore to remain relevant in the evolving global economic landscape.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The education top-ups, subsidies and monthly training allowances are unprecedented in scope and scale.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a huge investment in our people.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One of the common feedback from some graduates of "train-and-place" programmes is that they have difficulties in finding jobs on their own.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As this is intended to be a long-term policy, at substantial recurring cost to our country, the Government should measure if the investment is yielding satisfactory results.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If not, reviews, adjustments and changes will have to be made along the way.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, I would like to speak on support for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The underlying cost structure of our SMEs has changed significantly over the years.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I appreciate the near-term relief measures in the Budget to help them cope with the rising costs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some SMEs find it increasingly challenging to participate in Government projects as project scales increase, translating into higher capital and cashflow outlay and tender specifications.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government can be more thoughtful in running the tender process to be more inclusive.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We all know it is not easy for our SMEs to do R&D and incorporate AI development into their enterprises on their own, due to their smaller sizes and resource constraints.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They need Government support for funding and collaboration with researchers and universities, as well as partner companies upstream and downstream.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Otherwise, the digital divide between SMEs and MNCs will become wider.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore is a small economy, and our economy is expected to grow at a slower pace going forward.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It has become more urgent and important for our SMEs to source for more business and revenue overseas.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To develop their businesses beyond our shores, SMEs need to understand and adapt to the dynamics of foreign jurisdictions, with all their different jurisdictions and ways of doing business.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, there are opportunities to tap on the experience and skillsets of older professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) to assist SMEs in these aspects.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For senior PMETs who seek changes in their careers or who are not employed, will the Government consider designing a systematic, structured framework to match them with SMEs which require their experience, knowledge and skills in the relevant markets and sectors?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
