text: SMEs can leverage on their know-how, prior exposure to and familiarity with foreign markets to better navigate through the complexities and avoid potential pitfalls.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, I would like to speak on a topic which I have been following up on over the last few years, "Buy Singapore".

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is because it is a key pillar of our national food security, an issue which had been brought to the fore during the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must be prepared for other crises in the future and the more local food production services we have, the less vulnerable we are to supply disruptions.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must continue to support and boost this sector, and ensuring its viability, alongside others, such as manufacturing and financial services.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To strengthen food security, besides sector-friendly Government policies and financial support, we need to develop a whole ecosystem to make the agrifood sector a significant economic sector.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given a higher cost structure and lack of economy of scale, the strength of the Singapore dollar, our local produce is more expensive than imported produce.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To differentiate our local produce and justify their premium, we need to increase consumer awareness about the advantages and benefits of our local vegetables, fruits, eggs and fish, among others.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What public awareness and education programmes are in place to build up this knowledge and boost demand from our local consumers?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At Budget 2017, I appealed to the Government to do more to boost local demand by including a "Buy Singapore" requirement in their sourcing contracts.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A stronger official mandate will go a long way to boost demand.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will also send a signal to the market and consumers to support our own and encourage our local companies to keep improving.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, are we on track in the development of local expertise for this sector?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From agrifood practitioners to researchers, we need to nurture a new generation of talents in our technical institutions, polytechnics and universities to support the development of this relatively nascent sector, especially when we include the more cutting-edge developments, such as lab-grown protein and meat.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It was announced at Budget 2021 to help us move towards the "30 by 30" goal of producing 30% of Singapore's nutritional needs by 2030.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At the Budget debate in 2021, I had suggested that the Government includes agrifood developments in its green bond and loan issuances, and sizing them such that even small investors can participate in and do their part to support the growth of Singapore's agrifood sector.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Government share an update on what has been done to include our agrifood sector in our green finance market?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would also like to reiterate my appeal for the Government to consider more risk co-sharing with investors and banks for green and sustainability-linked projects.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Most of these will continue to be pioneering initiatives lacking track records.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government's support will provide green start-ups higher chances of bringing their visions to fruition.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Lastly, I would like to ask about the progress and impact on Flexible Work Arrangements (FWAs) on our workplace and economy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Has the Government conducted any measurement of the effectiveness and efficiency of this arrangement on public service delivery standards to date?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What have been the benefits and challenges of FWAs which had arisen in the past couple of years?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In particular, as multiple members of the family from different organisations may be working from home at the same time, how do we safeguard against the inadvertent exchange of confidential information and the potential misuse of such information?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What are the lessons the public sector had learnt which can be shared with private enterprises and organisations?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A deeper understanding of the relationship between FWAs and efficiency, information security and productivity can help us to come up with FWA policies that support and reinforce our global competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With this, I would like to conclude with my support for the Budget.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In his Budget Statement, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong spoke about AI as a general purpose technology, like electricity in internal combustion engine, the computer or the Internet as such technology, AI, indeed has the potential to touch every aspect of our lives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Like Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, I firmly believe in the transformative power of AI for the future of our shared economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In an earlier speech on amendments to the National Productivity Fund, I explained how AI carries both perils as well as promises.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But if we truly embrace this vision, I believe that we must also transform how we approach our policies in this AI age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This must go beyond pursuing excellence in AI research, embedding AI in Government services, upgrading our broadband infrastructure or even assure that our firms rapidly adopt AI.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Such goals outlined in the National AI Strategy 2.0 are indeed laudable but incomplete.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Rather, the impending structural shifts that our economy will face will alter the way that our businesses, workers and students will operate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: One can think of this as a complement to the Member Dr Tan Wu Meng as well as Mr Christopher de Souza's earlier speech, but not just about the policies of today but also of tomorrow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Researchers suggest that AI adopting firms tend to be larger, younger and relatively more productive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But to fully reap the benefits of AI in our economy, firms that are likely to fall behind, the SMEs, which are especially the incumbent firms in non-tech and non-professional sectors, must be presented with strong and urgent incentives to adopt AI.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Small firms are almost, by definition, that way because they have been relatively slower in seizing business opportunities and rationalising costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The owner of a "mama shop", a renovation contractor, a hawker stall or a car workshop may feel that AI has no direct implication for how they run their businesses and, hence, prefer to adopt a wait-and-see attitude toward adopting AI solutions for their company.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Pillar 2 allows for refunds of certain classes of investments to be treated as income rather than tax exemptions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This suits per additional investments in not just R&D and innovation, but also the adoption of AI-enabled digital and professional services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Yet, some words of caution are in order.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: First, such incentives will be greatest for the largest firms since these are the ones covered directly by BEPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But we must not forget SMEs and ensure that our "mom and pop" shops also see the strong benefits to pursuing Refundable Investment Credits, ideally through expanding outreach and promotion of the proposed scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And this applies, to my mind, especially for investments meant to simply increase production rather than those targeted specifically at the green transition or R&D.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: They may choose countervailing action and exercise the top-up over on their end, thereby undermining the attractiveness of the Refundable Investment Credit in the first place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is why the seeming consensus arrived at in the Budget-related wish lists put out by the big four accounting firms here, all of which stressed the importance of refundable tax credits, may be worrying if, indeed, the intent was to return to a pre-BEPS world where accounting firms identify sophisticated strategies to enable MNCs to whittle away at the effective tax rates, with the concurrence of our Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Third, we need to be aware that the traditional argument favouring tax in capital more favourably than labour, under the premise that doing so would stimulate productive investment, may have to be re-examined.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is because an AI-driven economy tends to be weightless, and encouraging investment in yet more physical capital is nowhere near as important as accumulating intangible knowledge capital.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Fourth, and most generally, it is imperative that we no longer regard tax competition as our primary strategy for attracting foreign capital, a point that I had made in this House before.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We should aim to create an environment where our businesses are AI-enabled and our workers are AI-savvy, which will naturally attract investment from abroad.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The Big Data machine-learning algorithms and large language models that are at the forefront of the AI revolution are increasingly concentrated in the hands of a few powerful firms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This calls for pre-emptive action by governments, especially those with deep pockets and sovereign wealth funds, to take active exposures in AI companies, whether in publicly traded firms or via private equity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This not only allows the public sector to enjoy a returns upside, but also to ensure that they have a voice in AI developments that is ultimately in the public interest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Of course, AI will not only alter the prospects for businesses but also our workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This implies that AI augmentation will lead to a compression in the distribution of abilities and skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: As such, those who have hitherto been able to distinguish themselves, perhaps because of their talent or industry, may now find that edge blunted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The upshot then is that we need to question the sorts of skills that we are pushing our workforce to acquire.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is certainly popular and sexy to suggest that the future economy will be in severe need of prompt engineers, cybersecurity specialists or digital marketers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But the current scarcity of such novel jobs will probably be relieved over the next few years, leaving it more likely that the skills involved will become enfolded into more traditional positions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Professionals of all stripes will need to learn the basics of delivering prompts through generative AI models, and marketers and salespeople will need to deliver their message across all media, including digital ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And while we can never be certain, old-school artisan or craftsman roles could well make a revival as robotics have yet to deliver the sort of sufficient quality or range of uses on this front.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Moreover, certain skills that we may have until recently thought were future-proof, such as coding, writing well or statistical analysis, may quickly become devalued when AI tools can do the job just as well, if not, better, for a fraction of the cost and time involved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Instead, it is soft human skills, originality and critical thinking, empathy and teamwork, leadership and communication that will be ever more important, and these are not as easily replicable by AI.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: These are not skills well captured by certifications alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Rather, they are nurtured through an emphasis on developing such ability in the classroom, even when they may not be formally evaluated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Or by self-reflection and feedback from managers and mentors, along with the concentrated efforts and experience over time in the workplace.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Even the most rudimentary models of human capital include not innate talent and years of schooling but also experience acquired from years of working.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: At this point, I declare that I work at an institution that has the potential to benefit from SkillsFuture, and this is some of the suggestions that I had suggested to the other Deputy Prime Minister earlier on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This means that allowing credits to be used not only for academic credentials but also for alternative learning modes, such as apprenticeship programmes or on-the-job training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I previously raised this possibility of such an expanded scope during the debate on the SkillsFuture Singapore Agency (Amendment) Bill, held in this House last year, and via various Parliamentary Questions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The offset from SkillsFuture would effectively mean a subsidised worker, which will both increase the attractiveness of taking on such apprentices while compensating the firm for the cost of on-the-job training provision.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Some may argue that the intent of SkillsFuture was to equip Singaporeans with new skills, not subsidise labour costs for businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But this misses the reality of how many modern skills need it and even the most evergreen ones are often acquired while doing the job, not before it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: A close friend of mine, who trained as an architect but eventually went on to a very successful career in finance, once shared that he was offered his first job at an investment bank despite his absent background, because they would have to teach him everything that he needed to know anyway.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Furthermore, training apprentices could ultimately leave for a position elsewhere, which also represents a risk for the business.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If we are truly concerned that companies may abuse the system to hire a stream of temporary workers with little transferable skills, we can always include a clause in the contract that requires a minimum duration of employment, post-apprenticeship, conditional on mutual agreement and reasonable performance, of course.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Such a change in how we value skills and training in an AI-enabled economy will become more necessary in the future, not less.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is not least because we cannot yet anticipate what kinds of jobs may become displaced by AI and what would become more important?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If anything, the lifespan of economically remunerative skills is likely to diminish.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But while I fully agree with the importance of infusing the mindset of lifelong learning into our workforce, we need to simultaneously stress that learning and applying must not be equated to grades and certificates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The WP supports this move, not least because we have been proposing some form of redundancy insurance since 2011.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In my response to the Budget last year, I further elaborated on the desirable features of such an unemployment insurance scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In a nutshell, this entails balancing the trade-off between providing a safety net for those who have lost a job, also encouraging those displaced workers to expeditiously return to the labour market, rather than relying on the payouts as a crutch.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Optimal schemes tend to combine reasonably generous salary replacement, albeit for limited time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If we accept that AI will alter how we work, it becomes self-evident that we also need to go upstream and rethink how the AI revolution will alter how we educate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: By this, I mean education for the masses, not just building a core of AI scientists and researchers, just to make ourselves a hub for AI innovation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: For starters, it is high time we internalise how straightforward knowledge accumulation and rote learning with constant repetition regurgitated through closed-book exams is no longer tenable, if it ever was in the "information is free" age of the Internet to begin with.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: AI will further erode the relevance of simply knowing more facts and figures, being the fastest at solving known problems or being able to memorise long lists of nomenclatures or taxonomies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Rather, we need to teach our kids how to filter information, to assess and evaluate, rather than to accept without questioning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This means that they will need to learn how to ask good questions and to identify the right from the wrong but, more often, to also recognise the new ones and know that there is not any clear right or wrong.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This, in turn, requires fostering a deep, intellectual curiosity in our students, one that instils the habits and imparts the tools necessary for critical interpretation and evaluation of data, as well as information.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Students need to be taught not so much what to think but how to think.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: That is why my party colleagues, Mr Pritam Singh and Ms He Ting Ru, emphasise the importance of access to information, so that we can encourage such thinking, even in the policy realm.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This will upend many of our traditional educational strategies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Indeed, it has even successfully drafted several Bills for legislators.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: While standardised testing has long been a mainstay of Asian society, the Keju was first introduced in China in the sixth century, and Indian Emperor Kharavela relied on competitive testing to select his officials in as far back as the first century BC, its continued use will need to be reviewed in light of the realities of the modern educational landscape.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But this does not mean that we eliminate assessment wholesale.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Rather, evaluations should be performed continuously and holistically.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We still need to impart numeracy and literacy, but these can be evaluated through dynamic debates and polished presentations through group projects and collaborative problem solving, and through the ability to pose quality questions as much as offer quality answers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I am aware of the subtle irony of this claim, coming from someone who has accumulated way too many academic credentials and taken way too many exams, and who still relies on teaching for a living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Be that as it may, I believe that we need to disabuse ourselves of the notion that the preferred path to professional, and personal, success lies solely in climbing the ladder of acquiring yet more academic qualifications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We inadvertently sell the rich diversity of gifts and talents of our population short, when we insist on holding fast to a mindset that the potential of a student is determined by how they fared in an exam when they were 12 or 16 years old.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Second, even as we implement AI in our pedagogy via the EdTech Masterplan 2030, we should not forget that customised learning, fostering digital literacy and equipping students with 21st century skills, all come back round to our teachers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Even as we fully empower our teachers with AI tools, we must also confer to them additional latitude to deliver the curriculum as they see fit, and make them facilitators rather than lecturers, or else learners will never fully exploit the full potential of AI.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Doing so will unlock what Sal Khan, founder of the online learning platform Khan Academy, characterised as "infinitely patient tutor ", a development that our tuition-obsessed nation will surely appreciate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This is something that AI, designed to riff off the existing corpus of knowledge, can never do.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have been in the Chamber for close to four and a half hours.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.15 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 2.56 pm until 3.15 pm.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In my view, Budget 2024 cares for people, helps businesses focus their attention on improving, upgrading and expanding both locally and internationally while ensuring that business costs are better managed with Government assistance.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2024 also boosts Singapore's premier position for attracting quality investments and helps create high-quality jobs for graduates coming out of our institutes of higher learning.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The big question before all of us is the need to remain committed to achieving these objectives as one people, one nation, one Singapore.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: With a cautiously optimistic outlook for 2024 and the economic stability that many of our trading partners are experiencing, Singapore businesses can breathe a sigh of relief.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: However, Singapore needs to remain vigilant in view of the current geopolitical tensions.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: An escalation in any of the current conflicts could significantly impact a small, open, trade-reliant nation like ours, potentially affecting energy stability, inflation and global commodity prices.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The business community welcomes many of the initiatives outlined in Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong's Budget 2024 speech.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The measures in the Budget to support and stimulate growth by managing rising business costs are greatly appreciated.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Given the four consecutive contractionary quarters faced by SMEs in 2023, as reported by OCBC's quarterly SME Index, this package is timely.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The Corporate Income Tax rebate provides temporary relief, enabling businesses to sustain operations and employment.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This intervention is a strategic move to alleviate financial pressures, encouraging firms to invest in productivity enhancements.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This could lead to a more resilient business environment and a win-win situation for the Government and business owners through greater economic activity and increased tax revenues.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The Enterprise Financing Scheme enhancements, including the SME Working Capital Loan increase and the enhanced maximum loan quantum for the trade loan, are also welcome developments.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: These adjustments will facilitate access to operational cashflow for SMEs and support businesses in internationalisation, ultimately reducing operating costs through leveraging comparative advantages in different sectors.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: These enhancements also facilitate businesses with greater access to financing and capital and to capture new growth areas.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I believe the SkillsFuture Credit top-up will not only nurture talent but also allow those unemployed to build skills in different sectors and improve their employability into new roles by pursuing full-time diplomas at polytechnics, ITEs or arts institutions.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This provides a win-win scenario for both individuals and businesses.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Individuals are well-equipped with better skills, lowering unemployment rates and pursuing jobs in sectors that offer better financial opportunities for their families.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses benefit from an increased talent pool with qualified individuals ready to dive into their sectors.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The extension of the credit to 30 June 2025 will also allow individuals more time to decide on the career paths more suited for them and consider additional expenses when deciding to attend the courses.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is very essential to bring along employers on board and change their mindset on investing in employees' training without fearing that they will leave after training.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: It is also important that employee training support includes workplace training, to improve the employability outcomes of our nation's investment in the training of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has highlighted, the most sustainable way to counter inflation is by bolstering our productivity by investing in human capital.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The investment in schemes aimed at improving R&D and productivity, alongside advancements in AI and the nationwide broadband network will drive local productivity growth and attract foreign direct investments into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The RIE2025 plan, with the NPF and the Financial Sector Development Fund (FSDF) are strategic initiatives designed to cement our status as a global hub for innovation, technology and financial services.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: By fostering R&D, promoting the commercialisation of innovative technologies and enhancing productivity, these programmes ensure our competitive edge in a high-value, efficient economic landscape.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: More importantly, these initiatives are progressive, ensuring that businesses lacking expertise and the ability to integrate with pre-existing technologies remain competitive and included.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding the uncertainties surrounding it, the implementation of Pillar Two of BEPS 2.0 on 1 January 2025 is a good strategic move for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond low corporate taxes, Singapore offers a conducive investment environment with a skilled talent pool, a stable and business-friendly political climate, low crime rates, a robust judicial system and top-tier educational opportunities.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: These factors make Singapore an attractive hub for MNCs, even with a potential increase in corporate tax rates.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I also want to highlight the measures in Budget 2024 to touch on a very important subject, which is enhancing the retirement adequacy of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The announcement for the closure of the Special Account and the transfer of the monies to the Retirement Account (RA) in 2025 is, in my view, a move in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: There will be short-term pain for a few, while there will be medium-term and long-term gains for many.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I also consider the most significant retirement-related move in the Budget to be the increase in the Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS), which will enable members to receive more income from CPF Life.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This is very significant in our society which is ageing fast and with many more Singaporeans living long, healthy and satisfying lives.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: With a prudent lifestyle, Singaporeans can retire and live gracefully in their golden years.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: However, I recognise the fact that for many of our fellow citizens, the most immediate goal is to reach the level of Full Retirement Sum (FRS), which remains at two times the BRS.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The lowering of this threshold will allow many more of our fellow citizens to enjoy the higher payout that comes with meeting the FRS.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Having some familiarity with how annuity payments are calculated and paid for, may I suggest that CPF LIFE and other annuity providers plan for these higher payouts for more citizens by increasing the duration of their fixed income portfolios?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: With interest rates at or close to the highest levels in the last decade, this is perhaps as good a time as any to increase the duration of their fixed income portfolios and enjoy the high rates that go with the longer duration.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Also, I would encourage the Government to re-energise its financial literacy campaign.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: While some of our fellow citizens are sophisticated, intelligent investors, many still do not understand basic concepts, such as the long-term benefits of compound interest.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I would also encourage the Government to formulate a detailed but simple delivery platform to explain these CPF changes to our senior citizens.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: We want every Singaporean to be well informed about the rationale for this move and how it will help them when the time comes for everyone in the near future.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In summary, this is a Budget that directly confronts the reality that cost-of-living pressures exist for individuals while rising costs for businesses are a major challenge.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: It balances these two issues while reducing the risk of overheating the economy and increasing inflation.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I believe this Budget will give businesses the necessary confidence to expedite their capital investment plans, which, in turn, will lead to growth in GDP and the creation of high value jobs.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In my view, the most important aspect of this Budget is that it provides for significant increase in benefits for individuals and companies without any new tax increases and without any need for any short-term deficit financing.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Maintaining fiscal discipline and protecting our Reserves is of paramount importance in what is likely to be a decade or two of rapid changes in the global economic environment with significant impact on a small, open economy like ours.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: That was my first and foremost reaction to this year's Budget Statement, aptly titled "Building Our Shared Future Together".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The annual Budget has always been about much more than how the Government spends in different areas.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Fundamentally, the Budget has always been about the People's Action Party (PAP) Government's agenda for governance – its plans, its priorities, its statement of intent – and undergirding all these, a manifestation of the PAP Government's ethos and core values in governance.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And for this year's Budget, the statement of intent is unmistakably about the 4G team's Forward Singapore agenda – to move Singapore and Singaporeans into an even brighter future.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In the Deputy Prime Minister’s words, Budget 2024 presents the first installation of plans in the Forward Singapore agenda.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This must imply subsequent installations to come – "akan datang" – and I look forward to the unveiling of these future plans in good time.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But as it is, the first installation of plans, as presented in Budget 2024 is, in my view, already breathtaking.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The plans are bold, they are ambitious and they brim with gumption.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But they are also plans I can describe in one phrase, that remind us that it takes two hands to clap, the Government, on the one hand, and citizens, whether individual or corporate and, oftentimes, the whole of society, on the other hand.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Government and citizens – two hands to clap.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The plans in the Forward Singapore agenda require the Government, citizens and the whole of society, to work ever more closely together, take action together, in order to make the plans happen.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This, for me, is the crux of Forward Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In other words, beyond having more information to facilitate further discourse, for me, the crux of Forward Singapore is really about action, taking action together, Government and citizens, individuals and corporates.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Redoubling our commitment to work with each other and build a shared future together.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Because for a Singapore this advanced in its development and with scant playbooks to follow, for a Singapore that is navigating uncharted waters in an increasingly complex and troubled world, it can no longer be about the Government delivering the goods and citizens merely receiving.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Going forward, it has to be about the Government and citizens figuring things out together, feeling the stones as we cross the river together.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: That is what our social compact going forward must look like.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, for the rest of my speech, I will talk about how we need to apply this basic orientation of action and collaboration between the Government and citizens in four areas under Forward Singapore and this Budget: housing, education, low-wage workers and healthcare.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The PPHS (Open Market) Voucher supports couples with a child or children and waiting to collect keys to their BTO flats to rent HDB flats temporarily from the open market.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is an important move by the Government to complement the PPHS, which the Government is already ramping up.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But for the Open Market Voucher to work, landlords – HDB flat owners – in the open market must play their part.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: As it is, we know anecdotally that landlords are less willing to rent to couples with a young child because of potential disamenities.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, it is not about rental price or rental market but it is about tenant profile.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Government cannot force or compel landlords to rent to couples with a young child.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Government can only provide the right scheme, the right market incentives, but the market must rise to the occasion and landlords have to do their part in order for the scheme to work.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Government is taking huge steps forward in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: One huge step is the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme to support more mature workers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: As for a second full-time diploma programme, the full tuition fee from a quick search online is typically around $12,000 per year, or $30,000, over 2.5 years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: On top of such subsidies, the Government is extending to the individual $4,000 in SkillsFuture Credit to cover more than half of the balance of the tuition fees.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, the out-of-pocket fees for a second full-time diploma comes up to about 10% of full tuition fees.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is a truly bold step and I think it will be a game-changer.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But indeed, if I were to have any criticism on the Level-Up Programme, it would be about this training allowance.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Because, generous as it is, I wish the training allowance had covered Singaporeans for up to 30 months, instead of 24 months, so that the entire duration of a full-time diploma programme can be more or less covered.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: That six months more of financial coverage for an adult learner with a family, with caregiving needs, will mean a world of difference.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But I think the difference it will make will be well-worth the cost.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But coming back to taking two hands to clap.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Government has made this bold move through the Level-Up Programme for more mature workers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think it is really up to our citizens, both individual and corporate, to work with the Government to make things work.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For individuals, to take the plunge and seize the opportunities to get a comprehensive skills reboot and secure for yourself a second wave in your career and life.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And for individuals, it is also about making and embracing an intergenerational classroom, where younger and more mature learners learn how to learn together.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This does not come naturally and it will take effort.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For corporates – enterprises and employers – they need to recognise the tremendous value of Singaporean jobseekers who have taken this skills reboot and operated in an intergenerational learning environment.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Recognise the tremendous value that this training provides, hire the jobseekers and offer them roles and packages that reflect their true value.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Another huge step taken in education in this Budget is the ITE Progression Award to help young ITE graduates get a diploma and move themselves onto a better career and wage trajectory.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is a huge step by the Government because it will uplift ITE graduates early on in their lives, reduce inequality and keep social mobility alive.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is another truly bold step, another game-changer in my mind, in the Forward Singapore agenda.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, I disagree with the Progressive Singapore Party (PSP), who has said that the $10,000 award upon graduation and to be paid into CPF Ordinary Account is not so helpful, because it creates differentiation among diploma graduates.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Well, the reality is, half of every cohort passes through our polytechnics and so, within our polytechnics, there are vastly different profiles of students with vastly different needs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, a differentiated approach for different polytechnic student profiles is pragmatic.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Therefore, the $10,000 CPF Award can be seen as helping diploma graduates coming through the ITE route to close the gap, just in terms of Ordinary Account contributions, that is equivalent to the first six years or so of their working lives.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Award helps them close this gap and helps them to catch up with their counterparts in terms of saving for a HDB flat.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is the right thing to do and I am glad that the Government has taken the bold and decisive step to do it.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But again, it takes two hands to clap.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, while the Government has taken this bold step, I hope more ITE graduates will be encouraged to take up this scheme, and upskill and uplift themselves.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And as importantly, I hope more ITE students, both current and future, will have a strong goal to work towards and be strongly motivated to do well in ITE to qualify for polytechnic.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The PWM works hand-in-hand with Workfare to uplift low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, there is really no fundamental ideological difference between minimum and progressive wages that warrants our rehashing and repeated debating in this House.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Rather, I think what this House should really discuss is how to make progressive wages work for our workers, how to translate policy into real outcomes on the ground.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And on this, it really takes two hands to clap.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The whole of society has to do its part.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: There have been instances of service buyers – corporate clients – reducing the workforce mix when calling for new tenders because of progressive wage.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In other words, because the wages of not just security officers but also senior security officers and security supervisors have to go up under the PWM, but the service buyer's budget remains the same, the service buyer cuts its requirement for senior security officers and supervisors in a new tender.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This runs against the spirit of progressive wages.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It causes our senior security officers and supervisors to lose out.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In order for the progressive wage policy to achieve real upliftment of low-wage workers, service buyers must be prepared to pay more.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I cheer the increase in per capita household income thresholds for various subsidy tiers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is timely and it will give more than a million Singaporeans higher healthcare subsidies and keep alive the promise of affordable healthcare for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Specifically, it will allow, amongst other things, more Singaporeans to requalify for the "blue" Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) card.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Government has heard and heeded the concerns of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But it takes two hands to clap and so, I hope with this enhancement and with the larger Healthier SG movement, all Singaporeans will really take ownership of their health and make full use of the infrastructure, programming and financing support provided by the Government to stay healthy and lead long and happy lives.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: While the Forward Singapore agenda reminds all of us of the need to each play our part, it is also a real luxury that we are able to talk about these exciting plans and have sufficient funds to back up these plans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Rather, it is the direct outcome of sound fiscal decisions taken year after year, over many years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Fiscal decisions, including the GST, starting in 1993, then 2002, 2007 and, most recently, 2022.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Our GST journey has spanned more than 30 years, more than half of our existence as an independent nation, taking the right decisions, time after time, steadily building up a sustainable revenue base for Singapore and designing a system of GST and transfers that is fair and progressive, does not hurt the poor and taxes primarily the higher-income Singaporeans and foreigners but benefitting all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is what successive PAP governments have done.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is also almost our entire Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC) today.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, had we taken the easy way out on GST each time —

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan, you have less than a minute.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: At the joint press conference on 6 February 2024, NTUC's Secretary-General and the President of the Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF), warned that we could expect a challenging year ahead.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Great power contestation and regional conflicts have disrupted global supply chains and reshaped economic activities, leading to a rising inflation, affecting both businesses and individuals around the world, including Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: NTUC also conducted our annual Economic Sentiments survey recently with 2,000 respondents.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: About two-thirds noted that their income has not kept up with living costs especially affecting our seniors.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This suggests prevailing insecurity, fear of job cuts and potential uptake in retrenchments in 2024.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: So, what does all these mean for our workers and for NTUC as a Labour Movement?

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Does it mean we will have to brace for tougher times?

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Yes, but we also need to seize opportunities for change and for transformation.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It is times like these that NTUC remains steadfast in our unwavering commitment to providing support for all our workers.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: My fellow Labour MPs will cover a range of topics that addresses the needs, the aspirations, the concerns of different segments of our workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: My speech will focus on three key areas.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: First, amid uncertainties, how the Labour Movement and NTUC will continue to journey with our workers.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I will make a call for workers and companies to join the union, for better protection as well as for business success.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Second, I will give an update on NTUC's efforts to support workers' upskilling through various schemes and initiatives.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And finally, I will continue to speak up for our middle-aged and middle-career workers who are facing significant challenges.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Recent wave of lay-offs globally and locally has heightened apprehensions among workers about job losses.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: An example is the Lazada Singapore retrenchment which has brought into focus the role and the value that unions can offer to all workers as well as to businesses.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And now, they are focused on building a strong partnership for the mutual benefit of the company and for all the workers that are affected.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Lazada's commitment to maintaining open communication with FDAWU is encouraging, underscoring the vital role the unions play in securing favourable terms for our workers, particularly during retrenchments.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I mentioned that many of the Lazada employees are PMEs.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: A senior account manager worked for 10 months and resigned in June 2023.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: During that period, she managed to close sales target for two separate teams, but she was told that if she was to leave earlier, she will not be eligible for the commission for her first team if she resigned.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: So, she sought the assistance of the Singapore Industrial and Services Employees' Union, after failing to convince the company herself.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The union represented her case and met with the management and eventually, the management investigated and agreed to pay the commission by the end of last year.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In the end, the member was grateful and maintained a positive relationship even as she left the company.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: PMEs or not, union members can benefit from NTUC membership on workplace issues.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But it is not just a matter of supporting only our workers.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: NTUC believes in achieving win-win outcomes by supporting businesses to grow the pie so that workers can benefit by sharing the gains.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: NTUC leans forward to support our unionised companies in hiring, in job placements, upskilling and training and, more recently, in business transformation.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Allow me to say an example of how NTUC supported our unionised company, Dyna-Mac Engineering Services Private Limited.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: During the oil price crunch and COVID-19 pandemic, the company was experiencing business downturn.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: A newly appointed Executive Chairman and CEO, Mr AC Lim, shared that he was at his wit's end trying to turn around the company, when the Shipbuilding and Marine Engineering Employees' Union introduced him to the company training committee initiative (CTC).

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Dyna-Mac took the leap of faith, formed the CTC and embarked on the OpsTech roadmap.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Through the process, the company reaffirmed their business direction and goals, and received support from the CTC Grant.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Today, Dyna-Mac is in the black and workers are sharing in the gains.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: So, when I joined Mr Lim at the last panel discussion on CTCs, he expressed strong appreciation for how NTUC has helped his businesses and his workers.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: When I tell this story, unions and even businesses around the world may not appreciate how a union can actually support businesses or even employers.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But with NTUC and Singapore, because of our unique tripartism, we were able to secure better outcomes for workers by not just supporting workers directly but also going upstream to support businesses.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It is in tough times that the value of NTUC will come to the fore, in protecting our workers and helping companies grow their businesses.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: So, I urge all companies and workers to consider joining the NTUC family because, as brothers and sisters, we will grow the business together and we will ensure we secure better wages, better welfare and better work prospects for all workers.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Next, I will speak about how NTUC plans to continue our support for workers' upskilling.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: NTUC has always maintained that for our economy to grow, our competitive advantage must be a skilled and quality workforce that is future ready.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But why is there an urgency now to step up our efforts in upskilling and training?

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: While all these advances are expected to enhance productivity and drive growth, there is an anticipated short-term impact on workers and their livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Last year, in the US, one of the longest labour disputes involving over 10,000 Hollywood Television and Movie Writers represented by The Writers Guild of America, along with 160,000 actors affiliated with other guilds, brought the entertainment industry to a standstill.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The writers' main concern was the extensive use of generative AI, such as ChatGPT, to create scripts, raising fears that studios may therefore exploit AI to replace screenwriters and to reduce fees.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: After negotiations, Hollywood writers secured control over AI to prevent its use as a tool to replace them.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Additionally, white-collar layoffs seen in companies like Google, Duolingo and UPS are increasingly tied to productivity-boosting technologies like machine learning.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This trend highlights AI's roles in automating routine tasks, affecting both blue- and white-collar jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This underscores the need for a "just transition", ensuring that as AI changes work, society and the economy, the transition is implemented fairly, equitably and with considerations for all workers and communities.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To navigate this transition, it is imperative for workers to engage in continuous learning, consistently updating our skills.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Our Founding Father, Mr Lee Kuan Yew, once referred a letter from the former chairman of the Japan Productivity Centre, Mr Kohei Goshi, who played a significant role in fostering a culture of productivity in Japan.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Goshi drew on the wisdom of a Chinese philosopher, Guanzi, and I quote, "一年之计，莫如树谷；十年之计，莫如树木；终身之计，莫如树人。" Translated, it means one may grow grains or trees for short-term gains but for longer rewards, one has to invest in growing men or in developing talents.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As we chart our way forward, NTUC pledges to continue championing our workers' interests to take action for them and with them.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I am heartened to share that despite the uncertainties of technological disruptions, 52% of workers foresee the need to upskill to adapt to the rise of AI, based on NTUC's annual Economic Sentiments survey.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: NTUC Learning Hub, for example, has recently launched the "X for Everyone" series of courses, addressing emerging technologies crucial for modern workplaces, such as generative AI, cybersecurity and cloud computing, as part of the Tech Talent Academy.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I encourage all workers to update their skills to remain proficient in the face of the rapid developments in these vital technologies.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Another initiative NTUC is working relentlessly in promoting upskilling is to drive the CTC, an institution to complement to SkillsFuture, and an initiative between employers and the unions to support businesses' transformation that can result in company-initiated training and skills upgrading for workers.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Since its inception in 2019, we have made tremendous progress.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Through OTR, Hydroflux formulated a business strategy plan identifying areas for digitalisation, talent development and growth opportunities.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Prior to the CTC initiative, sales staff faced limited career advancement opportunities.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But with a new plan in place, Hydroflux is committed to providing career development structures exemplified by success stories, like Ms Alyssa Lim, who transitioned from an air stewardess to now a sales role.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Ms Lim's dedication led to her promotion to a Senior Lifestyle Specialist role, showcasing the positive impact of CTCs and the implemented strategies.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: So, we hope more companies will work with NTUC in forming CTCs and developing strategic plans for both business and workforce development.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: NTUC urges companies to tap on the CTC Grant that helps to navigate trends, such as AI, support workers' upskilling and enhance business productivity.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Besides partnerships with the employers, NTUC also works with our SkillsFuture Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In June 2023, WSG piloted a Workplace Skills Recognition programme (WPSR) with NTUC and the National Centre of Excellence for Workplace Learning (NACE) in two sectors, the retail and the food services sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: NTUC has been working closely with SSG and NACE to introduce CTC companies within these two sectors to pilot and to embark on a Workplace Learning:READY Mark certification.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: With good ground feedback and success from companies, such as King's Cart Coffee Pte Ltd, NTUC will continue to work with SSG and NACE to onboard more CTC companies to this initiative.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In this regard, we hope that WPSR can be expanded to more sectors and availed to more companies for their benefit.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: NTUC remains committed to offering comprehensive support for workers navigating through career transitions.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: More details about this development will be announced shortly.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In my campaign speech in 2020 on national television, I spoke about this segment and that I will do my utmost to support them in their livelihood, to give them greater purpose and dignity.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I did so in Pasir Ris, bringing job opportunities, organising job fairs and career networking sessions and working with many Government agencies.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But despite these efforts, many still struggled, and I met them across the constituency.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I met this gentleman who was in his 50s when he decided to return from overseas to Singapore because of his son's National Service (NS).

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: He was confident he would secure a job easily, given his extensive experience in sales and also management.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: He applied for numerous jobs during COVID-19, got a few replies and a couple of interviews, but zero offers for two years.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Although it was not explicit, he sensed that companies find that his age could be a barrier.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Some even said he was overqualified for the post that he applied for.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This gentleman was not looking for a high-paying job.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: He was prepared to take a pay cut, learn new things, go into a new area and start all over.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But he was just not given the opportunity to do so.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: His wife has a health problem, his two children are not yet working, and he still has to put food on the table.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: At least that helped him to feel useful and helps to contribute to his family.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: After a year, he was finally offered a job at a fraction of his last drawn pay – even below what he could earn by driving Grab.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: He could not accept the offer and, as time passed, his confidence in himself, and also in the job market, dipped.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I recall receiving a message from him at 4.00 am one morning.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And it says: "Mr Tan, I am still struggling to get back to normal employment to deal with life.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Having worked so many years and so much effort to upgrade myself to stay relevant.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Why are people like me still struggling?" Well, thankfully he finally landed a good job after three to four years.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And, in between, he upgraded himself, took some courses and continued to persevere.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But his struggle is real and I think he is probably not the only one who faces the same problem.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We have to do more for people like him, especially given our ageing workforce and manpower shortage.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: That was why, during Budget last year, I called for the Government to provide more support for mid-career workers by expanding the SkillsFuture Career Transition Programme to more sectors, so that more workers can benefit from the scheme and also to consider introducing training allowance that was introduced during the COVID-19 for trainees under this scheme.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In my interactions over the last two weeks with many workers, including the gentleman I spoke about, these announcements are very welcomed and timely.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Many commented the schemes announced are well thought out and decisive, and for a group of workers that really face difficulties.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: (In Mandarin):   Esteemed colleagues in Parliament, since the announcement of the 2024 Budget, we have received a lot of positive feedback from workers.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Government has proposed many measures and schemes to support mid-career workers, uplift low-wage workers, assist young workers and families, help middle-aged workers obtain retirement adequacy and aid Singaporeans in coping with the cost of living.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These measures and schemes were proposed after listening to the feedback and voices of workers and have taken into account the recommendations from the NTUC's #EveryWorkerMatters Conversations report.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Our workers will benefit from the various plans and measures introduced by the Government.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: NTUC will continue to support workers in enhancing their skills, obtaining better wages, welfare and work prospects.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We also encourage workers to make good use of these schemes and measures introduced by the Government and NTUC.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As the saying goes, learning is like rowing upstream, not to advance is to retreat.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The same goes for building a career; not advancing is akin to retreating.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For society to progress and economy to grow, workers must upgrade and the tripartite partners must work together.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: United, we can help workers improve and create a better future. : The year 2024 is expected to bring challenges for both workers and businesses.

speaker: The Minister of State, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, echoing Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong's sentiment, and I quote, "Singapore can take heart that the country has navigated similar external disruptions and shocks in the past and each time had emerged stronger than before." Our resilience is evident in successfully weathering recent challenges, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, with tripartism at the very core of our efforts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is a well-considered budget that aims to strengthen our nation's resilience to withstand the challenges of an uncertain global economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We are entering an era of work that is marked by precarity, where job security is no longer a guarantee.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The climate crisis and new technologies like generative AI will bring about disruption and transformation to our economy, including the labour market in both speed and scale.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Jobs and skills obsolescence will persist and therefore workers of all collars and ages are now more vulnerable and understandably anxious about the way ahead.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Earlier this month, NTUC's annual Survey on Economic Sentiments echoed this same worry and anxiety on the ground, where more workers are concerned about losing their jobs compared to the preceding year.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: At the same time, there are ongoing challenges of inflation and rising costs of living.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: From groceries to electricity and water bills, Singaporeans who find themselves out of a job are facing increased financial strain in meeting their basic needs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: During this exceptional and critical time, it is therefore imperative for the Government to re-evaluate our approach to unemployment and job loss.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We must assure workers who find themselves involuntarily displaced or transitioning into more resilient careers that they will not be left behind without support.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We must also equip our workers with the resources and skills necessary to strengthen their employability.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Only by investing in our collective resilience and prosperity can Singapore prevent the adverse repercussions of economic restructuring and emerge stronger together.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To this end, I will focus on what I will call as the "2S" areas, of Support and Strengthening, for our workers: Support for the Unemployed, and Strengthening SkillsFuture and CET.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The first "S" of Support for the unemployed is a call I first made more than 10 years ago, here in this House in 2014.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: PMEs represent a segment of our workforce that are particularly precarious when they become unemployed, because they typically have more dependents to take care of but take a longer time to find a new job due to their age and expected income.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Upon re-entry to employment, there is also an increasing propensity for them to suffer from wage loss.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, I wish to highlight the anxieties that many Singaporeans face in our current employment climate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I will also talk about how we can better support our low-wage workers, by expanding the PWM to other sectors and exploring the Career Progression Model for skilled professions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is no secret that Singaporeans are anxious about the steady and unabating rise in our cost of living.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: All of us would have felt the impact of inflation when we buy our meals at hawker centres and when we pay our monthly utility bills.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Our survey also found that older workers felt this more acutely, likely due to the short runway they have till retirement.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The additional CDC Vouchers, the Cost-Of-Living Special Payment, U-Save and service and conservancy charges (S&CC) rebates will go some way in helping Singaporeans defray the rise in prices.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In addition to alleviating immediate cost-of-living pressures, Budget 2024 continues the Government's trend of increasing our social spend to cater to a rapidly ageing population and to ensure social mobility.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: During this term of Government, the budget allocated to MSF will increase by about 18%, from $3.9 billion in FY2020 to an estimated $4.6 billion in FY2024.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I fully support this, and I will speak more about the good work done by MSF during the COS debate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As we build our shared future together, we must retain our core identity as an inclusive society, a society where no one will be left behind.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The private sector and civil society can also do their part in the fight against inflation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: NTUC has rolled out various measures to help Singaporeans mitigate the rise in cost of living.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Initiatives, such as the $8 FairPrice Return Voucher for every $80 nett spend using CDC vouchers and the GST offset on 500 essential items, have helped many Singaporeans defray inflation.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: At Kopitiam, union members can enjoy a breakfast set starting from $2.20.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Transport workers continue to pay 60 cents for a cup of "kopi O" or "teh O" at over 50 canteens operated by the National Transport Workers' Union.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I was also heartened to read that DBS has extended its Five Million Hawker Meals initiative, which allows patrons of various hawker stalls who use the DBS PayLah! app to get up to $3 off their meals every Friday.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Hawkers in my Radin Mas constituency tell me that this has helped to boost business and my residents tell me that the $3 offset is indeed substantive.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I encourage more companies to join NTUC and DBS in helping to alleviate the cost-of-living pressures for everyone.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In Radin Mas, we launched the "It’s On Me" programme in 2021, where patrons to Redhill Food Centre and Telok Blangah Crescent Food Centre can pay a little extra when buying their own meals to treat someone else, someone who may be in need.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Since its launch in 2021, the programme has given away more than 100,000 free meals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beneficiaries have told me that they deeply appreciate how, as a community initiative, "It's On Me" does not require any means testing.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To further assist vulnerable residents, Radin Mas launched the EZ-Meals programme just last month.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beneficiaries can approach more than 80 participating hawker stalls within the constituency to offset $3 from the price of their meals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This helps to keep the cost of food low for some 200 beneficiaries while providing a wide variety of food options.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To help consumers find the best deals and stretch their dollar, the Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE) launched the Price Kaki app in 2019 to allow for an easy comparison of prices of daily essentials.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The app has since been downloaded by more than 150,000 users who use it to check the prices of over 10,000 daily essentials and about 75,000 cooked food items islandwide.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am also glad that HDB and Government Technology Agency (GovTech) had recently launched the Great Budget Meal Hunt, creating a portal to crowdsource budget meal recommendations located at HDB coffee shops.
