speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Together with Price Kaki, this will provide consumers with greater awareness and more choices to help them stretch their dollar.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Following the success of the Price Kaki app, CASE realised that, over time, we have built up a substantial number of "super users".

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They use the app daily and share deals with their family and friends, often by sending a screenshot of what they see on the app across their WhatsApp groups.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Price Kaki team has spoken to some of these super users, who tell us that they hope to be able to share these "lobangs" and promotions within their own neighbourhoods with other users using the app, so that we can build micro-communities of like-minded individuals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I call these users our "Price Kaki Champions" and we value their feedback.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: CASE will, therefore, enhance the app by launching a community feature in Price Kaki.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This new function will be available in a few days' time and will allow users to share reviews, in-store promotions and tips to better stretch their dollar.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We will also grow our community of Price Kaki Champions offline, so that we can bring the benefits of Price Kaki to as many consumers as possible.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These volunteers will help to suss out deals within their own neighbourhoods and teach others to use the Price Kaki app to find the best deals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As we grow our network of Price Kaki Champions, I am confident that we will further improve price transparency, promote cost-consciousness and empower consumers to make better value-for-money purchase decisions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: At NTUC, we believe that jobs are the best welfare and full employment is the best protection for our workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is especially true for our lower-wage brothers and sisters, who have seen their wages decrease in real terms in 2023.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I was, therefore, heartened to read how all three of our local banks, DBS, UOB and OCBC, are giving their junior staff a one-off payment to help them cope with cost-of-living pressures.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But beyond company-specific initiatives, NTUC has been relentlessly championing for a way to increase wages through upskilling skills and improving productivity.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We first conceptualised the PWM for the cleaning sector and expanded it to other sectors where outsourcing practices were common, such as security, landscape and lift and escalator maintenance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Members would have read news that countries with minimum wage policies are now starting to look towards the Singapore PWM, recognising that minimum wage had become a wage ceiling rather than a floor, resulting in stagnant wages in these countries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is a pivotal component of Singapore's strategy in pursuing sustainable income growth and plays a crucial role in uplifting the earning potential of workers across a spectrum of sectors and occupations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Despite initial concerns, empirical evidence has demonstrated that the implementation of PWM does not lead to job losses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This achievement is attributed to our tripartite process to establish consensus and buy-in, ensuring that any wage increases are acceptable and feasible for employers, thereby safeguarding against any adverse impacts on employment levels.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While the overarching goal of PWM is to improve the livelihoods of workers, achieving parity between their wages and those of university graduates, as suggested yesterday by the hon Member Mr Raj Joshua Thomas, poses challenges.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These challenges stem from the need to navigate various constraints, including ensuring that wage adjustments remain manageable for employers, contribute to the sustainable operation of businesses and do not jeopardise overall employment levels.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In sum, PWM adopts a pragmatic approach focused on raising wages sustainably.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: By adhering to this approach, PWM continues to serve as an effective tool for sustaining income progression while simultaneously addressing the diverse needs and complexities of both workers and employers within the broader economic landscape of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond our lower-wage workers, we must also uplift our skilled trade workers to develop their skills, attain mastery and build long-term careers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Having a skills-based, job-relevant diploma will certainly give a helpful boost to our ITE graduates.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: NTUC will work with agencies to develop Career Progression Models with specific career and accreditation pathways for skilled trade workers and essential workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The portal will allow PWM workers to view their PWM wages and job levels that their employers have placed them on.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Labour Movement commends MOM’s efforts in raising public awareness of PWM requirements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: NTUC will continue working with our Tripartite Partners to ensure compliance with PWM wages and requirements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: NTUC cares because every worker matters, and we will not hesitate to take strong action against any company which attempts to circumvent these PWM requirements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Inflation dynamics are still in flux and concerns about the cost of living will not go away.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But I am glad that the 4G team, led by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, have set their sights on addressing acute challenges that Singapore faces, such as tempering inequality and sustaining social mobility.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In building our shared future together, we must continue our tripartite efforts to expand PWM so that workers will continue to have good jobs and a growing income to combat inflation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: When Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong delivered the Budget two weeks ago, my immediate reaction as the Chairperson of the GPC for Manpower was that it was a Budget that had workers' interest at the very core.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Headlined by the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme with a second subsidised diploma and generous training allowance, workers would find significant help in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The natural question was whether the Budget had missed out on certain aspects of supporting workers and to ask for them during the debate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, we do know a single year’s of Budget does not make for robust and thoughtful national capabilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Each successive year’s Budget should build on each other.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is worth examining how this term of Government has built up critical employment infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Budgets from 2020 to 2022 were focused on preserving lives and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, the Jobs Growth Incentive (JGI) was highly successful in supporting local hires during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It also led to an increase of about 90,200 local hires.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This roughly translates to a significant spending of $8,700 per local worker who has benefited from the JGI.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Similarly, the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package provided jobs, traineeship opportunities and skills enhancement programmes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Over FY2020 to FY2021, $2.2 billion was set aside for SGUnited.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: From April 2020 to April 2022, more than 200,000 local jobseekers benefited.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Around eight of our 10 trainees secured employment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There was further progress in creating a more equitable society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Income inequality is now the lowest in over two decades.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is owed, in no small part, to the schemes to uplift lower-wage workers through expanding PWM and reforming the Local Qualifying Salary (LQS), as Member Melvin Yong had pointed out.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Progressive Wage Credit Scheme (PWCS) was launched in 2022 to support employers to adjust to the expanded PWM.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is complemented by raising the minimum qualifying salary under the WIS Scheme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: WIS was enhanced in 2020, 2023 and will be again in 2025.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Collectively, this will benefit around half a million Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Enabling Employment Credit was also created in 2023 to help workers with special needs or disabilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There were also decisive moves on Workplace Fairness and Platform Workers over this term of Government.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The net effect is a tapestry and trampoline of support schemes that help workers of all ages, abilities and skills.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This was built across successive Budgets, working with the unions and employers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Indeed, we must always find ways to improve on the Budgets to help Singaporeans further.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But we can do so today from a place of strength and comfort.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is from this foundation of strength that I would like to examine how we could support our younger workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our younger people are naturally anxious about transiting to the workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our year-long Every Worker Matters Conversations run by NTUC in 2023 also reflected similar sentiments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This year’s Budget builds capabilities to help our young Singaporeans to succeed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Investment in innovation and training systems can bring in new enterprises to create better jobs for them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, young Singaporeans still face two rather formidable challenges: one, transition to an economy shaped by AI and climate change; and two, navigating the workplace that ironically has more options and thus, harder to land on a desired career.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are at the doorsteps of a seismic shift in the economy with the rise of AI.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Just not too long ago, coding was deemed as the skill of the new economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even I was tempted to take up coding, but I could not really do it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It was almost a must-have for young people to seize new opportunities and thrive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet today, AI can already perform entry-level coding easily and some even for free.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can only imagine that, in time, it would be capable of, if not already so, sophisticated coding.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What does that leave for the many students and young people who have been learning coding in school?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And this is just coding that might be adversely impacted.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Most young people would need to work with AI regardless of their occupations or industries in the future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How do they work with AI, co-pilot it to become more creative and better in exercising human judgement?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: AI would lead to job creation and job losses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: AI advances and adoption by companies would be non-linear and, therefore, highly disruptive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The core job requirements and skills for many jobs would have changed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There would be a greater emphasis on analysis, working with clients and strategic thinking.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For our young Singaporeans and workers, they would either be riding this tremendous wave or be sunk by it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can we ensure that our youths are AI-ready?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Should IHLs include AI as part of all courses?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And do all our workers and educators now need to have AI booster courses?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The next challenge is that of green transition and the impact on jobs and training.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Take, for example, our nation's vision to achieve 100% cleaner energy vehicles by 2040.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: ITE currently offers automotive technology and engineering courses, which primes its students with appropriate skillsets for electric vehicles (EVs).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, what would happen to our workers who only have skills to repair internal combustion engines (ICE) vehicles?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Those students with mechanical engineering skills would need to acquire new skills quickly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Should they not be able to transition fast enough, they would be out of work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must embrace the green transition whether we like it or not.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Today, 52% of Singaporeans or young Singaporeans foresee the need to upskill to adapt to the rise of AI and this is especially so among our younger people.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They will need to retrain shortly after graduation if they find themselves on the wrong side of the economic transition.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At the heart of this endeavour lies the concept of a "just transition".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is more than just adapting to economic shifts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It embodies a worker-centric approach to ensuring that the transitions our workers undergo are fair, equitable and sustainable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This was also the point raised by Minister of State Desmond Tan.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To this, I wish to speak on key areas ensuring a “just transition" to the new economy for our young workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our workers and unionists appreciate that these are substantive support to transit into new careers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As part of a "just transition" for younger workers in trades that would be adversely impacted by large structural shifts of AI and green transition, I hope that the Government can provide similar support to our younger workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, one of the young persons we met was Darren, a 24-year-old ITE student studying business administration.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: He aspires to open an automotive workshop in the future but he would need automotive skills, especially those pertaining to EVs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: He would need support to pick up these skills to make the career transition.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Younger Singaporeans ITE and polytechnic diploma holders might take as long as five years before being able to tap on their SkillsFuture credits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Beyond this, there would be instances, such as in legal services, where a degree is needed for career transition.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would the Government consider also providing subsidies for second degrees?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, companies must also be fair and transparent with their employees in the use of AI and how it would impact them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is not desirable to stand in the way of progress, but it is equally undesirable to have sudden dislocation and displacement of workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The failure to manage the transition well might cause disturbances as large as what the US automakers faced with strikes by workers concerned by the job losses due to the transition to EVs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It was also what happened with the Writers Guild of America strike. "Just transition" also requires providing younger Singaporeans with more opportunities for transition.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Career trials for younger Singaporeans can help in navigating a complex workplace.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: WSG Career Trial encourages jobseekers above the age of 16 to go through a short-term trial before considering formal employment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The supply and diversity of these trials are needed to cater to the broad interests of our students.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Government consider enhancing subsidies to host companies to increase the supply of such career trials?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: NTUC has engaged more than 10,000 young people in a landmark Youth Task Force report last year to develop ways to help our younger Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It launched the NTUC Career Starter Lab to enable our younger people to transition smoothly to the workforce via career trials and mentorship.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement will always do its part alongside the Government to help our young workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It can equip our youth with invaluable skills and opportunities to pivot when necessary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to increase both the number and diversity of opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, the Ministry of Law (MinLaw) inked the memorandum of understanding for the Singapore-Shanghai Lawyers Exchange Programme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Lawyers can learn new skills from their counterparts and also enter new markets.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I hope that there can be more of such partnerships by other Ministries and businesses, especially that of our MNCs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Global Ready Talent Internship Programme encourages Singapore enterprises to train young local talent through local and overseas internships.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry look into expanding the reach of the programme to more host companies, whether based in Singapore or otherwise?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In doing so, we can forge a path towards a more just, equitable and sustainable future.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As our workforce ages and the aspirations of our workers changes, our Workers' Compact – our social and economic contract with our workers – must be renewed such that working towards better wages, welfare and work prospects continue to be a collective goal for workers, employers and the Government.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In our conversations, balancing caregiving duties with work responsibilities has become top of mind for our workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In a Singapore that is ageing rapidly with a smaller family nucleus, more workers are now caring for their senior loved ones, young children and infirm family members.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The going can get quite tough for our workers, many who are new generation two-shift workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: After a hard day’s work, they go home to immediately start on their second caregiving shifts at home, and it is Groundhog Day for as long as their loved ones need care.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our Labour Movement knows the importance of building up a strong ecosystem to empower and equip our working caregivers to stay in their jobs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In 1977, the NTUC set up its first childcare centre, which would eventually become MyFirstSkool, an island wide network of kindergartens and childcare centres that facilitates mothers returning to work with a peace of mind.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Since 2012, our Labour Movement had advocated better workplace conditions for nursing mothers under our Project Liquid Gold.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have called for family care and eldercare leave to be made mandatory since 2013, with one of the first calls being made by none other than Mdm Halimah Yacob herself.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Recently, I also made a call to employers to extend family care leave to include caring for aunts, uncles, nephews and nieces.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And yet, even with all of these, we recognise that FWAs would be a critical pillar in this ecosystem of support for our caregivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, the Unions have been advocating for FWAs since 1995, when we introduced FWAs in our collective agreement negotiations.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the heart of successful FWAs, a culture of trust must be created in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Workers must be responsible in the use and request of FWAs and be accountable for work outcomes as agreed with employers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Employers must create a culture sustainable for FWAs, redesigning their jobs for flexi-load, flexi-time and flexi-place, and re-engineering their organisations and management to embrace FWAs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe employers see FWAs as a tenable, sustainable way to retain and attract talent, but some of our SMEs may find it challenging to implement this on the ground in a productive manner.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For employers, FWAs must lead to productivity gains.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The NTUC, together with its partners, like the Institute for Human Resources Professionals, have started on this process of equipping and enabling our more progressive companies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unionised companies keen to use FWAs for talent management and productivity have strategised and reorganised themselves through CTCs and facilitated roadmapping exercises with the NTUC.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One such company is Chye Thiam Maintenance (CTM), which is unionised under our Building Construction and Timber Industries Employees' Union.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: CTM piloted, with the NTUC's Women and Family Unit, the "C U Back at Work" programme and this is aimed at attracting women caregivers to return to the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This success did not come easy, as the company had to re-engineer its HR processes and is now embarking on a digital scheduling programme.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In order to make FWAs a workplace norm, we must equip our companies with the necessary resources and expertise to execute this to achieve win-win employer-worker outcomes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This means availing organisational excellence tools and consulting expertise to our SMEs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This means providing our SMEs with plug-and-play technology software for managing flexi-time and flexi-place schedules.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This means facilitating SMEs with training programmes to upskill their workers and their potential pipeline of workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I call on the Government to consider FWAs as a critical workplace priority and to invest more resources to guide and equip our companies on its roll-out.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of our workers have chosen gig work and the shared economy as it affords them the gift of flexibility, and there is a certain romanticism in being able to have full control of your work life.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unlike the self-employed workers or "towkays" from yesteryears, most who run sole-proprietorships and are in control of their charge rates and their opening and closing hours, the majority of our platform workers today, such as private hire drivers, our delivery riders, by virtue of the fact that they depend on a shared platform with set rules and business guidelines for their livelihoods, are often subject to management controls by these platforms.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we argue that our drivers and riders can choose to move on to another platform if one fails them, the fact of the matter is that all platforms have their own set of rules and business priorities which our platform workers need to adhere to.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Over the weekend, I had a "lo hei" and kopi chat with some of our riders in Punggol.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is to achieve their incentive levels and not to "lose" the levels they have already achieved.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some expressed their angst on what they call "glitches" on the platform apps, where they do not get as many jobs as they get nearer to their incentives goals or are assigned jobs that are far away when actually, there are delivery riders nearby.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I also learnt that our riders are penalised if they are late to report to their shifts.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Yes, by the way, most platforms organise their riders by shift timings and our riders have to vie for the shift timings that they want.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And they tell me that they can be fined, even if they are late by mere seconds.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One rider shared that he was fined for being two minutes late.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I cannot fathom how stressful this is for our riders, battling traffic and road conditions and areas with poor signals.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I recall meeting Mr K, and this is not his real name, a food delivery rider several times over the past three years.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr K has late-stage cancer, but together with his family, have decided that he would continue work for as long as he can as a delivery rider.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Over the years, he has shown me how worried he is about his healthcare and retirement expenditures, and his family has reached out to me to find out more about CPF top-ups and the CPF Matched Retirement Savings Scheme.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lately, Mr K ran into an issue with his platform partner.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the end, we assisted Mr K financially, locally from the community.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As more Singaporeans choose to be in the shared economy and as more platform companies take root in Singapore and evolve their business models, our platform workers, their rights as workers and their grievances and aspirations must be represented in better, more impactful ways.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I call for additional protections and representation for our workers in the areas of earnings, benefits and welfare.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: More transparency must be given by the platforms.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For platform workers wishing to transit out of platform work, we must also prep for their long-term career resilience with upskilling.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I call for more accessibility to upskilling courses for our platform workers and livelihood support, while they are undergoing training.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am referring to our skilled tradesmen in professions, like plumbing, electrical work, air-conditioning servicing and mechanical repairs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our skilled tradesmen and women have forged fulfilling careers over the years, but as Singapore transformed itself economically over the years, these taken-for-granted but essential trades are at risk of a diminishing Singaporean worker base.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must continue to make these trades viable and exciting, with visible and attainable career pathways to attract new talent.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My work at the NTUC has allowed me to engage with our trade guilds and societies, and these engagements have yielded pragmatic insights into the matter.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given that master tradesmen are forged from a blend of strong foundations in theory and practical unique ground experiences, it makes sense that we strengthen and put into the foreground our apprenticeship programmes once again.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Guilds and unions are good grounds for finding master tradesmen and coupled with training programmes and institutions, apprenticeship programmes will allow for clear career pathways to be articulated and good livelihoods to be built – a career progression model!

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Besides youth workers, this also has good potential to be a second spring for our mid-careerists looking for a change in profession.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Singapore Plumbing Society recognised this and, with NTUC's facilitation, completed a roadmapping exercise earlier to structure training and career pathways for new members into the trade.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: More training funding support through the SkillsFuture mechanism can be availed to individuals embarking on such apprenticeship programmes.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: News platform, TODAY, reported that 13% of 1,000 plus Singapore workers surveyed by job portal Indeed.com were actively moonlighting in 2023.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They had done so because they feared being stranded should they be retrenched.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In the same TODAY report, one such individual, Mr Wong, aptly summed up this sentiment, "Nothing is certain.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses fail and people get retrenched", he said, "If one job doesn't work out, the other hopefully will." Unlike employees who have a stable job and moonlight as a "back-up", freelancers have no back-up plans.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Their work embodies a continual series of gigs, without assurance of job and income security.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2024 made significant policy shifts to better position our people and workers for the future.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: How might we, as a society, pave the way forward for our freelancers who may not fit into traditional employment and progression pathways?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: After all, own account workers make up close to 10% of the local workforce, with nearly 200,000 doing this as their main job.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This matters most where freelancing is the dominant mode of work, such as the creative, media, coaching and platform work sectors.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to outline to the House three precarities facing freelancers from these sectors and suggest five approaches in response.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: First, given the prevalence of sub-contracting, it is important to reinforce fair norms to address the precarity of the freelancer.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In the post-pandemic economy, firms are increasingly turning to micro-firms and freelancers for operational needs.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To achieve more with less, established firms in creative and media sectors would often parcel out work to micro-firms.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This lean sourcing approach is prevalent in the coaching sector, be it sports, art, enrichment or wellness coaching.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Some established firms that are main contractors have been passing on significant financial risks to micro-firms and freelancers through the sub-contracting model.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: These freelancers were owed fees for their work on the past two years' projects, which Company A was a sub-contractor.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Payment was also subject to the main contractor and client's full satisfaction with the project delivery.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Although such onerous terms had surfaced on occasions before the pandemic, Company A and fellow creative and media micro-firms shared that these terms became the norm post-pandemic, as part of the de-risking strategy of established firms.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: So how did this impact Company A and the freelancers it contracted?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Like other micro-firms, Company A was lean in staff and in cash.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: It tapped on freelancers for multiple concurrent projects and borrowed from banks and fintech firms to finance the projects.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Company A started delaying payments to its freelancers to muster enough cash to cover pressing loan instalments and the exorbitant lending rates of fintech firms.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: What alarmed me was that, just some months earlier, NTUC's National Instructors and Coaches Association (NICA), which I also serve, had handled a similar case, but in the wellness coaching sector.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In the case handled by NICA, those owed payments were freelance exercise instructors.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This meant that both firms, which were established and reputable for their works, had pledged to be progressive employers and service buyers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Although the relevant Tripartite Standards guide adopters to make part-payment to sub-contractors at project milestones, both main contractors did not do so.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Fellow Parliamentarian, Mr Ang Wei Neng, raised the same bugbear yesterday.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, the main contractors' inaction impacted the most vulnerable party in the link, the freelance worker.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This would introduce baseline protection for the thousands of freelance workers in the creative, media and coaching sectors, many of whom undertake work on fees and terms communicated through skimpy text messages.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This is commonplace because buyers are reluctant to write down agreements and freelancers are hesitant to insist.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Tripartite Standards that guide contracting with freelancers state that contracting parties should ink proper written agreements.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Proceeding without a proper written agreement means that freelancers would have a hard time pursuing payments, should buyers default.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To uphold the relevant Tripartite Standards, the Government could take a step in the direction of the Progressive Wage Mark (PW Mark).

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: MOM's PW Mark ensures that accredited firms and their sub-contractors compensate low-wage workers fairly.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In the same vein, the Government, as a buyer, could request its main contractors for creative, media or coaching work to adopt and uphold the Tripartite Standards' terms on contracting with freelancers, regardless of whether the freelancers were contracted directly or through sub-contractors.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: As in the case of the PW Mark, established firms that are the main contractors must, in turn, ensure the micro-firms that are their sub-contractors adopt and institute the relevant Tripartite Standards.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: By taking deliberate steps to reinforce fair norms, the Government can take the lead to curb freelancer precariousness arising from prevalent post-pandemic sub-contracting.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Even with the rising costs of business, freelancers in creative, media and coaching sectors share that it is an uphill battle to ensure their rates keep pace with costs.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, many reported that their rates had stagnated or declined slightly.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Seasoned freelancers have observed that, in recent years, project budgets have shrunk in tandem with intensified company restructuring and price competition.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Those affected by layoffs are also competing for freelance assignments.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Other freelancers noted that clients now expect them to do more work for the same rates.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: With fewer opportunities and unstable earnings, freelancers' decision-making for their finances can be hampered, for instance, choosing between setting aside monies for emergency funds for unexpected life events and investing in their business.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Some may even deprioritise purchasing insurance against workplace injuries and work liabilities, although such expenditure is necessary for peace of mind.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: If take-home earnings are unpredictable, freelancers would rather work than make time and effort to upskill or to market themselves.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This, in turn, compromises freelancers' ability to build a sustainable business model.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Freelancers have asked if the Government could consider their predicament, akin to the consideration by the Government to platform workers, including allowing platform workers to seek collective representation.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In the context of the creative, media and coaching sectors, the Government, in its capacity as service buyer, could engage representative freelancer-centred associations, such as NICA and VICPA, on changes to the cost of business for coaches and creatives and to set guidelines and principles on fair remuneration.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This allows the less visible yet vulnerable group of workers to collectively address the market gap.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Freelancers today must navigate perennial issues, such as inadequate insurance coverage, alongside new vulnerabilities, such as onerous obligations and unfair terms of buyers or suppliers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that an updated set of recommendations would provide freelancers and freelancer-centred associations for coaches, creatives and platform workers with pathways for expedient and affordable recourse against unfair terms, such as unreasonable leasing claims and the lack of work insurance provision or clear articulation on work safety protection.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Third, without a stable income stream and entitlements that employees have, freelancers are doubtful about their readiness and financial ability to weather life events.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Freelancers can gain from a boost in terms of support for upskilling and caregiving.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2024 is about uplifting workers and supporting workers with upskilling.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Freelancers coping with ageing parents seek enhanced support while those who seek to remain relevant in tandem with economic forces seek funding support for agile upskilling.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Many freelancers want to do right by their ageing parents.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Many hope to fulfil their ageing parents' wish to age-in-place.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To freelancers, supporting their parents to age-in-place means spending more time on caregiving and less time on income-earning.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Over time, these freelancers might have to contend with depleted CPF and savings, reduced client base and poorer financial resilience.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Caregivers who put in the hard work of caring for their loved ones at home should be recognised and supported, and not be left alone to worry about their own future.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Today, caregiving grants help families with caregiving expenses.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: We need to do more to take care of those who care for others.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: We need to assure them that their own retirement adequacy is assured even as they make hard trade-offs to forgo work opportunities.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: How might we help to alleviate the financial stress that arises when freelancers trade work for time and mind-space for caregiving?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Next, how might we introduce funding for agile upskilling by freelancers?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Many expect AI to transform work in the creative, media and coaching fields.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To employees, job scopes guide their work, whereas, to stay valuable, freelancers must quickly assimilate trends and technology to their methods.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Freelancers, too, are concerned about the pace of change and whether their business models can keep up.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: An agile approach to training is one that allows freelancers to right-skill just in time.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This requires the Government to allow and invite practitioners to take the lead in proposing what to train and how to train, especially if the know-how must be contextualised for the sector or profession.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, I hope that the Government, in particular, the Ministries and agencies overseeing the creative, media and coaching sectors, could consider working closely with NICA and VICPA, NTUC's affiliated associations for coaches and creatives, to develop freelancer-centred training support.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Parties could proactively curate right-skill just-in-time training and tie in subsidies and credits.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This ensures that cash-tight freelancers can afford the out-of-pocket training costs.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The SkillsFuture Level-Up programme is a step in the right direction and would be valuable to freelancers if it could be expanded to cater to their career fields.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I, therefore, urge the Tripartite Partners to step forward and take action together.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To recap, freelancers, particularly those in the creative, media and coaching sectors, are stressed by three precarities.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: First, the post-pandemic sub-contracting model threatens freelancers' income security.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Second, stagnated rates demoralise freelancers and erode their ability to sustain their livelihood.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Third, freelancers with less resources struggle to adapt to life stage needs and macroeconomic changes.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To address these three precarities, I hope the Government could consider five approaches.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In the same vein, could the Government, as a buyer, request its main contractors and their sub-contractors for creative, media or coaching work to adopt and uphold the Tripartite Standards' terms on contracting with freelancers?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Second, in the Government's capacity as a service buyer, they should engage the representative freelancer-centred associations, such as NICA and VICPA, on changes to the cost of business for coaches and creatives.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This allows a less visible yet vulnerable group of workers to collectively address the market gap.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The updated set of recommendations could provide freelancers and freelancer-centred associations for coaches, creatives and platform workers with pathways for expedient and affordable recourse against unfair terms, including unreasonable vehicle leasing claims.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Grants should recognise caregivers' labour and provide assurance for their retirement adequacy.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Fifth, work with NICA and VICPA to help freelancers keep pace with industry changes and seize opportunities.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: For example, develop targeted training support for freelancers alongside subsidies to cover both training and opportunity costs.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Budget 2024 charts a new chapter for workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In step with tripartism and an inclusive vision of success, these five approaches would boost freelancers' long-term capabilities and their confidence for the future.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Speaker, Sir, this has traditionally been a time when we, as a nation, delineate our goals and aspirations for the year ahead.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It is thus imperative that we renew our commitment and resolve to uplift society, as Singaporeans contend with job insecurity amid the rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I am uplifted by the central theme of this year's Budget: "Building our shared future together".

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As we continue to find ways to deal with the ever-evolving nature of world affairs, we must also set our eyes on how we can insulate and protect vulnerable Singaporeans from external shocks.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: My esteemed colleagues and I in the Labour Movement strongly support and welcome the plethora of measures introduced to alleviate the hardships that Singaporeans have experienced as a result of the external shocks, primarily from the ongoing conflicts around the world as well as improve all facets of society, amid increasing job insecurity and rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Nonetheless, I reckon that there are sufficient opportunities and scope to assist vulnerable workers better amid evolving global developments, especially our lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The best way to help workers cope with cost of living is through better wages and better jobs.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Speaker, Sir, in this speech, I will elaborate on how to further support our low-wage workers and also update on the M3 focus areas for efforts in assisting Malay/Muslims in the areas of employment and employability.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Low-wage workers are the backbone of our society as they keep Singapore going.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Engaged in the vital sectors, such as retail, hospitality and cleaning, they contribute significantly to the daily operations.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Their efforts uphold essential services, ensuring the functionality of the economy.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, recognising their importance and challenges is crucial in fostering economic resilience and societal well-being.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Last year, I reiterated that the formation of the Tripartite Workgroup on lower-wage workers is a testament to our commitment to ensure that the interests of our lower-wage workers are protected.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: For the past years, the collective support from various stakeholder groups to uplift the incomes of our lower-wage workers has been encouraging.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: For example, the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) enhancements, effective since January last year, were lobbied by NTUC to address rising costs of living.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The changes in WIS reflect the NTUC's strong commitment to support lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC, alongside our Tripartite Partners and various other stakeholder groups, will continue to remain committed to helping workers improve their income security and quality of life and give them confidence in navigating their careers, equipping them to participate in the new growth opportunities.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: But how can we work towards this goal and what are some areas we can continue to look into?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: However, this practice creates a sense of job insecurity and financial instability, especially for lower-wage and re-employed individuals.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It undermines the principle of recognising an employee's length of service, neglecting the dedication and experience they bring to the workplace.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Hence, it can lead to demotivation, reduced job satisfaction and higher turnover rate.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Recognising the length of service at the workplace is crucial, ensuring that employees, including re-employed staff, performing the same job receive fair and consistent treatment in terms of wages and benefits.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This approach promotes job stability, motivates employees and enhance overall job satisfaction.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It contributes to the more equitable and supportive work environment, aligning with the principles of fairness and recognition for long-serving individuals.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Enforcing these measures will foster a positive work culture and reinforce the Government's commitment to the welfare of its workforce.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC has identified two sectors for the implementation of PWM, namely, strata and facilities management as well as pest management.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: These sectors, such as cleaning and security, are outsourced sectors facing common challenges, such as cheap sourcing, which drives down wages.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC has conducted several engagements with stakeholders in the respective sectors and the response has been very encouraging thus far.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The Labour Movement will continue to explore the inclusion of these sectors within PWM and would like to call upon all our Tripartite Partners to work with us to do so.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We believe that this enhanced funding support from the Government is timely and will be pivotal transitional wage support for employers to adjust to upcoming mandatory wage increases for low-wage workers covered by Progressive Wage and Local Qualifying Salary (LQS) requirements.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Lastly, and on a related note, it is imperative that we look at parallel efforts to raise the LQS.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This adjustment not only protects the financial interests of the workforce but also reinforces the principle that gainful employment should provide a standard of living that reflects the economic realities of the society in which it operates.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In doing so, the LQS contributes to maintaining fair labour practices and fostering a more equitable and sustainable labour market.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, I call on the LQS to be perennially reviewed, especially amid global uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By aligning the LQS with the rising cost of living, authorities aim to ensure that employees receive salaries that are commensurate with the economic demands of the time.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: On a micro level, we are targeting specific groups, namely the platform workers, women, mature workers and the youth vis-à-vis career fairs, workshops and consultations.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: These platforms aim to exhort career and training opportunities, broaden their understanding of jobs in demand and skills required, and access job opportunities in the growing sectors.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As workers' aspirations evolve, our workers' compact, our socioeconomic contract with our workers must be renewed to achieve better wages, welfare and work prospects, which remains as a collective goal for workers, employers and the Government.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This includes support in, namely, career guidance, job matching and upskilling opportunities.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In conjunction with reintegration efforts by MENDAKI and other employment partners, close to 60 participants have successfully secured a job largely in sectors, such as education, healthcare, engineering, IT and finance.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Apart from employment opportunities, NTUC also provides upskilling avenues that make every worker a better worker and every job a better job.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Lifelong learning is a process of acquiring new skills and knowledge throughout one’s life, for personal or professional development.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC LearningHub (LHub) offers quality training solutions to help workers thrive and remain resilient in today’s digitally transformed economy and beyond.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: An individual who I would like to highlight is Ms Siti Nur Indra Jalal, 29 years old, formerly a financial advisor for five years with a desire to return to the corporate world through pivoting into a new sector.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: However, acquiring a new job was both challenging and daunting, especially during the pandemic period.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: To enhance her employability, Ms Indra enrolled into a six-month Community and Partnership Specialist programme at NTUC LHUB and is currently working as a Project Manager in Cybersecurity for an organisation.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: She intends to continue upgrading and equipping herself with essential skills through the courses provided by NTUC LHUB.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This shows that where there is a will, there will always be a way.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: From the reference above, it is a good example of a mid-career switch, and it is highly plausible, especially with the newly introduced Level-up programme by SkillsFuture for Singaporeans aged 40 and above.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, I urge Singaporeans to take full advantage on the readily available programmes to level up oneself and gain better employability.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC, alongside our tripartite partners and various other stakeholder groups, will remain committed to helping workers improve their income security and quality of life.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: These include ensuring financial protection for workers in case of work injury, improving housing and retirement adequacy, and enhancing representation for a brighter future. : Speaker, Sir, in closing, this year's Budget theme, "Building a Shared Future Together", has ignited a collective commitment to navigate global complexities and safeguard vulnerable Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: While applauding the Government's efforts to alleviate hardships, we must recognise opportunities for targeted support, particularly for lower-wage workers and communities.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Looking ahead, our focus would remain on addressing the challenges faced by the vulnerable workers, emphasising better wage and improved job opportunities as a solution to rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: With unwavering dedication, NTUC stands ready to champion the interests of Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: NTUC cares for the well-being of our workers coping with the rising living expenses and is committed to enhancing wages, conditions and better support to improve quality of life.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Rest assured, NTUC cares and will take action for you, with you, because Every Worker Matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: My fellow labour MPs have spoken for various segments of workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I will focus on advancing the interests of older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The Government and the tripartite partners have done a lot for our older workers over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: From lengthening employment to strengthening employability and augmenting retirement needs, there had been significant progress over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This was even so during the COVID-19 years, in sharp contrast to what happened in many other economies where many of their older workers lost their jobs and have the problem of coming back.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For the immediate term, older workers face the cost-of-living pressures like everyone else.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And I thank the Government for the Assurance Package and other cost-defraying measures in this and past Budgets to help Singaporeans cope with this pressure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Beyond the immediate pressures, older workers genuinely worry about other developments and for today, I will highlight three.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: There is the worry about the efficacy of ensuring longer work spans by just legislating higher retirement and re-employment ages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Because such legislation, important as they are, may likely come under pressure if it is not effectively combined with skills-building.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Two, the risk of skills obsolescence is increasing with accelerating changes in technology and business models.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For example, some industries are facing structural shifts, such as those brought about by the green transition and others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The pervasive impact of AI on how work will be carried out is also not a trivial matter for workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And this will increase the risk of premature displacement, despite legislated retirement and re-employment ages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Third, there continues to be ground feedback about the relative lack of equitable opportunity and access to training and skills upgrading for older workers compared to their younger counterparts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In NTUC's Every Worker Matters focus groups, six in 10 older workers who participated felt so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: They felt a relative lack of opportunity for training and skills-building compared to their younger counterparts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These challenges must be properly addressed so that our joint aim of enabling older workers to continue working and saving for retirement is not undermined by the evolving demographics in our country and by big environmental changes worldwide.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We, the NTUC, are also grateful for the enhancements to the Silver Support Scheme, the Matched Retirement Savings Scheme and specific initiatives under the Majulah Package, such as the Earn and Save Bonus, the Retirement Saving Bonus and the MediSave Bonus.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: All these efforts will increase the CPF savings of older workers and make for greater security in retirement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: However, it remains true that the most material way to help older workers financially in retirement is by adding to the effective working years and, here, I stress the world "effective" as opposed to legislated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: During NTUC's Every Worker Matters Conversations organised last year, we asked older workers who participated what they hoped to do when they reach the current retirement age of 63.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Many also asked when the Government will announce the next increase in statutory retirement and re-employment ages, since there is still a gap between the current ages and the goal of reaching the retirement age of 70 and the re-employment age of 65 by the year 2030.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I believe this is the pace that we need in order to reach those agreed goals by the year 2030, given the uncertainties that are inherent in the economic environment worldwide.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Next, I will speak on the subject of equity in opportunity and access to training so as to minimise the risk of premature displacement of our older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: NTUC found that more than nine in 10 older workers, besides wanting to continue working, they want to be continually trained.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These workers knew that training was critical to their remaining relevant in their jobs and they particularly worry about access to training opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This shows that the Government is alive to the important nexus between the older workers' training and their employment and their employability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Relevance is as salient as legislation in terms of bringing about an increase in effective working years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The question is, how to make that happen?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Yet, together with funding and for real outcomes, effective implementation is also key.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Therefore, we must scale-up mechanisms that can ensure actual implementation according to the intent in the workplace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This is why I fully support fellow labour MP Desmond Tan's call for employers to quickly work with the NTUC and our unions to form CTCs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I also want to thank Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat for recognising the value of the CTCs in his speech earlier today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: From NTUC, we pledge to work ever more closely with the Government in order to roll this out, not only in numbers but in effectiveness in order that we might be able to help as many workers as soon as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I ask all employers to form CTCs soonest and to work with NTUC and our unions to ensure that workers of all ages are given fair opportunity to be well-trained.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These workers will then help energise your company's growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The third area that needs tackling is that of age bias.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Older workers worry about age bias in several areas, namely, access to training as I mentioned, the availability of flexible work arrangements, so that they continue working while seeing to care needs and fair consideration as job seekers after being displaced.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Empirical research suggests that these fears about age bias have basis, and it requires tackling.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: NTUC and our unions will work closely with employers to advance the interest of workers and companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Beyond workplaces, there is also a growing need to expand and scale-up viable, accessible care services to cater to a rapidly ageing population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In the context of my focus today, I argue that this is important not only for the health and well-being of our seniors but also for the employability of their middle-aged working family caregivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: More of these family caregivers may then not need to quit work in order to undertake their care duties or, at least, to delay such an eventuality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Every year of continued working will significantly help with the retirement adequacy of the caregiver.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I urge the Government to work closely and intensively with trusted partners to further develop this ecosystem, so that Singapore and Singaporeans can truly enjoy the full benefits of better health, better care, better earnings and stronger retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: NTUC stands with our older workers as they confront job insecurity and the risk of skills obsolescence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We care, not just by asking for more or just by asking someone else to solve the problem or waiting for an invitation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: We put our ideas forward, we push for social change, make a real difference to their outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Because our workers are waiting for us to do that, and we will get it going and get it done.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: NTUC's approach is forward-looking, inclusive, action-oriented and practical, just like the PAP Government's.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I believe that this is the right and best way to secure sustainable good outcomes for workers and for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Working closely with the Government and tripartite partners, we will together build a better, more caring Singapore for workers of all ages.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In my speech today, I will first reflect on the asks I had made in Budget 2023; secondly, reiterate the critical role we, in this House, play in ensuring that we achieve sustained economic growth and put out a challenge to grow the economy at the top-end of the Government's target over the next decade; and thirdly, discuss the potential of AI to be a key engine of value creation and economic growth, and make four suggestions to this effect.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: During last year's Budget debate, I spoke for three groups who I saw, among my Woodlands residents, were being pushed to the limit of any reasonable measure of resilience that we would hope to see in our people.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I argued for a stronger trampoline for: one, ex-offenders, calling for more support to get them back into employment; two, people suffering from debt burdens – calling for social support measures to consider debt repayment needs; and three, people who had lost their jobs due to retrenchments, calling for higher quantums and longer durations of financial support and assistance with reskilling and finding new jobs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I am heartened that, a year later, each of these groups is getting more support.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, in basketball lingo, I am three for three, and these shifts have been long time coming, and I think it has taken some time for the external environment to get us to this tipping point.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But they are really good news for my Woodlands residents and for many other Singaporeans who need that stronger trampoline.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is indeed much to welcome in this year's Budget, as colleagues before me have said.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is clear that Budget 2024 was developed with the vision of Forward SG, with the vision of a society that is vibrant and inclusive, fair and thriving, resilient and united and a growing economy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is this last point that I wish to stress today – a growing economy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Growth allows us to provide our people and our enterprises with opportunities and better standards of living.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Growth allows us to fund the increasing demand for spending on childcare, education, housing, infrastructure, healthcare and support for an ageing population.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Growth allows us to tackle the greatest challenges of our time: climate change, energy transition, fighting inequality and the polarisation of society.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Growth allows us to uplift each generation one after the next, securing cohesion and trust in society.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, while it is well and good to talk about scrutiny and transparency and accountability and more support for every possible segment of our population, a critical role we must play in this House is to consider the impact of our interventions, our recommendations and our decisions on our ability to sustain the long-term growth of our economy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Budget 2024 places significant emphasis on sustaining economic growth by keeping Singapore attractive as an investment destination, riding economic and technology trends to capture new opportunities and enhancing human capital.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some might say that at our stage of our development and given the constraints we face, coupled with a less favourable external environment and global uncertainties, make it inevitable that we are entering into a slow growth era where eking out a 1% to 2% GDP growth is already an accomplishment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My humble challenge to the 4G leadership team is this: how might we achieve the top-end of that target and grow at 3%?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I have noted earlier the significant and important investment in SkillsFuture Level-Up.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I also welcome the commitments to invest in strengthening our competitive advantage through top-ups to RIE2025, the National Productivity Fund and the Financial Sector Development Fund.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The introduction of the Refundable Investment Credit addresses the need for more visibility and certainty for MNEs of how Singapore will retain its attractiveness as an investment destination in a BEPS 2.0 world, albeit perhaps a little belatedly, amid moves already announced by other jurisdictions, such as Japan, Thailand and the US.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For local enterprises, I am pleased to see that the Government is enhancing the Enterprise Financing Scheme, extending Skills Future Enterprise Credit and enhancing the Partnership for Capability Transformation Scheme, while also supporting enterprises to be sustainability-ready.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These initiatives accord priority to enterprises that embrace the need to restructure and transform, enterprises that are willing to invest in restructuring and transformation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In a world where technology is advancing rapidly, I welcome the investment in upgrading our national broadband network and in harnessing the power of AI across key sectors.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I had hoped, however, to hear that we could unlock further development of data centre capacity.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At this point, I declare my interest as the Managing Director and Senior Partner of a management consulting firm that does work in AI.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It seems that everyone has an opinion on AI today; whether we should develop our own large language model (LLM), whether we should pause on AI development, whether deepfakes should be regulated, and so on.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My belief is that we should be very focused on how AI development can enable new business models and productivity gains and thus, create value in Singapore and beyond.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We need to stay away from the hype and the noise, and anchor on value creation and on proven initiatives that will move the needle and not a bunch of what-ifs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: To this end, I would like to offer four suggestions to shape our AI policy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Talk to any large company and they have probably run a few AI proofs of concept by now.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some have already invested on platforms and models.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But companies today struggle to scale AI beyond pilots, and many of those platforms and models have nothing running on them.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The news headlines are all about the models and the tech.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In order for enterprises to unlock value from AI, the Government can provide support for them to go beyond proofs of concepts and pilots to deploying AI at scale.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The technology is rapidly evolving and there will be new options and substitutes.
