speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Even in the area of chips, where one chip has emerged as the workhorse of the AI industry, other chipmakers and big cloud companies are developing and deploying their own chips specially designed for AI workloads, and one would expect the AI chip landscape and the cost of these chips to evolve significantly over the next 12 to 18 months.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Moving from chips to platforms and models, in our work with companies to deploy enterprise scale-AI, we have often found that no one environment is the best for everything, whether it is in consideration of security, cost or feature set, and so on.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, let us be smart and strategic about what we invest in and when we invest.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Think, for example, of anti-money laundering using advanced AI/ML approaches that look at transaction data across banks, rather than a single bank, with greater accuracy and efficiency.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Government can be not only a catalyst, but an end-to-end orchestrator, pulling in multiple stakeholders to create new products and services that can create new value and revenue streams in Singapore and also in other markets.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This team can also provide functional leadership on the deployment of AI in internal functions across the Government and drive the end-to-end delivery of certain high impact use cases that can massively reduce cost and increase effectiveness in the Government itself.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is, of course, another reason for a stronger role of the centre when it comes to AI.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: AI will not only have significant implications for the economy, businesses or even for public services, like healthcare and education.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: AI will also have far-reaching implications for workers and society in ways that could have long-term consequences we never imagined.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The bleakest scenarios putting us on the path to a divided dystopia when machines replace man, the benefits accrue only to the rich minority, the middle class evaporates and a deep trust deficit leads to regular social and political instability.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How does the Government then confront these threats?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Will there need to be, at some time in the future, a complete change in the way we look at social welfare, in the way we look at tax policy and in the way we think about trust?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is the first Budget dedicated towards the goals of Forward Singapore, where Singaporeans collectively shape the next chapters on the way forward for our country.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Although the world we live in is more complex and uncertain, I am confident that we can forge ahead with resilience and optimism.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: To this end, there are four key themes on this year's Budget and plans that I wish to highlight.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: One, sustaining fiscal and economic strength amid challenges and improving three key trends relating to: (a) accelerating local businesses' growth in the new economy; (b) thriving in a digital age; and (c) enhancing social resilience and empathy.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore entered 2024 into a global landscape that is bleaker and more complex than prior years.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The Russian-Ukraine war persists, along with a new crisis in the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: China's economy remains soft, while Japan and the UK just entered into a technical recession with two quarters of declining growth.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While some bright spots include the surprising strength of the US economy, the flipside is that the interest rate decline has not yet happened and is expected to be higher for slightly longer.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Such realities underscore the need for Singapore to remain united, supported by discipline and foresight in our Government's fiscal policies.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I am, therefore, pleased that Budget 2024 is generous and, importantly, holistic.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: To me, the projected balanced fiscal position signals continued prudence while providing relief for immediate cost-of-living challenges and supporting longer-term capabilities, such as the upskilling of Singaporeans and business transformation.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Recognising the longer-term need to fund our future, I supported the GST increase in prior debates but requested more help for residents to cushion against higher inflation.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, I am heartened that our Government has continued to follow through on its commitment to support our people with the further enhancement of the Assurance Package.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Many residents I engaged over the Lunar New Year celebrations, including those at private condominiums, have expressed appreciation for the support.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As last year's growth was low at 1.1%, along with an outlook that remains challenging, can the Deputy Prime Minister share his thoughts on the sources and drivers of the factors supporting this more optimistic long-term growth forecast and how we can better achieve this target?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: To sustain economic strength, our businesses must be able to seize opportunities as they come.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, they repeatedly highlight labour and talent shortages, and this is also echoed by the SBF, that contrasts against the reality of continued low birth rates that are below replacement levels and jobs that are unattractive to our citizens.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: How may the Forward Singapore ethos apply so that the pursuit of economic growth, which may require more talents and foreign labour, that is not at all costs?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Should this continue, can the Deputy Prime Minister assure Singaporeans that other sources of revenue remain robust to support future expenditures and that there will be no further GST hikes in the foreseeable future?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister had explained last year that a considerable number of these funds were drawdown funds, where spending is certain to fulfil commitments today and on an ongoing basis.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Deputy Prime Minister clarify the time horizons for the utilisation of these funds to benefit Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As the FY2022 figure was much lower at $6.3 billion, can the Deputy Prime Minister also share if he expects such higher levels of funding and if the run-rate going forward will be at these higher levels?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I now turn to focus on accelerating the growth of our local businesses and SMEs, as they are the backbone of Singapore's economy.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Enhancements to the Enterprise Financing Scheme are also noteworthy.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Notably, the Budget has avoided more populist moves by going beyond handouts to encourage SMEs to transform for the longer term.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Businesses are, by nature, economic entities which transform the use of limited resource to produce goods and services that the market demands.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Those who can do so are better off and thrive in this new digital and green economy.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As such, I am glad to learn of the enhanced initiatives, such as allowing SMEs from more sectors to benefit from green loans and the Energy Efficiency Grant.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This is consistent with my suggestion at last year's COS debate for Government support to be more inclusive on transformational initiatives.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Another key thrust of Budget 2024 is the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This is a decisive push for mid-career workers to upskill and reskill, so that they can contribute in higher-value jobs and more exciting roles, in line with the broader transformational agenda.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Crucially, for SkillsFuture to be attractive, a mindset shift is also required by SMEs to see beyond the potential short-term constraints, like time-off given for staff development and, more importantly, to complement the programme by investing in training and job redesign for the longer term.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This will be a win-win situation for SMEs and their employees.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, while much is touted for SMEs to venture beyond their comfort zones, the fact is that transformation is challenging, especially in a high-cost environment, because the payback is uncertain and, often, not immediate.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As such, more funding from the Budget, by itself, is insufficient.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As most SMEs lack a dedicated strategy or training department, targeted facilitation is needed to guide them on how to effectively leverage Government support for meaningful transformation, so that they can learn by doing to build up expertise over time.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As the key nexus between the Government and SMEs in driving engagement and advisory, there is scope to improve the execution and effectiveness of SME centres and even TACs to support this agenda.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I will elaborate on this at the Ministry of Trade and Industry's COS debate.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore has made significant strides in our progress towards becoming a Smart Nation.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: But as the technology space is ever-evolving rapidly, so must our efforts.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As is always said, AI will not replace humans, but the person using AI will.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On the international stage, we are well-positioned to have an outsized influence on the responsible development of AI, amid bigger global powers competing for AI leadership.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: These are opportunities that Singapore must capture to stay relevant.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, while we pursue opportunities in AI and other frontier technologies on one end, we must have the right foundations in place, manage risks well and leave no one behind on the other.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As it is said, the art of progress is to preserve order amid changes and to preserve change amid order.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While a myriad of services, such as healthcare, postal and transportation, continue to be refreshed by new technologies, with a "digital-first, but not digital-only approach", it is crucial for the pace of change to be well-ordered, thoughtful and empathetic, especially for our senior residents and vulnerable communities.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: A digital society must also be reliable and secure for our residents and businesses to truly thrive within.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As we mature as a digitalised nation, organisations must step up their service resiliency and recoverability, with more robust contingency and crisis management plans.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As more systems become interconnected and interdependent, especially those in Government agencies that we rely on daily, greater IT-related and cybersecurity risks could have systemic impacts across our society and economy.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We will need to continue doubling down on multistakeholder efforts to bridge the digital divide as well as to manage the risks in this journey.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The Public Accounts Committee, which I am a member of, has also highlighted these key points in its recent report.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I hope more will be done in this area to frame future actions and public expectations.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I had previously emphasised the importance of an "all-hands-on-deck" approach by stakeholders in the ecosystem and would like to recognise the combined efforts of MHA, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), banks and telcos in reducing phishing scams and swiftly introducing measures to counter malware scams.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: But that said, scams are most prevalent and increasing in areas, such as jobs, e-commerce and fake friend scams, where they exploit victims' emotions and psychology for them to willingly part with their money.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Our agencies must be even more agile and responsive to combat scams with private sector and international partners.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As this has been a key issue impacting public safety and trust and which my residents are concerned about, I hope to hear more targeted measures in this area.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Youths form a crucial part of our society and are the Singapore's future.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: More concerning is that this trend extends from previous years, amid a backdrop of more permissive attitudes towards cannabis globally, as well as the continued emergence of new psychoactive substances and increasingly rampant use of vaporisers.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The formation of an Inter-Ministry Committee on Drug Prevention for Youths in 2023 was a good move.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to its plans to curb this alarming trend.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Key to our social fabric, too, is community cohesion.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I spoke on this issue at prior debates and understand work is still ongoing to establish a new unit dedicated to tackle protracted noise disputes and to enhance the current regime where mediation is voluntary.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While I look forward to an update on its progress and measures, I urge for all Singaporeans, aided by our agencies, to exercise restraint and empathy so that we can continue building cohesive and resilient communities.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, we have always been able to navigate obstacles better than others to emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While there are challenges ahead, I have no doubt we can surmount them in the uniquely Singapore way, as one united people.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I support the Budget and I am confident it will enable Singapore and Singaporeans to forge ahead with resilience and optimism, towards a shared future together.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some of the bigger challenges Singaporeans face in the coming year include the rising cost of living and economic uncertainty, with retrenchments on the rise.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While the causes of these issues are global trends, the Budget introduced by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong provides important measures to address these challenges for us in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In relation to the rising cost of living, significant financial assistance is being given out each month through a range of vouchers and, for the lowest income earners, the amounts being given out would be more than enough to cover the rising costs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am not aware of any other governments who are giving out such generous amounts to such a wide part of the population, but this does seem to be a direct way to address the issue.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The matter of retrenchments is one I wish to address in more detail.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am advisor to several unions, including the Advanced Manufacturing Employees Union.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is a union that started with being a union for the metal industry workers but has since repurposed itself to reflect the development of industries and the workforce it represents.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The evolution of this union is a reflection of the numerous waves of disruption it has helped the employees weathered over the years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this capacity, I am aware of the frontline challenges and efforts of our unions in dealing with retrenchments.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The labour MPs who spoke just before provided important examples of the work of our unions in dealing with retrenchment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And I encourage all employers and workers who are not already working with NTUC, to do so.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Overall, employment continued to grow in 2023, albeit at a slower pace than 2022, which suggests the post-pandemic spike in employment was moderating.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Most of the employment growth was in domestic-facing sectors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The upshot of these figures is that, against the backdrop of rising retrenchments, Singapore's economy is doing alright and there are opportunities for our workers to take up.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The continued growth of our job market has been possible, thanks to the creative approach to developing our economy, as outlined by Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat earlier in his speech.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has had some unique features in its employment market that have helped keep our unemployment rates low.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: First, there is less legislation and regulation as compared to many other markets.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, while this means less legislated employment rights for workers, it also means that employers are less concerned about making employment offers and employ people here.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Second, the efforts of the Government to bring in new business and industries have kept investment in Singapore robust, creating new jobs and many of these companies provide higher wages and drive up the general wages across the country.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Third, as there is currently little in way of direct unemployment benefits, people who lose jobs are highly motivated to find new jobs and do so.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this way, we create an environment that is conducive for job creation, hiring and incentivising people to work.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If one looks at the macroeconomic employment figures, the data looks alright for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The labour market remains tight with low unemployment, which means people who wish to work will have opportunities to do so.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Yet, notwithstanding the macro picture looking alright, there will be individuals who will still face disruption in their lives.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For those retrenched or facing unemployment, quite often, the cause has nothing to do with their own work performance but rather due to structural reasons, including their jobs or businesses getting disrupted.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In several earlier speeches in this House, I had spoken on how business cycles and lifespans of companies had gotten shorter, and industries and companies can go from boom to bust in a matter of years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This has already made the idea of lifetime employment with a single employer to the exception, rather than the rule, for many people in the private sector.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even if the industry and company remain, that does not mean the job will be there, and jobs are getting disrupted in a wide range of industries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the technology sector, for example, some of the jobs getting disrupted by AI are, ironically, the jobs of computer programmers and engineers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even in the movie industry, there was a dispute between the production houses and actors with arguments about whether and to what extent the industry was permitted to use the digital likeness of actors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was part of the reason large numbers of actors and workers in the media industry went on strike in the US.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It appears that what is being envisioned is payouts to those who may be unemployed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is not an easy area to navigate and even private providers of unemployment insurance in places like the US have stopped providing this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This suggests that they have not been able to find a financially sustainable way to provide this service.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Much of the feedback I have received from this also includes suggestions that the Government should have limits on the amounts that may be claimed and the duration, so that people are properly incentivised to return to work as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The scheme should perhaps start as a safety net of last resort, to cover people who may have more limited resources and should take into account factors, such as whether the employee received retrenchment benefits from their previous employer.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Related to this, I strongly support the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is a helpful programme for anyone whose industry or job has been disrupted and needs to pick up new skills.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The training allowance helps to take away some of the pain, particularly for lower-income workers, of getting a new job.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Also, as there is no age limit on this, older workers can also take advantage of this, even after they have retired.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Another structural issue we face in our job market is that wages at the lower-income levels had been stagnating relative to those at higher-income levels.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A number of measures have helped to address this issue, including rolling out the Progressive Wage Model and the WIS scheme, whereby the Government topped up salaries of lower-income workers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Both these schemes will continue with more generous funding available.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While most Members in this House support the WIS, I note the PSP does not seem to support it wholeheartedly and suggests this would create a "handout mentality".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Instead, they advocated a minimum wage of $2,200 a month, which they call a "living wage".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the reasons the Government is slow to impose a "blanket" minimum wage is that it is mindful that many of the lowest wages are in the lower-skilled sectors, affecting older workers and SMEs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If wages are pushed where a business cannot afford it, this may make these workers and the businesses they work in no longer financially viable.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What the Government has instead done is a two-pronged approach.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For those industries with profits to sustain higher wages, the PWM is being rolled out and this is better than a minimum wage because it guarantees not only a minimum wage, but wage increments for lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For workers whose wages remain low or those industries or jobs that are not part of the PWM yet, the WIS will kick in to provide an income supplement.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: WIS does not impose a burden on employers but meets the employee's need for a higher wage.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I believe this two-pronged model is a better one than the model proposed by PSP.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In my speech, I focused on those who may face difficulties with job losses or job disruption.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Based on the employment data last year, it was clear that the unemployment rate in Singapore remained low and jobs continued to be created.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, retrenchments also more than doubled last year from the year before, with most retrenched people getting a job within six months.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This means that for those who lose jobs, there are opportunities out there and it is important to keep trying for new jobs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For those who have lost jobs or who simply wish to retrain for better jobs, this provides support to do so, as it will cover course fees and also help subsidise some of the lost income with the training allowance.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If you have just lost your job, this would be particularly helpful as you can continue to earn while you train.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister also announced that he is looking into unemployment support going forward.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While schemes like that have had fallen short in other countries, I trust this will be important support for those who genuinely need it, especially if they are of limited means and did not receive much in way of retrenchment benefits or redundancy pay.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Therefore, I think the training grant and allowance will be two important pillars of support for those who are between jobs. : Mr Speaker, this Budget is an important one because it shows the Government "has our backs", and I have focused on the policies that help our workers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In my address today, I will concentrate on two primary areas: one, establishing a comprehensive SkillsFuture ecosystem that is inclusive; and two, ensuring equitable insurance protection for persons with disabilities and individuals on the autism spectrum.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Before I continue, may I declare that I lead a consultancy that provides selected short-form courses funded by SkillsFuture.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The newly introduced SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme offers substantial assistance to mid-career individuals looking to transit into new industries while managing family commitments.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This aligns with the objectives of the 2030 Enabling Masterplan to raise the employment rate of working age PwDs from 30% to 40%.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It is imperative that PwDs have equal access to CET programmes to acquire the essential skills needed to excel in today's job market.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I applaud the Government for its substantial support towards our PwDs in their CET endeavors.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Moreover, the rapid expansion of the Enabling Academy to offer over 700 accessible courses within just two years of its inception is commendable.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I am heartened by the collaborative efforts of the SkillsFuture team with disability advocacy organisations, like the Disabled People’s Association (DPA).

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, despite the Government's robust backing for PwDs, obstacles still remain.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Discussions and consultations with PwDs conducted by DPA have revealed that many PwDs encounter difficulties with CET providers who are unable to accommodate their specific needs, despite the PwDs being willing to provide guidance on how to do so.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This often results in PwDs being turned away or not receiving the necessary support to fully engage in CET programmes.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Those who have enrolled in SkillsFuture initiatives have also shared instances where instructors may not address their queries adequately, possibly due to a lack of knowledge and resources.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For instance, visually impaired individuals have requested screen-reader friendly document formats or image descriptions for diagrams, while autistic individuals have expressed a need for more specific and direct instructions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We need to acknowledge the challenges that PwDs face in their CET journey.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This should not be the experience of any individual in Singapore who seeks to enhance their skills and advance.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: To address these challenges, may I propose four key interventions?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In CET, reasonable accommodations refer to measures that enable PwDs to participate equally without imposing an undue burden on training providers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: SSG, in collaboration with the Enabling Academy, can work with training providers and industry partners to determine what constitutes reasonable accommodation.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This can include discussions on which industry courses to prioritise as well as provide the technical assistance for adaptations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In addition, clear communication and accessible recourse should be made available for PwDs when they encounter difficulties with training providers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I propose that we start with ATOs and CET centres offering long-form or industry-recognised courses.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This ensures that PwDs have access to courses that directly support employment or advancement at work.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Second, market technical assistance with the Capability Development Grant.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We must raise awareness as well as the utilisation of SG Enable's Capability Development Grant among training providers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This grant provides funding for customisation courses for PwDs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This data is not available in the Annual Reports of 2021 and 2022.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Many training providers outside the disability sector may not be aware of or are familiar with the grant utilisation.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Without this knowledge, the grant's effectiveness is limited.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: To address this, both the grant and SG Enable’s consultancy services should be promoted together to boost utilisation.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We must better equip our adult educators with skills to create accessible course materials.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Adult educators play a pivotal role in making learning accessible.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As content developers, they share the responsibility for ensuring its accessibility.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The Institute of Adult Learning (IAL) offers programmes for adult educators to meet the qualification requirements to run SSG-funded certifiable courses.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: While Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles are mentioned in IAL’s diploma programmes, the current depth does not ensure proficiency in creating accessible course materials.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: By integrating UDL practices into course development and setting minimum accommodation requirements, educators can reduce the need for accommodations after.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Fourth, accessible information on course and accommodations pre-enrolment.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Training providers should provide course information and accommodations in accessible format before enrolling to help learners make informed choices and prepare for course demands.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Doing so will underscore our commitment to PwDs in supporting their upskilling journey, on par with our support for those without disabilities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It is crucial that in our endeavours to empower PwDs through the Enabling Academy, we must strive to avoid unintentional segregation in their CET pursuits.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: While the Enabling Academy is a valuable complement to SkillsFuture programmes, particularly for disability types requiring significant course adjustments, an inclusive SkillsFuture ecosystem should promote an environment where both PwDs and individuals without disabilities can learn together.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: With the technical and financial support from SG Enable and other Government agencies, we can establish a comprehensive and inclusive SkillsFuture ecosystem.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Earlier this month, several Members and I myself brought attention to the necessity of enhancing insurance coverage for individuals with mental health conditions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We underscored the difficulties that individuals encounter when attempting to secure insurance for physical health issues that are separate from their mental health history.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: PwDs and individuals with autism encounter similar obstacles when navigating the insurance landscape beyond their existing conditions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These guidelines should elucidate the available avenues for recourse for individuals facing discrimination.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Presently, individuals have limited options for recourse, with the only available avenue being to appeal directly to MAS.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, the explanations provided by insurance companies in response to such appeals may be biased by their internal practices.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As we strive to raise the standards of equitable insurance coverage, I look forward to Singapore withdrawing its reservations on Article 25(e) of the UNCRPD in the near future.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It is a collective journey that we must undertake as a united Singapore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This journey serves as a poignant reminder of our shared vulnerability.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Anyone can face disabilities, whether temporarily or permanently, due to genetic factors or traumatic experiences.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We are all prone to illness and health challenges that may one day impede certain functions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These proposed initiatives are not solely focused on ensuring equal opportunities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: They are aimed at nurturing a society where every individual, regardless of their abilities or background, can flourish and make meaningful contributions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Let us work together to establish an inclusive SkillsFuture ecosystem and guarantee equitable insurance coverage for all.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: With this in mind, Mr Speaker, I lend my full support to Budget 2024.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, I applaud the Deputy Prime Minister, Mr Lawrence Wong, for his very clear statement in this year's Budget on the importance of the arts.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As he has said, they help to express our unique Singaporean culture, strengthen our shared bonds and make Singapore a distinctive home.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister has said that more diverse pathways will be offered so that every individual can strive to be the best possible version of themselves, and this statement was particularly resonant with me.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: He said that we must accord greater value to those who are skilled in technical hands-on abilities as well as those with the social and empathetic traits to excel in service jobs.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While the Deputy Prime Minister referred to the specific example of an ITE graduate who excelled brilliantly in his chosen path, let us also not forget the vast majority of people who work in non-white collar jobs who might not be superstars in their fields but whose labour and service is key to the functioning of our society.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Just as MOE encourages us to remember that every school is a good school, it must also be the case that every job is a good job, as long as it earns you an honest wage.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: And this is a point that many Members have made in the House over the last two days.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While this Budget highlights ITE students, members of the arts community also face struggles related to their wages and the misconceptions attached to the value of their role in society and their work.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Just this past weekend after the Budget Statement, I saw an artist friend lamenting on her Instagram stories that a potential customer had enquired about the prices for her embroidery art.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: When she explained that her work was priced in a certain way because she had to personally commit 40 hours of painstaking work by hand, the customer replied with a flippant, "Alrighty, maybe I'll get it on Taobao." To make things worse, the artist then found online stolen pictures of her work on Taobao, and these were being advertised by unscrupulous sellers who were purporting to recreate her designs for a fraction of her selling price.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This kind of careless disrespect for artistic work is something that many working artists in Singapore continue to face.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Better exposure to and awareness of the arts will help our communities to understand and, hopefully, better appreciate the important role that our arts workers play in our society.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To this end, the Government's plans to make the arts more accessible to all Singaporeans are indeed very welcome.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to the Committee of Supply debates that will allow us to further explore the opportunities presented for the arts community in this Budget Statement.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I will now move on to address two tax changes which were announced in the Budget, and I would be grateful for the Minister's clarifications on these.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Looking at the legislative history behind this concession, I note that the incentive was introduced in the Budget Statement delivered in 1983.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The then-Minister for Trade and Industry, Dr Tony Tan Keng Yam, stated that this would be, "An encouragement to creative talents, such as authors and composers." He continued that, "the concession will enable local publishers to offer better terms to authors and composers living in Singapore and abroad." He continued that, "foreign talents will find it worthwhile to get their works published here." In the year 2000, the concession was liberalised further to include royalty payments received by a composer, an author or a choreographer from music recording or film, dance or drama production businesses in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: When moving the Income Tax amendment Bill in that year, the then-Second Minister for Finance, Mr Lim Hng Kiang, once again described these changes as being put in place to "encourage the development of the arts and innovation in Singapore." Sir, I have some clarifications on the changes to the concession that have been announced in this year's Budget.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: First, what is the rationale behind these changes?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: From 2024 Budget materials, it is stated that the change will "ensure parity in the treatment of royalty income", which is fair enough in principle.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: But if the original intent behind the concession was to provide an incentive to encourage creative work, then I hope that the Minister is able to clarify the policy intentions now behind the revocation of the incentive.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My second clarification is on whether the incentive has served its purpose in encouraging the work of authors, composers and choreographers?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Minister be able to share the impact that the incentive has had over the years?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Does the Ministry have a sense of what the projected increase in revenue collection will be as a result of the rollback of this incentive?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The scope of qualifying deductible expenditure under this provision will now include designer fees or professional fees.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I fully understand that the valuation of artwork purchases is a complicated area but there are ways to alleviate the risks associated with the subjectivity of valuation.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: One way is to rely on valuations from trusted and accredited valuers, and we do have a number of them in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Another way could be to expand the pool of skilled valuation professionals in the space.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Art Galleries Associations of Taiwan and Korea, for example, have formal art appraisal and valuation arms.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: We have, in Singapore, our own Art Gallery Association of Singapore (AGAS) and, presently, it is entirely member-run.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While I understand that the Government has committed some resources to supporting AGAS' work on an ad-hoc project-basis or on a reimbursement basis, more can be done to assist the association in expanding its work so that its operational capabilities are on par with what similar associations in the region are able to offer.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It would be a good start, for example, if the Government were able to empower or sponsor AGAS to commission a study on how the local art gallery ecosystem can better support our economy.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This could be in the sphere of valuation or even in the area of general research into tax and economic policies which are relevant to the arts.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Tax benefits such as these will certainly contribute to the development and growth of our visual arts sector.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For Singapore to continue to prosper, we need our people to prosper.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Every Budget brought forth in this House signals the Government's intent in tackling both challenges of today and seizing future opportunities for the people of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Rising costs are an ever-present challenge globally and affect how we live in every way – from our kopi-peng to chicken rice, the transport we take to work to the way we are able to care for our loved ones.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This year's Budget Speech, delivered by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, set out various measures focused on mitigating the immediate impact of rising costs on household finances.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These include the U-Save and Service and Conservancy Charges (S&CC) rebates and additional Community Development Council (CDC) vouchers – tactically deployed to help Singaporeans navigate higher prices of food and electricity amidst the backdrop of global inflation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But even as we encourage marriages and families, we must also acknowledge the other factors contributing to our declining total fertility rate (TFR): stress and health conditions which affect fertility despite couples' best hopes, involuntary childlessness, inability to secure childcare options in line with parents' wishes, housing in estates far away from grandparents or workplaces, busy schedules which make it difficult for youth to date and lifestyle choices from younger men and women who choose to stay single.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Deputy Prime Minister has signalled the Government's clear intent in a Singapore built for families, however the effects of these policies are not immediate and our demographic challenges are pressing.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are not endowed with any natural advantages to fall back on, such as oil, vast land or precious metals.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The only resource we have is our people; and so, we have to invest in our human capital.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To this end, I am supportive of the boost given to the SkillsFuture Scheme to build an even better future for all.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My husband recounted a conversation that he had with a taxi driver to me.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Uncle asked where my husband was heading to – to which my husband replied he was heading to school.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Uncle said, "Wah, this age, still going to school ah?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Very good." My husband said, "Ya uncle, I'm studying part-time, must upgrade and learn new skills." Uncle replied, "But all these 'learn new skills' is for young people like you, not old people like me." Being under 40, neither my husband nor I are eligible for the enhanced SkillsFuture subsidies or the akan datang top-ups.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But uncle's perspective is shared by many of our older workers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beginning again or learning something new after 20 or 30 years of working is not easy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have shared in this House how proud I was of my parents, who had no choice after SARS to change course in their late 40s and 50s – my mum, from a homemaker to early childhood education.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My dad, from more than 30 years in the airlines to a training company with his peers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The direct way is to acquire certification – leading to a new role.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The less obvious route involves a journey into problem-solving and innovation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We sometimes associate SkillsFuture with mainly "jobs of the future" – from green sustainability, to coding and artificial intelligence (AI).

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But seemingly unrelated courses can benefit us too.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An illustration of this comes from the story of Apple.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In 1972, Steve Jobs purportedly took a calligraphy class at Reed College – despite knowing that the class would earn him no credit towards a degree.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: He reportedly learnt about typefaces and varying the space between different letter combinations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I quote, "None of this had any hope of any practical application in my life.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But 10 years later when we were designing the first Macintosh (Mac) computer, it all came back to me.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And we designed it all into the Mac." We ought to help citizens understand the application of SkillsFuture credits in this manner.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The knowledge and skills acquired through any learning is catalytic for generating fresh ideas and solving challenges by drawing from diverse disciplines.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This culture of continuous learning and curiosity is what will position ourselves as valuable assets.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We also need good public communication to support the mindset shifts required.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An article published on Channel NewsAsia (CNA) on 8 September 2023, highlights issues around utilisation rates of SkillsFuture.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Diving into utilisation rates by age bands, we can make some observations: 16.8% from 25 to 29; 38.8% from 30 to 39; 38.6% from 40 to 49; 37.1% from 50 to 59; and 26.4% for those above 60.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Utilisation rate in the 40 to 49 band is a signal of hope and we must encourage this.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The availability of the credit is one part of the puzzle.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, there are other considerations requiring a shift in attitudes and mindsets and flexibility in the employment ecosystem – families being willing to shoulder more caregiving responsibilities while one spends their evenings in class; enlightened employers providing employees the time-off to do so; and society being willing to support the gap in potential loss of income for gig economy workers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad that the NTUC is championing these efforts.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fundamentally, Singaporeans must know that SkillsFuture is an initiative that is more than chasing certificates.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a pathway to empowerment and progress.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also worry whether these skilling efforts will see fast enough change and we must consider how to supplement our workforce with talent in a way that is integrated with our Singaporean values and that brings additionality to our people.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Protectionism is on the rise and we are seeing disquiet and unrest born from a lack of economic opportunities and inequities – US-China relations keep the world on tenterhooks; the war between Russia and Ukraine rages on; and the world feels the effects from the humanitarian tragedy and hostilities in Gaza due to the Israel-Palestine crisis, even as more call for a permanent ceasefire.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yes, Singapore has worked hard and our reputation outsizes our 700 square kilometres or so.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But in a world where bigger countries threaten to dominate due to might and size, smaller countries like Singapore must navigate these turbulent waves.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Each move or statement we make comes with trade-offs we must think hard about.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And so, from the beginning, we have made it a point to emphasise rule of law, effective governance, balanced foreign relations amidst global tensions and staying open to the world.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore's ability to attract investment and have multinational corporations (MNCs) set up their regional headquarters here create jobs for our people.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In December 2023, Unilever announced its relocation of some roles based here to other markets across Asia.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Earlier this month, Electrolux also confirmed the closure of its Singapore regional office and relocated to Bangkok.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The UK recently launched the AI Futures Grant Scheme to attract AI researchers and engineers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Dubai has made a notable push for talent and investments through their D33 Economic Agenda and agile visa reforms.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Closer to home, Malaysia initiated their 2030 National Industrial Master Plan and Indonesia launched the Golden Visa programme for high-quality investments.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is a global war for talent and investments, and Singapore needs to be the hub for opportunities that attracts, but more importantly, builds and retains the talent to help our people to prosper.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a country where 90% of our food is imported from other countries and where we have no natural resources of our own – we have been fortunate to be able to attract investments, create jobs and build good foreign relations to help our country transform into a successful nation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While our reputation on the world stage outsizes our small land mass, let us not forget that this is an unlikely anomaly.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But tall buildings and magnificent infrastructure alone would be nothing without peace and stability both internally and externally.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are a unique society with different faiths, races and backgrounds.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As our people become more educated and their views grow more diverse, I would like to see more efforts through Forward SG to equip Singaporeans with the skills to have constructive and respectful discourses between the Government, private sector and our people; and the space to encourage effective ground-up changemaking.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Peace is not top-down, but instead must be supported by bottom-up efforts and must start from the young.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am concerned about our seniors, especially those who have complex and chronic health needs.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Obesity, diabetes, high-blood pressure – these are health conditions which threaten our quality of life.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through Healthier SG, I hope more can be done to encourage our seniors to go for regular health check-ups and connect with family doctors in their neighbourhood and more can be done early-on in their illness to prevent it from spiralling out of control and negatively impact healthy lifestyles.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is particularly important for older women – the ones who have sacrificed so much.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of them have been so busy looking after those around them, that they do not have time to look after themselves.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must do more to support the retirement adequacy and healthcare needs of older women and I would like to ask if the Government has considered nuancing the health schemes, given that many women have less CPF savings.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond chronic health conditions, loneliness can have an adverse effect the lives of our elderly too.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Sir, the many ideas shared in the House over the past three days showed the increasing social needs and growing funding required.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government will not be able to do this alone.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Over the decades, many hardworking individuals have built their roots here in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We prospered then because of that, and we must protect this now; continue to keep our hearts, society and workforce open so we can continue to achieve progress for our people, while being firm about our values as a country on the world stage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It delivers an optimistic and balanced first instalment towards implementation of Forward Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In doing so, I will focus on three values – equity, transparency and accountability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The last few years have seen a significant increase in the cost of living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Interest rates have increased, making mortgage payments difficult for many and there has also been an increase in the cost of rent, general goods and services, transport and food.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Many families are struggling to meet these costs and are being forced to make tough decisions about how to best provide for their children and families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Simply providing everyone with the same level of assistance is inequitable and does little to address structural or ongoing inequalities and disadvantage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We need to reassure families that assistance is available for everyone and that there is no shame or stigma associated with seeking or receiving assistance when needed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We also need to implement culturally appropriate community education campaigns to remind all Singaporeans what type of assistance is available and how to access that assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This is of particular importance to those families which may have become used to living with disadvantage or who, for socioeconomic, cultural or personal circumstances, are unable or unwilling to seek assistance when needed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We need to adopt a holistic, comprehensive case management approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Due to a range of factors, including the cost of professional care, many of those taking on short or long-term carer roles within the family home are from lower-income families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We need to acknowledge the significant financial and emotional burden that providing home care can have on individuals and ensure that those with caring responsibilities also receive the appropriate level of assistance and relief.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: They can also be expensive, particularly in the context of slowed or limited economic growth and the ongoing viability and affordability of such initiatives need to be considered.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: That is why we need to think long term and fiscally responsible and innovative in how we plan for our future and the future of our children and grandchildren.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In today's world, it is also important that we consider how social policy can be delivered in an environmentally sustainable way and, in turn, how environmental policy can be delivered in a socially responsible way.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While governments around the world are grappling with how to do this, unless we address the reality of climate change, the socioeconomic needs of our population will only increase and the cost of responding to these needs will only become more and more expensive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I will now make some comments about lifelong learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The European Commission defines Lifelong Learning as: "All purposeful learning activity undertaken throughout life with the aim of improving knowledge, skills and competencies with a personal, civic, social and/or employment-related perspective." This definition is preferred by many researchers and policymakers as it reinforces that lifelong learning is not confined to an employment context, but instead extends into the personal, civil and social contexts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This position is supported by the 1997 UNESCO Hamburg Declaration on Adult Learning, which notes: "Lifelong learning is important because it helps to develop the autonomy and sense of responsibility of people and communities; to reinforce the capacity to deal with the transformations taking place in the economy, in culture and in society; and to promote coexistence, tolerance and the informed and creative participation of citizens." Consistent with this declaration is the view that human capital is a key driver of economic development and that countries that invest the most in developing their human capital enjoy the most rapid and sustained economic growth and the highest quality of life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: If we only encourage those in established or influential positions to undertake learning and exclude those who are frequently considered less productive or deserving, we fail to address social disadvantage and we miss an opportunity to tap into a valuable resource.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Learning is an ongoing process of change and can occur in formal and informal settings, across multiple arenas and via multiple platforms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We also need to foster a flexible learning ecosystem that values and rewards curiosity, creativity and adaptability, rather than just grades or academic results and that prepares individuals to think and thrive in a rapidly changing and unpredictable world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We also need to further develop and foster partnerships among educational institutions, employers and community organisations, so as to create multiple coordinated pathways for lifelong learning and skills development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Measuring the impact of lifelong learning and its benefits is challenging.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, relying solely on hard indicators, such as economic growth or employment rates, may be counterproductive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: An effective culture of lifelong learning will benefit all of society, including social factors and sustainable development, and will assist to create an inclusive economy where the advantages of growth uplift everyone rather than disproportionately favouring the already affluent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Lifelong learning also assist employees to develop the capacity to think differently and to generate new perspectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This may lead to innovative outcomes and solutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Employers should encourage their employees to take time away from work to learn and then create an environment within their workspace where all employees can openly share knowledge, skills and ideas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Employers should also recognise and reward employees for their informal learning achievements and not just those qualifications gained in a structured environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Such a task force should actively seek inputs from people from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, young people and women entering or going back into the workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The study also reported that an increasing number of Singaporeans consider the rising cost of living when planning for retirement, including the cost of domestic help to assist care for them and their family as they age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: To achieve this goal, we need to explain the new Budget initiatives more clearly to all employees and employers and actively encourage and support all employees and employers to maximise the social and economic benefits of this new system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the Islamic prohibition of both earning and charging interest (riba) requires retirement funds from banks to establish alternative arrangements for their Muslim customers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The healthcare initiatives outlined in the Budget are intended to reduce healthcare costs for all Singaporeans, including the elderly and those living with chronic health conditions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As is happening across the globe, healthcare costs in Singapore are rising.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As our population ages, more and more people require increasingly expensive care and this cost inevitably falls on the consumer, insurers and the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: To assist offset these costs, I have several suggestions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The first is to recognise the personal and economic benefits of early intervention.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Many of us wait until later in life, sometimes too late, before we take measurable steps to protect our mental and physical health and well-being.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We need to do more to support and encourage young people to adopt and maintain a lifelong healthy lifestyle and perhaps this could be achieved through increased community education programmes targeted at children and young people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We also need to do more to attract and recruit suitably qualified healthcare professionals and to enhance the job satisfaction, professional development and career progression of our health professionals, and we do more to monitor and support the health and well-being of our health professionals, including those experiencing burnout.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While our healthcare sector continues to struggle with human resource issues, the provision of timely, targeted and professional healthcare will remain a challenge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We need to professionalise aged-care, and ensure that in-home care by affordable, professionally trained healthcare professionals is available when needed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: AI technology is developing far faster than any of us can ever hope to understand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However we need to be as prepared as possible for emerging technologies and be ready to embed these technologies into existing healthcare systems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By many measures, we are one of the safest countries in the world and it is only because of this that we are in a position to develop and implement all of the socioeconomic initiatives contained in this Budget.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The socioeconomic cost of a major cyber incident could be enormous and have far-reaching implications on public trust and confidence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Integrating human-centric design principles and robust safety protocols ensures that our Smart Nation Initiatives not only enhance convenience but also prioritise the well-being of individuals and communities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We also need to adopt an interdisciplinary approach to cybersecurity, integrating insights, methodology and expertise from various fields to comprehensively address complex security threats.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In view of such concerns, I speak to the House again on well-being and emphasise its role as a critical success factor to continued growth, to sustained growth.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In my Budget speech last year, I spoke of the need to consider a different model of progress that looked beyond economic growth.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: To be clear, I am not suggesting de-growth.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: On the contrary, what I am advocating for is a mindfulness and a slowing down that can help to unlock more potential in order to sustain or even to leapfrog growth.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Slowing down our minds and cutting away senseless busyness, to make time and space for things that nourish our hearts: one, family – to bear and nurture children because we desperately need to raise our total fertility rate (TFR); two, caring – to build stronger relationships and community to help alleviate costly institutional healthcare; and three, for dreaming – to nurture and actualise new aspirations.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: These are all desirables that Singaporeans expressed in many Forward Singapore conversations.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: How do we put these words into action?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I use an advertising sector parlance from my early career and offer this House three strategic actions towards a big, hairy, audacious goal – the twin goals of well-being and high growth.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: On the first, a National Well-being Index – because we love KPIs and what does not get measured does not get tracked.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Now that we have made mental health a national priority, how do we know if we are doing better?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And we would not, unless we start measuring and tracking.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: There are already ongoing national mental well-being surveys or studies, such as the Quality of Life Survey, which is helpful to track people’s level of satisfaction with their lives.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Well-being is not simply an existence of happiness or satisfaction.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is also the absence of dis-ease or dysfunctionality within our collective system.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, what we also need to monitor are figures such as the rate and incidences of mental health conditions, suicide rates as well as chronic disease rate, and factor all these into a set of indicators that makes sense.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We need to be accountable for all the strategies that have been announced by the national mental well-being task force and make the outcomes visible and trackable.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is human nature, that when people are unwell, they worry more and become more needy, whereas a people with high well-being will feel more secure and feel that they have more capacity to give.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It may sound easier said than done, but I offer a quick hack.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps what we need to do is start approaching complex and wicked problems with new lenses – a strengths-based lens instead of a scarcity lens, a trusting lens instead of a skeptical lens.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I spoke about this in my Adjournment Motion a few months ago on improving public rental housing to enable human thriving.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: What other policies need a fundamental shift in philosophy and thinking?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: There were two things in Deputy Prime Minister Wong’s Budget announcement that signalled to me that this shift is taking place and I am glad for it.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Removing the condition of the mother’s employment tells me that the Government respects the choices women are making, regardless of what they choose and that supporting children in their early years should not be conditional.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This reduces stress and enables families more freedom to navigate their caregiving needs, enhance their well-being and ensure that all children have an optimal early childhood start.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: To me, that is a very empathetic policy, showing an understanding of people’s worries and making a full commitment to support and invest in anyone who wishes to grow and upgrade themselves.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: There has no bond of any kind that has been announced to date tied to this training allowance, and I hope it stays that way, which signals to me the Government’s willingness to trust.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: To trust that citizens will make the best of the opportunity to create the desired outcomes for themselves, which is a better livelihood, and that itself is aligned with national interest.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In this year’s Committee of Supply, I will be making cuts on issues related to the preschool sector, caregiving, sustainability and integrating persons with special needs, with suggestions on how shifting the underlying philosophy and narratives of some policies to a strength- and trust-based lens can help us improve and accelerate outcomes without spending as much money.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As we transition and evolve our social compact from a less educated population leaning on intellectual elites to craft and implement policies as it was in the 1970s to the 1990s, we now have one of the most well-educated citizenry globally.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As we do this, we must recognise that we are somewhat new at this, and there may be some teething blues as we increase citizen participation and work more closely with one another.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Capability-building of facilitators who have ecosystem thinking, to be skilled at navigating cross-system cultures, mobilising people and building relationships across diverse sectors is key.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I recall in my first year as a Member of Parliament (MP), I sent an email to Deputy Prime Minister Mr Heng Swee Keat, who then forwarded it to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth Mr Edwin Tong.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In the email, I recommended the formation of a team of 100 organisational development-trained facilitators from diverse sectors.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I am not sure if they took up my suggestion but I do see many Public Service roles now titled “Community Engagement” and I see increase in efforts to train volunteers to help facilitate national dialogue sessions.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: As a social entrepreneur, I have first-hand experience of how tenacity and sustained commitment is needed for real and sustainable change to happen.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And it is not always easy to keep morale high as we go through the transition blues, messiness and pains as we will encounter along the way.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is also much easier to grouse and complain than to commit time and effort to create change.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And how do we keep people enthused to contribute and to stay the course?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: To shift this, we have to slow down our pace and appreciate what we already have and take time to appreciate one another.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   As the population ages, there is shortage of manpower and people's mental health is beginning to decline.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: How can we achieve a society that is less stressful, physically and mentally healthy and yet, continue to prosper?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In the face of these challenges, it is necessary for everyone not only to be willing to speak but also be willing to act.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Many people may have seen that there are many who can talk but very few who can truly do and are willing to do.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, the Government continues to implement digitalisation and encourages both individuals and businesses to transform.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Some residents complain that excessive mechanisation for efficiency has reduced the personal touch and I understand this very well.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: How can we strike a balance, using technology with a personal touch, making it convenient for us without sacrificing the interaction and communication between people?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This is something we should and must reflect on.
