text: That is what the Property Tax is designed to do – it is a wealth tax for those with more assets.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we do recognise that there are some groups – especially seniors and retirees – who may need some support to cushion the impact of the Property Tax increase; and this was highlighted by several Members including Ms Joan Pereira, Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Mr Yip Hon Weng.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, beyond the 24-month interest-free instalment plan – which I have announced in the Budget – those who face difficulties in paying, especially retirees and seniors, can approach IRAS for assistance.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Next, I should also deal with some specific questions on tax changes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ms Usha Chandradas asked about the withdrawal of the tax concession on royalty income accorded to authors, composers and choreographers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The concession was introduced in 1983 as she highlighted, at the time when Personal Income Tax rates were much higher.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Since then, tax rates have come down and the concession now benefits only a very small group of taxpayers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we have decided to withdraw the concession so as to ensure parity in the treatment of royalty income with other sectors.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But at the same time, we are putting in much more resources to provide additional broad-based support for the arts sector.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we are not withdrawing resources from the arts sector, we are putting in more resources for the arts sector.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There were also other tax-related suggestions from Ms Usha and other Members of Parliament, including Mr Don Wee, Mr Edward Chia, Ms Denise Phua and others.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to review them, taking into consideration their relevance for our tax regime, costs and benefits and of course consistency with international standards.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some Members, Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Mr Louis Chua and Mr Pritam Singh, had sought clarifications on the potential revenue impact of the BEPS Pillar Two moves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But these estimates have not taken into account how MNEs may respond and the possibility of their activities moving out of Singapore, thereby reducing our tax base.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we are really not sure where we will end up because there are so many unknowns.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I think no one is sure, to be clear.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The OECD has also made very clear these are estimates.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: No one can be sure what the actual impact will be.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: What we are doing is to engage the MNEs better to understand how they are likely to respond, especially taking into account some of the moves we have made in this Budget and we will certainly provide our own revenue estimates in due course.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In any case, any revenue impact from the Pillar Two moves will only materialise from FY2027.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, this is not something for this financial year.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are doing the detailed projections and we will come back with detailed revenue updates.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Of course, the actual amount of revenue gain and how long it will last will depend on how the competitive landscape evolves and also how much we have to re-invest into the economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several Members said that the whole point of BEPS is to tilt the playing field in favour of governments and make MNEs pay more taxes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I think Mr Louis Chua and Mr Jamus Lim highlighted that.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But there is theory and there is reality.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The reality is that MNEs have bargaining power and governments around the world are all finding ways to favour them and getting them to invest.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: You can read this for yourself in the media – just a few days ago, Japan said that it would give Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) up to $6.5 billion more in subsidies for a second plant and that will bring the total subsidies to TSMC to over $9 billion.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Earlier this month, the US also announced a $2 billion grant to GlobalFoundries – the largest grant from the CHIPS Act to date.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These are very generous subsidies that the major economies are giving to MNEs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These moves are absolutely necessary – so that we remain in the race for quality investments and create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is about the lives and livelihoods of Singaporeans and we will do whatever is necessary to safeguard this, especially in a world where competition will only get tougher.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I should also add that the above estimates do not take into account the impact of Pillar One, because all we have been talking about is Pillar Two.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But Pillar One has been delayed and if it is implemented, it will clearly be revenue-negative for Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: After taking into account all this, what is our fiscal position?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: All that was in the Occasional Paper and, indeed, this is what we have done.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The tax changes have come into effect, although we have not yet experienced the full revenue impact because we have been giving out some rebates.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We had also enjoyed some revenue upsides, some of it was due to sentiment-driven revenues, like Stamp Duty and Vehicle Quota Premiums; some of it due to stronger than expected Corporate Income Tax Revenues last year from a strong rebound amongst some companies post-COVID-19.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So overall, we are currently in a sound fiscal position.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And we are putting our resources to good use to address immediate concerns and also upcoming needs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I mean, this is no different from how one would manage your own personal finances.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Imagine if you are a homeowner planning for a major renovation in five years' time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: You start setting aside resources now for the major expenditure that has to be incurred.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: You do not wait until renovation starts then look for money and hope that it is there somehow.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the same way, we have set up Funds to meet real commitments and real spending needs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some of it are for recurring commitments, like the permanent GST Voucher, which we draw on year after year; for new commitments, like the Majulah Package; and for major spending needs that are coming up, like the Future Energy Fund – which will help to decarbonise our energy system.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There are countries that make major commitments without assurance of funding.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the US they call this "unfunded mandates" – pass laws for all sorts of provisions but find the money later, "Let us not worry about money now." That is not how we do things in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If this Government makes a commitment, we make sure it is properly funded.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If you look at our economic and fiscal situation, growth will come down.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Operating revenues will barely keep up with GDP growth and Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC) will also broadly maintain as a share of GDP over the medium-term.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We go through a rigorous process to do so with the Council of Presidential Advisers and the President but we do not expect this to increase given the more challenging investment environment.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, the expected long-term returns are applied on the reserves – or the net asset base – and we take half of that to generate the NIRC.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If we really had so much surpluses somehow streaming into the reserves, then the net asset base must be growing and the NIRC would be rising significantly as a share of GDP – but it has not and we do not expect it to do so in the coming years as well.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, operating revenues and NIRC maintaining as a share of GDP, which only means we must manage our expenditures well because only then can we continue running balanced budgets till the end of this decade.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Forward Singapore report has already outlined the broad range of policy areas we are reviewing and studying.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some have been announced – details have been given out in this Budget.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Others will be fleshed out in due course, as will the detailed fiscal requirements of these subsequent moves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will also update our medium-term expenditure and revenue projections.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Occasional Paper that we had published last year may not be so occasional after all.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will keep on updating it from time to time, so that everyone will have a sense of how our fiscal trends are unfolding, not just on a year-to-year basis, but over a five- to 10-year horizon.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We must continue to plan ahead, do our sums carefully and be upfront with Singaporeans on the costs of various proposals.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This approach of looking and planning ahead is a hallmark of our fiscal policy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It ensures that we are able to meet our collective aspirations and seize every opportunity that comes our way.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Perhaps, the Opposition takes a different view of fiscal management.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Certainly, they want the Government to use more of the reserves for current spending.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They suggest different ways of doing so – using revenue from land sales, waiving land cost for HDB flats, increasing the percentage of Net Investment Returns (NIR) that can be spent and so on – but in the end, they all come down to the same thing, which is to use more of the reserves today.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Basically, we will end up with less for ourselves in the future and we will also leave less behind for our children and the next generation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Eventually, NIRC will shrink as a percentage of GDP, the funding gap will increase and our children will have to pay more in taxes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, this is what many governments in the advanced economies are faced with.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Their debts are rising; their deficits are rising; and their fiscal systems are at risk of breaking.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many of them have some version of an independent budget office, but it has not helped at all.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Basically, no political party in these countries are prepared to dish out the hard truths.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, their policy debates are dominated by what some commentators call "fiscal fantasies".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The idea that all the funds can be raised from the rich, with close to zero consequences for the rest of the population.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Or they can kick the fiscal can down the road indefinitely – just continue to spend and leave it to their children or to those not yet born to solve the problems.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Let us not indulge in fantasy thinking – not in this House, not in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Having the resources to pursue a strong economy and a strong society, and to achieve good outcomes, is not a fairy tale.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is very much our Singapore reality, but it requires us to focus on prudence, fairness and sustainability.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: What we have is a unique and, certainly, a privileged position of strength.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We enjoy the benefits from savings from the past.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To continue on a sustainable path, we must maintain our commitment to set aside enough, not just for ourselves, but also for the future.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, I call on everyone in this House.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Let us commit to upholding these values – fiscal responsibility, discipline, ensure that our fiscal system meets the needs and aspirations of both current and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will present our case to Singaporeans, and ultimately, Singaporeans can decide what is the best fiscal approach to take Singapore forward.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are entering a different world, one that is messier, more dangerous and more unpredictable.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We want to refresh our social compact to keep our society strong and united in this troubled world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We want to build a better Singapore – not just for a few, but for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We want to refresh the Singapore Dream and build a Singapore that is vibrant and inclusive, fair and thriving, resilient and united.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The road ahead to this better Singapore will not be easy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we are all in this together and we all have a part to play.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Government will do more to provide opportunities and assurances at every stage of life and everyone in society should contribute towards our shared goals and aspirations in our own ways.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I take heart from the nation-building journey we have had so far.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As one united people, we have consistently turned our challenges into opportunities and our constraints into strengths.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have done it before, and I am confident we will do it again.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just a quick clarification for the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I acknowledge and thank him for stating very clearly that the Government will provide more information in response to some of the interventions that the various MPs have made.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I was trying to link it to the final subject matter that the Deputy Prime Minister covered about usage of reserves and so forth, or suggestions that were made by the Opposition, I think these were in a particular context.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It did not come up in this debate, but certainly, in previous debates where we talked about how we can make up for funding gaps vis-à-vis GST and all that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, the call for information actually is very much part of how the Opposition tries to understand or tries to work through a mechanism or framework of fiscal prudence as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will give you an example how we do that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Finance Minister talked about unemployment insurance and I think he made clear at his round-up speech that it will be financed through taxes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, I would be cautious to suggest that the Opposition essentially just wants to dig into the reserves because we do think about the financial prudence question quite carefully.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That was just a clarification for Finance Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second point is with regard to growth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think there were Members in the House in the course of the debate who talked about growth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But I think the key point here is sustainable growth and I think this is the real key going forward in this decade.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Because we have seen what happened one decade ago, about 10 years ago, the sort of debates we were having in this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government, basically Ministers, came out to say: we are slowing down growth, we have to, because the situation had changed so dramatically.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Going forward, I think the real question is not so much what I think one Member I heard saying, I make no apologies for growth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think we have to be careful if we go down that road, but to frame a conversation on sustainable growth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And then, I think there will be support for many policies that the Government proposes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There were instances in the past where, perhaps, infrastructure was not ready, for example.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why we have put in place processes, updated our planning processes, made sure that we plan our infrastructure well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why as I highlighted just now, I went through some pains to explain where the increase in foreign workers were coming from, the large part of it are Work Permit holders, especially in construction.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And there is a good reason for this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are ramping up our building programme for public housing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We need these workers to build our infrastructure and homes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These workers certainly do not compete with Singaporeans for jobs and the issue there really is about planning for infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why I said just now that we are making sure that we get the dormitories ready, making sure that we build more, making sure that we build better recreational centres for them, so that they are housed well and we can take care of their well-being.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, yes, we want sustainable growth, and we will pursue sustainable growth.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On Mr Singh's earlier points, I thank him for his clarification.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Now that we have implemented GST, as the WP said, with the 7%, now that it is done, we have accepted it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And would you then also say that the proposals to use more of the reserves by a higher share of NIRC are therefore no longer relevant and the WP is fully consistent with the PAP when it comes to our framework and rules for the use of the reserves?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think that is what I would have to respond with.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Earlier on in this debate, we had a bit of a back and forth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Now, we have no insight on those sort of matters.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I cannot make any promise here that we are reneging or stepping back on a commitment to look for revenues to fund some of these policy objectives; because we do not have an insight into those things.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: By and large, I think the vision, or whatever it is, before the WP in particular – I cannot speak for the entire Opposition – but we will have to work with the information that we have.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If it means that we have to look at all options, we will look at all options.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have been putting out more information already and we will continue to do so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If there is specific information that Members would like, we will be happy to reveal.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If there is no security or difficulties, we will certainly want to put them up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the basic point I was getting at is whether or not there is a difference in our fundamental fiscal philosophy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think that is important because there was a time when there was alignment in this House between the PAP and the WP.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There was a time under Mr Low Thia Khiang where it was very clear the ethos of fiscal responsibility was the same, across both sides of the House.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It seemed to me that this had changed under Mr Pritam Singh, that the position had changed under Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The WP, of course, is free to change its position, but I think it should be clear if this is so.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As far as the PAP is concerned, our position is quite clear.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It does not mean that policies cannot change.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Of course, we review, when circumstances change, we update our policies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But when it comes to certain fundamental principles and values like fiscal responsibility, a basic orientation, not just to look at today but for the future.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This must never be compromised; this must never change.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These principles were put in place by our founding leaders.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: They have continued under successive leaders of the PAP, and they will certainly continue under my watch.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think I have heard this before in this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The point again I would make in response to that is, indeed, I have to agree with the Finance Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: A People's Action Party Government yesterday would return the money that it has used from the Reserves as a matter of principle.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But today, a People's Action Party Government may not return the money it uses from the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I call the next Member, I just want to remind all Members.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: By all means, feel free to seek clarifications but do not make mini speeches.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I just want to bring up this point about the pre-funding of some of the major expenditures the Government committed.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I do agree with the Deputy Prime Minister that we should pre-fund some of these major commitments that we have.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It just demonstrates our prudence and our fiscal sustainability that the longer-term policy commitments are responsibly funded.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, it may also limit the overall fiscal impulse of a current Budget.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister: can he share whether the Government do take into consideration the utilisation of the earlier-funded packages to determine the total spending injection into the economy, so as to better calibrate the level of fiscal impulse to be injected in each Budget?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Just wanted to ask the Deputy Prime Minister: given that we continue to grow the base of the Reserves with half the contribution of NIRC, why is the incremental increase not as high as the previous years?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We take into consideration many factors when formulating the Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The fiscal impulse is just one of the many factors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But in thinking about the fiscal impulse, we do not look at the fund top-ups because these do not, as Mr Liang said, contribute to injections to the economy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When we calculate the fiscal impulse, we specifically look at injections into the economy; we look at the state of the economy and we assess what would an appropriate fiscal impulse be for the Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But aside from the fiscal impulse, there are many other factors that we need to take into consideration too – how much fiscal space we have, what kind of fiscal commitments do we have to make, what are the needs of businesses and households during this period and then how do we allocate our resources to build a Singapore that we all desire?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, these different considerations come together and we have to balance them in order to put together the Budget.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On NIRC, I have explained just now how this is calculated.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The broad strokes are: there is an expected long-term return, it is assessed and then we apply it on the net asset base.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In order to get a figure, we take half of it for the NIRC.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Generally, the NIRC flow is stable but there will be fluctuations from time to time, because we have to update the expected long-term returns every year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One is that there are many questions raised during the debate on the endowment and trust funds.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another Member who has raised quite a number of questions – which I am interested – was Ms Foo Mee Har.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can I seek clarifications from the Deputy Prime Minister on the following questions: one, what is the rate of drawdown of the various endowment and trust funds and what happened to the undrawn amounts, which I have discussed and sought answers during the Public Finance Motion; two, how the Government determines whether expenditures should be paid out of endowment funds and trust funds or the operating Budget.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My second question is: it was also observed that there is a fair amount of volatility in the overall Budget position, which was also pointed out by Ms Foo Mee Har.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, may I know what steps the Government is taking to increase so-called "Budget marksmanship" this year?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Maybe I should go through some of the numbers to substantiate my question.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not have the actual amount yet, but this revision of having a bigger deficit is on the back of what I have said yesterday; that in 2023, actually we have an unexpectedly large operating revenue in excess of our estimate, which is about $8 billion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, despite that, the revised overall budget deficit for 2023 actually is a bigger deficit.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I must say that that is puzzling and we seek clarification from the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the rate of drawdown: well, first of all, I should explain.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are a few of them but the bulk of our Funds are drawdown Funds.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That means we are actually drawing down on the Funds for specific spending needs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the rate of drawdown for these Funds, well, it will vary from Fund to Fund.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, GST Voucher Fund, almost two or three years we will need a top-up, because it is being drawn down and we are using it every year to fund the Permanent GST Vouchers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Majulah Package Fund will be different because it is really meant to support the Majulah Package.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It will be drawn down in the first instance, but then it will continue for some time because there will be people who are young seniors who will continue to benefit from such a Fund.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Future Energy Fund is a different Fund because, there, it is not something we will draw immediately but it is not also something that we will need only 20 or 30 years from now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We envisaged spending this, say, within a five- to 10-year time frame.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why we are setting aside resources now and massive resources are needed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have resources today – we set aside now to cover the spending.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the rate of drawdown will differ but the point is, all of the Fund information are published.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Members can look at them and see the rate of drawdown – what happens to the Funds, how they are used and if there are any undrawn amounts left behind, they will be co-mingled back with Government funds.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I mean, that is the rest of Government Funds.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I mean, this is how we will — But for most of the drawdown Funds, I would say, by and large, we expect almost all of them to be fully drawn down.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we do not think there will be an issue with any undrawn amounts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Endowment Funds are set up not to be drawn down but only to use the returns and they are set up with a very specific purpose, which is that whether in good times or bad times, whether the Government has money or no money, we want to ensure that through an endowment, we are able to generate the resources for specific groups of people.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why Edusave is set up as an Endowment Fund rather than a drawdown fund.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it is not contingent on whether there are Government resources or whether there are surpluses or whether there are additional monies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But students can be assured, in good years or bad years, that Edusave monies will always flow.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, these are the considerations behind the different types of Funds.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On volatility, actually before COVID-19, our fiscal marksmanship was not too bad.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It was within a range of within 4% to 5% of accuracy and that is comparable with many jurisdictions that we compare against.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The COVID-19 years, threw many of our assumptions off, but it is not just in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I mean, name me a forecaster who can predict turning points and get the timings right of these turning points.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The recent years of COVID-19 our forecast accuracy was not as good as we would like it to be but there is a reason for it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is because of the discontinuities, the disruptions, the sudden changes brought about by COVID-19 and we are determined to keep on doing better.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong mentioned just now that our NIRC, as a contribution to our GDP, is going to probably remain constant over the years.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: He mentioned that the current People's Action Party Government does not return Reserves to its people, whereas the past PAP Government does so.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I do not understand him because, are not returns from NIRC a way of returning money to the people – unless he is talking about a drawdown on Reserves?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not clear-cut to us whether this will continue.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It also depends on the revenue impact from BEPS – which as I said just now, is so uncertain.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There was a boost to corporate income tax revenue in these recent times, because we have seen a strong rebound among some companies; particularly in a post-COVID-19 environment – tourism, hospitality – some companies really just rebounded very strongly and that is why it has caused the revenue upsides and brought about the revenue upsides in corporate income tax revenue.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is too early to tell whether this can be sustained, so we will continue to monitor.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: To Mr Sitoh Yih Pin, the response that I gave to Deputy Prime Minister is a point of fact.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It was in response to what Deputy Prime Minister said about Mr Low having a certain position on the Reserves and that it had changed under me.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think this must be the third time he has mentioned it in this House and I have responded to it before and I responded to it the last time as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Global financial crisis – Government draws down, returns the money and I think there were some statements made about why it was doing that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This time round, Reserves are used for another emergency and they are not returned – just a simple statement of fact.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: So, is the Leader of the Opposition suggesting that the Government has to top-up the Reserve it drew during COVID-19 because that will be a massive amount and how are we going to fund it then?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: You have just made the case that I was making: in one situation, you can; another situation, you cannot.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: You have to look at the statements made when the money was returned, and then you see in a different situation a different context, there is a different explanation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just two areas of clarification for the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Does he believe that it is adequate to plan for retirement adequacy via risk-free returns instead of taking reasonable risks via a diversified, well-managed portfolio for the long term?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, in other words, if our investment entities are good enough for our collective reserves, why is it not good enough for individual Singaporeans' retirement reserves?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second is in relation to LRIS, which I mentioned during my speech as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Again, as the Deputy Prime Minister is now Deputy Prime Minister and soon to be Prime Minister, does he intend to still follow through on the Government's acceptance of the recommendation in 2016 on LRIS?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If so, when and, if not, why not?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I mean, if you want risk-free rates, then they will be much lower.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As I said, we will continue to study.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Once you smoothen that out – Mr Louis Chua is from finance – insurance does not come free, who pays for the insurance?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then, are you able to provide a better product than what is the current CPF rate?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Those are the considerations and we will continue to study.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are not saying never but we will continue to work on making the system better.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I understand that it is going to be funded by taxpayers and it is not an insurance scheme like what the Workers' Party has been proposing since 2006.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, I am a bit concerned now about the fiscal impact and the sustainability of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What is the quantum that is going to be given to the jobseekers and what is the duration of support that is going to be provided?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What might some of these domestic drivers be?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I would contend that the decision to hike GST would likely have contributed to domestic inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, the data used in the MAS study predates the GST hikes, but we have plenty of examples globally that VAT hikes do, indeed, spark inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, my first question to Deputy Prime Minister Wong is whether he still believes that the timing of raising GST was justified or if at least a postponement – especially given how the country has bumper tax receipts from other sources in recent years – may instead have been wise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As an aside, I would state that the Workers' Party categorically objects to the insinuation that we are less fiscally responsible, not least because while it is true that it is Deputy Prime Minister Wong's prerogative to think that the alternative levers of revenue that the Workers' Party has suggested are untenable, but is not true that we do not think about fiscal balances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My second question has to do with what Deputy Prime Minister Wong said about keeping Singapore competitive in the face of BEPS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Unlike what he said, I have no illusions, in fact, about the practicality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, the design of BEPS took into account the practicality of a race to the bottom and grants countries the right to apply a countervailing top-up tax if they believe that countries have not played by the rules or at least the spirit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, my fully non-theoretical question that I have for Deputy Prime Minister Wong is: what will the Government do if other countries choose to apply this tax top-up in response to a belief that our RIC contravenes the spirit of the refundable tax credit scheme?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Yes, it does impact on prices, but the impact is once-off.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If you look at the overall impact on inflation, actually, we have seen the impact on that monthly inflation when GST went up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But if you look at the subsequent trends down the rest of the month, inflation continues to moderate as it has in other advanced economies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I have explained what the key drivers were and neither will it cause us to have inflation remaining high because disinflation trend is happening globally, we are seeing similar trends in Singapore and our inflation rates are also coming down.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And to be very clear, even with the GST in place, we have deferred the impact of GST on the lower-income groups with the Assurance Package by more than five years for the vast majority of Singaporeans, and it is not even a temporary relief because, for the lower-income groups, we have enhanced the permanent GST Vouchers so that GST does not hurt the poor in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have gone through these debates extensively and I think we are in a good position to explain why the GST was needed and why, in fact, the additional revenues are needed because we can already see the rising expenditure trends very rapidly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It will happen in the next few years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If we had not done it at the time we did, when will be a good time to do it?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And if we were to do it this year or next year, will the Opposition therefore support it?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I think our approach is, let us do it correctly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Let us do it in good time, put in place, make sure that our fiscal system remains sound and always ensure that we have sufficient revenues to cover our spending.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is something that was discussed as part of the BEPS conversations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These sorts of refundable tax credits are allowed under BEPS rules.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is why we need to understand the realities of the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: One regarding the future of our fiscal reserves, the second regarding the social reserves, which I mentioned during the Budget Debate.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On our fiscal reserves, Mr Speaker, we know the world ahead is dreadfully uncertain but there may also be opportunities which allow Singapore, if luck and good policy favour us, to have possibly some exceptionally good years in future.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can I ask the Deputy Prime Minister regarding the idea of the SG Togetherness office, which could be under the PMO Strategy Group, will the Government give consideration to that, so that with that togetherness in our society, we will be better placed to ride the challenges and perhaps have some of those exceptionally good opportunities in future?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, hypothetically speaking, if there is indeed such a bumper year, maybe it will happen, we will consider it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But in reality, if you look at the facts and if you look at what is going to happen, this will not happen.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I mean, I cannot imagine that we will be able to produce surpluses that we used to have like in the past.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That was what I was trying to say.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Even if GDP grows, revenue will likely grow at the same rate of GDP; so will NIRC.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, always think in terms of a share of GDP, do not just think in absolute terms.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Is expenditure maintaining as a share of GDP?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So many programmes are being spent on all the things that we think are important.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, how do we then generate surpluses, as we used to in the 1980s or 1990s?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not going to be the same.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I think we just have to be realistic.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are in a different environment and we will do well just to be able to maintain balanced Budgets on our current settings.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the SG Togetherness office, there have been various proposals from Members – whether it was mental health, whether it is SG Togetherness – to keep on setting up offices in PMO, I think if we do that more and more, we will have many many offices in PMO and I am not sure that PMO will be equipped to handle all of these different functions.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I think the point is, they do not all need to be centralised within PMO.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are many things we want to achieve: mental health and well-being, togetherness, social mixing.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Ministries will be tasked to do this important work and we will continue to make sure we achieve good outcomes and, in the end, we will track and monitor these outcomes and publish them.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I have two questions for the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: But before I ask the two questions, I would like to first respond to what the Deputy Prime Minister said earlier about the Opposition asking to spend the Reserves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I wish to clarify that PSP is not asking for past Reserves to be spent.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: At the recent debate on public finances earlier this month, we have made it very clear that we are not asking for spending past Reserves.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: What has been accumulated stays there, but we are asking for a slowdown in the further accumulation of that Reserve.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: My first question is: the Deputy Prime Minister has said that MOF has done its five-year, 10-year fiscal projection; so, based on the Government's assessment, is there any need to raise GST further from now until 2030 to fund higher expenditures?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: My second question relates to the chart that the Deputy Prime Minister showed earlier, showing that the income growth of the bottom 20% is much higher than that for the top 20%.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: Can the Deputy Prime Minister clarify whether the income that is used here in this chart includes investment income like dividends and rental income as well as capital appreciation?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First, Ms Hazel Poa clarified that the PSP has not advocated using Past Reserves.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But the PSP has talked about using land proceeds.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, when we talk about Past Reserves, you may have a different definition, but the Constitution defines what Past Reserves is; and clearly, some of your proposals will require constitutional change and will require changes in our framework and using of Past Reserves as it is currently defined.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Number two, what was the second question again?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This was made clear in our Occasional Paper too, but as I said, this is up to 2030.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will continue to update this on a rolling basis, not just at every year's Budget, but from time to time, we will update the projections of our medium-term fiscal needs.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, post-2030, we will have to see what the picture is.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On income and whether the figures I showed just now included investment income, I have to confirm it.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I do not think it is all inclusive, particularly, capital appreciation, wealth-generated income.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It was also a point that Ms He mentioned just now in the debate regarding the Gini coefficient and the measure of Gini coefficient looks at income from work and does not include all sources of income.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Department of Statistics (DOS) is aware of this, and DOS is working on getting better income statistics, so that we can update our figures.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: With your indulgence, Sir, may I address Ms Poa's points, please?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: First, on whether there is really a wage gap between diploma graduates and ITE graduates who then go on to attain a diploma, I think it is not difficult to see that there is a real wage gap here.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Let us compare like for like and let us consider this baseline scenario.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: The cumulative wage gap between these two students, in this very simple baseline example, is quite clear.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: And we can look at variations to the baseline example, for example, a work-study diploma scenario, but any which way you look, there is a wage gap.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: The wage gap manifests from the start of our young graduates' working lives and it accumulates over time.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: On the wage gap between polytechnic and university graduates.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Yes, there is a gap, and it is an issue that has been discussed in this House – and, I am sure, will continue to be discussed in this House.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: The Government has already taken some steps to address the issue, for example, increasing the cohort university participation rate quite significantly so that more Singaporeans have the opportunity to meet their aspirations to get a degree.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: The Government is also working closely with industry, to leverage market forces, to uplift the wages of diploma graduates and close the gap.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: I know that behind the scenes, there is a lot of work that is going into this.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: My position as a backbencher is: I certainly hope so, but we cannot boil the ocean.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: The move in this Budget is a huge step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Focus first on the gap between ITE and polytechnic graduates, and I hope in time, we can extend the same basic policy intent to further address the gap between polytechnic and university graduates.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: But it will require resources, so we need to consider carefully, prudently and, most importantly, I think, if and when that time comes, it will require the whole of society to support such a policy direction.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: I hope I have provided the clarifications to Ms Poa.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: What Mr Xie is saying is that the wage gap is not so much that after they become diploma holders, they get lower salary, but that because they took a longer time to reach the point where they get the diploma and that, therefore, in terms of lifetime earnings, there is a gap.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: And I think that is the policy intent.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: In that case, Mr Speaker, I would like to follow up and ask Mr Xie if he thinks that, for any reason, any student has a delay in his studies and he ends up with a degree or whatever qualification and it is later than others, is it Mr Xie's position that Government ought to compensate for that difference in wages?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: I have never said that, so please do not put words in my mouth.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: There can be any infinite number of permutations and scenarios, but I think that the job of Government is to look at structural issues and find the best way forward to address structural issues.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: The starting point of this policy is that there is a structural gap between ITE graduates' starting pay and polytechnic graduates' starting pay.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: I have said that in my speech as well, if Ms Poa had listened to that, that is the starting point of my position, that I laid out in my speech.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: In COVID-19, it was more than $40 billion.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I know the Leader of the Opposition said he is not in Government, and I also said some months ago, we cannot assume it is a PAP Government forever.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I hope it is forever, but we cannot assume.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: So, I think, just for the next five minutes, can the WP teach me, assuming that you are in Government now, how do you top up $40 billion?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But the Government announced a 24-month instalment for property tax in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: You can pay by instalments, can you not?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: And Deputy Prime Minister also just mentioned that point.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I think, surely, if we can get a $40 billion surplus over the next X number of years, sure, it is a happy problem, but teach me how you are going to do that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Member has not answered the point on instalments.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: But on another point, I heard the hon Member Assoc Prof Jamus Lim as he spoke just now.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Not too long ago, he was talking in this House about pawning your assets and borrowing when interest rates were very low.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: Had we followed that advice, we would be in trouble today, because subsequently, interest rates rose.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: So, let us be very careful and let us be very conservative in our fiscal policies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, I said that had we locked it in at that time, we would be able to lock in a low interest rate, which actually, if anything, I would argue circumstances have proven to be the case, because interest rates have since risen and we did not lock it in at the time.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: In 1977, then-Foreign Minister, Mr S Rajaratnam, said about pawning our assets.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: When I had that debate with Assoc Prof Lim, I hesitated using the word "pawning".

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: But since Mr Rajaratnam used it in 1977, I think I can use it.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: What he said was interest rates are low, go and pawn your assets and go and reinvest.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: I said then, he was in a stage of euphoria.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: He is assuming that tomorrow will always be better than today.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: If we had used that approach, Singaporeans may be waking up thinking that today will be bleaker than yesterday and tomorrow darker than today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I am afraid I cannot speak for Mr Rajaratnam.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In a way, we do not need to replenish the reserves anymore, because we have actually accumulated more during the COVID-19 from the normal way that we are accumulating our reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Maybe the Deputy Prime Minister can confirm that, please.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I am sure people worked really hard on it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: So, in the context of the hard work and the request for more things to come under the Prime Minister's Office (PMO), I would like to reiterate that there are some issues that are really cross-cutting, despite the work that it entails, it really deserves to be sited within the PMO.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar
text: I think the other similar thing would be climate change, another cross-cutting issue, which has a National Climate Change Secretariat within the PMO.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Ministry of Communications and Information also drives our national AI strategy.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, again, I just want to appeal to Members, there is a desire for many things to be centralised.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am not sure, in fact, that more centralisation is always the best answer.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Over time, if we have a bigger and bigger portfolio, all residing within one Ministry, there will definitely be bandwidth issues.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Basically, the Government must work as a team, the Ministries must all work together.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There are clear goals we want to achieve and we will work together as a team to achieve them.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I heard many Members reminding yourselves not to prolong this Budget debate.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai, you still have clarifications?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I thought we are scheduled to end at 3.00 pm?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: But you yourself reminded everyone not to prolong it as well.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Anyway, if there are questions to be asked, I think we should take the debate seriously.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Which is why I gave you the floor.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: First of all, I would like to take what Deputy Prime Minister had said just now about the drawdown rate for the endowment and trust funds.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And I hope Deputy Prime Minister can clarify that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think Deputy Prime Minister is right to say that various funds have got various drawdown rates.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But by and large, I think we need to tell Singaporeans that for all the endowment and some of the trust funds, they are for social purposes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In other words, funds that are for social purposes, for the benefit of Singaporeans, the drawdown may potentially last for 20 years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And the funds for economic purposes, yes, it is less than five years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And I think that is a more accurate answer.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But, of course, I need the Deputy Prime Minister to confirm that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we should look at Endowment Funds separately.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Endowment Funds are created for a specific purpose so that whether good year or bad year, surplus or deficits, we do not have to worry.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There will always be a continued flow that will allow spending for that particular purpose, whether it is Edusave or other types of endowments.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But for the most part, and certainly many of the Funds we have created more recently, are largely drawdown Funds and they are not limited to economic purposes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is for the permanent GST Voucher Scheme and that is drawn down very quickly and topped up repeatedly, so that we can continue to fund the GST vouchers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, all of these drawdown Funds are drawn down, as Mr Leong himself highlighted, well within a reasonable period.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, the monies are all given back to Singaporeans in different ways.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: First, on the support scheme for the involuntarily unemployed.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: And secondly, Deputy Prime Minister mentioned about how they have been helping to ensure that there are more Singaporeans in senior positions in the financial sector.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I think that these senior executives in the financial sector earn higher salaries than in other industries and they are not the group that we are most concerned about.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, are there other sectors where lower- and middle-income Singaporeans are facing competition from foreigners that the Government is also paying the same level of attention to?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think, as I said, the parameters, the details will be released in due course.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On supporting Singaporeans in leadership positions, I gave Finance only as an example.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are certainly planning to grow the leadership pipeline across all fields, which I also stated in my speech, and not just in Finance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: First of all, I think one of the most important takeaways for this Budget debate is to have an accurate assessment of the cost-of-living crisis Singaporeans are facing today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, to that end, can I ask the Deputy Prime Minister to confirm whether he agrees with our points of view.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One, part of our inflation problem is self-inflicted – due to the GST, which he had explained is a one-off thing, and other tax increases.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But there is also the thing of escalating property prices, which has been an ongoing policies and also external environment-created phenomenon.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And two, Singaporeans have very little savings to cope with the crisis because, in our opinion, the schemes that the Government has put in in the past had not allowed the Singaporeans to build up their savings.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, as a result, this is a good opportunity when we are looking at how we restart and how we promote a new social compact, to think of new ways of doing things.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What the PSP has proposed is that do pay attention to more permanent schemes, rather than temporary handouts.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, this is the first question I wish the Deputy Prime Minister can confirm and opine on.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Because I would prefer you raise all the clarifications at one go.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think that would be a bit confusing.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I would rather you raise them all now.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: No, I would rather you raise them now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And second question, will the Government consider grandfathering the SA for Singaporeans who are above 55 years old now, going forward?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I do not have the specifics on the additional amount that the Government is paying.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The RA also enjoys and benefits from the same interest rate as the SA.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, almost everyone can transfer their monies from the SA to the RA, get the same interest rate because they can transfer up to the Enhanced Retirement Sum (ERS) because we have raised the ERS and they can get the same interest rate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And eventually, when they retire, they will benefit from higher retirement payouts through CPF LIFE.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Many commentators out there recognise that CPF LIFE is the best annuity product that anyone in Singapore can get today.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the cost-of-living crisis, whether it is self-inflicted – I thought I addressed that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The whole point of me going through some charts and addressing that, is to show this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If it were indeed self-inflicted and because of unique Singapore moves, then we would be standing out.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are not the only country facing inflation, higher prices.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, we have been managing it better than many other places.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And on top of that, as inflation has been coming down now, our inflation trends are also coming down.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I think we should take it in that context to understand what are the key drivers of inflation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Of course, domestic moves can contribute to inflation too.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: More demand for domestic services, wage pressures – that contributes to inflation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But if you look at the big picture and where the big drivers of global inflation are, I think I have set them up quite clearly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On minimum income, whether we have a target, our aim is to continue to push up, uplift lower-wage workers, but do so in a way that is sustainable and in a way where the increase in income is matched with increase in skills and productivity.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And that is the basis of our progressive wage approach.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And we will continue moving in this direction.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There have been suggestions from Labour MPs and Members to expand the progressive wage to new sectors.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will study all these suggestions and we will continue to work on this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Leong seems to suggest that handouts breed dependencies, but permanent schemes do not breed dependencies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But a poorly designed permanent scheme will breed dependencies permanently, forever.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we do not look at this or that, either one or the other.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have temporary relief measures where necessary, particularly, when inflation was higher in the last two years and in this Budget we are doing a little bit more as well.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I think Singaporeans understand why that is needed.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We also have structural schemes and in the structural schemes, these are not temporary at all.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We continue to fine-tune them, make sure that they are designed well, so that we are providing all the support and assurance we need while also upholding our key ethos of individual responsibility and self-reliance, and avoiding dependency and entitlement – something which Mr Leong himself cautioned against.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think it is important, Members of the House, to understand that the closure of the SA is not aimed at saving interest monies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I will provide a fuller explanation and clarification at the Committee of Supply speech on Monday.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I would urge Members to stay in the House and listen to that part of that speech, in particular.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have many, many esteemed financial experts in this House.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And for those members who want the flexibility after 55, they can always have the option to leave it in the OA.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the many people who feel that they have that ability to invest the monies wisely, they still have the option to invest their OA monies, whether it is in T-bills, in more secure investments.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think it is the option given back to them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In fact, if anything at all, at age 70, CPF Board does not have any option for members to continue to retain monies indefinitely.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If there is such a word, by 70, everyone has to decumulate.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What, I think, we gather from this is that the change in the Special Account is not because of the Government wanting to save money on the interest paid, but it is a matter of financial management principles.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I want to clarify that that is correct.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But generally, we still hold the opinion that the handout scheme has got a short-term nature and because it comes so often, it does create more dependency than a permanent scheme.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have completed the debate on the Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I propose to take a break now and we will resume the Sitting at 2.45 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I have revised the commencement time of the Committee of Supply — Yes, let me first put the question.
